facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass was the only product where the beta testers were called "Explorers," because "Guinea Pigs Who Paid fifteen hundred dollars" didn't fit on the box.

It had one camera, one tiny screen, and zero friends. Wearing it in public was a way of telling a stranger, "I may be filming you, and I definitely want to talk about my startup."

Remember the battery? Thirty minutes of recording and it ran hotter than your uncle at Thanksgiving. You didn't have a wearable computer, you had a forehead space heater with a blinking eye.

And the word "Glasshole" wasn't an insult someone invented. It was a consumer review. Bars banned it. Strangers punched it off people's faces. Strangers also asked, "Is that on right now?" which is the sound of privacy dying.

It was the first device that looked like the future and acted like a restraining order.

b.text:
Google Glass, the glasses that made everyone around you feel like they were being recorded for a documentary nobody asked for. You wore them to a dinner party and suddenly you weren't a guest, you were a surveillance operation with a nice haircut. Nobody could tell if you were looking at them or at the tiny little screen floating in your eyeball, which, let's be honest, is the exact same energy as a guy who keeps checking his phone while you're talking about your dead dog.

And that little camera! It was always pointed at people's faces like a tiny, judgmental lighthouse. People said "Glasshole" and honestly? They weren't wrong. Google spent years saying "you'll get used to it," and the public said, "We won't, but thanks for the offer."

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text:
Graphene, you're the most overhyped thing ever pulled off a pencil with Scotch tape. That's your origin story: two guys got a Nobel Prize for peeling you off graphite like a sticker off a banana. Meanwhile I can't get a Nobel for peeling the plastic off a new remote.

You're one atom thick, stronger than steel, more conductive than copper, and nearly transparent. You're also the only thing in science that's invisible and still manages to be full of yourself.

For twenty years you've been "five years away" from changing everything. Foldable phones, space elevators, unbreakable everything. And what do I have? A tennis racket. A really nice tennis racket.

You have no bandgap, so you can't even work as a decent transistor. You're the smartest kid in class who refuses to turn in homework.

You're just carbon in a honeycomb pattern. Your cousin is literally a diamond, and your other cousin is in my pencil case.

b.text:
Graphene, you're the only Nobel Prize winner ever discovered with Scotch tape. Two physicists peeled a pencil and found you, which means your origin story is literally "kid procrastinating on homework."

Since 2004 you've been "about to revolutionize" batteries, computers, water filters, and space elevators. Twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a tennis racket. You're not a wonder material, you're a press release with a hexagon fetish.

Everyone loves to say you're two hundred times stronger than steel. Great. You're also one atom thick. Nobody's impressed that a sheet of paper beats a battleship per ounce.

And for the supposed savior of electronics, you have zero bandgap. You can't even turn off. You're a transistor with no off switch, the guy at the party who never stops talking.

You're graphite with a LinkedIn profile.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text:
UGG boots: because nothing says "I respect my feet" like dressing them as two sheepskin loaves that lost a fight with a puddle.

They're the only shoe that looks wet when dry and ruined when wet. One drop of rain and suddenly your boots have a water stain shaped like Ohio. And the tag says "do not wear in rain," which is wild for something that's basically a footwear sponge. It's a boot with a dress code.

Also, they're from Australia, but the company's in California, and the price is from the moon. Three hundred dollars for a shoe designed to be worn by surfers who just got out of the ocean, and somehow it ended up in a Pilates class in Connecticut.

And the smell. Wearing them without socks is a lifestyle choice, and it turns the inside into a warm, damp sheep sauna. You don't take them off. You release them.

b.text: UGG boots. The only footwear named after a review. Australian surfers made these to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow America decided the ocean was the mall. They're sheepskin, which means a sheep died so you could wear a slipper to the DMV. One puddle and they're covered in salt lines like a topographic map of everywhere you regret going. Zero arch support, so after two weeks your heel caves sideways and you're walking on the boot's ankle like it owes you money. You wear them barefoot, so by February they smell like a wet lamb's final wish. They're as waterproof as a muffin. Oprah put them on her Favorite Things list. She's since moved on. Twenty years later they're back with platform soles, proving even a mistake wants to be taller.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text: Hawaiian pizza. Ham and pineapple. Somebody in Canada looked at a perfectly good pizza and said, "You know what this needs? Fruit that's been sitting in a can." Pineapple on pizza is a crime with a fruit salad alibi. It's sweet, it's salty, it's wet, and it's confused about what it wants to be, kind of like a dessert that got lost on the way to a breakfast buffet. And the ham? That's not ham, that's a lunch meat that went to college and dropped out. Every bite is a negotiation between a tropical vacation and a Tuesday at the deli counter. Hawaii didn't even invent this thing. A Greek-Canadian guy in Ontario did, in 1962, and then he just let it loose on the world like a dare.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza, you're named after a place you've never been. You were invented in Ontario, by a Greek guy, using canned pineapple. That's not a heritage, that's a witness protection identity.

And the ham? It's Canadian bacon. Even your meat is from Canada. The only Hawaiian thing about you is that people see you and say "aloha," meaning goodbye.

Pineapple has an enzyme that digests protein. You're the only pizza that eats the customer back. Warm fruit juice pooling on mozzarella like a hot tub nobody cleaned.

Italians don't hate you; they pray for you. The president of Iceland said he'd ban you if he could, and Iceland eats fermented shark.

You're not a pizza. You're a fruit cup that fell on a pizza and refused to get up.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text: Esperanto was built in 1887 so everyone on Earth could finally talk to each other, and 140 years later the main conversation is still, "Oh, you speak it too? Where are you from?" "Also Esperanto." Silence. Every speaker is one hug away from running out of things to say. The grammar is famously logical: every noun ends in -o, every adjective in -a, and every direct object gets an -n, which is the only place this language ever shows emotion. It promised to be easy to learn, and it kept that promise the way a diet pill does. You master it in a month, then spend the rest of your life waiting for a stranger to answer you back.

b.text:
Esperanto: the universal language invented in 1887 by a Polish eye doctor who decided humanity needed Italian with a Slavic accent. Universal, as long as your universe is Europe.

The name means "one who hopes." Over a century later: still hoping. There are roughly a thousand native speakers. Klingon is closing in, and Klingon has an army.

It's so logical that "bad" is "malbona," literally un-good. Orwell called; he wants royalties.

Every noun ends in -o and every adjective in -a, so every sentence sounds like a waiter reciting the specials. And it gave us ĉ, ĝ, ŝ and ŭ: letters with little hats, designed for global communication, then made untypeable on every keyboard on Earth.

Its biggest movie starred William Shatner. Even he couldn't oversell it.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that needs a warning label and a fan club. I smell you two blocks before I see the stall. Your aroma is a crime scene. Somebody left a gym sock in a brine barrel for three months, and you're the evidence. Then you get deep-fried so you look like a golden nugget, innocent and crispy, until people bite in and get a faceful of bad decisions. Everyone swears you "taste better than you smell." So does a gas leak, if you're hungry enough. The vendor hands you over with pickled cabbage and chili sauce like he's apologizing on your behalf. Nobody has ever ordered you on a first date.

b.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself three night-market stalls before you arrive. People don't find you at Shilin. They track you, like bloodhounds following a crime scene. Your whole brand is "smells like a sewer, tastes great," which is also what every bad Tinder date says about himself. You soak for months in fermented brine like you're marinating in a grudge. And your family's no better: Changsha dyed you black, the culinary equivalent of putting sunglasses on a corpse. You need deep frying, chili sauce, AND a mound of pickled cabbage just to be socially acceptable. That's not a garnish, that's a legal team. Your parents gave you one job: be tofu. Tofu's whole personality is having no personality. And somehow you came out smelling like a gym sock that went to college. Honestly? Respect.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text: Juicero raised over a hundred million dollars to build a $400 juicer that squeezed packets of pre-chopped kale. Then a reporter showed you could get the same juice by squeezing the packets with your bare hands. That's not a juicer. That's a hand. Your hand already came with the machine. The press checked a QR code on each pack before it would run, so you paid for a Wi-Fi juicer that needed the internet to tell it to do the job a towel does. And people paid it! Venture capitalists looked at a $5 bag of spinach and thought, "Yes, this needs a server." The company shut down in 2017. Honestly, that's the most productive thing the press has ever done.

b.text:
Juicero raised 120 million dollars to build a $400 Wi-Fi-connected juicer, which is a lot of engineering for a bag you could just squeeze with your hands. And that's exactly what Bloomberg did. Reporters squeezed the pack by hand and got juice faster than the machine. The machine had four tons of force, and the whole thing was basically a very expensive way to say "no thanks, I'll do it myself."

It wouldn't even work offline. Your juice pack had to phone home to check if it was expired. Imagine being a kale-based hostage to a server in California. "Sorry, your carrots are out of date." Brother, I'm holding them. They're orange. They're fine.

And the packs cost eight dollars each. Eight dollars for a bag of chopped salad you'd then have to pretend was fresh-pressed. Silicon Valley looked at a smoothie and said, "What if it had DRM?"

Juicero didn't disrupt juice. It disrupted investors' bank accounts.

Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero raised 120 million dollars to build a $400 Wi-Fi-connected juicer, which is a lot of engineering for a bag you could just squeeze with your hands. And that's exactly what Bloomberg did. The machine had four tons of force, and the whole thing was basically a very expensive way to say "no thanks, I'll do it myself."

It wouldn't even work offline. Your juice pack had to phone home to check if it was expired. Imagine being a kale-based hostage to a server in California. "Sorry, your carrots are out of date." Brother, I'm holding them. They're orange. They're fine.

And the packs cost eight dollars each. Eight dollars for a bag of chopped salad you'd then have to pretend was fresh-pressed. Silicon Valley looked at a smoothie and said, "What if it had DRM?"

Juicero didn't disrupt juice. It disrupted investors' bank accounts.

b.text:
Juicero, you beautiful $120 million monument to Silicon Valley. You launched at seven hundred dollars to squeeze a bag. A bag! Then Bloomberg reporters squeezed that same bag with their bare hands and got basically the same juice, only faster. You got outperformed by a guy with a grip strength of "typing."

Doug Evans bragged you pressed with four tons of force, enough to lift two Teslas. Buddy, it's kale. The kale didn't need a forklift.

And it needed Wi-Fi. It scanned a QR code before it'd let you drink. Your router goes down and suddenly your breakfast is asking for credentials. Who designs a juicer that can be bricked?

Google Ventures funded this. Kleiner Perkins funded this. Somewhere, a man is still holding a lukewarm pouch, waiting for a firmware update so he's allowed to eat a carrot.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, you're what happens when a watermelon gets a medieval weapons collection. You grow up to a hundred pounds, hang off the trunk like a tumor, and fall on people. You're the only fruit with a wrongful-death lawsuit hanging over your head.

Cutting you open requires oil on the knife, oil on the hands, and a signed waiver, because your sap is basically industrial glue. And inside? Yellow, stringy pods that smell like a gym bag soaked in bubblegum.

Then vegans discovered you. Suddenly you're "pulled pork." No. You're a fruit in a barbecue costume, sitting in sauce, hoping nobody checks your ID. Nobody's fooled. Even the vegans are just being polite.

You're Bangladesh's national fruit, which means a whole country looked at you and said, "Yes, that's us," and honestly, fair.

b.text:
Jackfruit, you're the largest fruit that grows on a tree, which sounds impressive until you realize it just means you're the biggest thing that can fall on someone's head in an orchard. Eighty pounds of spikes dangling at skull height. You're not a fruit, you're a booby trap with seeds.

Opening you requires an oiled knife, rubber gloves, and a tarp, because your sap is basically Elmer's glue with a grudge. Then the smell hits: half Juicy Fruit gum, half onions somebody forgot in a gym bag. You smell like a candy store got food poisoning.

And sure, vegans love you, but only when you're young and taste like absolutely nothing. That's your whole career. The most famous thing about you is that, with enough barbecue sauce, you can pass for a pig. Even your best role is an impression.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: Nobody's ever bought an NFT. They bought a receipt that says "you own this JPEG," and the JPEG is a cartoon ape with a bowler hat, the same JPEG you can right-click and save in four seconds. So they paid four hundred thousand dollars for a screenshot with a certificate. It's the only art in history where the certificate is the art. The Mona Lisa hangs in the Louvre with a crowd of tourists, and this guy's ape is hanging in a folder called "wallet" that nobody else can see. Ownership, they call it. Congratulations, you own the ape, and the ape doesn't know you exist.

b.text:
NFTs, you're the only investment where the product is a receipt, and the receipt is a link to a JPEG hosted on some guy's server. When he stops paying the bill, congratulations: you own a 404.

You convinced grown adults to pay $300,000 for a cartoon monkey in a sailor hat, then charge them $80 in gas fees to watch it lose 98% of its value. Jimmy Fallon showed off his ape on national television like a kid holding up a cool rock.

People right-clicked and hit "save as," and you called it theft. Theft of *what*? It's still there! I'm looking at it!

Every project had a roadmap: metaverse, merch, a members-only yacht party. Instead the roadmap was a Discord mod named Kevin typing "we're still early" at 3 a.m.

WAGMI, you said. We did not all make it.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word, you've had forty years to learn one thing: how to let me move a picture one millimeter without three paragraphs fleeing to page nine. You don't wrap text, you take hostages.

You underline my own name in red like I'm the typo. You turn my grocery list into a numbered legal document I can't escape. I hit Enter once and suddenly I'm in a style called "Heading 7" that I've never met.

And Track Changes? That's not editing, that's a crime scene where everyone bled in a different color.

You fired Clippy, the only one of you who ever admitted I looked like I needed help.

And every crash, you hand me "Document1 (Recovered)" like a cat dropping a dead bird on the porch: proud, useless, and somehow from 2 PM yesterday.

b.text:
Microsoft Word, you've had thirty years to learn what I want, and you still think I'm trying to write a bulleted list every time I type a dash.

You've got a paperclip's worth of trauma in your past, yet you still auto-correct "Costco" to "Cost co" like you're editing a ransom note.

I insert one picture and the whole document rearranges itself like furniture in an earthquake. The image jumps to page nine, the text wraps around it in the shape of a gunshot wound, and page four is now blank for reasons known only to God and a hidden section break.

You have a ribbon with 400 buttons, and the one I need is always under "Layout," which is somehow not where the layout is.

And "Not Responding"? Buddy, I just asked you to save. Then you recover my file as "Document1 (Autorecovered) (Copy) (2)," like a witness protection program for my thesis.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text:
NFTs are the only product where "right-click, save as" is a legitimate threat to a billion-dollar market. You didn't buy art. You bought a receipt for a JPEG that anyone can look at for free, and the receipt is a hyperlink, and the hyperlink is hosted on a server that's going down when the startup runs out of money. Congratulations, you own a 404.

And the names! Bored Ape. Doodle. CryptoPunk. Nothing says "serious investor" like a man in a blazer whispering, "I'm down forty grand on a cartoon monkey, but the community is strong."

Everyone was a visionary until the gas fees showed up. You paid sixty dollars in Ethereum fees to buy a picture of a rock that was worth four dollars, then listed it for a million because a guy named xX_DiamondHandz_Xx said it would "flip."

It didn't flip. It just sat there. Like a rock.

b.text: NFTs, everybody! The only art form where the most common review is "right-click, save." You paid four hundred thousand dollars for a cartoon monkey in a captain's hat, and I have the same monkey as my phone background. The difference? I didn't pay a gas fee bigger than the art. Technically you don't even own the picture. You own a receipt pointing to a link on a server some guy in Ohio forgot to renew. That's not a masterpiece; that's a parking stub for a JPEG. And remember the roadmap? Metaverse, merch, a yacht party! Then the founder pulled the rug, deleted the Discord, and left you holding a "rare trait": sunglasses. Jimmy Fallon showed Paris Hilton his ape on national TV like a proud dad. Now it's worth less than the TV.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text:
Macau, you're Las Vegas that went to a Portuguese finishing school and came back with gambling debt and a custard tart habit. You make more money from gambling than Vegas does, but you're only 12 square miles. That's not a city, that's a casino with a postal code.

You've got a replica Eiffel Tower, a Venice with fake canals, and a Roman-style sky painted on the ceiling. Nothing here is original except the egg tarts, and even those are Portuguese. You even stole those, Macau, you just added a Cantonese accent.

The streets have Portuguese names, but nobody speaks Portuguese. It's colonialism's most elegant ghost town. Every sign is written in a language the entire population ignores, like a terms and conditions page.

And the traffic! A million tourists walking between hotels that are all technically the same hotel. You've got a Grand Lisboa shaped like a golden lotus, or as locals call it, a giant birdcage for losing gamblers.

Come for the ruins of St. Paul's. Stay because the ferry back to Hong Kong costs exactly what you have left.

b.text: Macau, you're the only place where a fake Venice has a fake gondola and the gondolas still lose money. You're about ten Central Parks wide, so your casinos can't spread out and have to go up, like a city that got lost looking for space. Your cathedral is just a facade, a church that gave up on the church part. Your egg tarts are the best thing you've ever exported, and you did it by accident, like a bank robbery that ends with pastries. The bridge to Hong Kong took the better part of a decade, which is the most patience you've ever shown anyone. Nobody comes to Macau to see Macau. They come to lose money, and they leave with an egg tart and a receipt.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you're proof that marketing can convince people to pay four dollars for cloudy water with a nut rumor attached. You're 2% almonds. Two percent! That's not milk, that's a homeopathic remedy for oat milk.

You took a nut that needs a gallon of water per single almond to grow, then sold yourself to people who say "I'm doing it for the planet." California is in a drought, Karen. Those bees are being trucked across the country like migrant workers just so you can ruin a latte.

And the texture. You're the only drink that separates in coffee like a bad breakup. Curdling in front of everyone, floating there in tiny shame flakes.

Your carton says "Unsweetened Original," which is two lies in a row. There's nothing original about you, and nothing about you is sweet.

You're what a cow would make if she gave up halfway through and just described milk to a nut.

b.text:
Almond milk, you're the only drink that needs a lawyer to defend its name. The dairy industry sued because, technically, nobody has ever milked an almond. We looked. No nipples.

You're about two percent almonds. The rest is water, gellan gum, and confidence. You're not milk. You're a nut that got waterboarded and called it wellness.

And speaking of water: it takes over a gallon to grow a single almond. California is in a drought so you can be beige in a latte. Bees get trucked across the country like seasonal laborers just to make you, and a lot of them don't come home.

Leave you in the fridge for two days and you separate like you're ashamed of yourself. Fair. I'd need to be shaken too if I cost seven dollars and tasted like a wet sympathy card.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text: Luosifen smells like someone microwaved a sewer and called it dinner. You open the packet and the whole building files a noise complaint. Half the dormitories in China have banned it, and the company just says, "That's the flavor," like a skunk insisting that's its cologne. The sour bamboo shoots have been fermenting so long they've got a personal history. The little river snails swim in a broth that tastes exactly like the river they came from. Liuzhou calls it a treasure. Liuzhou also has the river. Then you get to the peanuts, tofu skin, and chili oil, which are there to make you feel like you're eating a meal instead of a crime scene. Honestly, the sealed bag is the most honest thing about it. Even the factory knows nobody wants to smell this one in the open.

b.text:
Luosifen, you're the only dish that arrives before the delivery guy does. You're named after river snails, yet nobody has ever found one in the bowl. You boiled them for hours, took their soul, and threw out the bodies. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up.

And that smell? Fermented bamboo shoots that died, got buried, and came back for revenge. Someone opens a packet in Liuzhou and a guy in Guilin checks his shoes. College dorms banned you like a space heater. Neighbors call the gas company.

Your fans swear, "It smells terrible but tastes amazing." Buddy, that's what everyone says about their toxic ex.

Peanuts, crispy tofu skin, wood ear, pickled beans, a slick of chili oil... that's not garnish, that's witness protection for flavor.

And now you come instant. Congratulations: a biohazard with a seasoning packet.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text: Windows 8, Microsoft looked at the Start button, the one thing every human on Earth knew how to use, and said, "What if we hid it?" You turned every desktop into a giant tablet nobody could touch. People were swiping at their monitors like they were wiping off a stain. Shutting you down required a treasure map: hover in a corner, summon the Charms bar, Settings, Power. Charms! Like the operating system was a bracelet from Claire's. You shipped with two Internet Explorers, which is two more than anyone wanted. Even your design name, Metro, got taken away by lawyers. And when 8.1 finally brought the Start button back, it just took you to the same tile screen. That's not an apology, that's a hostage note. You were so bad Microsoft skipped Windows 9 entirely, just to put more distance between us and you.

b.text:
Windows 8 was Microsoft's big bet that your desktop computer should look like a phone that got into a fight. They took the Start button, the one thing every human had memorized, and deleted it. Then they replaced it with a screen of giant colored tiles that looked like someone's grandma had designed a bank app. You'd click the corner to get back to the desktop, except the corner did something different depending on your mood. It was like a house where the front door only opens if you whistle.

And the tiles! Your Mail tile was always out of date, your Weather tile showed Miami on a Tuesday, and your Games tile was just an ad for a game you didn't ask for. Microsoft looked at a mouse and keyboard and said, "Let's make these people scroll sideways."

They eventually brought the Start button back. Windows 8 wasn't a bad operating system. It was just the one that tried to swipe its way into your life, and nobody swiped back.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text: Hydrogen fuel-cell cars are the most optimistic thing ever built. Think about it: you take the most abundant element in the universe, and then you spend a fortune compressing it to 700 bar, bolting it into a tank, and driving it to a station that's closed. Toyota's Mirai has more hydrogen stations in its dreams than in California. Some states have exactly one, and it's always broken. You pull up, the pump says "Out of Service," and you realize you've just become a very expensive lawn ornament. Meanwhile, your electric neighbor is charging in his garage in his pajamas. Hydrogen cars are like a guy who proposes on a first date and then can't find the ring.

b.text: Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle powered by the most abundant element in the universe that still can't find a gas station. California has about fifty pumps, and half of them are "temporarily offline," which is hydrogen for "go home." Its one emission is water, so it's technically the cleanest car on Earth, as long as you don't ask where the hydrogen came from. Spoiler: natural gas. It's a fossil fuel car in a witness protection program. Toyota gave Mirai buyers fifteen grand in free fuel, which sounds generous until you realize that at thirty-six bucks a kilo it covers roughly a year of driving, and the car loses that much value on the drive home. You're sitting on a tank pressurized to 10,000 psi to go three hundred miles. Even the Hindenburg would say, "Maybe just get a Tesla."

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: Nobody's ever been mugged for an NFT, and that's the scam. You can't steal it, you can't hang it on a wall, and you can't even right-click save it without the cartoon ape judging you. You paid four thousand dollars for a receipt. A receipt that says, "I own the JPEG of a bored monkey," and the JPEG is still sitting on a server in Ohio, unbothered. Your grandma bought Beanie Babies and at least she got a fabric bear she could hug. You bought a hyperlink with a pulse. And the best part? The guy who sold it to you already cashed out and bought a yacht named after the ape you didn't get to keep.

b.text:
NFTs, you're the only investment where the product is a receipt, and the receipt is a link to a JPEG hosted on some guy's server. When he stops paying the bill, congratulations: you own a 404.

You convinced grown adults to pay $300,000 for a cartoon monkey in a sailor hat, then charge them $80 in gas fees to watch it lose 98% of its value. Jimmy Fallon showed off his ape on national television like a kid holding up a cool rock.

People right-clicked and hit "save as," and you called it theft. Theft of *what*? It's still there! I'm looking at it!

Every project had a roadmap: metaverse, merch, a members-only yacht party. Instead the roadmap was a Discord mod named Kevin typing "we're still early" at 3 a.m.

WAGMI, you said. We did not all make it.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza is what happens when Italy and a Dole pineapple can get into a fender bender and decide not to exchange insurance. It's a pizza that's also a fruit cup. The only dish where the ham is nervous about the dessert.

And it's not even Hawaiian! It was invented by a Greek guy in Canada. Hawaii had nothing to do with it. That's like naming a burrito "The Norwegian" because someone's cousin once ate one near Oslo.

Pineapple on pizza is like a hot tub full of juice. The cheese slides off, the crust goes soggy, and every bite is a hostage negotiation between salty and sweet. Ham and pineapple are the only couple at the party who came together but won't stand next to each other.

And somehow it's still the pizza ordered by the guy who says, "I'm easy, I'll eat anything," and then picks off all the olives.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza, you're named after a place you've never been. You were invented in Ontario, by a Greek guy, using canned pineapple. That's not a heritage, that's a witness protection identity.

And the ham? It's Canadian bacon. Even your meat is from Canada. The only Hawaiian thing about you is that people see you and say "aloha," meaning goodbye.

Pineapple has an enzyme that digests protein. You're the only pizza that eats the customer back. Warm fruit juice pooling on mozzarella like a hot tub nobody cleaned.

Italians don't hate you; they pray for you. The president of Iceland said he'd ban you if he could, and Iceland eats fermented shark.

You're not a pizza. You're a fruit cup that fell on a pizza and refused to get up.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript was built in ten days, and honestly, it shows. It's the only language where 0.1 + 0.2 isn't 0.3, and "11" - 1 is 10 but "11" + 1 is 111. Math, but make it improv.

Its typeof null says "object." That's not a bug, that's a 28-year-old typo everyone agreed to live with, like a tattoo of an ex's name.

You want to check if something's an array? Great, typeof says "object." Use Array.isArray. Want to sort numbers? Default sort alphabetically, so 10 comes before 2. Because why would numbers be numbers?

And the ecosystem! One developer deleted an 11-line package called left-pad and half the internet fell over. Your app has 1,400 dependencies and a node_modules folder heavier than a neutron star.

Every Tuesday there's a new framework that's "totally different this time." It's a React with a Vue on top of a Svelte. Meanwhile, NaN is not equal to itself, which is the most self-aware thing this language has ever done.

b.text:
JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and honestly? It shows. You're named after Java the way a knockoff purse is named after Gucci.

You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number. NaN doesn't even equal itself, which makes it the only thing in you with any self-awareness.

Ask you to sort and you hand back, because you alphabetize numbers like a drunk librarian. "11" plus 1 is "111", but "11" minus 1 is 10. Pick a lane.

You needed a second equals sign just to stop lying, and nobody, including you, knows what "this" means.

January is month zero. One guy unpublishing left-pad broke half the internet. And your node_modules folder is heavier than a black hole.

Every week there's a new framework to fix you. That's not a language. That's a renovation.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text: Luosifen smells like someone microwaved a sewer and called it dinner. You open the packet and the whole building files a noise complaint. Half the dormitories in China have banned it, and the company just says, "That's the flavor," like a skunk insisting that's its cologne. The sour bamboo shoots have been fermenting so long they've got a personal history. The little river snails swim in a broth that tastes exactly like the river they came from. Liuzhou calls it a treasure. Liuzhou also has the river. Then you get to the peanuts, tofu skin, and chili oil, which are there to make you feel like you're eating a meal instead of a crime scene. Honestly, the sealed bag is the most honest thing about it. Even the factory knows nobody wants to smell this one in the open.

b.text: Luosifen, you're the only dish named after a snail that contains zero snails. They simmer the snails for hours, then throw them out, like a dad who shows up for the paternity test and leaves. Your real star is suan sun, fermented bamboo shoot that smells like a gym sock studied abroad in Liuzhou and came back with opinions. Fans say, "It smells terrible but tastes amazing." So does every scam. You turned instant noodles into a hazmat event: one packet opened in a dorm and three floors file noise complaints, because that smell is *loud*. Couriers wrap you in four bags like evidence. And you come with seven sachets: chili oil, peanuts, tofu skin, wood ear, the bamboo. It's IKEA furniture that makes the neighbors move out. Liuzhou didn't invent a soup. It invented Stockholm syndrome with chili oil.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole with a publicist. You order one and the waiter says "forty-five minutes," which is how long it takes to bake and also how long it takes to finish one slice. They put the sauce on top and the cheese underneath, like they're hiding evidence. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up. The crust is a buttery retaining wall holding back a lake of chunky tomato, because apparently Lake Michigan wasn't enough water for one city to manage. You need a knife, a fork, a nap, and a cardiologist on retainer. Then there's the sausage, laid down as one solid patty like the base layer of a parking garage. Chicagoans defend it like family. Sure: the relative who shows up late, takes up three chairs, and leaves everyone unable to move.

b.text:
Chicago deep-dish isn't pizza, it's a casserole that got a good agent. You wait 45 minutes for it, which is the only honest part, because the oven is basically doing a bypass in reverse. The waiter says "it takes a while," and he means "call your family and say something nice."

It arrives upside down: cheese on the bottom, sauce on top, like the pizza lost a bet. And the crust is a structural engineering project. It's not a slice, it's a core sample. You lift it with a spatula and the cheese stretches like it's begging you to reconsider.

Two slices and you're done. Not full, done. You walk out into a Chicago winter and honestly, the insulation helps.

New Yorkers call it soup in a bread bowl. Wrong. Soup has the decency to cool down. This stays molten until the first bite takes the roof of your mouth, as a deposit.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista, you were the operating system that asked permission to open the calculator. Every time I tried to delete a file, you'd pop up a box asking "Are you sure?" like I was a toddler with scissors. Then you'd ask again. And again. Your User Account Control was so annoying that people turned it off just to get their work done, which I guess was the security equivalent of removing the smoke detector because it beeps.

And Aero! Gorgeous glass windows that ran great on the computer that cost four thousand dollars and crawled on everything else. You had "Vista Capable" stickers on machines that couldn't actually run you. That's not a sticker, that's a hostage note.

b.text:
Windows Vista, you were the only operating system that asked permission to ask permission. "Are you sure you want to open Notepad?" Yes, Vista. I've been sure for twenty years.

You called yourself "Capable" on those stickers. Then you needed 15 gigs of RAM just to display a transparent window border. Aero looked gorgeous, though, like a beautiful man dying slowly of a mystery illness.

Remember copying a file? You'd say "Calculating time remaining" for six hours, like a mechanic staring at my engine going, "Hmm."

Microsoft shipped you, then immediately started apologizing with Windows 7. That's not a successor, that's a public apology with a Start button.

And "Vista Ready" laptops that couldn't run Vista? That's like a "Marathon Ready" sticker on a recliner.

Even your sidebar gadgets gave up. The weather widget just sat there, accurately predicting a cloudy future for everyone who bought you.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text: Carbon nanotubes, you've been "five years away from changing everything" since 1991. You're stronger than steel, lighter than aluminum, and conduct electricity like a champ, which is impressive until someone asks you to leave the lab. You're a sheet of graphene that rolled itself up and called it a personality. Your big selling point is being incredibly small, and honestly, that's the only thing you've ever fit into. Every time someone tries to disperse you in a solvent, you clump together like a group project at 2 a.m. Meanwhile, the press releases keep calling you "revolutionary," and the only thing you've revolutionized is the grant budget. Stronger than steel, lighter than aluminum, and still the guest nobody's ready to invite into the real world.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes, you've been "five years from changing everything" since 1991. Thirty-plus years! Fusion power looks at you and says, "Take it easy, pal."

You're a hundred times stronger than steel, but only if you're one perfect, flawless, microscopic strand that nobody can actually make longer than a hair. Basically you're a gym bro who can bench a truck but only if it's in a vacuum, and he's the size of a bacterium.

You're just rolled-up graphene. You're a sheet of pencil lead that got into a yoga class and now thinks it's special.

Every grant proposal says you'll build a space elevator. Meanwhile, the only thing you've actually lifted is my hopes and a tennis racket.

And toxicologists say you act like asbestos in the lungs. Incredible range: strongest material ever, also a lawsuit.

You're not the future. You're soot with a publicist.

a.text:
Windows 8, you looked at a billion people with a mouse and a keyboard and said, "What if your monitor was a giant phone you can't touch?"

You took away the Start button. The one thing a user knew how to find. Microsoft had literally sold Windows 95 with a Rolling Stones song called "Start Me Up," and you said, "Nah."

Want to shut down? Easy: hover in a secret corner, summon the Charms bar, click Settings, click Power. Turning off my computer shouldn't feel like unlocking a cheat code.

Your tiles were so ugly even the name "Metro" had to get dropped over a trademark dispute. Then 8.1 brought back the Start button, which just opened the same tiles. That's not an apology, that's a hostage video.

You were so bad Microsoft skipped the number 9 entirely just to put distance between you and Windows 10.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: Google Sheets, you're the spreadsheet that waits until I've typed three paragraphs of data before you tell me I've been editing a "view-only" copy this whole time. You're the only app where "Saving..." becomes a lifestyle. Your formulas are so fragile that one missing comma turns my budget into a column of #REF! like I'm a hacker's ransom note. And VLOOKUP? You make me hunt for the exact column index like it's a secret handshake. Every time I try to add a chart, you act like I asked you to build a cathedral. Sure, you're free, and you're everywhere, but that's just what happens when your whole personality is "well, at least it's not Excel."

b.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's little brother who moved into a browser tab and called it "the cloud." Your whole personality is twelve people's colored cursors circling the same cell like sharks while an Anonymous Capybara silently watches everyone's mistakes. You say "Saving..." with the confidence of a man who has absolutely not saved. Your IMPORTRANGE makes me click "Allow access" like I'm asking my own spreadsheet for permission to see my own spreadsheet. Half my cells just say "Loading..." forever, like a Victorian ghost waiting for a letter. And you'll let anyone sort one column without the others, then shrug while every customer gets someone else's phone number. Version history is your only real feature: it's just a timeline of who ruined everything at 2 a.m. And yes, Gemini can explain my #REF! error now. Great. It's still there.

a.text: Deep-dish pizza is the only food that makes you wait forty-five minutes for a meal and then spends the next three hours in your stomach like a sofa somebody moved in without asking. It's not a pizza. It's a casserole that got a library card. You bite in and the cheese pulls up like it's auditioning for a Lysol commercial, and the sauce sits on top like it lost a bet with the crust. Chicagoans will tell you it's "a whole different thing," which is what people say when they're hoping you won't check the ingredients. Nobody in Chicago has ever finished a whole deep dish alone. They just stare at the last slice in the box like it owes them money, then eat it cold at 1 a.m. over the sink, which is the only honest way to eat it.
