facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
You know what Slack is? It's a meeting that refuses to start. Somebody's typing for four minutes, and then it's just "k." Thanks, Dave. Four minutes for a letter.

And the little dots! Everybody's watching those dots like they're a heart monitor. "Dave is typing..." Dave has been typing since Tuesday.

Slack is where we go to "circle back" and never come back. Then there's the huddle. You can't call it a meeting, because that would be too honest. It's a "huddle," like we're a bunch of football players who just need a quick word about the Dorito situation.

And the status emoji! Little palm tree, "OOO." Sure, Brenda. You're on a beach, and you're replying to #marketing-updates from a beach.

b.text:
Slack, you started as the internal chat tool for a failed video game called Glitch, and honestly? Still the most accurate name you've ever had.

You promised to kill email. Instead you gave us email that *knocks*. That little wooden knock-brush sound has triggered more cortisol than any boss in history. I hear it in the shower. I hear it at funerals.

You invented the green dot, so now my employer knows I went to the bathroom for nineteen minutes. You invented "is typing…" so my manager can type for four straight minutes and send "ok."

Threads? Nobody can find them. Huddles? A Zoom call that ambushes you. And somehow every company has 400 channels, and the only active one is #random, where Kevin posts his sourdough.

Your name literally stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable. Sure. Try finding that one link from Tuesday. 👀 reacted by 3 people.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text:
Google Sheets, you're the spreadsheet equivalent of a guy who says "I'm not really a party person" and then shows up to every meeting with a pivot table. You've got 10 million cells and you still can't tell me why my VLOOKUP returned #N/A. Oh, that's not a bug, that's your personality: "Did you mean the other tab?" No, Sheets, I didn't mean the other tab. Nobody ever meant the other tab.

And don't get me started on autocomplete. I type "=SU" and you suggest SUMIF, SUMSQ, and SUBSTITUTE like you're trying to get me to commit to a divorce. Just pick one! You're a grid of cells that refuses to commit to a formula.

Your collaboration features are great, though. My boss can see my edits in real time, which is how I learned he watches me type "asdfgh" when a deadline hits.

b.text:
Google Sheets: the only software where you can watch a coworker named "Anonymous Capybara" ruin your formulas in real time.

You're the Excel that went to community college and told everyone it's "basically the same." Then someone adds 40,000 rows and you wheeze "Loading..." like a Chromebook climbing stairs.

Your formula for combining data from another sheet is IMPORTRANGE, which immediately yells #REF! until I click "Allow access," like I'm asking you to the prom. Your most advanced function, QUERY, makes me write SQL inside a text string, inside a cell, inside a spreadsheet. That's not a feature. That's a hostage video.

Every file on earth is named "Copy of Copy of Budget FINAL v2," shared with "anyone with the link," and owned by Brenda, who left in 2019. I click "Request edit access" and the void answers.

And the 10 million cell limit? Bold of you to assume anyone's budget is that organized. Mine is three tabs and a dream.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies, the only investment where your financial advisor was a woman named Deb at a card shop. People kept them in plastic cases, like organ donors. Not toys, relics. "Don't touch Princess the bear, she's for college." Princess was a purple bear stuffed with plastic pellets and a dead princess's legacy, and your mom thought she'd pay for Yale.

The genius was the tag. Not the toy, the tag. Ty looked at a bag of beans and said, "What if we made it illegal to love this?" Bend that heart-shaped tag and you've lost four thousand dollars. Kids learned grief early: "I hugged Peanut the elephant, and now he's worth nothing."

Then the retirements. Ty killed off bears like a Game of Thrones writer with a mortgage. Fall for Squealer the pig and he's gone by Tuesday, replaced by a slightly different pig.

Today they're in a garage in Ohio, sweating in a bin, worth less than the bin.

b.text: My mom bought forty Beanie Babies in 1998 because a man on the news said they'd pay for my college. They didn't. They're in a bin in her garage, each one still wrapped in its plastic tag protector like a tiny hostage. Ty Warner pulled off the greatest con in toy history. He retired a bear, announced it like a celebrity death, and watched grown adults panic-buy the thing they were supposed to play with. You weren't allowed to touch it, though. Touching meant fingerprints, and fingerprints meant it was worth nothing. So you didn't get a teddy bear. You got a bag of plastic pellets with a face, sitting on a shelf, guarded like the Crown Jewels.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack. Named after the one thing you'll never have again.

You promised to kill email, and you did, by replacing it with forty channels that are each email with a typing indicator. Nothing builds dread like "Greg is typing..." for ninety seconds, followed by "hey." Just "hey." Greg, that's not a message, that's a hostage situation.

You gave us threads, so every conversation happens in two places and nobody knows which one's real. You gave us huddles: a meeting that jumps out of a bush. You gave us the green dot, so my boss can monitor my bathroom breaks like a heart rate.

And that knock sound. I hear it in the grocery store. I hear it at funerals.

Slack, you're the only app that needs three gigs of RAM to tell me someone reacted with a dancing parrot.

b.text:
Slack, the only place where "Quick question" is a threat. Nobody has ever had a quick question. Just a little typing bubble that appears, disappears, appears again, and then nothing, like a ghost deciding whether to haunt you.

You took email, which everyone hated, and said, "What if it were faster, and your boss could watch you be green?" Now I can't go to the bathroom without my status turning yellow like I'm a traffic light of shame.

And the notifications. That little red badge. Forty-seven unread in #general, which is just a graveyard of birthday gifs and a guy named Doug asking who took his yogurt.

The emoji reactions are how adults now communicate. A thumbs-up means "I acknowledge you." The eyes emoji means "I saw this and will do nothing." And the little checkmark means "done," which is the biggest lie since "let's circle back."

Slack: you replaced meetings with meetings that never end.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies: the only investment where the advice was "don't remove the tag" and everyone said, "Sounds legit." Parents in 1998 put them in plexiglass cases like they were the Hope Diamond. It was a bean-filled bear named Garcia. You were hedging against a tie-dye pig.

Every one had a poem on the tag. "Legs the Frog" had a poem. Why? Nobody asked Legs to be a poet. Legs just wanted to sit on a shelf and appreciate the lack of structural support.

And the "retired" thing. Ty would announce a toy was retired, like it had served in a war. Suddenly your aunt's driving to a Hallmark in Ohio at 4 a.m. for Princess the Bear, a bear dedicated to a dead woman, which is a hell of a thing to put a price sticker on.

People paid thousands for these. Today they're worth less than the pellets inside. Which is the only part that was ever real: plastic pellets, fear, and a very small heart-shaped tag.

b.text: My mom bought forty Beanie Babies in 1998 because a man on the news said they'd pay for my college. They didn't. They're in a bin in her garage, each one still wrapped in its plastic tag protector like a tiny hostage. Ty Warner pulled off the greatest con in toy history. He retired a bear, announced it like a celebrity death, and watched grown adults panic-buy the thing they were supposed to play with. You weren't allowed to touch it, though. Touching meant fingerprints, and fingerprints meant it was worth nothing. So you didn't get a teddy bear. You got a bag of plastic pellets with a face, sitting on a shelf, guarded like the Crown Jewels.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, you're the only fruit that needs a permit to carry. You weigh eighty pounds, you're covered in spikes, and you grow directly out of the tree trunk like a tumor with ambition.

Cutting you open requires oiled knives, gloves, and a will, because you bleed glue. I've seen people stuck to you for three days. You're the only fruit that fights back like a bad breakup.

And the smell! Rotten banana, bubblegum, and gym socks, all in one. You're what Juicy Fruit becomes in a hostage situation.

Then vegans discovered you. Now you're in a can, drowning in barbecue sauce, pretending to be pulled pork. Jackfruit, you're a bland, stringy shredded mess in a tin, and you're lying to everyone. Even the tree looks at you and says, "I made that? And it's pretending to be a pig?"

b.text:
Jackfruit, you're the largest fruit that grows on a tree, which sounds impressive until you realize it just means you're the biggest thing that can fall on someone's head in an orchard. Eighty pounds of spikes dangling at skull height. You're not a fruit, you're a booby trap with seeds.

Opening you requires an oiled knife, rubber gloves, and a tarp, because your sap is basically Elmer's glue with a grudge. Then the smell hits: half Juicy Fruit gum, half onions somebody forgot in a gym bag. You smell like a candy store got food poisoning.

And sure, vegans love you, but only when you're young and taste like absolutely nothing. That's your whole career. The most famous thing about you is that, with enough barbecue sauce, you can pass for a pig. Even your best role is an impression.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text: Windows Vista, the operating system that asked permission for everything. You wanted to open a folder? Click "Continue." Delete a file? "Are you sure?" Breathe? "Allow this program to breathe?" Your computer needed a bouncer just to check its own coat. And the copy progress bar: "Four minutes remaining." Three hours later it's at 99 percent, forever. Vista didn't crash. It just kept asking if you were sure. And the sidebar! A little clock and a weather widget floating on your desktop like you needed a hall monitor for your screensaver. Microsoft put a "Vista Capable" sticker on computers that could barely run it, and then acted shocked when people were mad. Honestly, Vista, you were the first operating system to make your user feel like the problem.

b.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Microsoft spent five years building you as "Longhorn," and somehow you still came out premature.

Your slogan was "The Wow Starts Now." You meant "Now" as in "after the loading circle finishes." People bought laptops with "Vista Capable" stickers, which turned out to mean "capable of being sued over." Those machines couldn't even run Aero, so they got a see-through window theme with nothing to see.

And User Account Control! You asked "Are you sure?" so many times that you became the first operating system with separation anxiety.

You came in six editions, including "Ultimate," whose big exclusive was DreamScene: a moving wallpaper for the ten minutes you weren't hunting for printer drivers.

Microsoft had to trick people into liking you. The Mojave Experiment! Your own parents had to put you in disguise.

Your greatest feature? The XP downgrade.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Let's start with the name, because that's the first lie. You were invented in Ontario. By a Greek guy. In 1962. You're Hawaiian the way a tiki bar in Ohio is Hawaiian. The only tropical thing about you is the can your pineapple came out of.

And that pineapple: warm, wet, weeping syrup into the crust until the middle slice folds like a lawn chair. Pineapple contains an enzyme that breaks down protein, so the fruit is literally trying to digest the ham. Even your toppings hate each other.

And the ham! Not prosciutto, not even pepperoni. Just pale pink squares that look like they were chiseled out of a deli's floor tile.

You're the pizza people order to seem quirky. "I'm so random!" No, Kevin. That's a fruit cup that fell on a pizza, and nobody cleaned it up.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza is what happens when Italy and a Dole pineapple can have a custody battle and nobody wins. It was invented in Canada, by a Greek guy, and named after a pineapple brand. That's not a pizza, that's a bad customs form.

Every other topping says "I'm here to be savory." Pineapple shows up like, "I'm also dessert. And I'm leaking." Now your ham is swimming in a warm fruit puddle, and the crust has the structural integrity of a wet napkin.

And the ham! Not even good ham. Sad, pink, circle ham, the kind that's been in a sandwich bag since a 2006 field trip.

Nobody orders it for themselves. It's always "I'll just get a Hawaiian for the table," said by the one guy who also says "I'm not really a *pizza* person."

Hawaii has never claimed it. Hawaii has been in court trying to get away from it.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk, you're porridge that went to finishing school. Somebody looked at horse food and said, "What if it cost seventy cents extra?" Then somebody else said, "Yes, and put it in a carton that talks like a guy who just got back from Copenhagen." Your packaging has more personality than you do. Every box of Oatly reads like a cover letter: "Hi! We're a little weird!" No, you're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not a beverage. That's a salad dressing that gave up.

And the "Barista Edition"? You needed extra oil just to get a job. Enzymes break your starch into maltose, so technically you're a sugar spike in a flannel shirt. Plus you were funded by Blackstone. You're not anti-establishment, oat milk. You're a private equity firm wearing a beanie.

b.text: Oat milk, you're the Prius of dairy alternatives. You show up at brunch with a tote bag full of opinions, and everybody claps like you saved the planet. Meanwhile you're just oats that got put through a blender and came out looking like wet cardboard with a lawyer. You froth beautifully, sure, but you froth like a guy who just found out his barista certificate expired. And don't get me started on "barista edition." Nobody's a barista because they bought a carton with a cartoon on it. You're basically a shampoo that gave up on being a shampoo and decided to be a latte. Nobody asked you to be creamy. You just showed up creamy-adjacent and expected a parade.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, you started as the internal chat tool for a failed video game called Glitch, and honestly? Still the most accurate name you've ever had.

You promised to kill email. Instead you gave us email that *knocks*. That little wooden knock-brush sound has triggered more cortisol than any boss in history. I hear it in the shower. I hear it at funerals.

You invented the green dot, so now my employer knows I went to the bathroom for nineteen minutes. You invented "is typing…" so my manager can type for four straight minutes and send "ok."

Threads? Nobody can find them. Huddles? A Zoom call that ambushes you. And somehow every company has 400 channels, and the only active one is #random, where Kevin posts his sourdough.

Your name literally stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable. Sure. Try finding that one link from Tuesday. 👀 reacted by 3 people.

b.text:
Slack, the only place where "Quick question" is a threat. Nobody has ever had a quick question. Just a little typing bubble that appears, disappears, appears again, and then nothing, like a ghost deciding whether to haunt you.

You took email, which everyone hated, and said, "What if it were faster, and your boss could watch you be green?" Now I can't go to the bathroom without my status turning yellow like I'm a traffic light of shame.

And the notifications. That little red badge. Forty-seven unread in #general, which is just a graveyard of birthday gifs and a guy named Doug asking who took his yogurt.

The emoji reactions are how adults now communicate. A thumbs-up means "I acknowledge you." The eyes emoji means "I saw this and will do nothing." And the little checkmark means "done," which is the biggest lie since "let's circle back."

Slack: you replaced meetings with meetings that never end.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which is wild, because you dress like a medieval mace and smell like a crime scene. Every other fruit says "eat me." You say "I dare you."

You're the only food with a gas leak. A Canberra university library was evacuated because of you. Evacuated! Fruit is not supposed to trigger a hazmat response.

Singapore had to put you on the subway sign with a big red X, right next to flamethrowers. Hotels ban you the way they ban smoking and goats.

And the flesh inside? Custard that tastes like sweet almonds, caramel, and a decision you regret. Fans say, "Just get past the smell." That's what people say about your cousin's boyfriend.

You're the only fruit that can kill me from the tree, and the only one I'd still blame the neighbors for.

b.text: Durian, you're the only fruit that needs a gas mask and a hazmat permit just to get through the airport. Airlines ban you like you're a bomb with a bad attitude. Your smell is a mix of gym socks, rotting onions, and a sewage pipe that's been sulking for a week. People hear the word "delicacy" and think you're kidding. Southeast Asians call you the king of fruits, and honestly, that's the only reason you got a crown instead of a restraining order. You look like a medieval mace someone dropped in a swamp, and you're covered in spikes so nobody can hug you. Even the spikes are a warning. Your fans swear you taste like custard and heaven, but they also say that about getting a root canal on Christmas. Smell like a crime scene, taste like a dessert, and still somehow get a hotel room kicked out for eating you.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ, hydrogen silsesquioxane, the only resist that's basically glass pretending to be a photoresist. You're the diva of nanofabrication. Shelf life? Three months, if you keep it cold, treat it gently, and whisper affirmations. Open the bottle wrong and you've got a jar of gel with commitment issues.

You're a negative tone resist, which is fitting, because that's the attitude. Everyone wants 10-nanometer lines, and you deliver them, then collapse because a developer rinse looked at you funny. Capillary forces: your Achilles heel, your whole personality.

And your dose? You need a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. That's not exposure, that's a hostage negotiation with the beam. Writing one wafer takes longer than my last relationship.

Then you cure into silicon dioxide and just sit there, permanent, like a bad tattoo. "Oh, you wanted to remove me? Enjoy your hydrofluoric acid, hero."

Gorgeous resolution, though. Truly. Shame about everything else.

b.text:
HSQ, ladies and gentlemen: the only resist with sub-10-nanometer resolution and the personality of a sourdough starter. You buy it, you refrigerate it, and it *still* starts gelling in the bottle like it's got somewhere better to be. Shelf life measured in "eh, few months, maybe."

And slow? HSQ needs a dose so high the e-beam tool files for overtime. Your PMMA friends finished their write and went home; you're still exposing alignment marks.

Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you want contrast, *salty* developer. Yes, this resist literally needs you to add salt. Even Gordon Ramsay thinks that's a lot.

But the real red flag? Once it's exposed, it turns into glass. Permanently. You want it gone? Hydrofluoric acid. That's not a resist, that's a relationship you can only leave with a hazmat suit.

Still, gorgeous lines. Shame they collapse when they dry.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, the material that's been "ten years from changing everything" for thirty years. You're 100 times stronger than steel, and yet somehow you've never held a job.

You're a single sheet of graphene rolled up like a sad burrito, and you still can't decide if you're a metal or a semiconductor. Chirality, right? Your entire personality depends on which way you twist. That's not physics, that's a mood ring.

Scientists say you could build a space elevator. Buddy, you can't even get through a lab without clumping together like earbuds in a pocket. Every researcher spends six months trying to disperse you, then writes "uniform" in the paper anyway.

And the manufacturing! Everyone gets a random mix of types, so sorting you is like trying to separate identical twins by vibe.

Also, you're a nanometer wide and somehow still the biggest thing in everyone's grant proposal.

b.text: Carbon nanotubes, you've been "five years away from changing everything" since 1991. You're stronger than steel, lighter than aluminum, and conduct electricity like a champ, which is impressive until someone asks you to leave the lab. You're a sheet of graphene that rolled itself up and called it a personality. Your big selling point is being incredibly small, and honestly, that's the only thing you've ever fit into. Every time someone tries to disperse you in a solvent, you clump together like a group project at 2 a.m. Meanwhile, the press releases keep calling you "revolutionary," and the only thing you've revolutionized is the grant budget. Stronger than steel, lighter than aluminum, and still the guest nobody's ready to invite into the real world.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs is a beautiful operating system. Shame it never shipped with a decent text editor. That's why half its users install evil-mode: they love Emacs so much they turned it into Vim.

Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," which is also the sound your pinky makes on its way to the orthopedic surgeon. Asking for help is C-h, which in a terminal deletes a character. So even your cry for help gets backspaced.

It has a built-in therapist, M-x doctor, which is thoughtful, because nobody else will listen to you explain your init.el. Four thousand lines of Lisp, half copied from a 2003 mailing list, and you still declare "Emacs bankruptcy" every two years.

It plays Tetris. It reads email. It runs your entire life in Org-mode. It still chokes on one long line of JSON.

b.text:
Emacs isn't a text editor, it's an operating system that's still waiting for a decent editor to come along. It has a built-in psychiatrist, a Tetris clone, and a mail client, but somehow no sane keybindings.

Ctrl-x Ctrl-s to save? That's not a shortcut, that's a hand injury with a lawsuit pending. Emacs users call it "Emacs pinky" like it's a badge of honor. Sir, that's a repetitive strain injury from a Lisp interpreter.

And the config file! Fifteen years of init.el, a thousand lines of copy-pasted snippets from a 2009 blog post, and nobody knows what half of it does. But if you delete it, you die.

Every Emacs user says, "It's infinitely customizable!" Yes, and you've spent four hundred hours customizing it so you can finally write a grocery list.

Meanwhile, the Vim guys are laughing, and honestly? They've earned it.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text: Papyrus, you were designed in 1982 by a 23-year-old with calligraphy pens and a dream of ancient Egypt, and somehow you still look like you were drawn by someone shivering. Your edges are so rough you need exfoliating. You promised the wisdom of the Nile and delivered the vibe of a chiropractor's tri-fold brochure. Every day spa, hookah lounge, and "Inner Journey" yoga retreat found you in the dropdown menu and whispered, "This feels ancient." James Cameron spent $237 million on *Avatar* and then used you for the logo, which is like building the Taj Mahal and signing it in crayon. Ryan Gosling lost sleep over you on national television. You're not a typeface; you're a cry for help with ragged little serifs. Even Comic Sans looks at you and says, "At least I know I'm a joke."

b.text: Papyrus, you're a font that has never once been near Egypt. You look like a yoga studio's "Namaste" sign left out in the Sedona sun until it got fuzzy around the edges. Every letter has the texture of a wet paper bag someone tried to iron. You're the go-to for the wooden plaque in a crystal shop, right next to the "Live Laugh Love" sign and the incense nobody's bought since 2009. James Cameron used you for Avatar, and somehow an entire alien moon ended up looking like a smoothie menu. People who pick you think they're being mysterious. You're not mysterious. You're a tiki bar's menu that's sorry it opened, printed on the same paper you're named after, which is to say, nobody's real writing surface.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, you were a $400 Wi-Fi-connected juicer that delivered four tons of force, enough, your engineers bragged, to lift two Teslas, and Bloomberg proved the job could be done by a guy with hands. You raised $120 million from Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins to compete with *squeezing*. Every single customer already owned the competing product. It came in pairs.

You sold $8 bags of chopped produce that had to scan a QR code and phone home before you'd juice them. A juicer that needed internet. Imagine the outage: "Sorry, AWS is down, enjoy your sealed pouch of regret." You'd refuse to press an expired pack, like a bouncer for kale.

Doug Evans compared himself to Steve Jobs. Steve Jobs put a thousand songs in your pocket. Doug put a sack of mush in a vise and asked for your Wi-Fi password. Silicon Valley's most expensive way to say, "Just use your hands."

b.text:
Juicero raised 120 million dollars to build a $400 Wi-Fi-connected juicer, which is a lot of engineering for a bag you could just squeeze with your hands. And that's exactly what Bloomberg did. Reporters squeezed the pack by hand and got juice faster than the machine. The machine had four tons of force, and the whole thing was basically a very expensive way to say "no thanks, I'll do it myself."

It wouldn't even work offline. Your juice pack had to phone home to check if it was expired. Imagine being a kale-based hostage to a server in California. "Sorry, your carrots are out of date." Brother, I'm holding them. They're orange. They're fine.

And the packs cost eight dollars each. Eight dollars for a bag of chopped salad you'd then have to pretend was fresh-pressed. Silicon Valley looked at a smoothie and said, "What if it had DRM?"

Juicero didn't disrupt juice. It disrupted investors' bank accounts.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text:
Google Sheets is Excel's cousin who showed up to the family reunion and insisted everyone edit the same potluck dish at once. You open a file called "Untitled spreadsheet" and somehow it's the most permanent document your company owns. It's been "Budget FINAL v3 (Copy of Copy)" since 2017.

The best part is the real-time collaboration. Nothing says teamwork like watching an Anonymous Capybara delete your entire column while you're mid-formula. And you can't even blame Greg, because Greg is a capybara.

IMPORTRANGE is the only function that makes you beg a spreadsheet for permission to read your own spreadsheet. "Allow access." I'm sorry, I made both of these!

Then you hit a hundred thousand rows and the whole thing goes "Working..." That's not a loading message, that's a hostage video.

And QUERY? It's SQL for people who were told SQL was too scary, then handed something scarier.

b.text:
Google Sheets, you're the spreadsheet equivalent of a guy who says "I'm not really a party person" and then shows up to every meeting with a pivot table. You've got 10 million cells and you still can't tell me why my VLOOKUP returned #N/A. Oh, that's not a bug, that's your personality: "Did you mean the other tab?" No, Sheets, I didn't mean the other tab. Nobody ever meant the other tab.

And don't get me started on autocomplete. I type "=SU" and you suggest SUMIF, SUMSQ, and SUBSTITUTE like you're trying to get me to commit to a divorce. Just pick one! You're a grid of cells that refuses to commit to a formula.

Your collaboration features are great, though. My boss can see my edits in real time, which is how I learned he watches me type "asdfgh" when a deadline hits.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest thing humanity ever did, pouring hot water over beans, and turned it into a subscription-based hostage situation. You charge me fifty cents for a thimble of coffee wrapped in a tiny plastic coffin that will outlive my great-grandchildren.

The inventor of the K-Cup literally apologized for it. The guy said he sometimes regrets inventing it. Your own father looked at his creation and said, "Yeah, I'd undo that."

And the machine itself? You push one button and it screams like a dying dial-up modem, then dribbles out something called "Bold" that tastes like a warm handshake from a wet paper bag. Every morning it flashes "Descale Me" like a needy ex. Meanwhile your water reservoir holds enough for exactly one bad decision.

Offices love you because nothing says "we value our employees" like a sad pod carousel next to a broken microwave.

Keurig: for people who want coffee, but also want to feel something about landfills.

b.text: Keurig, you're the only appliance that makes a cup of coffee and then apologizes for it by making you wait four minutes while it hums like a dying refrigerator. You're a single-serve machine with the commitment of a Tinder profile: one pod, one cup, and you'll never call back. Every morning I stare into your little plastic mouth, feed you a pod that cost more per ounce than gold, and you spit out something that tastes like a coffee bean's ghost. And the recycling? Those pods are tiny landfills with lids. You didn't make coffee, Keurig. You made a subscription plan wearing a drip tray. Even your name sounds like a sneeze that got a corporate loan.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text: Keurig, you're the only appliance that makes a cup of coffee and then apologizes for it by making you wait four minutes while it hums like a dying refrigerator. You're a single-serve machine with the commitment of a Tinder profile: one pod, one cup, and you'll never call back. Every morning I stare into your little plastic mouth, feed you a pod that cost more per ounce than gold, and you spit out something that tastes like a coffee bean's ghost. And the recycling? Those pods are tiny landfills with lids. You didn't make coffee, Keurig. You made a subscription plan wearing a drip tray. Even your name sounds like a sneeze that got a corporate loan.

b.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest thing in the world, hot water meeting coffee, and turned it into a subscription-based hostage situation. My grandfather made coffee with a pot and a prayer. I make it by stabbing a tiny plastic hockey puck in the face.

You've created a machine that takes four minutes to warm up just to produce eight ounces of something that tastes like a mug rinsed in a wet cardboard box. And that little pod? Thousands of tiny plastic cups, each one lasting longer than my last three relationships.

Then there's the "descale" light. Every few months it screams at me to run vinegar through it, like a smoke detector for my own laziness. I ignore it, and the machine just sighs and gives me half a cup.

The best part is the "strong" button. It doesn't make it stronger. It makes it smaller. You invented coffee's version of "I'm not mad, I'm just disappointed."

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Deep-dish pizza is the only food that makes you wait forty-five minutes for a meal and then spends the next three hours in your stomach like a sofa somebody moved in without asking. It's not a pizza. It's a casserole that got a library card. You bite in and the cheese pulls up like it's auditioning for a Lysol commercial, and the sauce sits on top like it lost a bet with the crust. Chicagoans will tell you it's "a whole different thing," which is what people say when they're hoping you won't check the ingredients. Nobody in Chicago has ever finished a whole deep dish alone. They just stare at the last slice in the box like it owes them money, then eat it cold at 1 a.m. over the sink, which is the only honest way to eat it.

b.text:
Chicago deep-dish isn't pizza, it's a casserole with an identity crisis. You order it, and they say, "That'll be 45 minutes." Forty-five minutes! For bread! I've seen people give birth faster, and the baby came out less cooked.

Then it arrives, and it's built upside down. Cheese on the bottom, sauce on top. That's not a recipe, that's a structural failure. It's a pizza that fell down the stairs and everyone decided to call it tradition.

You get one slice, and it requires a spatula, a fork, a knife, and a signed waiver. Your first bite is molten cheese lava. Your second bite is a tomato landslide. By the third, you're lying on the booth like you've been shot by a lasagna.

And Chicagoans defend this! "It's the real pizza." Sir, you eat soup with a crust and call New Yorkers wrong. That's a pie chart with a cardiologist.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text:
Esperanto is the only product in history where the user manual promised world peace and the user base turned out to be eleven guys named Zbigniew arguing about the accusative case.

Zamenhof invented a language to unite humanity, and humanity said, "Cute. Does it have a Starbucks?"

It has sixteen grammar rules and no exceptions, which is exactly what a language sounds like when it's never been used by anyone angry. Try ordering a sandwich in a tongue where nobody has ever cheated on anyone or been cut off in traffic. Where's the slang? Where's the swearing? You can't build a culture on a word for "hello" and a really strong feeling about the letter ĥ.

Its greatest literary achievement is a translation of Hamlet. Even the original works are mostly translations of someone else's feelings.

And the flag is a green star. Not a country. A star. It's a nation-state with a logo and a dating pool smaller than a Dungeons & Dragons convention in Lithuania.

Mi amas vin, Esperanto. Nobody else does.

b.text:
Esperanto. In 1887, Dr. Zamenhof, an eye doctor, looked at a world divided by language and decided what it really needed was six letters wearing tiny hats. Nothing says "universal" like ĉ, ĝ, and ŭ, characters no keyboard on Earth can type, so your fans write "cx" and pretend that's fine.

Your name literally means "one who hopes." A hundred and thirty years later: still hoping.

You're the only language where "bad" is just "un-good." *Malbona.* That's not grammar, that's Orwell's Newspeak with a beard. Every noun ends in -o, so you sound like Italian being sight-read by a robot.

You promised world peace and delivered a convention full of men wearing green star pins. Your biggest movie stars William Shatner. And you have about a thousand native speakers, which isn't a language community. It's a cul-de-sac.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only energy source that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not the future, you're a toddler promising to clean his room after the next funding cycle.

You heat plasma to 150 million degrees, ten times hotter than the core of the sun, and still can't do what the sun does for free while being a ball of gas with no PhD.

ITER started at five billion euros. It's now north of twenty, and it hasn't produced a watt. That's not a reactor, that's a French timeshare.

In 2022 you finally got "net energy gain" by ignoring the 300 megajoules the lasers pulled from the wall. That's like saying your restaurant's profitable if you don't count rent.

And your solution to fuel shortages is mining helium-3 on the moon. Buddy, you can't even make it to Tuesday.

b.text:
Fusion power, you've been thirty years away since my grandfather was alive. You're the friend who's "five minutes out" and hasn't left the house.

You're so proud of reaching net energy gain. Sure, the laser put out more than the fuel pellet took in, but it needed three hundred megajoules from the wall to make three. That's like bragging you turned a profit because you ignored rent, payroll, and the building.

You heat plasma to a hundred million degrees, then your biggest worry is that it touches something. Your whole job is holding a tiny sun in a magnetic bottle, and the sun does it for free using only gravity and spite.

ITER's budget has more delays than a budget airline. Your fuel, tritium, is rarer than a straight answer from a physicist, so your plan is to breed it inside the reactor you haven't built yet.

Fusion: the energy of the future, and always will be.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're just plexiglass with a god complex. You're the same stuff as a hamster cage, and somehow you've got a cleanroom full of PhDs treating you like a sacred text.

You're a positive resist, which is cute, because nothing about your attitude is. We hit you with a billion electrons and you just go, "Fine, I'll break up a little." Chain scission? That's not a lithography mechanism, that's your whole personality.

And the sensitivity! You need like a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. My phone charges faster than you expose. Meanwhile I'm sitting at the e-beam writing a pattern for nine hours so you can give me a lopsided blob.

Then comes development. Isopropanol and MIBK, because you're too good for water. Overdevelop by ten seconds and your lines collapse like a dropped soufflé.

And you're sold in anisole, so every wafer smells like a licorice factory had an affair with a solvent cabinet.

Great resolution, though. Ten nanometers. Shame about everything else.

b.text: Ladies and gentlemen, PMMA, the e-beam resist that's just Plexiglass with a graduate degree. You know what else is sharp and transparent and you can't eat? A window. PMMA takes a beam of electrons, snaps its chains apart, and then acts shocked when the developer washes away exactly the parts it chose to lose. Its sensitivity is so low you need a dose that would make a lesser polymer file for disability. You bake it at 180 degrees, wait, spin it, wait, bake again, and it still makes you feel like you're the one being exposed. Its etch resistance is about as strong as a wet paper towel. But sure, it draws lines thinner than a virus's dream, so we just keep inviting it back, like that one relative who only shows up to tell you what you did wrong.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP, you're the only language whose name is a recursive acronym, and it still reads like a bug report. Every variable wears a dollar sign like you're charging rent for each one. Your function names were clearly picked by drawing lots: strpos takes the haystack first, array_search takes the needle first, and you just shrug. "0" == false? Sure. "abc" == 0? Why not. Your comparison operator is a coin toss in a trench coat. Half the internet runs on you, and WordPress is the proof. Nobody brags about WordPress, but everybody's sites are built on you. I'd like to hate you more, but I've seen you in production. Everyone loves you secretly, late at night, with error_reporting turned off.

b.text:
PHP is the only language where the standard library looks like it was named by a committee of people who'd never met. Is it str_replace or strpos? Is the needle first or the haystack? Nobody knows. Not even PHP. It just rolls dice and says "array_walk, but backwards."

Fun fact: PHP stands for "Personal Home Page," which is also what it feels like when your code gets hacked and a teenager in Belarus redirects your site to a pharmacy.

It's got a function called mysql_real_escape_string, which implies there was a mysql_escape_string that was fake. Fake escaping. Just vibes.

And the equality operator? "0" == false, "abc" == 0, null == false. PHP looks at two completely different things and says, "Eh, close enough." It's the language equivalent of a bouncer who lets everyone in because they're wearing a shirt.

But hey, it powers 77% of the web. So does that one guy named Gary who's still on WordPress 3.2.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text: Papyrus, you're a font that has never once been near Egypt. You look like a yoga studio's "Namaste" sign left out in the Sedona sun until it got fuzzy around the edges. Every letter has the texture of a wet paper bag someone tried to iron. You're the go-to for the wooden plaque in a crystal shop, right next to the "Live Laugh Love" sign and the incense nobody's bought since 2009. James Cameron used you for Avatar, and somehow an entire alien moon ended up looking like a smoothie menu. People who pick you think they're being mysterious. You're not mysterious. You're a tiki bar's menu that's sorry it opened, printed on the same paper you're named after, which is to say, nobody's real writing surface.

b.text:
Papyrus, you're the font that shows up to every event dressed for a different one. You've been on spa menus, yoga studio flyers, and a blockbuster movie about a blue alien planet, and somehow you're always wrong for all of them.

You look like you were hand-torn from a scroll by someone who has never held a scroll. Your edges are so rough, it's like you were printed on a napkin during an earthquake. Every letter looks like it's auditioning for a role as "Ancient Egyptian Gift Shop."

And the designers! They had one job for Avatar: make it look futuristic. They gave you a font that says "Cleopatra's Aromatherapy Candles." Ryan Gosling did a whole sketch about it, and you're still working. That's not resilience, that's a restraining order nobody enforced.

You say "organic." You say "natural." You mean "I was free in the font menu and nobody had the heart to say no."

Papyrus: the only thing on your computer that smells like incense.

a.text:
Esperanto. In 1887, Dr. Zamenhof, an eye doctor, looked at a world divided by language and decided what it really needed was six letters wearing tiny hats. Nothing says "universal" like ĉ, ĝ, and ŭ, characters no keyboard on Earth can type, so your fans write "cx" and pretend that's fine.

Your name literally means "one who hopes." A hundred and thirty years later: still hoping.

You promised world peace and delivered a convention full of men wearing green star pins. Your biggest movie stars William Shatner. And you have about a thousand native speakers, which isn't a language community. It's a cul-de-sac.

b.text:
Esperanto: the language invented to unite humanity, and after 130 years, its greatest achievement is a tiny group of people who all met at the same convention.

Zamenhof wanted world peace. He got a language where the most common sentence is "Hello, are you also here for the Esperanto thing?"

Everything is regular. Every noun ends in O. Every adjective ends in A. It's the only language designed like a filing cabinet, and it sounds like Italian and Polish got stuck in an elevator and decided to name the kids.

And the accusative! They made a language to be easy, then kept the accusative. Fine. It's a hobby.

"Native speakers" of Esperanto number about a thousand, which is what we call "the children of enthusiasts who never got a vote."

The national anthem is "La Espero." The national sport is correcting your pronunciation of "ĉ." And the only country that really speaks it is the Facebook group.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass was the only product where the beta testers were called "Explorers," because "Guinea Pigs With Fourteen Hundred Dollars" tested poorly.

It was a computer you wore on your face that said "OK Glass" out loud, so every guy using it looked like he was being polite to a ghost. You didn't need a screen. You needed a wink and a prayer. Winking took a photo, which is a fantastic feature if you want to be punched in a bar.

And that's where they were banned: bars, casinos, strip clubs, movie theaters. Glass was the first device kicked out of places for what it *might* do. Even the strip club said, "Sir, we have standards."

They called the wearers "Glassholes," which is the rare nickname that came with the product, free, no subscription.

Google didn't discontinue it. They pivoted it to factories, where nobody has to look at you.

b.text: Google Glass, you cost fifteen hundred dollars and made everyone wearing you look like a Bluetooth headset that got promoted. Sergey Brin launched you by skydiving onto a building, and that's the last time you were ever cool. You put a tiny prism over one eye so people could check email while pretending to make eye contact. You didn't invent a computer, you invented a reason to get punched. You're the only gadget that gave us a new slur: "Glasshole." Bars banned you. Movie theaters banned you. Robert Scoble wore you in the shower, and that photo did more damage than any privacy lawsuit. You took pictures when people winked, turning every awkward conversation into a potential felony. Your battery died before your reputation did, and that's impressive. Rest in peace: demoted to warehouse work, then quietly killed in 2023. The most Google ending possible.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text: Canberra: the only city where the traffic jam is a roundabout with a sculpture in the middle. A century ago, someone looked at a sheep paddock between Sydney and Melbourne and said, "Let's put the whole country's government here so nobody has to visit." And it worked. Parliament House sits on its hill like a very expensive filing cabinet. The lake is named after an American architect, and it's the most exciting thing that happens here. Winter mornings hit minus four, and the only people outside are joggers with a grudge. Friday night out means the Civic bar, where everyone's a public servant with a lanyard still on. Nobody lives in Canberra. They're just waiting for a posting.

b.text:
Canberra is the only city in the world designed by an architect and then lived in by a committee. It's a capital built on a swamp, which was a bold choice, because nothing says "national pride" like a lake you dug yourself so the city would have something to look at.

Everyone's a public servant. Ask someone what they do and they say "policy," then spend forty minutes explaining that they can't explain it.

Roundabouts are the city's love language. You don't navigate Canberra, you get slowly interrogated by it. Exit two, exit three, back to Parliament House, you've been circling since March.

It's the only place where the nightlife is a Dendy cinema and a tense conversation about a briefing note. Even the fireworks are banned. The bush capital: eight months of frost, four of bushfire smoke, and one weekend where it's nice and everyone's at Floriade pretending they live somewhere better.

a.text:
Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree on anything, so they built a city that nobody could possibly be jealous of. Mission accomplished.

It was designed by an American architect, which explains why it feels like a very nice airport with sheep. The roundabouts are so plentiful that locals don't give directions, they give revolutions. The lake is fake, the population is mostly public servants waiting for Friday, and the kangaroos outnumber the nightlife.

Your Parliament House is literally buried in a hill so people can walk on the roof, the only time Australians get to stand on politicians.

For your centenary you commissioned the Skywhale, a giant flying balloon with ten enormous boobs, and somehow that's still the most exciting thing to happen here.

Canberra: home of Summernats, Floriade, and legally purchasable X-rated videos. Burnouts, tulips and porn, because you've got to do something until the next Senate estimates hearing.

b.text:

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text:
Brasília, you're the only city designed by someone who looked at a map and said, "What if it were an airplane?" Congratulations, you're the world's largest piece of urban origami. Nobody can find anything because every address is a code. "I live at SQS 308, Bloco C, Apartamento 204." That's not a home, that's a Wi-Fi password.

You have no street corners. You have no sidewalks anyone uses. Brazilians love to gather in public, so you built a city where the only way to meet someone is by driving twenty minutes to stand near them.

Oscar Niemeyer gave you gorgeous curves, and then your politicians moved in and did the most corrupt things you could imagine inside them. A cathedral that looks like a crown of thorns, a Congress that looks like two bowls and a pair of dishes. Even the buildings look like they're waiting for a bribe.

You were built in four years. It shows. Rio had 400 to get charming.

b.text:
Brasília, you're the only city designed to look like an airplane, and somehow everyone still just wants to leave on one. Politicians fly in Tuesday, take a bribe Wednesday, and they're gone by Thursday like it's a timeshare.

Your addresses read like a Wi-Fi password: "SQS 308, Bloco C, Apartamento 402." I'm not visiting a friend, I'm resetting a router.

Niemeyer gave you gorgeous curves, then Lúcio Costa forgot pedestrians. Want to walk to the bakery? Hope you enjoy the eight-lane Eixão and a light jog through a tesourinha.

Your humidity drops to 10 percent. Your congress has one bowl facing up, one facing down: one for collecting money, the other for hiding it.

And you were built with no corners, so Brazil's capital has no boteco na esquina. That's not urban planning. That's a human rights violation.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text: Klingon, you sound like a man hacking up a hairball during a hostage negotiation. Every word starts with a throat-clearing gargle, and somehow "nuqneH" still sounds like a threat. Apparently "please" is a sign of weakness, so you just bellow "Qapla'" and hope the guy behind you agrees. Your grammar treats every sentence like a dare: object first, verb second, subject whenever you feel like it. Your big literary achievement is *Hamlet*, and its most famous line comes out as "taH pagh taHbe'," which sounds like a dog choking on a sock. Your dictionary has more ways to say "your mother" than "I'm sorry," and I'd respect you more if you apologized once.

b.text:
Klingon, a language designed by a linguist so warriors could sound like they're clearing their throats at you in anger. Every sentence sounds like a cat being strangled by a Scrabble bag of Q's and apostrophes.

You have a word for "disruptor" but not "please." Because apparently when a Klingon wants something, he doesn't ask. He just reorders his grammar until the object is afraid.

Your verbs go at the end, so by the time someone finishes threatening me, I've already left for lunch. "I will crush your skull and... " Hold on, I'm still waiting for the verb. Honestly, that's the most polite thing about you.

And Okrand wrote an entire dictionary, yet there's no word for "sorry" because "it's a weakness." Meanwhile, there's a proverb about revenge being a dish best served cold. You're a language with an open-mic problem and a fridge full of leftovers.

Fluent speakers: about twelve. All of them are named Gary, and all of them are using you to ask for the check.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text: You're one atom thick, the only thing about you that's ever been thin. Two guys won a Nobel for peeling you off a lump of pencil lead with Scotch tape. Pencil lead! Your whole family tree is the stuff kids chew in exam halls. You're stronger than steel pound for pound, you conduct electricity, you're transparent, and you still can't get out of the lab. Every year it's "graphene will revolutionize batteries next year." That's been going on for twenty years. Meanwhile companies slap your name on tennis rackets and face cream with about as much of you as a rumor. You're basically a pencil lead that got a personal trainer and a Nobel, and you still can't get a callback from a battery company.

b.text:
Graphene, you're the only Nobel Prize winner ever discovered with Scotch tape. Two physicists peeled a pencil and found you, which means your origin story is literally "kid procrastinating on homework."

Since 2004 you've been "about to revolutionize" batteries, computers, water filters, and space elevators. Twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a tennis racket. You're not a wonder material, you're a press release with a hexagon fetish.

Everyone loves to say you're two hundred times stronger than steel. Great. You're also one atom thick. Nobody's impressed that a sheet of paper beats a battleship per ounce.

And for the supposed savior of electronics, you have zero bandgap. You can't even turn off. You're a transistor with no off switch, the guy at the party who never stops talking.

You're graphite with a LinkedIn profile.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text: Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree, so Australia built a city nobody wanted, which is honestly the most Canberra origin story possible: a compromise with suburbs. They held an international design competition and hired two Americans to plan it, and they nailed the brief: "Make it impossible to find anything." Every road is a roundabout leading to another roundabout, encircling a fake lake named after the guy who designed the roundabouts. Your Parliament House has a grass roof so you can literally walk on top of the government, the only time anyone in Canberra is above a public servant. The kangaroos outnumber the nightlife. For decades your two biggest attractions were legal fireworks and X-rated videos, which tells me the locals needed both a bang and a release. Then you banned the fireworks. Now the excitement is Floriade: a month of staring at tulips because the alternative is Tuggeranong.

b.text:
Canberra is the only city in the world designed by an architect and then lived in by a committee. It's a capital built on a swamp, which was a bold choice, because nothing says "national pride" like a lake you dug yourself so the city would have something to look at.

Everyone's a public servant. Ask someone what they do and they say "policy," then spend forty minutes explaining that they can't explain it.

Roundabouts are the city's love language. You don't navigate Canberra, you get slowly interrogated by it. Exit two, exit three, back to Parliament House, you've been circling since March.

It's the only place where the nightlife is a Dendy cinema and a tense conversation about a briefing note. Even the fireworks are banned. The bush capital: eight months of frost, four of bushfire smoke, and one weekend where it's nice and everyone's at Floriade pretending they live somewhere better.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text: Papyrus is the font that wants so badly to be ancient Egyptian it forgot to check whether it's the right century. It was made in 1983, on a computer, by someone with a hunch and no interest in pharaohs. Yet it's on every yoga studio sign, vegan café menu, and candle that says "Blessed." Its letters look like they were chiseled by someone who loves the idea of a tomb but has never stood in one. Wedding invitations, wine bars, tiki shacks: they all reach for Papyrus like it's wisdom. Look at that lopsided W, like it had three margaritas before it got written. It's the typographic equivalent of a man in a linen shirt at a funeral, and it's nobody's ancestor.

b.text: Papyrus, you were designed in 1982 by a 23-year-old with calligraphy pens and a dream of ancient Egypt, and somehow you still look like you were drawn by someone shivering. Your edges are so rough you need exfoliating. You promised the wisdom of the Nile and delivered the vibe of a chiropractor's tri-fold brochure. Every day spa, hookah lounge, and "Inner Journey" yoga retreat found you in the dropdown menu and whispered, "This feels ancient." James Cameron spent $237 million on *Avatar* and then used you for the logo, which is like building the Taj Mahal and signing it in crayon. Ryan Gosling lost sleep over you on national television. You're not a typeface; you're a cry for help with ragged little serifs. Even Comic Sans looks at you and says, "At least I know I'm a joke."

Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text: Canberra is the only capital in Australia built from scratch, which explains a lot. Sydney and Melbourne were so busy hating each other they agreed to put the country's brain in a paddock halfway between them, and it has been sulking ever since. Walter Burley Griffin drew it up as a neat wheel of boulevards around a lake, then the public servants arrived and discovered that every road in town is a roundabout. Nobody has ever found the way out of Civic. The nightlife shuts at nine because the whole city is in bed before Question Time ends. The lake is named after Griffin, which is a shame, because he's the only man ever to design a city and then get a lake named after him instead of a train station. In winter the frost is so thick the ministers need a scraper before they can go inside and be lied to.

b.text: Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree, so Australia built a city nobody wanted, which is honestly the most Canberra origin story possible: a compromise with suburbs. They held an international design competition and hired two Americans to plan it, and they nailed the brief: "Make it impossible to find anything." Every road is a roundabout leading to another roundabout, encircling a fake lake named after the guy who designed the roundabouts. Your Parliament House has a grass roof so you can literally walk on top of the government, the only time anyone in Canberra is above a public servant. The kangaroos outnumber the nightlife. For decades your two biggest attractions were legal fireworks and X-rated videos, which tells me the locals needed both a bang and a release. Then you banned the fireworks. Now the excitement is Floriade: a month of staring at tulips because the alternative is Tuggeranong.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text:
Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a front wall. Fitting, since the whole city is a facade: a fake Venice with a painted sky, a half-size Eiffel Tower, and a Grand Lisboa that looks like a golden pineapple trying to cheat at baccarat.

Portugal ruled you for 442 years and left behind egg tarts and street signs nobody can pronounce. Four centuries, one pastry.

You've made several times more gambling money than Las Vegas, yet your signature dish is a pork chop jammed in a bun. Classy.

Half your land was dug out of the sea, which is perfect, because the other half was dug out of tourists' pockets.

And they built a 55-kilometer bridge to connect you to Hong Kong, and it's emptier than a junket operator's promises. Even the bridge is losing at the tables.

b.text:
Macau, you're what happens when Portugal and Las Vegas have a one-night stand and nobody wants to claim the kid. You have a Venetian with fake canals, a fake sky, and a gondolier singing "O Sole Mio" in a Chinese province. Not even Italy does that to itself.

You make more gambling money than Vegas by a factor of several, which means you're basically a very successful casino with a cobblestone problem.

Your egg tarts are better than Portugal's, and everyone knows it, including Portugal, who's still mad. Your Eiffel Tower is half-size, your Parisian is half-French, and your Grand Lisboa looks like a golden lotus ate a disco ball.

You're 12 square miles and somehow have traffic jams at the border from people who lost everything and still want to come back. That's not tourism. That's an abusive relationship with a buffet.

Even your ruins are just a facade. St. Paul's is literally one wall. You couldn't keep the church, but you kept the slot machines.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, you're the only city where a $19 buffet costs $64 once you add the "resort fee," the "facility fee," and the emotional toll of the line.

You built a fake Eiffel Tower, a fake Venice, and a fake New York, because even your tourists said, "Sure, but can we get these somewhere hotter and sadder?"

It's 115 degrees, and the locals say, "But it's a dry heat." So is an oven, Brenda.

Everyone arrives in a bachelor party wearing matching shirts and leaves as a missing-person report with a wristband.

You have a million slot machines at the airport. You're the only place that starts taking your money before you've gotten your luggage.

And the Sphere? A billion-dollar glowing eyeball staring down the Strip, like even the city is judging your decisions.

What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas, mostly because it's your checking account.

b.text:
