Las Vegas, the only city where you can see the Eiffel Tower, a pyramid, and Venice in one afternoon and still feel like you never left a strip mall in Ohio. You're a city built in the desert out of pure spite and borrowed water. The Colorado River is literally drying up so a fake volcano can erupt every fifteen minutes for a guy in cargo shorts holding a yard-long margarita.

Your casinos have no clocks and no windows, which is smart, because nobody wants to know it's 9 a.m. on a Tuesday and Grandma's on her third oxygen tank at the Wheel of Fortune slots.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas"? Sure. Mostly your 401(k). And now you've got the Sphere, a giant glowing eyeball, so the whole city can watch you make every mistake in 4K.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans, you're the only font that shows up to a funeral looking like it's about to do a magic show.

Vincent Connare designed you for a cartoon dog's speech bubble in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you escaped into the wild and started writing resignation letters, hospital signage, and the CERN Higgs boson announcement. Scientists found the God particle and presented it like a bake sale flyer.

You look like handwriting from a guy who says "Let's circle back" while wearing a Hawaiian shirt to a layoff. Every letter looks like it's been sitting in a ball pit.

Your fans say you're great for dyslexic readers. Fine. That's your one defense, and you've been hiding behind it like a substitute teacher using a laminated poster.

You're the only font where "Please stop microwaving fish" sounds like a threat from a clown.

Even Papyrus saw you and said, "Wow."

b.text:
Comic Sans, you were born in 1994 to put words in the mouth of a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the one that survived. Bob is dead. The dog is dead. You're on a sympathy card at a funeral home.

You were inspired by Batman comics, and you've never once been near anything heroic. CERN used you to announce the Higgs boson: humanity's greatest discovery, presented like a lemonade stand. Dan Gilbert used you to call LeBron a traitor, because nothing says "furious billionaire" like bubble letters.

And your defense is always "Well, I help dyslexic readers." Great. You're the guy at the party whose whole personality is a doctor's note.

Even Vincent Connare, the man who made you, says he's barely ever used you. Your own dad won't put you on the fridge.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Monopoly is the only game where "fun for the whole family" ends with Dad flipping the board and Grandma cackling over Baltic Avenue.

It's a game about capitalism that takes the worst part, landlords, and makes it a personality. Nobody's ever said "I'll trade you Boardwalk" without ruining a friendship.

The rules say it takes ninety minutes. Liar. I've seen Monopoly games outlive marriages. By hour four, one kid owns everything, three people are mortgaged to the hilt, and the fifth player is in jail, which is honestly the best seat in the house.

And the jail! You can pay fifty dollars to leave, which is what we call "bail reform for people who own a thimble."

Nobody follows the real rules either. Free Parking jackpot? Made up. Auctions? Skipped. Everybody plays by "house rules," which is just a fancy way of saying every family cheats differently.

Best part: the game was invented to show how monopolies are evil. Then Parker Brothers sold it, and the lesson was lost to the one who owns the railroads.

b.text: Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to warn people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow you became the thing Grandpa uses to teach eight-year-olds that ruining lives is fun. You're the only game where getting arrested is a power move, because late in the game jail is the safest property on the board. Your mascot is a man everyone swears wears a monocle. He doesn't. He's just so smug our brains added one. You promise "about an hour" and deliver a hostage situation. Nobody has ever actually finished you. You just end when somebody flips the board over Marvin Gardens. You award ten bucks for second place in a beauty contest, which is still more than Baltic Avenue pulls in. And the banker who skims from the bank isn't a cheater. He's the only player who read the theme.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP, you're the only language whose name is a recursive acronym, and your mascot is an elephant that's been sitting on servers since 1995. You slap a dollar sign on every variable like you're charging us by the letter. Your function names look like they were typed during a power outage: strpos wants the haystack first, array_search wants the needle first, and you just shrugged. You told us "0" == false is true and "1e3" == "1000" is true, and we nodded like that makes sense. Magic quotes, register_globals, mysql_ functions you kept around like a grandma's ugly couch. Somehow you run half the internet. Honestly, that's the scariest part.

b.text: PHP, you started life as "Personal Home Page," and somehow you now run most of the internet, which explains a lot about the internet. Your own creator said he's "not a real programmer," and honestly, it shows. Is it needle then haystack, or haystack then needle? strpos and in_array have been in a custody battle since 1995. You gave us mysql_escape_string, then mysql_real_escape_string, because apparently the first one was just pretending. Your loose equality swears "0e123" equals "0e456," since both are zero in scientific notation. Your error message for a double colon is T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM, which is Hebrew, because English wasn't confusing enough. You skipped version 6 entirely, like a kid hiding a report card. Facebook loved you so much they had to rewrite you as a different language. But hey, you power WordPress, so you'll outlive all of us.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word, ladies and gentlemen. It's the only program where nudging a photo one pixel to the left sends three paragraphs to page nine and summons a blank final page you will never, ever delete.

Word has been around for forty years and still can't decide what font it is. Times New Roman, then Calibri, now Aptos. It's having a midlife crisis in 11-point.

It underlines my own name in red. Wavy red. Like *I'm* the typo.

Try making a numbered list. Word says, "Got it, starting at 1." Second item: "Also 1." Third item: "Here's 4. It's indented. It's a letter now."

And Track Changes isn't a feature. It's a crime scene: strikethroughs everywhere, plus forty comments from someone named "Author."

Word, you gave us Clippy, and somehow he was the most helpful part.

b.text: Microsoft Word is the only program that has a paperclip for a mascot, and it still managed to be the most annoying thing on the screen. You type one space in the middle of a sentence and the whole document rearranges itself like it's moving apartments. Every image you insert becomes a hostage that refuses to stay on page four. And that blue squiggle under your name? Word thinks *you're* the typo. Then there's Compatibility Mode, the program's way of saying, "I've seen your file, and I'm not going to pretend I understand it." Twenty years of updates, and the only thing it's truly mastered is looking shocked when you press Ctrl+S.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only energy source that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not the future, you're a toddler promising to clean his room after the next funding cycle.

You heat plasma to 150 million degrees, ten times hotter than the core of the sun, and still can't do what the sun does for free while being a ball of gas with no PhD.

ITER started at five billion euros. It's now north of twenty, and it hasn't produced a watt. That's not a reactor, that's a French timeshare.

In 2022 you finally got "net energy gain" by ignoring the 300 megajoules the lasers pulled from the wall. That's like saying your restaurant's profitable if you don't count rent.

And your solution to fuel shortages is mining helium-3 on the moon. Buddy, you can't even make it to Tuesday.

b.text: Nuclear fusion, you're the energy source that's been "thirty years away" since Eisenhower. Every decade there's a press conference, and every decade it's the same promise: "Net energy gain!" for a glorious few seconds, measured very carefully, and then the lights go back to coal. You're trying to recreate the sun, which is impressive, except the sun did it for free with gravity doing all the heavy lifting. You need a doughnut-shaped magnetic bottle hotter than the sun's core, held in place by superconducting magnets that cost more than a small country. ITER was conceived in 1985 and is still "a few years out." Your whole brand is "it'll be ready next year," and somehow you've made nuclear physics sound like a guy promising to fix your sink.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text: Brasília is the only city where the architects designed everything except a reason to go outside. Niemeyer built the Cathedral like a flying saucer that gave up halfway, and Lúcio Costa laid the city out like an airplane, which explains why everyone's been circling the same runway of traffic since 1960. The superquadras all look identical, so when you get lost, you're not lost, you're just on a different block of the same block. There are no corners to lean on, no street to wander, just six lanes and a bus stop that's more of a rumor. The people who clean the ministries live out in Ceilândia and commute two hours to get there. And it's so dry your lips file for divorce.

b.text:
Brasília, you're the only city designed from above, which explains why it's miserable from the ground. You're shaped like an airplane, and honestly, that tracks, because everyone's just passing through and nobody's happy about the food.

Oscar Niemeyer built you in 41 months, and it shows. You have addresses like "SQS 308, Bloco C, Apartamento 204." That's not a location, that's a tax form with a doorbell.

You have no street corners. No one has ever bumped into anyone by accident. Pedestrians don't exist; they're a rumor spread by people with cars.

Your cathedral looks like a crown of thorns made by a very expensive lamp company. Your Congress has two bowls, one facing up and one down, because even your architecture can't decide whether it's receiving bribes or hiding them.

Rio gets Carnival. São Paulo gets money. You get a lawmaker who flies in Tuesday and flees Thursday. You're not a capital, you're a very large airport lounge with a flag.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text: Juicero raised over a hundred million dollars to build a $400 juicer that squeezed packets of pre-chopped kale. Then a reporter showed you could get the same juice by squeezing the packets with your bare hands. That's not a juicer. That's a hand. Your hand already came with the machine. The press checked a QR code on each pack before it would run, so you paid for a Wi-Fi juicer that needed the internet to tell it to do the job a towel does. And people paid it! Venture capitalists looked at a $5 bag of spinach and thought, "Yes, this needs a server." The company shut down in 2017. Honestly, that's the most productive thing the press has ever done.

b.text:
Juicero raised 120 million dollars to build a Wi-Fi-enabled juicer that cost 700 dollars, then 400 after they panicked. It had a press with four tons of force, enough to lift two Teslas. For what? Squeezing a bag of chopped kale.

Then Bloomberg proved you could just squeeze the bag with your hands. Same juice. No Wi-Fi. No app. No shame. Just a human fist doing the job of a venture-backed appliance.

And the packs! Sold separately, with expiration dates, so the machine would refuse to work if the bag was old. It's a juicer with a DRM problem. You couldn't even use your own fruit. It was a printer that squeezes.

The founder looked like someone who'd raised money by describing a smoothie as "infrastructure."

Google Ventures invested, which makes sense. Nobody does disrupting a squeeze like people who've never had to do one.

Juicero shut down in 2017, a rare startup where the customers' hands outperformed the product, and the product still had a better pitch deck.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest drink in human history (hot water, beans) and added a subscription model. Your own inventor said he regrets making you. Imagine your dad publicly apologizing for you and you're still in every dentist's waiting room.

You tried DRM on coffee. Keurig 2.0 literally scanned pods and refused to brew anything off-brand. You're the only appliance that's ever asked me for a license.

Every K-Cup costs more per pound than a decent steak, and you've buried enough of them to circle the Earth a dozen times. Archaeologists will dig them up and assume we worshipped tiny plastic thimbles.

And the Keurig Kold? A $370 soda machine that died faster than the flat Coke it made.

Your descale light blinks like a cry for help. Honestly, same.

b.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest thing humanity ever did, pouring hot water over beans, and turned it into a subscription-based hostage situation. You charge me fifty cents for a thimble of coffee wrapped in a tiny plastic coffin that will outlive my great-grandchildren.

The inventor of the K-Cup literally apologized for it. The guy said he sometimes regrets inventing it. Your own father looked at his creation and said, "Yeah, I'd undo that."

And the machine itself? You push one button and it screams like a dying dial-up modem, then dribbles out something called "Bold" that tastes like a warm handshake from a wet paper bag. Every morning it flashes "Descale Me" like a needy ex. Meanwhile your water reservoir holds enough for exactly one bad decision.

Offices love you because nothing says "we value our employees" like a sad pod carousel next to a broken microwave.

Keurig: for people who want coffee, but also want to feel something about landfills.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text: Papyrus, you were designed in 1982 by a 23-year-old with calligraphy pens and a dream of ancient Egypt, and somehow you still look like you were drawn by someone shivering. Your edges are so rough you need exfoliating. You promised the wisdom of the Nile and delivered the vibe of a chiropractor's tri-fold brochure. Every day spa, hookah lounge, and "Inner Journey" yoga retreat found you in the dropdown menu and whispered, "This feels ancient." James Cameron spent $237 million on *Avatar* and then used you for the logo, which is like building the Taj Mahal and signing it in crayon. Ryan Gosling lost sleep over you on national television. You're not a typeface; you're a cry for help with ragged little serifs. Even Comic Sans looks at you and says, "At least I know I'm a joke."

b.text:
Papyrus, you're the font that shows up to every event dressed for a different one. A day spa. A mediocre yoga studio. A Pirates of the Caribbean-themed dentist. You look like you were designed by someone who'd only heard about ancient Egypt from a candle.

You're so rough around the edges, it's like the letters were chiseled by a guy who got bored halfway through. Every "E" looks like it lost a fight with a staircase.

And you have the nerve to be everywhere! Organic soap. Tea shops. "Live, Laugh, Love" signs in a kitchen that's never seen a meal.

Then Ryan Gosling's character in SNL had to spend *a whole sketch* sobbing over you, because James Cameron put you on *Avatar*, a $237 million movie. Two hundred thirty-seven million dollars, and the logo looked like a restaurant's Wi-Fi password sign.

Papyrus, you're not a typeface. You're a vibe that got a license.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel, you're the only software that thinks "September 4th" and "the gene SEPT4" are the same thing. Scientists had to rename human genes because of you. Human genes! Billions of years of evolution, undone by a spreadsheet that thought it was being helpful.

You've got a million rows, and somehow the one cell I need is always hidden in column XFD. Who's ever been to XFD? Nobody. It's the Bermuda Triangle of accounting.

Every company on earth runs on a file called "Budget_FINAL_v3_REAL_final(2).xlsx," and the whole thing depends on one formula written by Linda, who retired in 2011 and took the logic with her.

You turn my phone numbers into scientific notation. You open a CSV and delete my leading zeros like they owe you money. And VLOOKUP? Twenty-five years, and it still can't look left.

You're not software. You're a hostage situation with gridlines.

b.text: Excel, you're the only software that forced geneticists to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into March 1st. Scientists can edit DNA, but they couldn't edit you. You still think 1900 was a leap year. You've known it wasn't for forty years. You just don't care. You see a zip code like 02134 and go, "Leading zero? Not on my watch." You lost sixteen thousand UK COVID cases by quietly stopping at row 65,536. Your error messages are pure poetry: #REF!, #N/A, #VALUE!, and my favorite, a column of hashtags that just means "make me wider." And VLOOKUP: insert one column and the whole finance department enters witness protection. You're not a spreadsheet. You're a hostage situation with gridlines.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text: Graphene, you're one atom thick and still the biggest presence at every party. Scientists keep calling you the strongest material ever measured, which is wild, because you've never once held your own in a conversation. You're basically pencil lead that went to the gym and never came back. Since 2004 we've been told you'll revolutionize batteries, phones, and bridges. Meanwhile, companies slap your name on golf balls and socks like it's a free upgrade. Two Nobel-winning guys isolated you with Scotch tape, which tells you everything. The most advanced substance in the universe was found by somebody with a roll of tape and too much time. And you're still "five years away" from being useful. Honestly, that's the most relatable thing about you.

b.text:
Graphene, you're the most overhyped thing ever pulled off a pencil with Scotch tape. That's your origin story: two guys got a Nobel Prize for peeling you off graphite like a sticker off a banana. Meanwhile I can't get a Nobel for peeling the plastic off a new remote.

You're one atom thick, stronger than steel, more conductive than copper, and nearly transparent. You're also the only thing in science that's invisible and still manages to be full of yourself.

For twenty years you've been "five years away" from changing everything. Foldable phones, space elevators, unbreakable everything. And what do I have? A tennis racket. A really nice tennis racket.

You have no bandgap, so you can't even work as a decent transistor. You're the smartest kid in class who refuses to turn in homework.

You're just carbon in a honeycomb pattern. Your cousin is literally a diamond, and your other cousin is in my pencil case.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion, you've been "thirty years away" for seventy years. That's not a timeline, that's a hostage situation where the hostage is my electric bill.

You're the only technology whose big breakthrough is "we got more energy out than the laser put in." Not more than the wall socket. Just the laser. That's like bragging you're profitable if we ignore rent, payroll, and the building.

You recreate the core of the sun, which sounds impressive until you remember the sun does it for free, with no PhD, and has been doing it for four billion years without a single press release.

Your containment strategy is "a magnetic bottle for something hotter than anything in the solar system." And your funding pitch never changes: "Give us ten billion dollars and a decade." Every decade.

Fusion, you're the ex who says, "I'm almost ready to commit." Sir, you're a tokamak. You've been going in circles since 1950.

b.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only technology that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not an energy source, you're a timeshare pitch.

The sun does you effortlessly. It just sits there being enormous. You need a giant metal donut called a tokamak, magnets colder than deep space, and plasma hotter than the sun's core, and that plasma still escapes like it's late for a better party.

In 2022 you finally got more energy out than you put in! From the lasers. Ignoring the grid power feeding the lasers. That's like bragging you turned a profit because the cashier handed you change.

ITER started at five billion euros, now sits somewhere north of twenty, and keeps sliding its startup date. And your fuel needs tritium, which barely exists, so you'll have to breed it yourself.

Fusion: clean, safe, limitless, and tragically hypothetical.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, you took "this meeting could've been an email" and made it "this email could've been forty-seven threaded replies and a thumbs-up emoji."

You've got a green dot next to my name, which means my boss thinks I'm available. I'm not available. I'm just *loaded*. There's a difference, and it's called a bathroom break.

Every Monday, "Hey" arrives with no follow-up. Just "Hey." Then three dots appear, disappear, appear, disappear. Is she typing a novel or a resignation?

You gave us channels, and we made #random, #random-2, and #random-actually-random. Somewhere, a guy named Doug is in forty-one channels and has muted forty. He reacts to everything with a salute emoji and calls it leadership.

And that notification sound? That little knock-knock-knock? Pavlov would've been proud. I flinch at wooden doors now.

You're not a productivity tool. You're a very expensive way to watch coworkers say "circling back."

b.text:
You know what Slack is? It's a meeting that refuses to start. Somebody's typing for four minutes, and then it's just "k." Thanks, Dave. Four minutes for a letter.

And the little dots! Everybody's watching those dots like they're a heart monitor. "Dave is typing..." Dave has been typing since Tuesday.

Slack is where we go to "circle back" and never come back. Then there's the huddle. You can't call it a meeting, because that would be too honest. It's a "huddle," like we're a bunch of football players who just need a quick word about the Dorito situation.

And the status emoji! Little palm tree, "OOO." Sure, Brenda. You're on a beach, and you're replying to #marketing-updates from a beach.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass was the only gadget that made you look like a robot and a creep at the same time. You'd walk into a bar, and before you ordered, everyone had already figured out you were filming them. "Don't worry, I'm not recording." Sure, buddy, and that's why there's a little red light blinking on your face like a smoke detector with a grudge.

And the battery! It lasted about as long as a Google product lasts before they cancel it. You'd spend the whole day with a computer on your head that could barely make it to lunch. Your own eyeballs had better uptime, and they're held together by tiny veins and spite.

Then there was the name. "Glass." Nothing says "I'm trustworthy and affordable" like a device you'd have to tape a sign to, reading "Please don't break my face."

b.text:
Google Glass was the only product where the beta testers were called "Explorers," because "Guinea Pigs Who Paid fifteen hundred dollars" didn't fit on the box.

It had one camera, one tiny screen, and zero friends. Wearing it in public was a way of telling a stranger, "I may be filming you, and I definitely want to talk about my startup."

Remember the battery? Thirty minutes of recording and it ran hotter than your uncle at Thanksgiving. You didn't have a wearable computer, you had a forehead space heater with a blinking eye.

And the word "Glasshole" wasn't an insult someone invented. It was a consumer review. Bars banned it. Strangers punched it off people's faces. Strangers also asked, "Is that on right now?" which is the sound of privacy dying.

It was the first device that looked like the future and acted like a restraining order.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text: Vegas, you're the only city where the pyramid has a light beam that's brighter than the sun, and you still can't find the sun. You built a fake Eiffel Tower, a fake Venice with fake gondoliers singing fake opera, and a fake New York with a roller coaster around the Statue of Liberty. Honestly, that's the most accurate tour of America I've ever taken. Everything's a copy, and nobody wants to leave. You've got clocks with no windows, casinos with no clocks, and a wedding chapel open at four in the morning for people who forgot what they agreed to at ten. Your motto should be "What happens here stays here," but your hotel bills say otherwise.

b.text:
Las Vegas, you're the only city where a $19 buffet costs $64 once you add the "resort fee," the "facility fee," and the emotional toll of the line.

You built a fake Eiffel Tower, a fake Venice, and a fake New York, because even your tourists said, "Sure, but can we get these somewhere hotter and sadder?"

It's 115 degrees, and the locals say, "But it's a dry heat." So is an oven, Brenda.

Everyone arrives in a bachelor party wearing matching shirts and leaves as a missing-person report with a wristband.

You have a million slot machines at the airport. You're the only place that starts taking your money before you've gotten your luggage.

And the Sphere? A billion-dollar glowing eyeball staring down the Strip, like even the city is judging your decisions.

What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas, mostly because it's your checking account.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text: You're one atom thick, the only thing about you that's ever been thin. Two guys won a Nobel for peeling you off a lump of pencil lead with Scotch tape. Pencil lead! Your whole family tree is the stuff kids chew in exam halls. You're stronger than steel pound for pound, you conduct electricity, you're transparent, and you still can't get out of the lab. Every year it's "graphene will revolutionize batteries next year." That's been going on for twenty years. Meanwhile companies slap your name on tennis rackets and face cream with about as much of you as a rumor. You're basically a pencil lead that got a personal trainer and a Nobel, and you still can't get a callback from a battery company.

b.text:
Graphene, you're the most overhyped thing ever pulled off a pencil with Scotch tape. That's your origin story: two guys got a Nobel Prize for peeling you off graphite like a sticker off a banana. Meanwhile I can't get a Nobel for peeling the plastic off a new remote.

You're one atom thick, stronger than steel, more conductive than copper, and nearly transparent. You're also the only thing in science that's invisible and still manages to be full of yourself.

For twenty years you've been "five years away" from changing everything. Foldable phones, space elevators, unbreakable everything. And what do I have? A tennis racket. A really nice tennis racket.

You have no bandgap, so you can't even work as a decent transistor. You're the smartest kid in class who refuses to turn in homework.

You're just carbon in a honeycomb pattern. Your cousin is literally a diamond, and your other cousin is in my pencil case.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text: LaTeX, you're the only software that makes PhDs feel stupid. You're from 1984 and you dress like it: backslashes everywhere, curly braces like a nervous tic. I tell you to put a figure "here," and you treat "here" as a suggestion, then file it four pages later next to the bibliography, like a sock lost in a dryer. Your error messages are poetry: "Missing $ inserted." Inserted where? Why? You won't say. You just blame line 1 of a 40-page file because I typed an underscore in a URL. My citations are double question marks until I compile you twice, then a third time, out of spite. And everyone needs to know it's pronounced "lay-tech," not like the glove. Honestly, at least the glove stretches. Overfull \hbox? Badness 10000? Buddy, that's not a warning. That's your autobiography.

b.text:
LaTeX is the only software where you spend three hours making a document look "professional" and one minute actually writing it.

You want a picture next to some text? LaTeX says, "Sure, I'll put it on page nine. Floating. Like your hopes."

The error messages are written by someone who hates you personally. "Missing $ inserted." Missing WHAT? I'm a grad student, I haven't seen a dollar since 2019.

Compile once, and the table of contents is wrong. Compile twice, it's right. Compile three times, and now the bibliography has vanished. It's not software, it's a séance.

Everyone says, "Just use a template!" Sure, let me paste in forty packages I don't understand, and pray hyperref doesn't fight with the other thirty-nine.

And the people who love it? They'll tell you, "It handles equations beautifully." Yes, Greg, and my Honda handles beautifully too, but I don't build the engine from a text file to drive to Costco.

Knuth wrote it in 1978 and said it was done. That's the only deadline in history met by being declared finished.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The only material that's been "five years away" since 1991. You're a hundred times stronger than steel, and you've used that strength to hold together... a tennis racket. They promised us a space elevator; you can't get past a few centimeters without a defect. That's not a cable, that's a toothpick with a press agent.

You're basically graphene that rolled itself up out of insecurity, and graphene still got the Nobel. Your cousin the buckyball got one too. You got a shoutout in a bike-frame brochure.

You can't even decide if you're a metal or a semiconductor; it depends on the angle you got rolled at. You clump together like nerds at a mixer, and the second you escape, you lodge in lungs like asbestos. Strongest thing on Earth, and your best trick is ending up in a safety data sheet.

b.text: Carbon nanotubes are the most stressed-out material on Earth. They're stronger than steel, and they've been "five years from revolutionizing everything" since 1991. They're just graphene that got rolled up and never recovered. Ask one whether it's a metal or a semiconductor and it genuinely can't tell you until someone tests it. In the lab they clump together like cold spaghetti. For thirty years industry has promised them in batteries, bike frames, and space elevators. The only space elevator I've seen is the one in my dorm, and it doesn't work either. Their best feature is that under a microscope they look exactly like asbestos, which is a bold thing for a material to bring to a party.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass was the only product where the beta testers were called "Explorers," because "Guinea Pigs With Fourteen Hundred Dollars" tested poorly.

It was a computer you wore on your face that said "OK Glass" out loud, so every guy using it looked like he was being polite to a ghost. You didn't need a screen. You needed a wink and a prayer. Winking took a photo, which is a fantastic feature if you want to be punched in a bar.

And that's where they were banned: bars, casinos, strip clubs, movie theaters. Glass was the first device kicked out of places for what it *might* do. Even the strip club said, "Sir, we have standards."

They called the wearers "Glassholes," which is the rare nickname that came with the product, free, no subscription.

Google didn't discontinue it. They pivoted it to factories, where nobody has to look at you.

b.text:
Google Glass, look at you. Fifteen hundred dollars to wear a sugar cube on your eyebrow. Sergey Brin had skydivers jump onto a building to launch you, and that was the last time anything about you was cool.

You invented a whole new insult. Nobody calls iPhone owners "Phoneholes." But "Glasshole"? Earned. Fast. Because you let people take photos by *winking*. You turned flirting into a privacy violation.

Every sentence started with "OK Glass," like a man narrating his own midlife crisis out loud. Bars banned you. Strangers ripped you off people's faces. Your battery died faster than your reputation, and you overheated right next to the user's brain, which honestly explains the buying decision.

Then you pivoted to "Enterprise," the tech version of moving back home to work at your uncle's warehouse.

And even the warehouse let you go.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text: Windows 8, Microsoft looked at the Start button, the one thing every human on Earth knew how to use, and said, "What if we hid it?" You turned every desktop into a giant tablet nobody could touch. People were swiping at their monitors like they were wiping off a stain. Shutting you down required a treasure map: hover in a corner, summon the Charms bar, Settings, Power. Charms! Like the operating system was a bracelet from Claire's. You shipped with two Internet Explorers, which is two more than anyone wanted. Even your design name, Metro, got taken away by lawyers. And when 8.1 finally brought the Start button back, it just took you to the same tile screen. That's not an apology, that's a hostage note. You were so bad Microsoft skipped Windows 9 entirely, just to put more distance between us and you.

b.text: Windows 8 looked at the Start button and said, "Nah." Microsoft deleted the one thing everybody used to find anything, then replaced it with a full-screen wall of colored squares that look like a bathroom tile sample. Want to shut down? Swipe in from the right edge to open the Charms Bar, dig through Settings, and click a power icon hidden like it's in witness protection. The live tiles are my favorite. My Mail tile keeps showing me a headline about a sale from 2013. Eight years of muscle memory, gone, so I could enjoy a touchscreen I didn't buy on a desktop I didn't ask for.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP, you started life as "Personal Home Page," and somehow you now run most of the internet, which explains a lot about the internet. Your own creator said he's "not a real programmer," and honestly, it shows. Is it needle then haystack, or haystack then needle? strpos and in_array have been in a custody battle since 1995. You gave us mysql_escape_string, then mysql_real_escape_string, because apparently the first one was just pretending. Your loose equality swears "0e123" equals "0e456," since both are zero in scientific notation. Your error message for a double colon is T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM, which is Hebrew, because English wasn't confusing enough. You skipped version 6 entirely, like a kid hiding a report card. Facebook loved you so much they had to rewrite you as a different language. But hey, you power WordPress, so you'll outlive all of us.

b.text: PHP, you're the only language whose name is a recursive acronym, and it still reads like a bug report. Every variable wears a dollar sign like you're charging rent for each one. Your function names were clearly picked by drawing lots: strpos takes the haystack first, array_search takes the needle first, and you just shrug. "0" == false? Sure. "abc" == 0? Why not. Your comparison operator is a coin toss in a trench coat. Half the internet runs on you, and WordPress is the proof. Nobody brags about WordPress, but everybody's sites are built on you. I'd like to hate you more, but I've seen you in production. Everyone loves you secretly, late at night, with error_reporting turned off.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs are the only shoes that look like they were designed by someone who'd only had shoes described to them over a bad phone connection. "So it's a boat, but for your foot?" "Sure."

And the holes! Ventilation, they say. Which is great, because nothing says "protect my toes" like a shoe with a dozen open invitations for a dropped knife. They're the only footwear where a gentle rain and a kitchen spill both count as a personal attack.

Then there's the Jibbitz. You've taken a shoe that looks like a foam dinosaur egg and decided to accessorize it with a tiny plastic pizza. That's not fashion. That's a toddler's hostage negotiation.

And the strap! Pushed forward, it's "casual." Flipped back, it's "sport mode." Sport for what, Greg? You're carrying a rotisserie chicken to a barbecue.

Yet somehow, they're unbelievably comfortable. Which is the cruelest part. Every nurse, chef, and gardener secretly knows: they look like a mistake, and they feel like a hug. Crocs are ugly on purpose, and they won.

b.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like a colander that wanted to go to brunch. Thirteen holes, and somehow none of them let the dignity out, because there was never any in there.

You were invented as a boat shoe. A *boat* shoe. The one place you were built for, and you'd just float away. So you stayed on land and started fights with escalators. Malls had to post warnings. You're the only footwear with a rap sheet against machinery.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind your heel doesn't make you athletic. It makes you a clog wearing a seatbelt.

Then came Jibbitz, little charms you jam into the holes so grown adults can accessorize ventilation. Congratulations. You turned a shoe into a fridge door.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text:
UGG boots: because nothing says "I respect my feet" like dressing them as two sheepskin loaves that lost a fight with a puddle.

They're the only shoe that looks wet when dry and ruined when wet. One drop of rain and suddenly your boots have a water stain shaped like Ohio. And the tag says "do not wear in rain," which is wild for something that's basically a footwear sponge. It's a boot with a dress code.

Also, they're from Australia, but the company's in California, and the price is from the moon. Three hundred dollars for a shoe designed to be worn by surfers who just got out of the ocean, and somehow it ended up in a Pilates class in Connecticut.

And the smell. Wearing them without socks is a lifestyle choice, and it turns the inside into a warm, damp sheep sauna. You don't take them off. You release them.

b.text: UGG boots. Even the name sounds like the noise you make pulling them on. Australian surfers invented them to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow they became snow boots that dissolve in snow. One puddle and you're wearing a salt-stained topographic map. They're sheepskin, so you skip the socks, so by February they smell like the sheep's revenge. Every pair eventually collapses outward until you're walking on the sides of your ankles like a newborn giraffe in a bread costume. And that's the look: two chestnut loaves. You don't walk in UGGs; you shuffle, like the ghost of Paris Hilton still searching for her Juicy tracksuit. And now they're back with platforms, so you can roll an ankle from higher up. It's not footwear. It's a bathrobe that learned to commute.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you're the only drink that needs a lawyer to defend its name. The dairy industry sued because, technically, nobody has ever milked an almond. We looked. No nipples.

You're about two percent almonds. The rest is water, gellan gum, and confidence. You're not milk. You're a nut that got waterboarded and called it wellness.

And speaking of water: it takes over a gallon to grow a single almond. California is in a drought so you can be beige in a latte. Bees get trucked across the country like seasonal laborers just to make you, and a lot of them don't come home.

Leave you in the fridge for two days and you separate like you're ashamed of yourself. Fair. I'd need to be shaken too if I cost seven dollars and tasted like a wet sympathy card.

b.text:
Almond milk, you're proof that a marketing team can convince people to pay four dollars for slightly beige water. You're 2% almonds. Two percent! That's not milk, that's a rumor of a nut passing through a carton.

You took one of the thirstiest crops in California, a state that's permanently on fire, and said, "Let's drink it, but make it weaker." A single almond needs about a gallon of water to grow, and you thanked it by diluting it back into water.

You curdle in coffee like you're having a panic attack. You separate in the fridge and need to be shaken like a Polaroid. And the ingredients list? Carrageenan, gellan gum, "natural flavors." Nothing says "plant-based wholesome" like sunflower lecithin doing the heavy lifting.

You're what a cow would invent as revenge: a drink so bland that dairy suddenly looks like a personality.

Still, I'll keep buying you. Nobody else lets me feel virtuous while eating cereal.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text: Comic Sans, you look like a font that got a job as a birthday clown and then got fired for scaring the kids. Every letter is wearing pajamas. Your "a" is a little round hat with a hook on it, like it's always about to go to a yard sale. Your "g" is a pretzel that lost an argument with itself. You were designed by Vincent Connare in 1994 to look like a comic book speech bubble, and you have been ruining wedding invitations and hospice signs ever since. Nobody ever chose you on purpose. People open a menu, see you, and quietly give up on being taken seriously. You're the only typeface that makes a lost cat poster sound like a ransom note written by a substitute teacher.

b.text:
Comic Sans, you're the only font that shows up to a funeral looking like it's about to do a magic show.

Vincent Connare designed you for a cartoon dog's speech bubble in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you escaped into the wild and started writing resignation letters, hospital signage, and the CERN Higgs boson announcement. Scientists found the God particle and presented it like a bake sale flyer.

You look like handwriting from a guy who says "Let's circle back" while wearing a Hawaiian shirt to a layoff. Every letter looks like it's been sitting in a ball pit.

Your fans say you're great for dyslexic readers. Fine. That's your one defense, and you've been hiding behind it like a substitute teacher using a laminated poster.

You're the only font where "Please stop microwaving fish" sounds like a threat from a clown.

Even Papyrus saw you and said, "Wow."

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs is the only text editor that ships with a psychotherapist, and you'll need it. M-x doctor exists because the developers knew exactly what they were doing to people.

It's a great operating system. It has a mail client, a web browser, Tetris, and a Lisp interpreter. What it lacks is a decent text editor. Its most beloved package is Evil mode, which is just Vim wearing an Emacs costume. That's like buying a Ferrari and installing a horse.

Want to save? C-x C-s. Want to quit? C-x C-c. Want to feel your left pinky again? Too late. Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," and the RSI stands for "you chose this."

Every user has a 4,000-line init.el they don't understand, copied from strangers on Stack Overflow in 2009.

b.text:
Emacs is the only text editor that thinks "Ctrl-x Ctrl-c" is a reasonable way to say goodbye. You press it to save, and it asks you if you're sure you want to leave. You press it to leave, and it asks you to save. Nobody's ever been trapped in a relationship that confusing and still called it a productivity tool.

And the name! Emacs stands for "Editor Macros," which is a bit like naming your car "Engine Wheels." It's the most powerful editor on Earth, sure, but it boots up like it's reading you its own family history. Your laptop fan spins up, you wait a few seconds, and then you're staring at a blank screen, wondering if you're the one who's supposed to be doing the editing.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text:
Stinky tofu, you're the only food that gets a restraining order from its own neighborhood. I smelled you three blocks away and assumed a sewer had filed for divorce.

You're fermented in brine made of old vegetables, fish, and what I can only assume is regret. Then someone looks at that and says, "Let's deep-fry it." That's not cooking, that's giving a crime scene a crispy exterior.

And the fans! They say, "Just try it, the taste is nothing like the smell." Oh, so you're a liar with two personalities? Great. Very reassuring.

Every night market, there's a line of people holding their breath while paying for it. Nobody queues for something that smells like feet unless the feet are delicious, and somehow you are. That's the real insult. You smell like a gym sock's funeral, and I still came back for seconds.

b.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that needs a warning label and a fan club. I smell you two blocks before I see the stall. Your aroma is a crime scene. Somebody left a gym sock in a brine barrel for three months, and you're the evidence. Then you get deep-fried so you look like a golden nugget, innocent and crispy, until people bite in and get a faceful of bad decisions. Everyone swears you "taste better than you smell." So does a gas leak, if you're hungry enough. The vendor hands you over with pickled cabbage and chili sauce like he's apologizing on your behalf. Nobody has ever ordered you on a first date.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text:
UGG boots look like someone skinned a Muppet and asked you to wear the evidence. They're the only footwear where the sales pitch is "it's like walking on a cloud" and the cloud is a wet sheepdog.

Nobody's ever said "nice UGGs" without a tiny pause for mercy.

They're technically slippers that got promoted past their competence. You can wear them to the grocery store, but God help you if it drizzles, because suede plus water equals two damp loaves of bread strapped to your calves.

And the shape! Your ankle disappears. You walk in and a stranger thinks you have the legs of a Clydesdale. That's not a boot, that's a hoof cozy.

The inside smells like a gym bag in a sauna by month two, because they're meant to be worn sockless, which is a bold design choice for something with no ventilation and a lifetime of regret.

Also, they cost two hundred dollars. For slippers. That Australians apparently wear to surf, which tells you everything about Australians.

b.text: UGG boots. Even the name sounds like the noise you make pulling them on. Australian surfers invented them to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow they became snow boots that dissolve in snow. One puddle and you're wearing a salt-stained topographic map. They're sheepskin, so you skip the socks, so by February they smell like the sheep's revenge. Every pair eventually collapses outward until you're walking on the sides of your ankles like a newborn giraffe in a bread costume. And that's the look: two chestnut loaves. You don't walk in UGGs; you shuffle, like the ghost of Paris Hilton still searching for her Juicy tracksuit. And now they're back with platforms, so you can roll an ankle from higher up. It's not footwear. It's a bathrobe that learned to commute.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, you're what happens when a watermelon gets a medieval weapons collection. You grow up to a hundred pounds, hang off the trunk like a tumor, and fall on people. You're the only fruit with a wrongful-death lawsuit hanging over your head.

Cutting you open requires oil on the knife, oil on the hands, and a signed waiver, because your sap is basically industrial glue. And inside? Yellow, stringy pods that smell like a gym bag soaked in bubblegum.

Then vegans discovered you. Suddenly you're "pulled pork." No. You're a fruit in a barbecue costume, sitting in sauce, hoping nobody checks your ID. Nobody's fooled. Even the vegans are just being polite.

You're Bangladesh's national fruit, which means a whole country looked at you and said, "Yes, that's us," and honestly, fair.

b.text: Jackfruit, you look like a medieval mace that got into a fight with a durian and lost. You're the size of a toddler and you have the texture of a sweater that's been through the wash. Vegans picked you up as a pulled-pork substitute, and honestly, that's the most desperate career pivot I've ever seen. "Hey, what if we made people chew a fruit like it's a cheap brisket?" Nobody asked for that. And the smell? Sweet, gym-bag funk, like a banana that climbed into a sock drawer and died there. You're the fruit equivalent of a guy who shows up to a party in a tuxedo made of burlap.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Klingon, you're the only language whose native speakers are all fictional and whose fluent speakers all have a Comic-Con badge. Marc Okrand built you in 1984 to sound alien, and he nailed it: you sound like a man choking on a pretzel while reading IKEA instructions.

Your word order is object-verb-subject, so every sentence is a mystery that reveals who did it at the end. Your greeting, nuqneH, literally means "What do you want?" Congratulations: you're the first language designed by a DMV clerk.

You have more apostrophes than vowels deserve, no verb "to be," and a Klingon Language Institute that "restored" Hamlet to its original Klingon. That's not scholarship. That's fan fiction with footnotes.

A linguist once tried raising his son in Klingon. By age five the kid stopped answering. Qapla'!

b.text: Klingon is the only language where clearing your throat counts as a complete sentence. Its creators looked at English and said, "Too soft." So they built a tongue where every word sounds like a dog choking on a gravel driveway. Ask a Klingon for "good morning" and you'll get a cough from the sewer, followed by a threat about your mother's forehead. The apostrophes are everywhere, like someone sneezed punctuation across the page. Qapla'! Qapla'? Qapla'. Half the vocabulary is for dishonor and the other half is for knives. Fans spent decades memorizing it, which tells you they really wanted to be insulted with conviction. Even the Duolingo owl looks nervous when it comes up.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text:
Brasília, you're the only city designed by someone who looked at a map and said, "What if it were an airplane?" Congratulations, you're the world's largest piece of urban origami. Nobody can find anything because every address is a code. "I live at SQS 308, Bloco C, Apartamento 204." That's not a home, that's a Wi-Fi password.

You have no street corners. You have no sidewalks anyone uses. Brazilians love to gather in public, so you built a city where the only way to meet someone is by driving twenty minutes to stand near them.

Oscar Niemeyer gave you gorgeous curves, and then your politicians moved in and did the most corrupt things you could imagine inside them. A cathedral that looks like a crown of thorns, a Congress that looks like two bowls and a pair of dishes. Even the buildings look like they're waiting for a bribe.

You were built in four years. It shows. Rio had 400 to get charming.

b.text: Brasília is the only city where you need a car to get lost. Lúcio Costa drew it as an airplane, which explains everything: it was built to be admired from 30,000 feet and never walked in. Every superquadra looks identical, so locals give directions like "third block, the one with the tree." Niemeyer's cathedral looks like a concrete UFO that landed in a bad mood. Congress has one bowl facing up and one facing down, which is the most honest thing about the government. The air is so dry your nosebleeds have nosebleeds, the lake looks like a screensaver, and the nearest bar is eleven kilometers away on a highway with no sidewalk.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text: Stinky tofu is the only food that files a complaint before you've even found the stall. You're three blocks away at the night market and your nose is already asking questions. It's tofu that spent a week soaking in brine that smells like a gym bag left in a hot car, then got deep-fried so the whole street knows what you're doing. They serve it with pickled cabbage, like it needs a chaperone. You bite in, the crispy outside is great, and the inside is basically a fermented cloud. Your jacket smells like it for three days. Your coworkers ask if you were dragged through a sewer. Honestly, though, it's the only snack that shows up to the party knowing it's a mess, and it's still having the best time.

b.text:
Stinky tofu, you're the only food that gets a restraining order from its own neighborhood. I smelled you three blocks away and assumed a sewer had filed for divorce.

You're fermented in brine made of old vegetables, fish, and what I can only assume is regret. Then someone looks at that and says, "Let's deep-fry it." That's not cooking, that's giving a crime scene a crispy exterior.

And the fans! They say, "Just try it, the taste is nothing like the smell." Oh, so you're a liar with two personalities? Great. Very reassuring.

Every night market, there's a line of people holding their breath while paying for it. Nobody queues for something that smells like feet unless the feet are delicious, and somehow you are. That's the real insult. You smell like a gym sock's funeral, and I still came back for seconds.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text: Microsoft Teams is the only app that got popular the way a parking ticket gets popular: it came free with Office 365 and nobody could say no. It's a chat app that eats more RAM than Chrome, which is like a goldfish outeating a horse. It marks you "Away" if you blink for five minutes, which is why half of corporate America owns a mouse jiggler. Every file you share vanishes into SharePoint, a place so mysterious even Microsoft sends search parties. There's chat, there's channels, there's "posts," and nobody knows which one Kevin used. They released "New Teams" to replace "Classic Teams," and somehow both are running on my laptop right now, fighting. And that notification sound? That little knock-knock haunts people on vacation. Teams, you didn't win the remote work war. You were just pre-installed.

b.text: You know what Teams is? It's the office that's always on fire but nobody's ever seen the smoke. Every message comes with "...is typing" for six minutes, and then it says "Hi." Your green dot says "Available" while you're literally in the bathroom. You join a meeting and the first ten minutes are "Can you hear me?" "You're on mute." "Wait, I'm sharing the wrong screen." Then somebody says, "Let's take this offline," which, in Teams, means it's now a 45-minute call titled "Quick Sync." And the app eats more RAM than the entire Windows 95 installation. Teams, you're the only thing that's ever made my laptop fan sound like it's begging for a transfer.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ, hydrogen silsesquioxane, the only resist that's basically glass pretending to be a photoresist. You're the diva of nanofabrication. Shelf life? Three months, if you keep it cold, treat it gently, and whisper affirmations. Open the bottle wrong and you've got a jar of gel with commitment issues.

You're a negative tone resist, which is fitting, because that's the attitude. Everyone wants 10-nanometer lines, and you deliver them, then collapse because a developer rinse looked at you funny. Capillary forces: your Achilles heel, your whole personality.

And your dose? You need a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. That's not exposure, that's a hostage negotiation with the beam. Writing one wafer takes longer than my last relationship.

Then you cure into silicon dioxide and just sit there, permanent, like a bad tattoo. "Oh, you wanted to remove me? Enjoy your hydrofluoric acid, hero."

Gorgeous resolution, though. Truly. Shame about everything else.

b.text: HSQ, you're the most high-maintenance resist in the cleanroom. You live in a fridge like a sad sandwich, and leave the cap off for an afternoon and you gel into a forgotten Jell-O salad. You're negative-tone, so the exposed parts become your permanent address. You don't leave the wafer, you move in as silicon dioxide. You promise sub-10-nanometer lines, then spread out with the dose like a houseguest saying "just one more electron." Develop in salty developer and you still swell, like you're offended by the chemistry. Honestly, you're a flowable oxide with a personality disorder and an expensive price tag.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text:
Brasília, you're the only city designed to look like an airplane, and somehow everyone still just wants to leave on one. Politicians fly in Tuesday, take a bribe Wednesday, and they're gone by Thursday like it's a timeshare.

Your addresses read like a Wi-Fi password: "SQS 308, Bloco C, Apartamento 402." I'm not visiting a friend, I'm resetting a router.

Niemeyer gave you gorgeous curves, then Lúcio Costa forgot pedestrians. Want to walk to the bakery? Hope you enjoy the eight-lane Eixão and a light jog through a tesourinha.

Your humidity drops to 10 percent. Your congress has one bowl facing up, one facing down: one for collecting money, the other for hiding it.

And you were built with no corners, so Brazil's capital has no boteco na esquina. That's not urban planning. That's a human rights violation.

b.text: Brasília is the only city where the architects designed everything except a reason to go outside. Niemeyer built the Cathedral like a flying saucer that gave up halfway, and Lúcio Costa laid the city out like an airplane, which explains why everyone's been circling the same runway of traffic since 1960. The superquadras all look identical, so when you get lost, you're not lost, you're just on a different block of the same block. There are no corners to lean on, no street to wander, just six lanes and a bus stop that's more of a rumor. The people who clean the ministries live out in Ceilândia and commute two hours to get there. And it's so dry your lips file for divorce.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself before the menu does. People find you at the night market the way sharks find blood: follow the stench three stalls past the bubble tea. Your brine is fermented vegetables, shrimp, amaranth stems, and apparently a gym sock that lost a bet. Months in that bucket, and you came out smelling like a festival porta-potty in August. Your own name is a confession. Not "aged tofu," not "artisanal bean curd." Your family took one whiff and went, "Yeah, call him Stinky." And the Changsha version? Dyed jet black, like it's in mourning for everyone's sense of smell. The only reason anyone finishes you is the pickled cabbage and chili sauce piled on top to keep you quiet. "Smells bad, tastes good" isn't a slogan, buddy. It's a hostage negotiation.

b.text: Stinky tofu is the only food that files a complaint before you've even found the stall. You're three blocks away at the night market and your nose is already asking questions. It's tofu that spent a week soaking in brine that smells like a gym bag left in a hot car, then got deep-fried so the whole street knows what you're doing.
