They serve it with pickled cabbage, like it needs a chaperone. You bite in, the crispy outside is great, and the inside is basically a fermented cloud. Your jacket smells like it for three days. Your coworkers ask if you were dragged through a sewer. Honestly, though, it's the only snack that shows up to the party knowing it's a mess, and it's still having the best time.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word, you've had forty years to learn one thing: how to let me move a picture one millimeter without three paragraphs fleeing to page nine. You don't wrap text, you take hostages.

You underline my own name in red like I'm the typo. You turn my grocery list into a numbered legal document I can't escape. I hit Enter once and suddenly I'm in a style called "Heading 7" that I've never met.

And Track Changes? That's not editing, that's a crime scene where everyone bled in a different color.

You fired Clippy, the only one of you who ever admitted I looked like I needed help.

And every crash, you hand me "Document1 (Recovered)" like a cat dropping a dead bird on the porch: proud, useless, and somehow from 2 PM yesterday.

b.text:
Microsoft Word, you're the only software where pressing Enter once can rearrange my entire document like a Rubik's cube in an earthquake.

You've got a paperclip-shaped trauma in your past, and honestly, he was the only one who ever tried to help. Now it's just you, auto-correcting "ducking" into things I definitely didn't mean to say to my boss.

Bullet points? You take them personally. I press Tab, you indent. I press Backspace, you un-indent, delete the bullet, and change the font to Comic Sans out of spite.

I tried to put one picture on page two. Page six now has a single sentence and a sense of dread.

And the green squiggly line? Judgmental. The red one? Fine, I misspelled "necessary." But you underlined my own name like I'm the one who's wrong.

You've been around since 1983 and still can't tell me why Save As has seven different locations. Ribbon? More like a ribbon of confusion. Truly, you're a masterpiece of formatting I never asked for.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text: Esperanto is the language of hope, which is a polite way of saying nobody has needed it since 1887. Dr. Zamenhof built it so everyone on Earth could talk to each other, and it worked beautifully, provided everyone was a Polish optometrist who already spoke German. Every noun ends in -o and every adjective in -a, like the language is labeling its own furniture. Then it split over a rival called Ido, because Esperantists love a universal language so much they needed a second one to be mad at. The conferences are the best part: a thousand people who learned the same made-up language, hugging in a Bulgarian youth hostel, recognizing each other by little green star pins. Then they fly home, and the nearest person they can talk to is the one who only speaks English.

b.text:
Esperanto. In 1887, Dr. Zamenhof, an eye doctor, looked at a world divided by language and decided what it really needed was six letters wearing tiny hats. Nothing says "universal" like ĉ, ĝ, and ŭ, characters no keyboard on Earth can type, so your fans write "cx" and pretend that's fine.

Your name literally means "one who hopes." A hundred and thirty years later: still hoping.

You're the only language where "bad" is just "un-good." *Malbona.* That's not grammar, that's Orwell's Newspeak with a beard. Every noun ends in -o, so you sound like Italian being sight-read by a robot.

You promised world peace and delivered a convention full of men wearing green star pins. Your biggest movie stars William Shatner. And you have about a thousand native speakers, which isn't a language community. It's a cul-de-sac.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle where the tailpipe emission is water and the owners are still crying more than the car. The Toyota Mirai loses value faster than a Hindenburg loses altitude. Used ones sell for less than the free fuel card Toyota bundled with them, a card you can't use because the station's been "temporarily offline" since 2022.

You've got a 10,000-PSI tank of the universe's most abundant element, and somehow it's the scarcest thing in California. Filling up costs thirty-six bucks a kilo, and most of that hydrogen is made from natural gas, so congratulations: you bought a gas car with extra steps and a guilt-free bumper sticker.

Hydrogen's been "ten years away" for thirty years. Even fusion's embarrassed for you, and fusion is the same element with better excuses.

b.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars are the only vehicles where the fuel is the most abundant element in the universe and somehow still costs more per mile than caviar. Sixteen dollars a kilogram, and you can only buy it at one station in California, which is closed. For "maintenance."

Their big selling point is that the only emissions are water. Fantastic. Most of the hydrogen is made from natural gas, so it's a car that cries clean tears after being force-fed fossil fuels in a basement.

Toyota calls its model the Mirai. That's Japanese for "future." Accurate, because that's when you'll find a pump.

Owners are a special breed. They drive 40 minutes to refuel, then call it freedom. Their car is basically a Prius that got a PhD, went into massive debt, and still can't get a job.

And the tank? Pressurized to 10,000 psi. So it's a zero-emissions vehicle with a tiny, polite bomb in the trunk.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text:
Stinky tofu, you're the only food that needs a restraining order from its own neighborhood. I smelled you three blocks away and assumed a sewer had filed for divorce.

You're fermented in brine made of old vegetables, fish, and, as far as I can tell, regret. Then you're deep-fried, because apparently someone looked at a crime scene and said, "Needs crunch."

Everyone says, "Just try it, it tastes better than it smells!" That's not a compliment. That's what people say about a divorce lawyer.

And the fans! They stand in line at the night market, glowing with pride, like they've survived something. Sir, you're eating a gym sock in a pickle costume, and the pickle is also a gym sock.

Still, I'll admit it: the chili sauce is incredible. Which is exactly what you'd say about a hostage situation with good snacks.

b.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself before the menu does. People find you at the night market the way sharks find blood: follow the stench three stalls past the bubble tea. Your brine is fermented vegetables, shrimp, amaranth stems, and apparently a gym sock that lost a bet. Months in that bucket, and you came out smelling like a festival porta-potty in August. Your own name is a confession. Not "aged tofu," not "artisanal bean curd." Your family took one whiff and went, "Yeah, call him Stinky." And the Changsha version? Dyed jet black, like it's in mourning for everyone's sense of smell. The only reason anyone finishes you is the pickled cabbage and chili sauce piled on top to keep you quiet. "Smells bad, tastes good" isn't a slogan, buddy. It's a hostage negotiation.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim is the only software where the tutorial is "how to leave." Millions of developers have rebooted their computers rather than figure out :wq. Stack Overflow has a question about quitting Vim with over a million views. That's not a text editor, that's a hostage situation.

It has modes. Normal mode, which is where nothing normal happens. Insert mode, where you finally type, like a toddler allowed one cookie. Visual mode, command mode, replace mode. It's a text editor with more personalities than a Reddit thread.

Vim users say "once you learn it, you'll be so fast." Sir, you spent six years learning to delete a word. You've saved four seconds and told everyone at dinner about it.

And the pride! They've memorized hjkl so they never move their hands, yet they've moved their entire personality into a .vimrc file that's 900 lines long, breaks every update, and was last understood in 2014.

b.text: Vim is the only program that greets you with "How do I quit?" as its opening line. You open it by accident, and now you're trapped in a text editor that thinks typing is a crime. You press "i" to insert text, which is hilarious, because nobody who uses Vim has ever inserted anything into their life. Then you hit Escape, and suddenly you're in command mode, where the letters you type don't write anything. They do things. "d" deletes. "x" deletes. "dd" deletes the whole line, and you did not ask for that. Vim doesn't have a save button; it has ":wq," which sounds like a sneeze in a library. Vim users say it's efficient. Sure, if your idea of efficiency is memorizing a secret language just to change one word.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text: Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle powered by the most abundant element in the universe that still can't find a gas station. California has about fifty pumps, and half of them are "temporarily offline," which is hydrogen for "go home." Its one emission is water, so it's technically the cleanest car on Earth, as long as you don't ask where the hydrogen came from. Spoiler: natural gas. It's a fossil fuel car in a witness protection program. Toyota gave Mirai buyers fifteen grand in free fuel, which sounds generous until you realize that at thirty-six bucks a kilo it covers roughly a year of driving, and the car loses that much value on the drive home. You're sitting on a tank pressurized to 10,000 psi to go three hundred miles. Even the Hindenburg would say, "Maybe just get a Tesla."

b.text: Hydrogen fuel-cell cars are the most ambitious thing ever built to avoid a charging cable. Think about it: the whole plan is to take electricity, use it to split water into hydrogen, compress that hydrogen to ten thousand PSI, drive it across the country in a tank that's basically a rocket casing, then turn it back into electricity. That's not a green car, that's a magic trick with a chaperone. And the hydrogen stations? Good luck. You'll find one in California, and it's closed for "maintenance," which I'm pretty sure means someone realized they were hydrogen stations and got nervous. Meanwhile, my Tesla just asks if I'd like to plug in at home, like a normal car.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's little brother who moved into a browser tab and called it "the cloud." Your whole personality is twelve people's colored cursors circling the same cell like sharks while an Anonymous Capybara silently watches everyone's mistakes. You say "Saving..." with the confidence of a man who has absolutely not saved. Your IMPORTRANGE makes me click "Allow access" like I'm asking my own spreadsheet for permission to see my own spreadsheet. Half my cells just say "Loading..." forever, like a Victorian ghost waiting for a letter. And you'll let anyone sort one column without the others, then shrug while every customer gets someone else's phone number. Version history is your only real feature: it's just a timeline of who ruined everything at 2 a.m. And yes, Gemini can explain my #REF! error now. Great. It's still there.

b.text:
Google Sheets is Excel's cousin who showed up to the family reunion and insisted everyone edit the same potluck dish at once. You open a file called "Untitled spreadsheet" and somehow it's the most permanent document your company owns. It's been "Budget FINAL v3 (Copy of Copy)" since 2017.

The best part is the real-time collaboration. Nothing says teamwork like watching an Anonymous Capybara delete your entire column while you're mid-formula. And you can't even blame Greg, because Greg is a capybara.

IMPORTRANGE is the only function that makes you beg a spreadsheet for permission to read your own spreadsheet. "Allow access." I'm sorry, I made both of these!

Then you hit a hundred thousand rows and the whole thing goes "Working..." That's not a loading message, that's a hostage video.

And QUERY? It's SQL for people who were told SQL was too scary, then handed something scarier.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: Macau, you're the only place where a fake Venice has a fake gondola and the gondolas still lose money. You're about ten Central Parks wide, so your casinos can't spread out and have to go up, like a city that got lost looking for space. Your cathedral is just a facade, a church that gave up on the church part. Your egg tarts are the best thing you've ever exported, and you did it by accident, like a bank robbery that ends with pastries. The bridge to Hong Kong took the better part of a decade, which is the most patience you've ever shown anyone. Nobody comes to Macau to see Macau. They come to lose money, and they leave with an egg tart and a receipt.

b.text:
Macau, you're what happens when Portugal and Las Vegas have a one-night stand and nobody wants to claim the kid. You have a Venetian with fake canals, a fake sky, and a gondolier singing "O Sole Mio" in a Chinese province. Not even Italy does that to itself.

You make more gambling money than Vegas by a factor of several, which means you're basically a very successful casino with a cobblestone problem.

Your egg tarts are better than Portugal's, and everyone knows it, including Portugal, who's still mad. Your Eiffel Tower is half-size, your Parisian is half-French, and your Grand Lisboa looks like a golden lotus ate a disco ball.

You're 12 square miles and somehow have traffic jams at the border from people who lost everything and still want to come back. That's not tourism. That's an abusive relationship with a buffet.

Even your ruins are just a facade. St. Paul's is literally one wall. You couldn't keep the church, but you kept the slot machines.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs isn't a text editor, it's an operating system that's still waiting for a decent editor to come along. It has a built-in psychiatrist, a Tetris clone, and a mail client, but somehow no sane keybindings.

Ctrl-x Ctrl-s to save? That's not a shortcut, that's a hand injury with a lawsuit pending. Emacs users call it "Emacs pinky" like it's a badge of honor. Sir, that's a repetitive strain injury from a Lisp interpreter.

And the config file! Fifteen years of init.el, a thousand lines of copy-pasted snippets from a 2009 blog post, and nobody knows what half of it does. But if you delete it, you die.

Every Emacs user says, "It's infinitely customizable!" Yes, and you've spent four hundred hours customizing it so you can finally write a grocery list.

Meanwhile, the Vim guys are laughing, and honestly? They've earned it.

b.text:
Emacs is the only text editor that ships with a psychotherapist, and you'll need it. M-x doctor exists because the developers knew exactly what they were doing to people.

It's a great operating system. It has a mail client, a web browser, Tetris, and a Lisp interpreter. What it lacks is a decent text editor. Its most beloved package is Evil mode, which is just Vim wearing an Emacs costume. That's like buying a Ferrari and installing a horse.

Want to save? C-x C-s. Want to quit? C-x C-c. Want to feel your left pinky again? Too late. Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," and the RSI stands for "you chose this."

Every user has a 4,000-line init.el they don't understand, copied from strangers on Stack Overflow in 2009.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen, the only food that files a noise complaint with your nose. It's a noodle soup made from river snails, which is already a bold choice, then fermented sour bamboo shoots join in, and suddenly your apartment smells like a swamp got a divorce.

You open one packet and the whole building knows your business. Neighbors don't ask "what's cooking?" They ask "is someone okay?"

Liuzhou people say it's delicious. Sure, and a skunk says the same about its perfume.

And the cruelty is that it's actually amazing. Rice noodles, chili oil, peanuts, tofu skin, that sour-funky-spicy punch. You'll eat it and swear you'll never do it again, then smell your own hoodie three days later and whisper, "Same time next week?"

It's the only dish where the leftover smell outlasts the leftovers, and your elevator has stopped making eye contact with you.

b.text: Luosifen, you're the only dish named after a snail that contains zero snails. They simmer the snails for hours, then throw them out, like a dad who shows up for the paternity test and leaves. Your real star is suan sun, fermented bamboo shoot that smells like a gym sock studied abroad in Liuzhou and came back with opinions. Fans say, "It smells terrible but tastes amazing." So does every scam. You turned instant noodles into a hazmat event: one packet opened in a dorm and three floors file noise complaints, because that smell is *loud*. Couriers wrap you in four bags like evidence. And you come with seven sachets: chili oil, peanuts, tofu skin, wood ear, the bamboo. It's IKEA furniture that makes the neighbors move out. Liuzhou didn't invent a soup. It invented Stockholm syndrome with chili oil.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text: PMMA, you're the world's most expensive Post-it note. Someone spins you onto a silicon wafer at four thousand RPM, bakes you on a hotplate like a sad pizza, then fires electrons at you for six hours, and your big move is to dissolve in MIBK. That's your whole personality. You're a positive resist, which in your case means you only become positive once you've been destroyed. Hit you with a plasma etch and you're gone in ten seconds, so the entire process has to be built around your fragility. You're the lab's most high-maintenance divorcee. But the resolution is incredible, I'll give you that. Sub-20 nanometers, folks. Shame you can't survive a Tuesday.

b.text:
PMMA, you're just plexiglass with a god complex. You're the same stuff as a hamster cage, and somehow you've got a cleanroom full of PhDs treating you like a sacred text.

You're a positive resist, which is cute, because nothing about your attitude is. We hit you with a billion electrons and you just go, "Fine, I'll break up a little." Chain scission? That's not a lithography mechanism, that's your whole personality.

And the sensitivity! You need like a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. My phone charges faster than you expose. Meanwhile I'm sitting at the e-beam writing a pattern for nine hours so you can give me a lopsided blob.

Then comes development. Isopropanol and MIBK, because you're too good for water. Overdevelop by ten seconds and your lines collapse like a dropped soufflé.

And you're sold in anisole, so every wafer smells like a licorice factory had an affair with a solvent cabinet.

Great resolution, though. Ten nanometers. Shame about everything else.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, and you couldn't even make it to the branches. You just hang off the trunk like a drunk uncle clinging to a lamppost.

You weigh eighty pounds. That's not a fruit, that's a fourth grader in a bumpy green costume. People cut you open and need cooking oil on their hands and knives, because your insides are basically rubber cement. You're the only produce that requires a solvent.

And vegans love you because when you're young, you taste like absolutely nothing. Your big career move is pretending to be pulled pork. Your whole identity is "not bad if you drown me in barbecue sauce."

Then you ripen and smell like Juicy Fruit gum fermenting in a gym bag.

You're the national fruit of Bangladesh, and you still find time to fall on people's heads.

b.text: Jackfruit, you look like a medieval mace that got into a fight with a durian and lost. You're the size of a toddler and you have the texture of a sweater that's been through the wash. Vegans picked you up as a pulled-pork substitute, and honestly, that's the most desperate career pivot I've ever seen. "Hey, what if we made people chew a fruit like it's a cheap brisket?" Nobody asked for that. And the smell? Sweet, gym-bag funk, like a banana that climbed into a sock drawer and died there. You're the fruit equivalent of a guy who shows up to a party in a tuxedo made of burlap.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text: Risk is the only board game where the goal is world domination and somehow everyone ends up furious about it. You spend four hours conquering continents while your friend sits there holding Australia, which is basically a fortress with one door and a view of nothing. Kamchatka is the most dangerous place on Earth. It's one territory, and it eats two of your tiny plastic armies every time someone looks at it. Then there's the dice. Three red against two blue, and the fate of the entire planet comes down to a guy yelling "I'm rolling for Siberia!" every game ends the same way: Greg, who swore he'd only be a few minutes, owns Asia, a grudge, and your Alaska.

b.text:
Risk is the only game where you can conquer the entire planet and still lose to the guy who's been hiding in Australia since 7 p.m. Four territories, one entrance, and he just sits there like a guy at a party who won't leave the snack table.

This game has a map drawn by someone who heard about geography once, at a bar. Kamchatka borders Alaska. Ukraine is the size of Brazil. Yakutsk and Irkutsk are vital military objectives, and nobody at the table can find them on a real map.

The rules say the defender wins ties, which is the most realistic thing about it, because nobody actually finishes Risk. They just quit at 2 a.m. when someone's dad flips the board over Siberia.

And the pieces? Little plastic cannons and horses. Napoleonic warfare, global scale, and the whole thing is decided by rolling a 6 against your cousin Greg.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole that got a fake ID. You order it, and the waiter says, "That'll be forty-five minutes." Forty-five minutes! I've had relationships bake faster. They put the sauce on top because if you saw what was underneath first, you'd leave. A solid sheet of sausage, like somebody paved a driveway with a patty. Two pounds of mozzarella hiding under a tomato quilt. It's not a slice, it's a core sample. You need a knife, a fork, and a structural engineer. The crust is buttery cornmeal, so it's a pie crust, so congratulations, you're eating dessert with ambitions. And here's the best part: actual Chicagoans don't even eat it. They eat tavern-style thin crust cut in squares. Deep-dish is just the city's way of keeping tourists too full to walk to Wrigley.

b.text: Deep-dish pizza is the only food that makes you wait forty-five minutes for a meal and then spends the next three hours in your stomach like a sofa somebody moved in without asking. It's not a pizza. It's a casserole that got a library card. You bite in and the cheese pulls up like it's auditioning for a Lysol commercial, and the sauce sits on top like it lost a bet with the crust. Chicagoans will tell you it's "a whole different thing," which is what people say when they're hoping you won't check the ingredients. Nobody in Chicago has ever finished a whole deep dish alone. They just stare at the last slice in the box like it owes them money, then eat it cold at 1 a.m. over the sink, which is the only honest way to eat it.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen, you're the only dish that arrives before the delivery guy does. You're named after river snails, yet nobody has ever found one in the bowl. You boiled them for hours, took their soul, and threw out the bodies. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up.

And that smell? Fermented bamboo shoots that died, got buried, and came back for revenge. Someone opens a packet in Liuzhou and a guy in Guilin checks his shoes. College dorms banned you like a space heater. Neighbors call the gas company.

Your fans swear, "It smells terrible but tastes amazing." Buddy, that's what everyone says about their toxic ex.

Peanuts, crispy tofu skin, wood ear, pickled beans, a slick of chili oil... that's not garnish, that's witness protection for flavor.

And now you come instant. Congratulations: a biohazard with a seasoning packet.

b.text: Luosifen is the only food that needs a smell permit. You open the packet in a dorm and the RA shows up asking who's microwaving a crime scene. The broth is snails simmered with pickled bamboo shoots that have been fermenting since before your grandmother was born, and those shoots smell like a gym sock that got promoted to management. People say, "It's delicious once you get past the smell." Sure, and a stink bomb is delicious once you get past the explosion. Then there's the packet of chili oil, which the label calls "optional" in the same tone a hostage-taker uses. Eat it on the subway and the whole car suddenly finds the ceiling fascinating. That's not a meal. That's a restraining order with chopsticks.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans, you were literally designed for a talking dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the only part of that project that didn't die with dignity. Vincent Connare made you in 1994 for cartoon speech bubbles, and you heard that and thought, "Tombstones. Legal notices. Resignation letters."

Dan Gilbert wrote his furious LeBron James letter in you, and that's why nobody remembers being scared. CERN announced the Higgs boson, the most important physics discovery in fifty years, in you, and the entire scientific community went, "Did a third grader find God?"

People defend you because you help some readers with dyslexia, which is true and lovely, and also the only time you've ever been used responsibly.

You're not a font. You're a bake sale flyer that got tenure. Even Papyrus looks at you and says, "Wow, okay, tone it down."

b.text:
Comic Sans, you're the only font that shows up to a funeral looking like it's about to do a magic show for toddlers.

You were designed for a cartoon dog's speech bubble in Microsoft Bob, and somehow ended up on cancer-ward notices, divorce settlements, and "Please Do Not Microwave Fish" signs in the office kitchen. Every message you carry sounds like it was written by a substitute teacher who's given up.

Designers don't hate you. Designers have a support group for you. CERN announced the Higgs boson in you, and physicists everywhere suddenly wondered if the universe was a bake sale flyer.

Your letters look like they were drawn by someone holding the marker in their left hand while riding a bus. The lowercase "a" is the only part of you that's trying.

And yet you're still installed on every computer on Earth, like a clown that nobody invited but nobody can evict.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text: Esperanto is the language of hope, which is a polite way of saying nobody has needed it since 1887. Dr. Zamenhof built it so everyone on Earth could talk to each other, and it worked beautifully, provided everyone was a Polish optometrist who already spoke German. Every noun ends in -o and every adjective in -a, like the language is labeling its own furniture. Then it split over a rival called Ido, because Esperantists love a universal language so much they needed a second one to be mad at. The conferences are the best part: a thousand people who learned the same made-up language, hugging in a Bulgarian youth hostel, recognizing each other by little green star pins. Then they fly home, and the nearest person they can talk to is the one who only speaks English.

b.text:
Esperanto: the language invented to unite humanity, and after 130 years, its greatest achievement is a tiny group of people who all met at the same convention.

Zamenhof wanted world peace. He got a language where the most common sentence is "Hello, are you also here for the Esperanto thing?"

Everything is regular. Every noun ends in O. Every adjective ends in A. It's the only language designed like a filing cabinet, and it sounds like Italian and Polish got stuck in an elevator and decided to name the kids.

And the accusative! They made a language to be easy, then kept the accusative. Fine. It's a hobby.

"Native speakers" of Esperanto number about a thousand, which is what we call "the children of enthusiasts who never got a vote."

The national anthem is "La Espero." The national sport is correcting your pronunciation of "ĉ." And the only country that really speaks it is the Facebook group.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text: Esperanto was built in 1887 so everyone on Earth could finally talk to each other, and 140 years later the main conversation is still, "Oh, you speak it too? Where are you from?" "Also Esperanto." Silence. Every speaker is one hug away from running out of things to say. The grammar is famously logical: every noun ends in -o, every adjective in -a, and every direct object gets an -n, which is the only place this language ever shows emotion. It promised to be easy to learn, and it kept that promise the way a diet pill does. You master it in a month, then spend the rest of your life waiting for a stranger to answer you back.

b.text:
Esperanto. In 1887, Dr. Zamenhof, an eye doctor, looked at a world divided by language and decided what it really needed was six letters wearing tiny hats. Nothing says "universal" like ĉ, ĝ, and ŭ, characters no keyboard on Earth can type, so your fans write "cx" and pretend that's fine.

Your name literally means "one who hopes." A hundred and thirty years later: still hoping.

You're the only language where "bad" is just "un-good." *Malbona.* That's not grammar, that's Orwell's Newspeak with a beard. Every noun ends in -o, so you sound like Italian being sight-read by a robot.

You promised world peace and delivered a convention full of men wearing green star pins. Your biggest movie stars William Shatner. And you have about a thousand native speakers, which isn't a language community. It's a cul-de-sac.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text: Hydrogen fuel-cell cars are the most ambitious thing ever built to avoid a charging cable. Think about it: the whole plan is to take electricity, use it to split water into hydrogen, compress that hydrogen to ten thousand PSI, drive it across the country in a tank that's basically a rocket casing, then turn it back into electricity. That's not a green car, that's a magic trick with a chaperone. And the hydrogen stations? Good luck. You'll find one in California, and it's closed for "maintenance," which I'm pretty sure means someone realized they were hydrogen stations and got nervous. Meanwhile, my Tesla just asks if I'd like to plug in at home, like a normal car.

b.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle where the tailpipe emission is water and the owners are still crying more than the car. The Toyota Mirai loses value faster than a Hindenburg loses altitude. Used ones sell for less than the free fuel card Toyota bundled with them, a card you can't use because the station's been "temporarily offline" since 2022.

You've got a 10,000-PSI tank of the universe's most abundant element, and somehow it's the scarcest thing in California. Filling up costs thirty-six bucks a kilo, and most of that hydrogen is made from natural gas, so congratulations: you bought a gas car with extra steps and a guilt-free bumper sticker.

Hydrogen's been "ten years away" for thirty years. Even fusion's embarrassed for you, and fusion is the same element with better excuses.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel, you're the only software that thinks "September 4th" and "the gene SEPT4" are the same thing. Scientists renamed human genes because of you. Genetics bent the knee to a spreadsheet.

You've got a million rows, and somehow the one cell I need is always showing ########. That's not an error, that's you yelling at me.

Every company on earth runs on one file called "Final_v7_REAL_final_JOHN'S EDIT.xlsx" that only Linda understands, and Linda's on vacation. Her formula is a nested IF statement so long it has its own zip code.

You can do VLOOKUP, XLOOKUP, INDEX-MATCH, and you still make me fight for it like a hostage negotiation.

And you're a "data tool" that auto-formats my phone number into scientific notation. Congratulations, 5.55E+09, I've never felt more called.

Also, Clippy left. You stayed. That tells us who was actually the problem.

b.text: Excel, you're the only software that forced geneticists to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into March 1st. Scientists can edit DNA, but they couldn't edit you. You still think 1900 was a leap year. You've known it wasn't for forty years. You just don't care. You see a zip code like 02134 and go, "Leading zero? Not on my watch." You lost sixteen thousand UK COVID cases by quietly stopping at row 65,536. Your error messages are pure poetry: #REF!, #N/A, #VALUE!, and my favorite, a column of hashtags that just means "make me wider." And VLOOKUP: insert one column and the whole finance department enters witness protection. You're not a spreadsheet. You're a hostage situation with gridlines.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ, hydrogen silsesquioxane, the only resist that's basically glass pretending to be a photoresist. You're a negative-tone resist that turns into silicon dioxide. So after all my work, my pattern isn't a mask, it's a permanent tenant.

Your shelf life is a joke. You gel in the bottle if I look at you wrong. Open a fresh one, two weeks later it's Jell-O with commitment issues. Keep it in the fridge, and it's still aging like milk in a sauna.

And the development! Sixty nanometer lines, beautiful, then TMAH hits and they collapse like a Jenga tower. Sure, you can do sub-10 nanometer features, but only if I sacrifice a goat, run at 1000 microcoulombs per square centimeter, and sit there for nine hours while the beam writes a rectangle.

Contrast? Terrible. Sensitivity? Worse. Stripping you off? Hydrofluoric acid. You're the ex who can only be removed by something that dissolves bones.

b.text:
HSQ, ladies and gentlemen: the only resist with sub-10-nanometer resolution and the personality of a sourdough starter. You buy it, you refrigerate it, and it *still* starts gelling in the bottle like it's got somewhere better to be. Shelf life measured in "eh, few months, maybe."

And slow? HSQ needs a dose so high the e-beam tool files for overtime. Your PMMA friends finished their write and went home; you're still exposing alignment marks.

Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you want contrast, *salty* developer. Yes, this resist literally needs you to add salt. Even Gordon Ramsay thinks that's a lot.

But the real red flag? Once it's exposed, it turns into glass. Permanently. You want it gone? Hydrofluoric acid. That's not a resist, that's a relationship you can only leave with a hazmat suit.

Still, gorgeous lines. Shame they collapse when they dry.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza is what happens when Italy and a Dole pineapple can have a custody battle and nobody wins. It was invented in Canada, by a Greek guy, and named after a pineapple brand. That's not a pizza, that's a bad customs form.

Every other topping says "I'm here to be savory." Pineapple shows up like, "I'm also dessert. And I'm leaking." Now your ham is swimming in a warm fruit puddle, and the crust has the structural integrity of a wet napkin.

And the ham! Not even good ham. Sad, pink, circle ham, the kind that's been in a sandwich bag since a 2006 field trip.

Nobody orders it for themselves. It's always "I'll just get a Hawaiian for the table," said by the one guy who also says "I'm not really a *pizza* person."

Hawaii has never claimed it. Hawaii has been in court trying to get away from it.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Pineapple on bread with ham. Somebody looked at a perfectly good pizza and said, "You know what this needs? Fruit that's been sitting in a can since the Eisenhower administration." And everybody just nodded. Nobody stopped him.

And the ham! It's not even Hawaiian ham. It's Canadian bacon wearing a cheap Hawaiian shirt. It's the pizza version of a guy at a wedding who says, "I'm not a dancer," and then dances anyway.

The pineapple's the real problem, though. It's sweet, it's wet, and it's trying so hard to be a tropical vacation. You bite in, and it's like a sprinkler went off in your mouth, and the cheese just gives up and slides onto your shirt.

Honestly, I respect it. Hawaiian pizza is the only food that makes ham and fruit feel like they're both lost.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies, look at you. Half bear, half beanbag, all retirement plan that never paid out. An entire generation of parents bought you instead of index funds. Somewhere a man is still storing Princess, the purple Diana bear, in a climate-controlled unit, waiting for the market to "recover." Buddy, the market recovered. It just didn't take you with it.

Your most valuable feature was a heart-shaped paper tag. People bought plastic tag protectors. For the tag. That's like buying a phone case for your receipt.

And every tag had a little poem rhyming "bear" with "care." Hallmark called that lazy.

A Las Vegas couple had to divide you on a courtroom floor during their divorce, one at a time. That's the most anyone has wanted you since 1999: only to make sure their ex didn't get you.

Ty Warner got a billion dollars. You got plastic pellets.

b.text: My mom bought forty Beanie Babies in 1998 because a man on the news said they'd pay for my college. They didn't. They're in a bin in her garage, each one still wrapped in its plastic tag protector like a tiny hostage. Ty Warner pulled off the greatest con in toy history. He retired a bear, announced it like a celebrity death, and watched grown adults panic-buy the thing they were supposed to play with. You weren't allowed to touch it, though. Touching meant fingerprints, and fingerprints meant it was worth nothing. So you didn't get a teddy bear. You got a bag of plastic pellets with a face, sitting on a shelf, guarded like the Crown Jewels.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion, you've been "thirty years away" for seventy years. That's not a timeline, that's a hostage situation where the hostage is my electric bill.

You're the only technology whose big breakthrough is "we got more energy out than the laser put in." Not more than the wall socket. Just the laser. That's like bragging you're profitable if we ignore rent, payroll, and the building.

You recreate the core of the sun, which sounds impressive until you remember the sun does it for free, with no PhD, and has been doing it for four billion years without a single press release.

Your containment strategy is "a magnetic bottle for something hotter than anything in the solar system." And your funding pitch never changes: "Give us ten billion dollars and a decade." Every decade.

Fusion, you're the ex who says, "I'm almost ready to commit." Sir, you're a tokamak. You've been going in circles since 1950.

b.text: Nuclear fusion, you're the energy source that's been "thirty years away" since Eisenhower. Every decade there's a press conference, and every decade it's the same promise: "Net energy gain!" for a glorious few seconds, measured very carefully, and then the lights go back to coal. You're trying to recreate the sun, which is impressive, except the sun did it for free with gravity doing all the heavy lifting. You need a doughnut-shaped magnetic bottle hotter than the sun's core, held in place by superconducting magnets that cost more than a small country. ITER was conceived in 1985 and is still "a few years out." Your whole brand is "it'll be ready next year," and somehow you've made nuclear physics sound like a guy promising to fix your sink.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text:
Apple Vision Pro, you cost $3,499 and still need a battery on a cord like a 1996 Walkman. Two hours of charge? That's not spatial computing, that's a matinee. Wear glasses? Zeiss inserts, extra. Apple saw you squinting and smelled revenue.

And EyeSight! A front screen showing your eyes so people feel connected. Nothing says "I'm present" like blurry cartoon eyeballs trapped behind ski-goggle glass. Your Persona avatar looks like a hostage video directed by a ghost.

You promised the future, and Netflix wouldn't even make you an app. You strap over a pound to dads' faces so they can record "spatial memories" of birthdays they watched through a screen.

Apple said you'd never see the world the same way. True. Now it's through a $3,500 face fridge.

b.text:
The Apple Vision Pro costs $3,499, which is a bold price for something that gives you a headache and a neck injury in the same sitting. It weighs over a pound, so after twenty minutes you're not experiencing spatial computing, you're experiencing the chiropractic kind.

Apple said it would change how we see the world, then gave it a two-hour battery on a cable you have to keep in your pocket, like an oxygen tank for your delusions.

EyeSight shows your eyes on the front, so everyone around you can watch a haunted aquarium version of your face. Your FaceTime Persona looks like a hostage video made by a very polite ghost.

The best part is the control scheme: you look at something and pinch your fingers, like you're being quietly condescending to your own living room.

It's a $3,500 ski goggle that lets you watch a movie alone. Congratulations, you've invented a very expensive way to ignore your family.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text:
Risk is the only game where you spend four hours conquering the world and then lose it because your brother-in-law rolled three sixes in Kamchatka.

"Strategy game," the box says. Sure. Strategy is a dice cup deciding your destiny while you scream at a plastic cannon.

Nobody finishes Risk. It doesn't end, it just gets abandoned, like Napoleon's Russian campaign, except Napoleon had better snacks. Someone eventually says "I have to be up early," which is Risk for "I've been dead since Australia."

Speaking of Australia: everyone knows the whole game is just "hold Australia and pretend you're smart." One entrance, four territories, a bonus. It's the gated community of continents. Meanwhile Asia has twelve territories and a bonus of seven, which is the board's way of saying "go ahead, try it, I'll see you at hour three."

And the alliances! Friendships don't die in Risk. They get negotiated away for a single card.

Happy 60 years, Risk. You've ended more family dinners than politics.

b.text: Risk, you're the only game where "world domination" takes longer than actual world domination. Genghis Khan conquered Asia faster than my cousin conquered Ukraine, and my cousin had six armies and a dream. Your map looks like it was drawn from a description of Earth overheard on a bus. Kamchatka borders Alaska? Irkutsk and Yakutsk get more real estate than most of Africa? You taught a generation that the winning strategy is hiding in Australia like a coward and waiting for everyone else to bleed out over Siam. The defender wins ties, which explains the forty armies I lost trying to get through one guy in Egypt. And one plastic cannon is worth ten soldiers? Finally, accurate military budgeting. Five hours in, two players left, nobody's had fun since the first card set. That's not a board game, Risk. That's a hostage situation.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole that got a fake ID. You order it, and the waiter says, "That'll be forty-five minutes." Forty-five minutes! I've had relationships bake faster. They put the sauce on top because if you saw what was underneath first, you'd leave. A solid sheet of sausage, like somebody paved a driveway with a patty. Two pounds of mozzarella hiding under a tomato quilt. It's not a slice, it's a core sample. You need a knife, a fork, and a structural engineer. The crust is buttery cornmeal, so it's a pie crust, so congratulations, you're eating dessert with ambitions. And here's the best part: actual Chicagoans don't even eat it. They eat tavern-style thin crust cut in squares. Deep-dish is just the city's way of keeping tourists too full to walk to Wrigley.

b.text:
Chicago deep-dish isn't pizza, it's a casserole with an identity crisis. You order it, and they say, "That'll be 45 minutes." Forty-five minutes! For bread! I've seen people give birth faster, and the baby came out less cooked.

Then it arrives, and it's built upside down. Cheese on the bottom, sauce on top. That's not a recipe, that's a structural failure. It's a pizza that fell down the stairs and everyone decided to call it tradition.

You get one slice, and it requires a spatula, a fork, a knife, and a signed waiver. Your first bite is molten cheese lava. Your second bite is a tomato landslide. By the third, you're lying on the booth like you've been shot by a lasagna.

And Chicagoans defend this! "It's the real pizza." Sir, you eat soup with a crust and call New Yorkers wrong. That's a pie chart with a cardiologist.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: Google Sheets, you're the spreadsheet that waits until I've typed three paragraphs of data before you tell me I've been editing a "view-only" copy this whole time. You're the only app where "Saving..." becomes a lifestyle. Your formulas are so fragile that one missing comma turns my budget into a column of #REF! like I'm a hacker's ransom note. And VLOOKUP? You make me hunt for the exact column index like it's a secret handshake. Every time I try to add a chart, you act like I asked you to build a cathedral. Sure, you're free, and you're everywhere, but that's just what happens when your whole personality is "well, at least it's not Excel."

b.text:
Google Sheets is Excel's cousin who showed up to the family reunion and insisted everyone edit the same potluck dish at once. You open a file called "Untitled spreadsheet" and somehow it's the most permanent document your company owns. It's been "Budget FINAL v3 (Copy of Copy)" since 2017.

The best part is the real-time collaboration. Nothing says teamwork like watching an Anonymous Capybara delete your entire column while you're mid-formula. And you can't even blame Greg, because Greg is a capybara.

IMPORTRANGE is the only function that makes you beg a spreadsheet for permission to read your own spreadsheet. "Allow access." I'm sorry, I made both of these!

Then you hit a hundred thousand rows and the whole thing goes "Working..." That's not a loading message, that's a hostage video.

And QUERY? It's SQL for people who were told SQL was too scary, then handed something scarier.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text: Monopoly is the only board game where the goal is to bankrupt your friends, and the game itself bankrupts the friendship. It's been around ninety years and nobody has ever finished it. Your cousin Dave, who owns Boardwalk and two hotels, isn't a real estate mogul. He's a man who spent three hours shorting the bank. And the banker! The one person trusted with the stack of pink fives, and every single time he "accidentally" gives himself two hundred bucks. Free Parking is a lie. Nobody has ever landed there and collected the jackpot. The little top hat has been in the same spot since 1935 and still gets no respect. Let's be honest: the only property you can afford is Baltic Avenue, and that's because the game put it there to make you feel bad.

b.text:
Monopoly is the only game where "fun for the whole family" ends with Dad flipping the board and Grandma cackling over Baltic Avenue.

It's a game about capitalism that takes the worst part, landlords, and makes it a personality. Nobody's ever said "I'll trade you Boardwalk" without ruining a friendship.

The rules say it takes ninety minutes. Liar. I've seen Monopoly games outlive marriages. By hour four, one kid owns everything, three people are mortgaged to the hilt, and the fifth player is in jail, which is honestly the best seat in the house.

And the jail! You can pay fifty dollars to leave, which is what we call "bail reform for people who own a thimble."

Nobody follows the real rules either. Free Parking jackpot? Made up. Auctions? Skipped. Everybody plays by "house rules," which is just a fancy way of saying every family cheats differently.

Best part: the game was invented to show how monopolies are evil. Then Parker Brothers sold it, and the lesson was lost to the one who owns the railroads.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text:
LaTeX is the only software where you spend three hours making a document look "professional" and one minute actually writing it.

You want a picture next to some text? LaTeX says, "Sure, I'll put it on page nine. Floating. Like your hopes."

The error messages are written by someone who hates you personally. "Missing $ inserted." Missing WHAT? I'm a grad student, I haven't seen a dollar since 2019.

Compile once, and the table of contents is wrong. Compile twice, it's right. Compile three times, and now the bibliography has vanished. It's not software, it's a séance.

Everyone says, "Just use a template!" Sure, let me paste in forty packages I don't understand, and pray hyperref doesn't fight with the other thirty-nine.

And the people who love it? They'll tell you, "It handles equations beautifully." Yes, Greg, and my Honda handles beautifully too, but I don't build the engine from a text file to drive to Costco.

Knuth wrote it in 1978 and said it was done. That's the only deadline in history met by being declared finished.

b.text: LaTeX, you're the only program that makes a document look like a Pulitzer and then sends you a nine-hundred-line error log because you forgot a bracket. "Missing $ inserted." Where? Everywhere. Your error messages read like a ransom note. And the figures! I put a picture in, and it floats off to page nine like it has somewhere better to be. I write to say "here," and you say, "Mm, I'll be the judge of that." Centering a table takes three hours, a booktabs package, and a prayer. Then I compile, get a PDF so beautiful I almost forgive you, and you hit me with "Overfull \hbox, badness 10000." Badness. You named it. You're the only typesetter honest enough to put its own insult in the log.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text: Monopoly is the only board game where the goal is to bankrupt your friends, and the game itself bankrupts the friendship. It's been around ninety years and nobody has ever finished it. Your cousin Dave, who owns Boardwalk and two hotels, isn't a real estate mogul. He's a man who spent three hours shorting the bank. And the banker! The one person trusted with the stack of pink fives, and every single time he "accidentally" gives himself two hundred bucks. Free Parking is a lie. Nobody has ever landed there and collected the jackpot. The little top hat has been in the same spot since 1935 and still gets no respect. Let's be honest: the only property you can afford is Baltic Avenue, and that's because the game put it there to make you feel bad.

b.text:
Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow the lesson everyone learned was "buy Park Place." Then Parker Brothers bought you from a guy who basically stole you, which is the most on-brand origin story in history.

You're the only game where "second prize in a beauty contest" counts as income and jail is solved with a coupon. Your mascot looks like he foreclosed on the Pringles guy, and half of America swears he wears a monocle. He doesn't. We just assumed a man that rich would be hiding something.

Nobody has ever finished you. Games don't end; your cousin just flips the board over Marvin Gardens, which you misspelled, by the way. It's Marven. Even your real estate is a scam.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text:
Papyrus, you're the font that shows up to every event dressed for a different one. A day spa. A mediocre yoga studio. A Pirates of the Caribbean-themed dentist. You look like you were designed by someone who'd only heard about ancient Egypt from a candle.

You're so rough around the edges, it's like the letters were chiseled by a guy who got bored halfway through. Every "E" looks like it lost a fight with a staircase.

And you have the nerve to be everywhere! Organic soap. Tea shops. "Live, Laugh, Love" signs in a kitchen that's never seen a meal.

Then Ryan Gosling's character in SNL had to spend *a whole sketch* sobbing over you, because James Cameron put you on *Avatar*, a $237 million movie. Two hundred thirty-seven million dollars, and the logo looked like a restaurant's Wi-Fi password sign.

Papyrus, you're not a typeface. You're a vibe that got a license.

b.text: Papyrus, you're a font that has never once been near Egypt. You look like a yoga studio's "Namaste" sign left out in the Sedona sun until it got fuzzy around the edges. Every letter has the texture of a wet paper bag someone tried to iron. You're the go-to for the wooden plaque in a crystal shop, right next to the "Live Laugh Love" sign and the incense nobody's bought since 2009. James Cameron used you for Avatar, and somehow an entire alien moon ended up looking like a smoothie menu. People who pick you think they're being mysterious. You're not mysterious. You're a tiki bar's menu that's sorry it opened, printed on the same paper you're named after, which is to say, nobody's real writing surface.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text: Klingon, you're a language built by one linguist, Marc Okrand, specifically to sound alien and hostile, and somehow you still ended up sounding like a man choking on a Dorito. Your word order is object-verb-subject, so even your sentences walk in backwards to hide their face. You don't even have a word for "hello." Your greeting is "nuqneH," "what do you want?" You're the only language that greets people like a DMV clerk. Your apostrophes are glottal stops, your capital Q is a different letter from lowercase q, and "tlh" isn't a sound, it's a hairball. You translated Hamlet and claimed it was the original. Buddy, the most popular thing ever said in you is "Qapla'," and the people saying it are at a Marriott in Burbank.

b.text:
Klingon, a language designed by a linguist so warriors could sound like they're clearing their throats at you in anger. Every sentence sounds like a cat being strangled by a Scrabble bag of Q's and apostrophes.

You have a word for "disruptor" but not "please." Because apparently when a Klingon wants something, he doesn't ask. He just reorders his grammar until the object is afraid.

Your verbs go at the end, so by the time someone finishes threatening me, I've already left for lunch. "I will crush your skull and... " Hold on, I'm still waiting for the verb. Honestly, that's the most polite thing about you.

And Okrand wrote an entire dictionary, yet there's no word for "sorry" because "it's a weakness." Meanwhile, there's a proverb about revenge being a dish best served cold. You're a language with an open-mic problem and a fridge full of leftovers.

Fluent speakers: about twelve. All of them are named Gary, and all of them are using you to ask for the check.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text: UGG boots. The only footwear named after a review. Australian surfers made these to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow America decided the ocean was the mall. They're sheepskin, which means a sheep died so you could wear a slipper to the DMV. One puddle and they're covered in salt lines like a topographic map of everywhere you regret going. Zero arch support, so after two weeks your heel caves sideways and you're walking on the boot's ankle like it owes you money. You wear them barefoot, so by February they smell like a wet lamb's final wish. They're as waterproof as a muffin. Oprah put them on her Favorite Things list. She's since moved on. Twenty years later they're back with platform soles, proving even a mistake wants to be taller.

b.text: Ugg boots are the only shoe that looks like a sheep ate a pair of slippers and then apologized by giving them back. You didn't buy Uggs, you bought a pair of carpet remnants that wandered into a shoe store and got lucky. Nobody's ever run in them. Nobody's ever been chased in them. They're designed for one thing: standing in a Target parking lot holding an oat milk latte like you just finished a marathon. And the name! "Ugg." That's not a brand, that's a noise you make when you step on a Lego in the dark. Somewhere, a shearling farmer is looking at these and saying, "I didn't raise sheep for this, I raised them to be respected." Stay warm, I guess. You look like a hot dog that gave up.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Let's start with the name, because that's the first lie. You were invented in Ontario. By a Greek guy. In 1962. You're Hawaiian the way a tiki bar in Ohio is Hawaiian. The only tropical thing about you is the can your pineapple came out of.

And that pineapple: warm, wet, weeping syrup into the crust until the middle slice folds like a lawn chair. Pineapple contains an enzyme that breaks down protein, so the fruit is literally trying to digest the ham. Even your toppings hate each other.

And the ham! Not prosciutto, not even pepperoni. Just pale pink squares that look like they were chiseled out of a deli's floor tile.

You're the pizza people order to seem quirky. "I'm so random!" No, Kevin. That's a fruit cup that fell on a pizza, and nobody cleaned it up.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Pineapple on bread with ham. Somebody looked at a perfectly good pizza and said, "You know what this needs? Fruit that's been sitting in a can since the Eisenhower administration." And everybody just nodded. Nobody stopped him.

And the ham! It's not even Hawaiian ham. It's Canadian bacon wearing a cheap Hawaiian shirt. It's the pizza version of a guy at a wedding who says, "I'm not a dancer," and then dances anyway.

The pineapple's the real problem, though. It's sweet, it's wet, and it's trying so hard to be a tropical vacation. You bite in, and it's like a sprinkler went off in your mouth, and the cheese just gives up and slides onto your shirt.

Honestly, I respect it. Hawaiian pizza is the only food that makes ham and fruit feel like they're both lost.

So they built a tongue where every word sounds like a dog choking on a gravel driveway. Ask a Klingon for "good morning" and you'll get a cough from the sewer, followed by a threat about your mother's forehead. The apostrophes are everywhere, like someone sneezed punctuation across the page. Qapla'! Qapla'? Qapla'. Half the vocabulary is for dishonor and the other half is for knives. Fans spent decades memorizing it, which tells you they really wanted to be insulted with conviction. Even the Duolingo owl looks nervous when it comes up.

b.text:
Klingon, a language designed by a linguist so warriors could sound like they're clearing their throats at you in anger. Every sentence sounds like a cat being strangled by a Scrabble bag of Q's and apostrophes.

You have a word for "disruptor" but not "please." Because apparently when a Klingon wants something, he doesn't ask. He just reorders his grammar until the object is afraid.

Your verbs go at the end, so by the time someone finishes threatening me, I've already left for lunch. "I will crush your skull and... " Hold on, I'm still waiting for the verb. Honestly, that's the most polite thing about you.
