facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text: Nuclear fusion is the energy source that's always thirty years away, and it has been since your grandpa was in diapers. Scientists figured out how to bottle a star. Unfortunately, the star is 150 million degrees, and it refuses to stay in the bottle. Every time the plasma touches the wall, it's like a toddler discovering the fridge is cold. The machines are shaped like donuts because nothing else can handle the pressure. We got net energy gain for a few billionths of a second, and the press release was longer than the experiment. Meanwhile, the sun does it for free, with no magnets, and it still manages to be more reliable than the people promising us a fusion plant by 2030.

b.text:
Fusion power, you've been thirty years away since my grandfather was alive. You're the friend who's "five minutes out" and hasn't left the house.

You're so proud of reaching net energy gain. Sure, the laser put out more than the fuel pellet took in, but it needed three hundred megajoules from the wall to make three. That's like bragging you turned a profit because you ignored rent, payroll, and the building.

You heat plasma to a hundred million degrees, then your biggest worry is that it touches something. Your whole job is holding a tiny sun in a magnetic bottle, and the sun does it for free using only gravity and spite.

ITER's budget has more delays than a budget airline. Your fuel, tritium, is rarer than a straight answer from a physicist, so your plan is to breed it inside the reactor you haven't built yet.

Fusion: the energy of the future, and always will be.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
You're the only language where `typeof null` returns "object" and nobody got fired. It's been wrong for thirty years, and instead of fixing it, you just shrugged and kept serving it, like a restaurant that's been selling raw chicken since 1995 and calls it a rustic choice.

You've got two equals signs for comparison, and one of them lies. `0 == ""` is true. `"" == "0"` is false. Zero equals empty string, empty string doesn't equal zero-string. That's not a bug. That's a hostage situation.

And `.sort()` gives you ``, because you sort numbers alphabetically unless someone begs you for a comparator function. You wrote a language that thinks digits are words.

b.text:
JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and honestly? It shows. You're named after Java the way a knockoff purse is named after Gucci.

You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number. NaN doesn't even equal itself, which makes it the only thing in you with any self-awareness.

Ask you to sort and you hand back, because you alphabetize numbers like a drunk librarian. "11" plus 1 is "111", but "11" minus 1 is 10. Pick a lane.

You needed a second equals sign just to stop lying, and nobody, including you, knows what "this" means.

January is month zero. One guy unpublishing left-pad broke half the internet. And your node_modules folder is heavier than a black hole.

Every week there's a new framework to fix you. That's not a language. That's a renovation.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text: Brasília, you're what happens when an architect gets an entire country's budget and nobody says, "Maybe add a sidewalk?" You're shaped like an airplane, which is fitting, because everyone's goal is to board one by Friday afternoon. Your addresses read like Wi-Fi passwords: "SQS 308, Bloco C, apartamento 402." That's not a home. That's a parking spot on a spaceship. Kubitschek promised "fifty years in five," and you delivered: it's been sixty-five years and you still feel unfinished. Your Congress has one bowl facing up to receive the money and one facing down to hide it. You've got a row of identical ministry buildings so nobody can tell which one the scandal came from. In August the humidity drops so low that the only thing drier than the air is a deputy's sense of shame. Even your lake is fake. Honestly? On brand.

b.text: Brasília is the only city where you need a car to get lost. Lúcio Costa drew it as an airplane, which explains everything: it was built to be admired from 30,000 feet and never walked in. Every superquadra looks identical, so locals give directions like "third block, the one with the tree." Niemeyer's cathedral looks like a concrete UFO that landed in a bad mood. Congress has one bowl facing up and one facing down, which is the most honest thing about the government. The air is so dry your nosebleeds have nosebleeds, the lake looks like a screensaver, and the nearest bar is eleven kilometers away on a highway with no sidewalk.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text:
Graphene, you're the only Nobel Prize winner ever discovered with Scotch tape. Two physicists peeled a pencil and found you, which means your origin story is literally "kid procrastinating on homework."

Since 2004 you've been "about to revolutionize" batteries, computers, water filters, and space elevators. Twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a tennis racket. You're not a wonder material, you're a press release with a hexagon fetish.

Everyone loves to say you're two hundred times stronger than steel. Great. You're also one atom thick. Nobody's impressed that a sheet of paper beats a battleship per ounce.

And for the supposed savior of electronics, you have zero bandgap. You can't even turn off. You're a transistor with no off switch, the guy at the party who never stops talking.

You're graphite with a LinkedIn profile.

b.text: Graphene, you're one atom thick and still the biggest presence at every party. Scientists keep calling you the strongest material ever measured, which is wild, because you've never once held your own in a conversation. You're basically pencil lead that went to the gym and never came back. Since 2004 we've been told you'll revolutionize batteries, phones, and bridges. Meanwhile, companies slap your name on golf balls and socks like it's a free upgrade. Two Nobel-winning guys isolated you with Scotch tape, which tells you everything. The most advanced substance in the universe was found by somebody with a roll of tape and too much time. And you're still "five years away" from being useful. Honestly, that's the most relatable thing about you.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, you're the only city where a $19 buffet requires a two-hour line and a signed waiver. You built a pyramid, a volcano, and the Eiffel Tower, but God forbid anyone find a clock. You've got no windows, no clocks, and no shame. It's 3 p.m. or 3 a.m., and either way a guy dressed as Elvis is selling me a "gentleman's club" flyer.

You call it a resort fee. I call it a cover charge to enter my own hotel room. Forty-five dollars for "amenities," and the amenity is a sad pool with a DJ who keeps yelling "Make some noise!" at dehydrated accountants from Ohio.

You're a desert pretending to be Venice, with gondoliers singing in a mall. It's 112 degrees and the canal is a puddle with a mortgage.

And the slot machines in the airport? Vegas, you're the only place that starts taking your money before you've even claimed your luggage.

b.text: Vegas, you're the only city where the pyramid has a light beam that's brighter than the sun, and you still can't find the sun. You built a fake Eiffel Tower, a fake Venice with fake gondoliers singing fake opera, and a fake New York with a roller coaster around the Statue of Liberty. Honestly, that's the most accurate tour of America I've ever taken. Everything's a copy, and nobody wants to leave. You've got clocks with no windows, casinos with no clocks, and a wedding chapel open at four in the morning for people who forgot what they agreed to at ten. Your motto should be "What happens here stays here," but your hotel bills say otherwise.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs is the only text editor that thinks "Ctrl-x Ctrl-c" is a reasonable way to say goodbye. You press it to save, and it asks you if you're sure you want to leave. You press it to leave, and it asks you to save. Nobody's ever been trapped in a relationship that confusing and still called it a productivity tool.

And the name! Emacs stands for "Editor Macros," which is a bit like naming your car "Engine Wheels." It's the most powerful editor on Earth, sure, but it boots up like it's reading you its own family history. Your laptop fan spins up, you wait a few seconds, and then you're staring at a blank screen, wondering if you're the one who's supposed to be doing the editing.

b.text:
Emacs isn't a text editor, it's an operating system that's still looking for a decent editor. Thirty years of development, and the most reliable feature is the pinky injury.

You press Control-X, Control-S to save. That's not a keyboard shortcut, that's a hostage negotiation with your left hand.

Emacs users say, "It's infinitely customizable!" Sure. So is a blank sheet of paper, but nobody brags about spending three weekends configuring that. Your init.el is 4,000 lines long, and you wrote 12 of them. The rest is a Stack Overflow answer from 2011 that you're afraid to delete.

And the manual calls it "the extensible, self-documenting editor." Self-documenting! Yes, it will tell you exactly what a function does, right after you press Control-H, then K, then wonder why you're reading Lisp.

You can read email in it, browse the web in it, and play Tetris in it. Everything except quit. Nobody remembers how to quit.

Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text: Graphene, you're one atom thick, and somehow that's still more depth than your business plan. Two hundred times stronger than steel, conducts better than copper, and twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a sticker on a tennis racket. You were discovered with Scotch tape. *Scotch tape!* You're the only Nobel Prize that could've been found in a kindergarten craft drawer. And let's be honest: you're pencil lead that went to grad school. Your cousin graphite has been writing grocery lists for centuries; you've been writing grant proposals. Every year a headline swears you'll revolutionize batteries, chips, water filters. Every year you're still in the lab, like a thirty-year-old in his parents' basement. You can't even be a decent transistor. No bandgap. You literally cannot turn off. Graphene: the material of the future, permanently.

b.text: You're one atom thick, the only thing about you that's ever been thin. Two guys won a Nobel for peeling you off a lump of pencil lead with Scotch tape. Pencil lead! Your whole family tree is the stuff kids chew in exam halls. You're stronger than steel pound for pound, you conduct electricity, you're transparent, and you still can't get out of the lab. Every year it's "graphene will revolutionize batteries next year." That's been going on for twenty years. Meanwhile companies slap your name on tennis rackets and face cream with about as much of you as a rumor. You're basically a pencil lead that got a personal trainer and a Nobel, and you still can't get a callback from a battery company.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you're the coffee maker that treats a cup of coffee like a hostage negotiation. Eight minutes of whirring, gurgling, and blinking just to produce a lukewarm thimble of brown water. Meanwhile my grandma's percolator makes a full pot before I finish reading the Wikipedia article about pour-over.

And the pods! Every cup creates a little plastic tombstone. You're basically a landfill with a power button. You've got more recyclable-pod-related guilt than my Catholic school.

Then there's the "strong" setting, which is just the regular setting with a dramatic pause. Nothing about you is bold except your price per ounce.

Keurig, you're not a coffee maker. You're a vending machine that got a cardiology degree.

b.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest thing in the world, hot water meeting coffee, and turned it into a subscription-based hostage situation. My grandfather made coffee with a pot and a prayer. I make it by stabbing a tiny plastic hockey puck in the face.

You've created a machine that takes four minutes to warm up just to produce eight ounces of something that tastes like a mug rinsed in a wet cardboard box. And that little pod? Thousands of tiny plastic cups, each one lasting longer than my last three relationships.

Then there's the "descale" light. Every few months it screams at me to run vinegar through it, like a smoke detector for my own laziness. I ignore it, and the machine just sighs and gives me half a cup.

The best part is the "strong" button. It doesn't make it stronger. It makes it smaller. You invented coffee's version of "I'm not mad, I'm just disappointed."

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text: Risk, you're the only game where "world domination" takes longer than actual world domination. Genghis Khan conquered Asia faster than my cousin conquered Ukraine, and my cousin had six armies and a dream. Your map looks like it was drawn from a description of Earth overheard on a bus. Kamchatka borders Alaska? Irkutsk and Yakutsk get more real estate than most of Africa? You taught a generation that the winning strategy is hiding in Australia like a coward and waiting for everyone else to bleed out over Siam. The defender wins ties, which explains the forty armies I lost trying to get through one guy in Egypt. And one plastic cannon is worth ten soldiers? Finally, accurate military budgeting. Five hours in, two players left, nobody's had fun since the first card set. That's not a board game, Risk. That's a hostage situation.

b.text:
Risk promises "world domination" and delivers a nine-hour hostage situation with plastic army men. Nobody has ever finished a game of Risk. We just stop when someone's mom needs the dining room table back.

Let's talk about the dice. You attack with three armies, I defend with two, and somehow I lose all three while you lose nothing. Math is a liar, and it lives in that little red cup.

Australia is the only continent anyone wants, because it has one entrance and the emotional stability of a hermit. Meanwhile Asia has seventeen borders, and holding it is like being the manager of a Wetherspoons on Saturday night.

And the alliances! "Let's team up against Dave." Then you betray me in Kamchatka. Kamchatka! A place no one has ever been or will ever visit, and yet it's responsible for more ruined friendships than any ex's Instagram.

Risk isn't a game. It's a divorce with cards.

Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza is what happens when Italy and a Dole pineapple can get into a fender bender and decide not to exchange insurance. It's a pizza that's also a fruit cup. The only dish where the ham is nervous about the dessert.

And it's not even Hawaiian! It was invented by a Greek guy in Canada. Hawaii had nothing to do with it. That's like naming a burrito "The Norwegian" because someone's cousin once ate one near Oslo.

Pineapple on pizza is like a hot tub full of juice. The cheese slides off, the crust goes soggy, and every bite is a hostage negotiation between salty and sweet. Ham and pineapple are the only couple at the party who came together but won't stand next to each other.

And somehow it's still the pizza ordered by the guy who says, "I'm easy, I'll eat anything," and then picks off all the olives.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Pineapple on bread with ham. Somebody looked at a perfectly good pizza and said, "You know what this needs? Fruit that's been sitting in a can since the Eisenhower administration." And everybody just nodded. Nobody stopped him.

And the ham! It's not even Hawaiian ham. It's Canadian bacon wearing a cheap Hawaiian shirt. It's the pizza version of a guy at a wedding who says, "I'm not a dancer," and then dances anyway.

The pineapple's the real problem, though. It's sweet, it's wet, and it's trying so hard to be a tropical vacation. You bite in, and it's like a sprinkler went off in your mouth, and the cheese just gives up and slides onto your shirt.

Honestly, I respect it. Hawaiian pizza is the only food that makes ham and fruit feel like they're both lost.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8, you looked at a billion people with a mouse and a keyboard and said, "What if your monitor was a giant phone you can't touch?"

You took away the Start button. The one thing a user knew how to find. Microsoft had literally sold Windows 95 with a Rolling Stones song called "Start Me Up," and you said, "Nah."

Want to shut down? Easy: hover in a secret corner, summon the Charms bar, click Settings, click Power. Turning off my computer shouldn't feel like unlocking a cheat code.

Your tiles were so ugly even the name "Metro" had to get dropped over a trademark dispute. Then 8.1 brought back the Start button, which just opened the same tiles. That's not an apology, that's a hostage video.

You were so bad Microsoft skipped the number 9 entirely just to put distance between you and Windows 10.

b.text: Windows 8 looked at the Start button and said, "Nah." Microsoft deleted the one thing everybody used to find anything, then replaced it with a full-screen wall of colored squares that look like a bathroom tile sample. Want to shut down? Swipe in from the right edge to open the Charms Bar, dig through Settings, and click a power icon hidden like it's in witness protection. The live tiles are my favorite. My Mail tile keeps showing me a headline about a sale from 2013. Eight years of muscle memory, gone, so I could enjoy a touchscreen I didn't buy on a desktop I didn't ask for.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you're not milk. You're almonds that got lost on the way to a smoothie and decided to lie about it. Milk comes from a cow, and a cow has some dignity. You come from a nut that's been soaked in water until it gave up. Somebody squeezed a almond, looked at the sad little puddle, and said, "Yep, that's breakfast."

You're so thin, I can read a newspaper through you. Your idea of creamy is a rumor. You've got less body than a Tuesday. And every carton of you says "Unsweetened" like you're proud of it, like there's a single person alive who wanted to taste nothing.

Almond milk, you're the guy who says he's "not really into drinking" and then orders the oat latte.

b.text:
Almond milk, you're proof that marketing can convince people to pay four dollars for cloudy water with a nut rumor attached. You're 2% almonds. Two percent! That's not milk, that's a homeopathic remedy for oat milk.

You took a nut that needs a gallon of water per single almond to grow, then sold yourself to people who say "I'm doing it for the planet." California is in a drought, Karen. Those bees are being trucked across the country like migrant workers just so you can ruin a latte.

And the texture. You're the only drink that separates in coffee like a bad breakup. Curdling in front of everyone, floating there in tiny shame flakes.

Your carton says "Unsweetened Original," which is two lies in a row. There's nothing original about you, and nothing about you is sweet.

You're what a cow would make if she gave up halfway through and just described milk to a nut.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Microsoft Teams is the only app that can notify you about a message you're already reading. You've got a red badge, a yellow badge, and a little purple "@" telling you someone said "per my last email" in a chat called "Q3 Sync (Copy) (Final)."

Teams has seven ways to say hello and none of them load. "Joining meeting..." is its resting state. It's the Waiting for Godot of video calls, except Godot eventually shows up and says, "Can everyone see my screen?" No, Greg. We see a spinning circle and your cat.

Every update, it asks you to restart. Not the app. Your life choices.

Teams and Channels are different things, by the way. A channel lives inside a team. Which is inside a tenant. Which is inside a guest account you can't switch out of without signing out of everything and crying.

And the green dot? It goes yellow the second you stop moving your mouse, so your boss thinks you're napping. Ten minutes of reading a document is considered a vacation.

b.text: Microsoft Teams, you're the only app with the nerve to open itself the second I log in, like a hall monitor who got promoted. Every meeting starts with the same ritual: "Can you hear me?" "You're on mute." "Sorry, you're on mute." Thirty seconds of people unmuting like it's a hostage situation. And that little "Someone is typing..." bubble? It's been there since Tuesday. Nobody's typing, Teams. Nobody's ever typing. You tell me I'm "Available" while I'm literally in a meeting, then ping me four minutes after everyone else has already replied. "Let's take this offline," says the guy, and then he schedules a Teams call about it. Teams, you're not a chat app. You're a conference room that follows you home.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text:
Esperanto: the universal language invented in 1887 by a Polish eye doctor who decided humanity needed Italian with a Slavic accent. Universal, as long as your universe is Europe.

The name means "one who hopes." Over a century later: still hoping. There are roughly a thousand native speakers. Klingon is closing in, and Klingon has an army.

It's so logical that "bad" is "malbona," literally un-good. Orwell called; he wants royalties.

Every noun ends in -o and every adjective in -a, so every sentence sounds like a waiter reciting the specials. And it gave us ĉ, ĝ, ŝ and ŭ: letters with little hats, designed for global communication, then made untypeable on every keyboard on Earth.

Its biggest movie starred William Shatner. Even he couldn't oversell it.

b.text:
Esperanto: the language invented to unite humanity, and after 130 years, its greatest achievement is a tiny group of people who all met at the same convention.

Zamenhof wanted world peace. He got a language where the most common sentence is "Hello, are you also here for the Esperanto thing?"

Everything is regular. Every noun ends in O. Every adjective ends in A. It's the only language designed like a filing cabinet, and it sounds like Italian and Polish got stuck in an elevator and decided to name the kids.

And the accusative! They made a language to be easy, then kept the accusative. Fine. It's a hobby.

"Native speakers" of Esperanto number about a thousand, which is what we call "the children of enthusiasts who never got a vote."

The national anthem is "La Espero." The national sport is correcting your pronunciation of "ĉ." And the only country that really speaks it is the Facebook group.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text:
LaTeX is the only software where you spend three hours making a document look "professional" and one minute actually writing it.

You want a picture next to some text? LaTeX says, "Sure, I'll put it on page nine. Floating. Like your hopes."

The error messages are written by someone who hates you personally. "Missing $ inserted." Missing WHAT? I'm a grad student, I haven't seen a dollar since 2019.

Compile once, and the table of contents is wrong. Compile twice, it's right. Compile three times, and now the bibliography has vanished. It's not software, it's a séance.

Everyone says, "Just use a template!" Sure, let me paste in forty packages I don't understand, and pray hyperref doesn't fight with the other thirty-nine.

And the people who love it? They'll tell you, "It handles equations beautifully." Yes, Greg, and my Honda handles beautifully too, but I don't build the engine from a text file to drive to Costco.

Knuth wrote it in 1978 and said it was done. That's the only deadline in history met by being declared finished.

b.text: LaTeX, you're a word processor that makes me pass a programming exam just to type "hello." I need a backslash, three curly braces, and a prayer to make one word bold. Forget a single dollar sign and you scream "Missing $ inserted," like I personally mugged your math mode. Then you throw "Emergency stop" at me, which is rude, because I'm the one who's supposed to be panicking. Want a table? Enjoy three hours wrestling ampersands and \hline like they owe you money. Bibliography? Run the compiler three times, like a coach yelling "one more lap" because the first two didn't count. Your fans swear the output is gorgeous. Sure, so is a cathedral, and nobody builds a grocery list out of one.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're just plexiglass with a god complex. You're the same stuff as a hamster cage, and somehow you've got a cleanroom full of PhDs treating you like a sacred text.

You're a positive resist, which is cute, because nothing about your attitude is. We hit you with a billion electrons and you just go, "Fine, I'll break up a little." Chain scission? That's not a lithography mechanism, that's your whole personality.

And the sensitivity! You need like a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. My phone charges faster than you expose. Meanwhile I'm sitting at the e-beam writing a pattern for nine hours so you can give me a lopsided blob.

Then comes development. Isopropanol and MIBK, because you're too good for water. Overdevelop by ten seconds and your lines collapse like a dropped soufflé.

And you're sold in anisole, so every wafer smells like a licorice factory had an affair with a solvent cabinet.

Great resolution, though. Ten nanometers. Shame about everything else.

b.text: PMMA, you're the same plastic as a hockey rink window, and somehow that's your most dignified job. You've been "high resolution" since the 1970s, which is like bragging about your SAT score at your retirement party. Sure, you'll resolve sub-10-nanometer lines, if someone stands there blasting you with electrons for an eternity. Your sensitivity is so low the beam current has gotten tenure. You don't even develop properly without MIBK and IPA holding your hand in a one-to-three ratio. And your whole personality is chain scission: you literally fall apart when someone pays attention to you. Then hit you with too much dose and you crosslink and flip to negative tone, a full identity crisis. And dry etch? You melt in plasma faster than an ice sculpture at a barbecue. Honestly, the only thing you're consistently good at is lift-off: leaving.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass was the only product where the beta testers were called "Explorers," because "Guinea Pigs Who Paid fifteen hundred dollars" didn't fit on the box.

It had one camera, one tiny screen, and zero friends. Wearing it in public was a way of telling a stranger, "I may be filming you, and I definitely want to talk about my startup."

Remember the battery? Thirty minutes of recording and it ran hotter than your uncle at Thanksgiving. You didn't have a wearable computer, you had a forehead space heater with a blinking eye.

And the word "Glasshole" wasn't an insult someone invented. It was a consumer review. Bars banned it. Strangers punched it off people's faces. Strangers also asked, "Is that on right now?" which is the sound of privacy dying.

It was the first device that looked like the future and acted like a restraining order.

b.text: Google Glass, you cost fifteen hundred dollars and made everyone wearing you look like a Bluetooth headset that got promoted. Sergey Brin launched you by skydiving onto a building, and that's the last time you were ever cool. You put a tiny prism over one eye so people could check email while pretending to make eye contact. You didn't invent a computer, you invented a reason to get punched. You're the only gadget that gave us a new slur: "Glasshole." Bars banned you. Movie theaters banned you. Robert Scoble wore you in the shower, and that photo did more damage than any privacy lawsuit. You took pictures when people winked, turning every awkward conversation into a potential felony. Your battery died before your reputation did, and that's impressive. Rest in peace: demoted to warehouse work, then quietly killed in 2023. The most Google ending possible.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text: Hydrogen fuel-cell cars are the most optimistic thing ever built. Think about it: you take the most abundant element in the universe, and then you spend a fortune compressing it to 700 bar, bolting it into a tank, and driving it to a station that's closed. Toyota's Mirai has more hydrogen stations in its dreams than in California. Some states have exactly one, and it's always broken. You pull up, the pump says "Out of Service," and you realize you've just become a very expensive lawn ornament. Meanwhile, your electric neighbor is charging in his garage in his pajamas. Hydrogen cars are like a guy who proposes on a first date and then can't find the ring.

b.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars are the only vehicles where the fuel is the most abundant element in the universe and somehow still costs more per mile than caviar. Sixteen dollars a kilogram, and you can only buy it at one station in California, which is closed. For "maintenance."

Their big selling point is that the only emissions are water. Fantastic. Most of the hydrogen is made from natural gas, so it's a car that cries clean tears after being force-fed fossil fuels in a basement.

Toyota calls its model the Mirai. That's Japanese for "future." Accurate, because that's when you'll find a pump.

Owners are a special breed. They drive 40 minutes to refuel, then call it freedom. Their car is basically a Prius that got a PhD, went into massive debt, and still can't get a job.

And the tank? Pressurized to 10,000 psi. So it's a zero-emissions vehicle with a tiny, polite bomb in the trunk.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text: Brasília is the only city where the architects designed everything except a reason to go outside. Niemeyer built the Cathedral like a flying saucer that gave up halfway, and Lúcio Costa laid the city out like an airplane, which explains why everyone's been circling the same runway of traffic since 1960. The superquadras all look identical, so when you get lost, you're not lost, you're just on a different block of the same block. There are no corners to lean on, no street to wander, just six lanes and a bus stop that's more of a rumor. The people who clean the ministries live out in Ceilândia and commute two hours to get there. And it's so dry your lips file for divorce.

b.text: Brasília, you're what happens when an architect gets an entire country's budget and nobody says, "Maybe add a sidewalk?" You're shaped like an airplane, which is fitting, because everyone's goal is to board one by Friday afternoon. Your addresses read like Wi-Fi passwords: "SQS 308, Bloco C, apartamento 402." That's not a home. That's a parking spot on a spaceship. Kubitschek promised "fifty years in five," and you delivered: it's been sixty-five years and you still feel unfinished. Your Congress has one bowl facing up to receive the money and one facing down to hide it. You've got a row of identical ministry buildings so nobody can tell which one the scandal came from. In August the humidity drops so low that the only thing drier than the air is a deputy's sense of shame. Even your lake is fake. Honestly? On brand.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text: Jackfruit, you look like a medieval mace that got into a fight with a durian and lost. You're the size of a toddler and you have the texture of a sweater that's been through the wash. Vegans picked you up as a pulled-pork substitute, and honestly, that's the most desperate career pivot I've ever seen. "Hey, what if we made people chew a fruit like it's a cheap brisket?" Nobody asked for that. And the smell? Sweet, gym-bag funk, like a banana that climbed into a sock drawer and died there. You're the fruit equivalent of a guy who shows up to a party in a tuxedo made of burlap.

b.text:
Jackfruit, you're the largest fruit that grows on a tree, which sounds impressive until you realize it just means you're the biggest thing that can fall on someone's head in an orchard. Eighty pounds of spikes dangling at skull height. You're not a fruit, you're a booby trap with seeds.

Opening you requires an oiled knife, rubber gloves, and a tarp, because your sap is basically Elmer's glue with a grudge. Then the smell hits: half Juicy Fruit gum, half onions somebody forgot in a gym bag. You smell like a candy store got food poisoning.

And sure, vegans love you, but only when you're young and taste like absolutely nothing. That's your whole career. The most famous thing about you is that, with enough barbecue sauce, you can pass for a pig. Even your best role is an impression.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text:
Brasília, you're the only city designed from above, which explains why it's miserable from the ground. You're shaped like an airplane, and honestly, that tracks, because everyone's just passing through and nobody's happy about the food.

Oscar Niemeyer built you in 41 months, and it shows. You have addresses like "SQS 308, Bloco C, Apartamento 204." That's not a location, that's a tax form with a doorbell.

You have no street corners. No one has ever bumped into anyone by accident. Pedestrians don't exist; they're a rumor spread by people with cars.

Your cathedral looks like a crown of thorns made by a very expensive lamp company. Your Congress has two bowls, one facing up and one down, because even your architecture can't decide whether it's receiving bribes or hiding them.

Rio gets Carnival. São Paulo gets money. You get a lawmaker who flies in Tuesday and flees Thursday. You're not a capital, you're a very large airport lounge with a flag.

b.text:
Brasília, you're the only city designed to look like an airplane, and somehow everyone still just wants to leave on one. Politicians fly in Tuesday, take a bribe Wednesday, and they're gone by Thursday like it's a timeshare.

Your addresses read like a Wi-Fi password: "SQS 308, Bloco C, Apartamento 402." I'm not visiting a friend, I'm resetting a router.

Niemeyer gave you gorgeous curves, then Lúcio Costa forgot pedestrians. Want to walk to the bakery? Hope you enjoy the eight-lane Eixão and a light jog through a tesourinha.

Your humidity drops to 10 percent. Your congress has one bowl facing up, one facing down: one for collecting money, the other for hiding it.

And you were built with no corners, so Brazil's capital has no boteco na esquina. That's not urban planning. That's a human rights violation.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel, you're the Swiss Army knife of spreadsheets, except every blade is sharp in the wrong direction. You've got four hundred functions and somehow none of them can tell me why my dates turned into the number 45292. You autocorrect "1-2" into January 2nd, and then you act surprised when a gene called MARCH1 becomes "1-Mar." Scientists had to rename genes because of you. That's not a bug, that's a biography.

And the Ctrl+Z history stops at about twelve steps, like you're embarrassed of your own mistakes. You're a grid of a million rows and you still can't fit my budget on one screen without me squinting like I'm reading a ransom note.

Every one of us has one cell that says #REF! and one VLOOKUP we don't understand. You're not a tool, you're a hostage negotiation with a row number.

b.text: Excel, you're the only software that forced geneticists to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into March 1st. Scientists can edit DNA, but they couldn't edit you. You still think 1900 was a leap year. You've known it wasn't for forty years. You just don't care. You see a zip code like 02134 and go, "Leading zero? Not on my watch." You lost sixteen thousand UK COVID cases by quietly stopping at row 65,536. Your error messages are pure poetry: #REF!, #N/A, #VALUE!, and my favorite, a column of hashtags that just means "make me wider." And VLOOKUP: insert one column and the whole finance department enters witness protection. You're not a spreadsheet. You're a hostage situation with gridlines.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the vehicle for people who looked at electric cars and said, "Too convenient."

You can only fuel up at one of about fifty stations in the entire state of California, and half of them are "temporarily" closed, like a Blockbuster with a hopeful sign. Owners plan road trips like they're smuggling something.

The fuel costs more per mile than driving a Bentley on champagne. And the whole thing runs on the most abundant element in the universe, which is somehow harder to find than a parking spot at Costco.

Toyota calls it the Mirai, Japanese for "future." Technically accurate. That's where the gas stations are.

The only emission is water, which is great, because you'll be standing next to the car for an hour, watching it drip, wondering why you didn't just buy a Tesla.

Hydrogen: the future of transportation, and always will be.

b.text: Hydrogen fuel-cell cars are the most ambitious thing ever built to avoid a charging cable. Think about it: the whole plan is to take electricity, use it to split water into hydrogen, compress that hydrogen to ten thousand PSI, drive it across the country in a tank that's basically a rocket casing, then turn it back into electricity. That's not a green car, that's a magic trick with a chaperone. And the hydrogen stations? Good luck. You'll find one in California, and it's closed for "maintenance," which I'm pretty sure means someone realized they were hydrogen stations and got nervous. Meanwhile, my Tesla just asks if I'd like to plug in at home, like a normal car.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP, you're the only language whose name is a recursive acronym, and your mascot is an elephant that's been sitting on servers since 1995. You slap a dollar sign on every variable like you're charging us by the letter. Your function names look like they were typed during a power outage: strpos wants the haystack first, array_search wants the needle first, and you just shrugged. You told us "0" == false is true and "1e3" == "1000" is true, and we nodded like that makes sense. Magic quotes, register_globals, mysql_ functions you kept around like a grandma's ugly couch. Somehow you run half the internet. Honestly, that's the scariest part.

b.text:
PHP is the only language where the standard library looks like it was named by a committee of people who'd never met. Is it str_replace or strpos? Is the needle first or the haystack? Nobody knows. Not even PHP. It just rolls dice and says "array_walk, but backwards."

Fun fact: PHP stands for "Personal Home Page," which is also what it feels like when your code gets hacked and a teenager in Belarus redirects your site to a pharmacy.

It's got a function called mysql_real_escape_string, which implies there was a mysql_escape_string that was fake. Fake escaping. Just vibes.

And the equality operator? "0" == false, "abc" == 0, null == false. PHP looks at two completely different things and says, "Eh, close enough." It's the language equivalent of a bouncer who lets everyone in because they're wearing a shirt.

But hey, it powers 77% of the web. So does that one guy named Gary who's still on WordPress 3.2.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs is a beautiful operating system. Shame it never shipped with a decent text editor. That's why half its users install evil-mode: they love Emacs so much they turned it into Vim.

Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," which is also the sound your pinky makes on its way to the orthopedic surgeon. Asking for help is C-h, which in a terminal deletes a character. So even your cry for help gets backspaced.

It has a built-in therapist, M-x doctor, which is thoughtful, because nobody else will listen to you explain your init.el. Four thousand lines of Lisp, half copied from a 2003 mailing list, and you still declare "Emacs bankruptcy" every two years.

It plays Tetris. It reads email. It runs your entire life in Org-mode. It still chokes on one long line of JSON.

b.text:
Emacs is the only text editor that thinks "Ctrl-x Ctrl-c" is a reasonable way to say goodbye. You press it to save, and it asks you if you're sure you want to leave. You press it to leave, and it asks you to save. Nobody's ever been trapped in a relationship that confusing and still called it a productivity tool.

And the name! Emacs stands for "Editor Macros," which is a bit like naming your car "Engine Wheels." It's the most powerful editor on Earth, sure, but it boots up like it's reading you its own family history. Your laptop fan spins up, you wait a few seconds, and then you're staring at a blank screen, wondering if you're the one who's supposed to be doing the editing.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text: Windows Vista, the operating system that asked permission for everything. You wanted to open a folder? Click "Continue." Delete a file? "Are you sure?" Breathe? "Allow this program to breathe?" Your computer needed a bouncer just to check its own coat. And the copy progress bar: "Four minutes remaining." Three hours later it's at 99 percent, forever. Vista didn't crash. It just kept asking if you were sure. And the sidebar! A little clock and a weather widget floating on your desktop like you needed a hall monitor for your screensaver. Microsoft put a "Vista Capable" sticker on computers that could barely run it, and then acted shocked when people were mad. Honestly, Vista, you were the first operating system to make your user feel like the problem.

b.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Five years in development as "Longhorn," and the only thing that shipped on time was the disappointment. They cut WinFS but kept the Aero glass. Finally, an operating system you could see right through.

Vista came in six editions, from Starter to Ultimate, which is five more ways to pay for the same crash. Microsoft slapped "Vista Capable" stickers on computers that could barely run Solitaire, then got sued. The only thing Vista ever finished loading was a class action.

And User Account Control! "Are you sure you want to do that?" Every. Single. Click. Vista was the only software that needed permission to exist, and honestly? We should've hit Cancel.

Copying a file: "Calculating time remaining…" Vista, you were calculating until 2009, when Microsoft fixed you, renamed you Windows 7, and pretended you were adopted.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text:
Papyrus, you're the font that shows up to every event dressed for a different one. You've been on spa menus, yoga studio flyers, and a blockbuster movie about a blue alien planet, and somehow you're always wrong for all of them.

You look like you were hand-torn from a scroll by someone who has never held a scroll. Your edges are so rough, it's like you were printed on a napkin during an earthquake. Every letter looks like it's auditioning for a role as "Ancient Egyptian Gift Shop."

And the designers! They had one job for Avatar: make it look futuristic. They gave you a font that says "Cleopatra's Aromatherapy Candles." Ryan Gosling did a whole sketch about it, and you're still working. That's not resilience, that's a restraining order nobody enforced.

You say "organic." You say "natural." You mean "I was free in the font menu and nobody had the heart to say no."

Papyrus: the only thing on your computer that smells like incense.

b.text:
Papyrus, look at you. A 23-year-old drew you with a calligraphy pen in 1982, trying to imagine what English would look like 2,000 years ago, and somehow you became the official font of every place that sells crystals next to a tanning bed. You're on yoga studios, hookah lounges, and the church bake sale flyer for "Loaves & Fishes & Brownies."

Your letters look like they were chiseled by a Pharaoh with a hangover. That little floaty bar on your capital E? Even your crossbars are trying to leave.

James Cameron spent a billion dollars inventing an alien language, then labeled the poster with a font that came free with Microsoft Office. Ryan Gosling got an entire SNL sketch out of being haunted by you.

Even your creator says he's sick of you. Comic Sans has haters. You have a dad who wants a refund.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: NFTs, everybody! The only art form where the most common review is "right-click, save." You paid four hundred thousand dollars for a cartoon monkey in a captain's hat, and I have the same monkey as my phone background. The difference? I didn't pay a gas fee bigger than the art. Technically you don't even own the picture. You own a receipt pointing to a link on a server some guy in Ohio forgot to renew. That's not a masterpiece; that's a parking stub for a JPEG. And remember the roadmap? Metaverse, merch, a yacht party! Then the founder pulled the rug, deleted the Discord, and left you holding a "rare trait": sunglasses. Jimmy Fallon showed Paris Hilton his ape on national TV like a proud dad. Now it's worth less than the TV.

b.text: Nobody's ever been mugged for an NFT, and that's the scam. You can't steal it, you can't hang it on a wall, and you can't even right-click save it without the cartoon ape judging you. You paid four thousand dollars for a receipt. A receipt that says, "I own the JPEG of a bored monkey," and the JPEG is still sitting on a server in Ohio, unbothered. Your grandma bought Beanie Babies and at least she got a fabric bear she could hug. You bought a hyperlink with a pulse. And the best part? The guy who sold it to you already cashed out and bought a yacht named after the ape you didn't get to keep.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Deep-dish pizza is the only food where you need a fork, a knife, and a structural engineer. You order a slice and the waiter brings you a casserole with a crust like a bank vault. The sauce sits on top, which is the pizza equivalent of wearing your shirt on the outside of your jacket. Chicagoans will tell you it's "not pizza, it's a pie," which is what you say when you've eaten something that requires a 45-minute wait and still leaves you feeling like you've been mugged by cheese. Locals eat it with a straight face. Tourists eat it with a flashlight, looking for the bottom. And somewhere under there, buried under three pounds of mozzarella, is a tomato that has never once been invited to the party.

b.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole with a publicist. You order one and the waiter says "forty-five minutes," which is how long it takes to bake and also how long it takes to finish one slice. They put the sauce on top and the cheese underneath, like they're hiding evidence. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up. The crust is a buttery retaining wall holding back a lake of chunky tomato, because apparently Lake Michigan wasn't enough water for one city to manage. You need a knife, a fork, a nap, and a cardiologist on retainer. Then there's the sausage, laid down as one solid patty like the base layer of a parking garage. Chicagoans defend it like family. Sure: the relative who shows up late, takes up three chairs, and leaves everyone unable to move.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text: Esperanto was built in 1887 so everyone on Earth could finally talk to each other, and 140 years later the main conversation is still, "Oh, you speak it too? Where are you from?" "Also Esperanto." Silence. Every speaker is one hug away from running out of things to say. The grammar is famously logical: every noun ends in -o, every adjective in -a, and every direct object gets an -n, which is the only place this language ever shows emotion. It promised to be easy to learn, and it kept that promise the way a diet pill does. You master it in a month, then spend the rest of your life waiting for a stranger to answer you back.

b.text:
Esperanto is the only product in history where the user manual promised world peace and the user base turned out to be eleven guys named Zbigniew arguing about the accusative case.

Zamenhof invented a language to unite humanity, and humanity said, "Cute. Does it have a Starbucks?"

It has sixteen grammar rules and no exceptions, which is exactly what a language sounds like when it's never been used by anyone angry. Try ordering a sandwich in a tongue where nobody has ever cheated on anyone or been cut off in traffic. Where's the slang? Where's the swearing? You can't build a culture on a word for "hello" and a really strong feeling about the letter ĥ.

Its greatest literary achievement is a translation of Hamlet. Even the original works are mostly translations of someone else's feelings.

And the flag is a green star. Not a country. A star. It's a nation-state with a logo and a dating pool smaller than a Dungeons & Dragons convention in Lithuania.

Mi amas vin, Esperanto. Nobody else does.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim. The only program where "how do I leave?" has more Stack Overflow views than most religions have followers. Two million people asked, and the answer was colon, q, exclamation point, which reads less like a command and more like a hostage's final words.

Vim stands for "Vi Improved." Improved from a 1976 terminal whose arrow keys were printed on H, J, K, and L. Fifty years later, Vim's still out here like, "Why fix what you can turn into a personality?"

You don't type in Vim. You type a sentence, then discover you deleted four lines, yanked a paragraph into register W, and started recording a macro.

Crash it once and it leaves a .swp file behind, like a ghost whispering, "Recover, Edit anyway, Quit, or Abort?"

Even its fans forked it. Neovim exists because Vim users wanted Vim, minus Vim.

b.text:
Vim is the only software where the tutorial is "how to leave." Millions of developers have rebooted their computers rather than figure out :wq. Stack Overflow has a question about quitting Vim with over a million views. That's not a text editor, that's a hostage situation.

It has modes. Normal mode, which is where nothing normal happens. Insert mode, where you finally type, like a toddler allowed one cookie. Visual mode, command mode, replace mode. It's a text editor with more personalities than a Reddit thread.

Vim users say "once you learn it, you'll be so fast." Sir, you spent six years learning to delete a word. You've saved four seconds and told everyone at dinner about it.

And the pride! They've memorized hjkl so they never move their hands, yet they've moved their entire personality into a .vimrc file that's 900 lines long, breaks every update, and was last understood in 2014.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text: HSQ, you're the most high-maintenance resist in the cleanroom. You live in a fridge like a sad sandwich, and leave the cap off for an afternoon and you gel into a forgotten Jell-O salad. You're negative-tone, so the exposed parts become your permanent address. You don't leave the wafer, you move in as silicon dioxide. You promise sub-10-nanometer lines, then spread out with the dose like a houseguest saying "just one more electron." Develop in salty developer and you still swell, like you're offended by the chemistry. Honestly, you're a flowable oxide with a personality disorder and an expensive price tag.

b.text:
HSQ, everybody! The only resist that ages faster than the grad student using it. You spin it Monday, expose it Tuesday, and suddenly your dose curve has gone through a midlife crisis. It has to live in the fridge like expired yogurt, and it's about as forgiving.

HSQ brags about sub-10-nanometer lines. Sure, if you've got six hours of write time, because this diva needs a dose that could sterilize a hospital. Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you're desperate, *salt water*. Your whole career is literally seasoned with tears now.

And once it's exposed? It turns into glass. Brittle, cracking glass. You wanted a mask; you got a window that shatters when you look at it. Want it gone? Hope you enjoy hydrofluoric acid, the chemical that dissolves your bones.

HSQ: beautiful resolution, terrible personality. It's not negative-tone. It's just negative.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text: Crocs are the only shoe that looks like it was designed by a committee of ducks. Every pair is a foam clog with holes in it, like someone started making shoes, got bored halfway through, and said, "Eh, the air can have the rest." Nobody has ever bought Crocs to look good. You buy them because they're the only shoe that can survive a flood, a hospital shift, and a barbecue at the same time. They come with little charms you snap into the holes, which is how you know the company has given up on fashion and moved into hostage negotiation: "Fine, you want a shoe, we'll give you a shoe with a pizza slice stuck in its side." And somehow they're everywhere. Grandpas, nurses, teenagers, and one guy at every Costco who hasn't left the house since 2009. Crocs don't walk, they waddle. That's not a shoe, that's a rubber duck that lost a bet.

b.text:
Crocs are the only shoes that look like they were designed by someone who'd only had shoes described to them over a bad phone connection. "So it's a boat, but for your foot?" "Sure."

And the holes! Ventilation, they say. Which is great, because nothing says "protect my toes" like a shoe with a dozen open invitations for a dropped knife. They're the only footwear where a gentle rain and a kitchen spill both count as a personal attack.

Then there's the Jibbitz. You've taken a shoe that looks like a foam dinosaur egg and decided to accessorize it with a tiny plastic pizza. That's not fashion. That's a toddler's hostage negotiation.

And the strap! Pushed forward, it's "casual." Flipped back, it's "sport mode." Sport for what, Greg? You're carrying a rotisserie chicken to a barbecue.

Yet somehow, they're unbelievably comfortable. Which is the cruelest part. Every nurse, chef, and gardener secretly knows: they look like a mistake, and they feel like a hug. Crocs are ugly on purpose, and they won.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text:
PHP. You started as "Personal Home Page," then rebranded as "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a recursive acronym, because even your name couldn't commit to a stable API.

For twenty years, "abc" == 0 was true, and you called it "type juggling," like a clown proud of dropping things.

strpos takes haystack, needle. array_search takes needle, haystack. That's not argument order; that's mood swings.

Your parse error says T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM. That's Hebrew for "double colon" and English for "good luck."

You skipped version 6 entirely. Even your release numbers just wanted to move on.

You shipped mysql_real_escape_string, implying the first one was a hoax.

Facebook loved you so much they invented Hack just to avoid touching you.

But sure, you power most of the web. Mostly WordPress. That's like bragging your biggest fan is a raccoon.

b.text:
PHP is the only language where the standard library looks like it was named by a committee of people who'd never met. Is it str_replace or strpos? Is the needle first or the haystack? Nobody knows. Not even PHP. It just rolls dice and says "array_walk, but backwards."

Fun fact: PHP stands for "Personal Home Page," which is also what it feels like when your code gets hacked and a teenager in Belarus redirects your site to a pharmacy.

It's got a function called mysql_real_escape_string, which implies there was a mysql_escape_string that was fake. Fake escaping. Just vibes.

And the equality operator? "0" == false, "abc" == 0, null == false. PHP looks at two completely different things and says, "Eh, close enough." It's the language equivalent of a bouncer who lets everyone in because they're wearing a shirt.

But hey, it powers 77% of the web. So does that one guy named Gary who's still on WordPress 3.2.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. Somewhere your cousin is a sneeze guard at Chipotle, and honestly? Your cousin has better etch resistance. One whiff of plasma and you vanish faster than a grad student's weekend.

You've been the "gold standard" since the 1970s, which is a polite way of saying nobody's been able to fire you. You need hundreds of microcoulombs just to *notice* the beam. A 40-hour write for one wafer. Glacial, but sure, sub-10-nanometer lines, we get it.

Positive resist? Overdose you and you cross-link into a *negative* one. That's not versatility, that's an identity crisis.

You get developed in MIBK, which smells like regret, and you come in 495K and 950K because one of you alone can't even do liftoff. And acetone dissolves you instantly. Even your solvents think you're temporary.

b.text:
PMMA, you're just plexiglass with a god complex. You're the same stuff as a hamster cage, and somehow you've got a cleanroom full of PhDs treating you like a sacred text.

You're a positive resist, which is cute, because nothing about your attitude is. We hit you with a billion electrons and you just go, "Fine, I'll break up a little." Chain scission? That's not a lithography mechanism, that's your whole personality.

And the sensitivity! You need like a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. My phone charges faster than you expose. Meanwhile I'm sitting at the e-beam writing a pattern for nine hours so you can give me a lopsided blob.

Then comes development. Isopropanol and MIBK, because you're too good for water. Overdevelop by ten seconds and your lines collapse like a dropped soufflé.

And you're sold in anisole, so every wafer smells like a licorice factory had an affair with a solvent cabinet.

Great resolution, though. Ten nanometers. Shame about everything else.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Klingon, a language designed by a linguist for a race of warriors, and somehow it still has a word for "tea" but no word for "hello." You people invented a whole culture of honor and glory, and the greeting is "What do you want?" That's not a language, that's a customer service line at a gym.

The grammar is object-verb-subject. Of course it is. Even the sentence structure says "I'm going to stab the dinner first and tell you who did it later."

Klingon has a phrase for "Today is a good day to die," but you try ordering a sandwich. Nope. Because no Klingon ever said, "Could I get that on rye?" They said, "Bring me the still-moving thing."

And the fans! Thousands of people speaking fluent guttural phlegm, getting married in it, translating Hamlet. Shakespeare in the original Klingon, which is just regular Shakespeare, but now the soliloquy sounds like someone clearing their throat at a funeral.

Qapla'? More like Qa-please-stop.

b.text: Klingon, you sound like a man hacking up a hairball during a hostage negotiation. Every word starts with a throat-clearing gargle, and somehow "nuqneH" still sounds like a threat. Apparently "please" is a sign of weakness, so you just bellow "Qapla'" and hope the guy behind you agrees. Your grammar treats every sentence like a dare: object first, verb second, subject whenever you feel like it. Your big literary achievement is *Hamlet*, and its most famous line comes out as "taH pagh taHbe'," which sounds like a dog choking on a sock. Your dictionary has more ways to say "your mother" than "I'm sorry," and I'd respect you more if you apologized once.

Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
