a.text: Vim is the only program that greets you with "How do I quit?" as its opening line. You open it by accident, and now you're trapped in a text editor that thinks typing is a crime. You press "i" to insert text, which is hilarious, because nobody who uses Vim has ever inserted anything into their life. Then you hit Escape, and suddenly you're in command mode, where the letters you type don't write anything. They do things. "d" deletes. "x" deletes. "dd" deletes the whole line, and you did not ask for that. Vim doesn't have a save button; it has ":wq," which sounds like a sneeze in a library. Vim users say it's efficient. Sure, if your idea of efficiency is memorizing a secret language just to change one word.

b.text:
Vim, you're the only text editor with its own hostage negotiation thread. Millions of people have viewed the Stack Overflow question on how to leave you. That's not a user base, that's a missing persons report.

You have modes. Normal mode, where typing does nothing normal, and Insert mode, hidden behind the letter "i" like a secret menu.

Your fans move the cursor with h, j, k, l because a terminal from 1976 printed arrows on those keys. That's not efficiency, that's Stockholm syndrome on the home row.

Every Vim user has a 900-line .vimrc copied from a stranger and is too scared to touch it. And when you crash, you leave .swp files behind like a burglar who signs the guestbook.

Even your own kids forked you into Neovim. That's not a fork. That's an intervention.

Goodnight! :wq… :q!… ESC ESC ESC…

You look like you were hand-torn from a scroll by someone who has never held a scroll. Your edges are so rough, it's like you were printed on a napkin during an earthquake. Every letter looks like it's auditioning for a role as "Ancient Egyptian Gift Shop."

And the designers! They had one job for Avatar: make it look futuristic. They gave you a font that says "Cleopatra's Aromatherapy Candles." Ryan Gosling did a whole sketch about it, and you're still working. That's not resilience, that's a restraining order nobody enforced.

It was made in 1983, on a computer, by someone with a hunch and no interest in pharaohs. Yet it's on every yoga studio sign, vegan café menu, and candle that says "Blessed." Its letters look like they were chiseled by someone who loves the idea of a tomb but has never stood in one. Wedding invitations, wine bars, tiki shacks: they all reach for Papyrus like it's wisdom. Look at that lopsided W, like it had three margaritas before it got written. It's the typographic equivalent of a man in a linen shirt at a funeral, and it's nobody's ancestor.

You say "organic." You say "natural." You mean "I was free in the font menu and nobody had the heart to say no."

Papyrus: the only thing on your computer that smells like incense.

b.text: Papyrus, you were designed in 1982 by a 23-year-old with calligraphy pens and a dream of ancient Egypt, and somehow you still look like you were drawn by someone shivering. Your edges are so rough you need exfoliating. You promised the wisdom of the Nile and delivered the vibe of a chiropractor's tri-fold brochure. Every day spa, hookah lounge, and "Inner Journey" yoga retreat found you in the dropdown menu and whispered, "This feels ancient." James Cameron spent $237 million on *Avatar* and then used you for the logo, which is like building the Taj Mahal and signing it in crayon. Ryan Gosling lost sleep over you on national television. You're not a typeface; you're a cry for help with ragged little serifs. Even Comic Sans looks at you and says, "At least I know I'm a joke."

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza is what happens when Italy and a Dole pineapple can have a custody battle and nobody wins. It was invented in Canada, by a Greek guy, and named after a pineapple brand. That's not a pizza, that's a bad customs form.

Every other topping says "I'm here to be savory." Pineapple shows up like, "I'm also dessert. And I'm leaking." Now your ham is swimming in a warm fruit puddle, and the crust has the structural integrity of a wet napkin.

And the ham! Not even good ham. Sad, pink, circle ham, the kind that's been in a sandwich bag since a 2006 field trip.

Nobody orders it for themselves. It's always "I'll just get a Hawaiian for the table," said by the one guy who also says "I'm not really a *pizza* person."

Hawaii has never claimed it. Hawaii has been in court trying to get away from it.

b.text: Hawaiian pizza. Ham and pineapple. Somebody in Canada looked at a perfectly good pizza and said, "You know what this needs? Fruit that's been sitting in a can." Pineapple on pizza is a crime with a fruit salad alibi. It's sweet, it's salty, it's wet, and it's confused about what it wants to be, kind of like a dessert that got lost on the way to a breakfast buffet. And the ham? That's not ham, that's a lunch meat that went to college and dropped out. Every bite is a negotiation between a tropical vacation and a Tuesday at the deli counter. Hawaii didn't even invent this thing. A Greek-Canadian guy in Ontario did, in 1962, and then he just let it loose on the world like a dare.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text:
Apple Vision Pro: the only device where you pay $3,500 to be told your living room isn't good enough. It's a ski mask for people who want to look at spreadsheets in the void.

It weighs about a pound and a half, so after twenty minutes you don't have spatial computing, you have a chiropractor. And the battery lasts two hours, tethered to a pack in your pocket, so you're basically walking a tiny, expensive dog.

Apple said it was the future of work. The future of work is a man in Cupertino pinching the air like he's trying to catch a very slow fly.

And the "EyeSight" feature, where your eyes appear on the front? It's like a haunted Snapchat filter. Your family sees a creepy digital ghost of you, and you see them as a fuzzy video feed of people you're ignoring.

Three thousand five hundred dollars. For that I could buy a nice TV, a couch, and friends to sit on it.

b.text: Apple Vision Pro, everybody! Thirty-five hundred dollars to look like a scuba diver lost in a Best Buy. Apple insists it's not VR, it's "spatial computing," which is like calling a fanny pack "hip luggage." It's so heavy they had to throw in a second strap, and the battery's a separate brick on a cord, so you're basically a lamp that walks. Two hours of charge! That's not a computer, that's a matinee. Then there's EyeSight, the screen that shows your eyes on the front, so your family can watch a dim, blurry you stare at nothing. Most honest feature Apple's ever made. Netflix wouldn't even make an app. Netflix! They're on smart fridges! And your Persona looks like a hostage video filmed inside the uncanny valley.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's cousin who got into tech because you could "share a link." Congrats: now forty Anonymous Capybaras can watch me botch a VLOOKUP in real time. Your whole personality is "All changes saved in Drive," which is a weird flex when the change was Kevin sorting one column and detaching every employee from their salary. Version history isn't a feature; it's a crime scene. IMPORTRANGE says "Loading..." the way my dad said he was going out for milk. You've got a QUERY function that's just SQL in a fake mustache, yet you freeze if I paste more than twelve rows. And #REF! isn't an error message; it's you shrugging in all caps. You cap out at ten million cells. Ten million. You're the only spreadsheet with a bedtime.

b.text:
Google Sheets: the only software where you can watch a coworker named "Anonymous Capybara" ruin your formulas in real time.

You're the Excel that went to community college and told everyone it's "basically the same." Then someone adds 40,000 rows and you wheeze "Loading..." like a Chromebook climbing stairs.

Your formula for combining data from another sheet is IMPORTRANGE, which immediately yells #REF! until I click "Allow access," like I'm asking you to the prom. Your most advanced function, QUERY, makes me write SQL inside a text string, inside a cell, inside a spreadsheet. That's not a feature. That's a hostage video.

Every file on earth is named "Copy of Copy of Budget FINAL v2," shared with "anyone with the link," and owned by Brenda, who left in 2019. I click "Request edit access" and the void answers.

And the 10 million cell limit? Bold of you to assume anyone's budget is that organized. Mine is three tabs and a dream.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk, you're what happens when a bowl of oatmeal gets ghosted and decides to live in a carton. You're not milk. You're oatmeal that went through a breakup and is now "finding itself" in a Brooklyn coffee shop.

You cost seven dollars, and for that, you taste like a wet cereal bowl that someone rinsed with regret. Baristas call you "creamy." You're not creamy. You're just thick, like the guy at the party explaining his podcast.

You separate in hot coffee like you've got commitment issues, then leave a gritty film at the bottom that feels like drinking a handshake from a sandcastle.

And the label says "Barista Edition." Barista Edition? Oh good, you've got a job title now. Cow's milk never needed a LinkedIn.

Your whole personality is "I'm not dairy." Congratulations. Neither is drywall, and it's got a better shelf life.

b.text:
Oat milk, you're porridge that went to finishing school. Somebody looked at horse food and said, "What if it cost seventy cents extra?" Then somebody else said, "Yes, and put it in a carton that talks like a guy who just got back from Copenhagen." Your packaging has more personality than you do. Every box of Oatly reads like a cover letter: "Hi! We're a little weird!" No, you're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not a beverage. That's a salad dressing that gave up.

And the "Barista Edition"? You needed extra oil just to get a job. Enzymes break your starch into maltose, so technically you're a sugar spike in a flannel shirt. Plus you were funded by Blackstone. You're not anti-establishment, oat milk. You're a private equity firm wearing a beanie.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text: Esperanto is the language of hope, which is a polite way of saying nobody has needed it since 1887. Dr. Zamenhof built it so everyone on Earth could talk to each other, and it worked beautifully, provided everyone was a Polish optometrist who already spoke German. Every noun ends in -o and every adjective in -a, like the language is labeling its own furniture. Then it split over a rival called Ido, because Esperantists love a universal language so much they needed a second one to be mad at. The conferences are the best part: a thousand people who learned the same made-up language, hugging in a Bulgarian youth hostel, recognizing each other by little green star pins. Then they fly home, and the nearest person they can talk to is the one who only speaks English.

b.text:
Esperanto is the only product in history where the user manual promised world peace and the user base turned out to be eleven guys named Zbigniew arguing about the accusative case.

Zamenhof invented a language to unite humanity, and humanity said, "Cute. Does it have a Starbucks?"

It has sixteen grammar rules and no exceptions, which is exactly what a language sounds like when it's never been used by anyone angry. Try ordering a sandwich in a tongue where nobody has ever cheated on anyone or been cut off in traffic. Where's the slang? Where's the swearing? You can't build a culture on a word for "hello" and a really strong feeling about the letter ĥ.

Its greatest literary achievement is a translation of Hamlet. Even the original works are mostly translations of someone else's feelings.

And the flag is a green star. Not a country. A star. It's a nation-state with a logo and a dating pool smaller than a Dungeons & Dragons convention in Lithuania.

Mi amas vin, Esperanto. Nobody else does.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text: LaTeX, you're the only software that makes PhDs feel stupid. You're from 1984 and you dress like it: backslashes everywhere, curly braces like a nervous tic. I tell you to put a figure "here," and you treat "here" as a suggestion, then file it four pages later next to the bibliography, like a sock lost in a dryer. Your error messages are poetry: "Missing $ inserted." Inserted where? Why? You won't say. You just blame line 1 of a 40-page file because I typed an underscore in a URL. My citations are double question marks until I compile you twice, then a third time, out of spite. And everyone needs to know it's pronounced "lay-tech," not like the glove. Honestly, at least the glove stretches. Overfull \hbox? Badness 10000? Buddy, that's not a warning. That's your autobiography.

b.text: LaTeX, you're a word processor that makes me pass a programming exam just to type "hello." I need a backslash, three curly braces, and a prayer to make one word bold. Forget a single dollar sign and you scream "Missing $ inserted," like I personally mugged your math mode. Then you throw "Emergency stop" at me, which is rude, because I'm the one who's supposed to be panicking. Want a table? Enjoy three hours wrestling ampersands and \hline like they owe you money. Bibliography? Run the compiler three times, like a coach yelling "one more lap" because the first two didn't count. Your fans swear the output is gorgeous. Sure, so is a cathedral, and nobody builds a grocery list out of one.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk, you're porridge that went to finishing school. Somebody looked at horse food and said, "What if it cost seventy cents extra?" Then somebody else said, "Yes, and put it in a carton that talks like a guy who just got back from Copenhagen." Your packaging has more personality than you do. Every box of Oatly reads like a cover letter: "Hi! We're a little weird!" No, you're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not a beverage. That's a salad dressing that gave up.

And the "Barista Edition"? You needed extra oil just to get a job. Enzymes break your starch into maltose, so technically you're a sugar spike in a flannel shirt. Plus you were funded by Blackstone. You're not anti-establishment, oat milk. You're a private equity firm wearing a beanie.

b.text:
Oat milk, you're what happens when a bowl of oatmeal gets ghosted and starts a podcast. You're not milk. You're porridge that went through a breakup and a juice cleanse.

You cost eight dollars a carton, and the only reason is that a barista called you "creamy" once and you've been unbearable ever since. Cows have been doing this for ten thousand years for free. You needed an enzyme and a marketing team.

You separate in hot coffee like you're being deposed. You curdle at the first sign of acid, then expect me to drink you anyway.

And the label! "Barista Edition." For what? Standing near a espresso machine? You're a beige liquid with a gym membership.

Your whole personality is that you're not almond milk, which is the lowest bar in the dairy aisle, and somehow you still tripped over it. Sweet, slimy, smug. Basically a Sunday brunch in a carton.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ, hydrogen silsesquioxane, the only resist that's basically glass pretending to be a photoresist. You're a negative-tone resist that turns into silicon dioxide. So after all my work, my pattern isn't a mask, it's a permanent tenant.

Your shelf life is a joke. You gel in the bottle if I look at you wrong. Open a fresh one, two weeks later it's Jell-O with commitment issues. Keep it in the fridge, and it's still aging like milk in a sauna.

And the development! Sixty nanometer lines, beautiful, then TMAH hits and they collapse like a Jenga tower. Sure, you can do sub-10 nanometer features, but only if I sacrifice a goat, run at 1000 microcoulombs per square centimeter, and sit there for nine hours while the beam writes a rectangle.

Contrast? Terrible. Sensitivity? Worse. Stripping you off? Hydrofluoric acid. You're the ex who can only be removed by something that dissolves bones.

b.text: Let's talk about HSQ, the e-beam resist that's basically a diva. You spin it on, bake it, expose it, and it's supposed to be your friend, but it's secretly already becoming glass. Leave the bottle in the fridge too long and it gels into a sad, cloudy paste, like a relationship that stopped talking to you. Develop it in TMAH and it still acts like it's doing you a favor. And lift-off? Forget it. Once HSQ is exposed, it's SiO2 with a attitude, and it's not leaving your substrate without a fight. It's the only thing in the cleanroom that's been baked, exposed, and developed, and still wants to be left alone.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text: Crocs are shoes designed by someone who saw a bath mat and thought, "Yes, but what if it had holes so my feet could breathe while I pretend I'm a surgeon at a Cracker Barrel?" They look like the foam that sits on a hot dog's bun. They're the only footwear where the heel is basically a suggestion. You can't run in them, you can't hike in them, and you definitely can't sneak up on anyone, because every step sounds like a duck being slowly squeezed. And somehow they're on the feet of grown adults who own a mortgage. Nobody wears Crocs to look good. You wear Crocs because you've accepted that your feet have given up, and you've decided the shoe should match that energy. Honestly, respect. You're the only person at the Target parking lot who's fully at peace.

b.text:
Crocs are the only shoes that look like they were designed by someone who'd only had shoes described to them over a bad phone connection. "So it's a boat, but for your foot?" "Sure."

And the holes! Ventilation, they say. Which is great, because nothing says "protect my toes" like a shoe with a dozen open invitations for a dropped knife. They're the only footwear where a gentle rain and a kitchen spill both count as a personal attack.

Then there's the Jibbitz. You've taken a shoe that looks like a foam dinosaur egg and decided to accessorize it with a tiny plastic pizza. That's not fashion. That's a toddler's hostage negotiation.

And the strap! Pushed forward, it's "casual." Flipped back, it's "sport mode." Sport for what, Greg? You're carrying a rotisserie chicken to a barbecue.

Yet somehow, they're unbelievably comfortable. Which is the cruelest part. Every nurse, chef, and gardener secretly knows: they look like a mistake, and they feel like a hug. Crocs are ugly on purpose, and they won.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, you've been "five years from changing everything" since 1991. Thirty-plus years! Fusion power looks at you and says, "Take it easy, pal."

You're a hundred times stronger than steel, but only if you're one perfect, flawless, microscopic strand that nobody can actually make longer than a hair. Basically you're a gym bro who can bench a truck but only if it's in a vacuum, and he's the size of a bacterium.

You're just rolled-up graphene. You're a sheet of pencil lead that got into a yoga class and now thinks it's special.

Every grant proposal says you'll build a space elevator. Meanwhile, the only thing you've actually lifted is my hopes and a tennis racket.

And toxicologists say you act like asbestos in the lungs. Incredible range: strongest material ever, also a lawsuit.

You're not the future. You're soot with a publicist.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The only material that's been "five years away" since 1991. You're a hundred times stronger than steel, and you've used that strength to hold together... a tennis racket. They promised us a space elevator; you can't get past a few centimeters without a defect. That's not a cable, that's a toothpick with a press agent.

You're basically graphene that rolled itself up out of insecurity, and graphene still got the Nobel. Your cousin the buckyball got one too. You got a shoutout in a bike-frame brochure.

You can't even decide if you're a metal or a semiconductor; it depends on the angle you got rolled at. You clump together like nerds at a mixer, and the second you escape, you lodge in lungs like asbestos. Strongest thing on Earth, and your best trick is ending up in a safety data sheet.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Microsoft Teams is the only app that marks me "Away" after five minutes of deep thought but keeps me "Available" for three hours after I've died. It's not software. It's a hall monitor in a purple vest.

Teams eats more RAM than the game I'm pretending not to play. It launches on startup uninvited, then takes four minutes to load a chat that just says "ok."

Where are my files? SharePoint. Where's SharePoint? Nobody knows. Teams ships them off like a kid to boarding school.

Then they gave us "New Teams," which is Old Teams with a fresh coat of lag. IT has told me to "clear the cache" so often I do it in my sleep.

Nobody chose Teams. It came free with Office. Fitting, since so did Clippy.

b.text: Microsoft Teams, you're the only app with the nerve to open itself the second I log in, like a hall monitor who got promoted. Every meeting starts with the same ritual: "Can you hear me?" "You're on mute." "Sorry, you're on mute." Thirty seconds of people unmuting like it's a hostage situation. And that little "Someone is typing..." bubble? It's been there since Tuesday. Nobody's typing, Teams. Nobody's ever typing. You tell me I'm "Available" while I'm literally in a meeting, then ping me four minutes after everyone else has already replied. "Let's take this offline," says the guy, and then he schedules a Teams call about it. Teams, you're not a chat app. You're a conference room that follows you home.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, the only city that looked at the Mojave Desert and said, "You know what this needs? Venice." Nothing says Italian romance like a gondolier singing in a mall next to a Cheesecake Factory.

You built a half-size Eiffel Tower, a fake New York, and a pyramid, because why visit the world when you can visit its gift shop?

No clocks, no windows, and carpet designed by a migraine, all so you won't notice you've been feeding a penny slot since Tuesday.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas." Yeah. Especially your money. And the $45 resort fee for a pool you couldn't use because a bachelor party from Ohio was in it.

And Lake Mead's drying up so fast they keep finding bodies. Even the mob's secrets can't stay in Vegas anymore.

b.text: Vegas, you're the only city where the pyramid has a light beam shooting into space, and somehow the most depressing thing is the hotel. You've got a fake Venice with a gondolier who's clearly on a break from his real job at the Gap. Eiffel Tower at 1/4 scale, so the French are just fine with you as long as you keep the Eiffel Tower a little embarrassed. Your slogan is "What happens here stays here," which is a lie, because I've seen what happens here, and it's all showing up on my credit card statement in the spring. You run on oxygen that's pumped into casinos so nobody notices the clock. Your buffets are all-you-can-eat, which is a dare. You're a city built on the idea that the house always wins, and honestly, Vegas, you're the house.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8 was the only operating system that made you feel like a burglar in your own computer. You'd boot up, and there's no Start button. Microsoft just removed it, like a doctor deciding you've never needed a pulse.

Instead, you got a screen of giant colorful tiles, designed for tablets, which you didn't own, running on a desktop, which you did. Every app opened full-screen, so checking the weather meant your entire monitor said "72 degrees" at you in a font the size of a billboard.

And how do you shut it down? Hover your mouse in the top-right corner, wait for the Charms bar to appear like a shy ghost, click Settings, then Power. Four steps to turn off a computer. People Googled it. Millions of people Googled how to turn off their computer.

Then came the hot corners, where moving your mouse an inch too far opened things you didn't ask for.

Microsoft eventually apologized with 8.1 by bringing back the Start button. It just opened the tiles. That's not an apology. That's a hostage returning your shoe.

b.text: Windows 8 looked at the Start button and said, "Nah." Microsoft deleted the one thing everybody used to find anything, then replaced it with a full-screen wall of colored squares that look like a bathroom tile sample. Want to shut down? Swipe in from the right edge to open the Charms Bar, dig through Settings, and click a power icon hidden like it's in witness protection. The live tiles are my favorite. My Mail tile keeps showing me a headline about a sale from 2013. Eight years of muscle memory, gone, so I could enjoy a touchscreen I didn't buy on a desktop I didn't ask for.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text: Juicero built a $400 Wi-Fi press whose entire job was squeezing a bag. Not a fruit. A bag. Somebody looked at a pouch of pre-chopped kale and decided it needed a computer. Then a reporter showed everyone you could wring the packs out with your bare hands, and the venture capitalists went quiet, like they'd just realized their $120 million bought a very expensive pair of hands. The press checked a QR code before it would crush your spinach. That's the most Silicon Valley sentence ever written: the machine needed permission to juice. The packs cost about five bucks each, so you were paying premium prices to do what a Capri Sun does on its own.

b.text:
Juicero, you were a $400 Wi-Fi-connected juicer that delivered four tons of force, enough, your engineers bragged, to lift two Teslas, and Bloomberg proved the job could be done by a guy with hands. You raised $120 million from Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins to compete with *squeezing*. Every single customer already owned the competing product. It came in pairs.

You sold $8 bags of chopped produce that had to scan a QR code and phone home before you'd juice them. A juicer that needed internet. Imagine the outage: "Sorry, AWS is down, enjoy your sealed pouch of regret." You'd refuse to press an expired pack, like a bouncer for kale.

Doug Evans compared himself to Steve Jobs. Steve Jobs put a thousand songs in your pocket. Doug put a sack of mush in a vise and asked for your Wi-Fi password. Silicon Valley's most expensive way to say, "Just use your hands."

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text: Excel, you're the Swiss Army knife of spreadsheets, except every blade is rusty and one of them is just a tiny cursor that's been stuck in a cell since 1998. You've got 17,000 functions and I still can't find the one that sums things without you auto-converting my zip codes into scientific notation. You turned "1-2" into a date. Nobody asked you to. Your autocorrect thinks my gene names are calendar events. And your formulas? One missing parenthesis and suddenly I'm staring at #VALUE! like it's a personal insult. Forty years in, you still can't tell me what I did wrong. You just sit there, green triangle in the corner, judging me.

b.text:
Excel, you're the only software so powerful that scientists had to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into a date. You didn't adapt to biology; biology adapted to you. Type a phone number and you lop off the leading zero like it owes you money. Enter a credit card number and you serve back 4.53E+15, as if I'm splitting dinner with a physicist.

You still think 1900 was a leap year. It wasn't. You've known for decades. You just don't care.

You're running entire national economies and you still panic over merged cells. The UK lost sixteen thousand COVID cases because someone used your old .xls format and you quietly ran out of rows. No warning. Just vibes.

And VLOOKUP only looks right. Thirty years we spent squinting at #N/A before you finally invented XLOOKUP, like a guy who learns to turn left at fifty.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk, you're what happens when a bowl of oatmeal gets ghosted and starts a podcast. You're not milk. You're porridge that went through a breakup and a juice cleanse.

You cost eight dollars a carton, and the only reason is that a barista called you "creamy" once and you've been unbearable ever since. Cows have been doing this for ten thousand years for free. You needed an enzyme and a marketing team.

You separate in hot coffee like you're being deposed. You curdle at the first sign of acid, then expect me to drink you anyway.

And the label! "Barista Edition." For what? Standing near a espresso machine? You're a beige liquid with a gym membership.

Your whole personality is that you're not almond milk, which is the lowest bar in the dairy aisle, and somehow you still tripped over it. Sweet, slimy, smug. Basically a Sunday brunch in a carton.

b.text:
Oat milk, you are porridge that got a publicist. Somebody looked at the breakfast of Victorian orphans and said, "What if it cost six dollars and had a font?"

Your carton talks to me. Oatly, I'm trying to make coffee, not get into a pen-pal situation with a beverage that writes like a substitute teacher who wants to be called "Dave."

You're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not milk, that's a salad dressing that gave up. And they had to add enzymes to turn your starch into sugar so you'd taste like something. You're the only "health drink" that spikes my blood sugar like a Pop-Tart.

There's a "Barista Edition" now. Oat milk, there are two editions of you. Moby-Dick has fewer editions than you.

And you're beige. You make every latte look like dishwater with ambition.

Horses eat oats for free, and they still look embarrassed for us.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text: Risk, you're the only game where "world domination" takes longer than actual world domination. Genghis Khan conquered Asia faster than my cousin conquered Ukraine, and my cousin had six armies and a dream. Your map looks like it was drawn from a description of Earth overheard on a bus. Kamchatka borders Alaska? Irkutsk and Yakutsk get more real estate than most of Africa? You taught a generation that the winning strategy is hiding in Australia like a coward and waiting for everyone else to bleed out over Siam. The defender wins ties, which explains the forty armies I lost trying to get through one guy in Egypt. And one plastic cannon is worth ten soldiers? Finally, accurate military budgeting. Five hours in, two players left, nobody's had fun since the first card set. That's not a board game, Risk. That's a hostage situation.

b.text: Risk is the only board game where the map is the villain. Australia is one continent with four borders, and somehow it's the thing everyone wants to fight over. Kamchatka is a Russian peninsula nobody could find if you paid them, and it becomes the most important place on Earth for six straight hours. You know the game's dragging when you're hoping someone rolls a three just to end the suffering. The dice are cheap six-siders you shake in a cup, so entire wars get decided by two guys who could lose a continent in the time it takes to say "I'm not mad, I'm just disappointed." And there's always that guy eliminated since nine o'clock, still sitting at the table holding his cards like a hostage negotiation, begging someone to betray their ally and save him. Nobody has ever finished Risk. You just stop when the pizza's cold.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista, the only operating system that asked "Are you sure?" before letting you breathe. You wanted to open Notepad? Cancel or Allow. You clicked Allow? Are you *really* sure? It had the confidence of a bouncer and the competence of a toddler.

Microsoft promised "Wow." Users said "Why?" Then "Where's my RAM?" Then "Where's my printer driver?" Then "Where's XP?"

It launched with a sticker that said "Vista Capable," which turned out to mean "Capable of displaying a sad blue spinning circle on your brand-new laptop."

Copying a file took so long that Vista estimated "20 minutes remaining," then "3 days," then "Discovering..." forever. Aero looked gorgeous, like a Ferrari with no engine.

Apple made an entire ad campaign out of mocking you, Vista, and the worst part is Microsoft just sat there, clicked Allow, and said "Yes, I'm sure."

b.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Five years in development as "Longhorn," and the only thing that shipped on time was the disappointment. They cut WinFS but kept the Aero glass. Finally, an operating system you could see right through.

Vista came in six editions, from Starter to Ultimate, which is five more ways to pay for the same crash. Microsoft slapped "Vista Capable" stickers on computers that could barely run Solitaire, then got sued. The only thing Vista ever finished loading was a class action.

And User Account Control! "Are you sure you want to do that?" Every. Single. Click. Vista was the only software that needed permission to exist, and honestly? We should've hit Cancel.

Copying a file: "Calculating time remaining…" Vista, you were calculating until 2009, when Microsoft fixed you, renamed you Windows 7, and pretended you were adopted.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text: Keurig, you're the only appliance that makes a cup of coffee and then apologizes for it by making you wait four minutes while it hums like a dying refrigerator. You're a single-serve machine with the commitment of a Tinder profile: one pod, one cup, and you'll never call back. Every morning I stare into your little plastic mouth, feed you a pod that cost more per ounce than gold, and you spit out something that tastes like a coffee bean's ghost. And the recycling? Those pods are tiny landfills with lids. You didn't make coffee, Keurig. You made a subscription plan wearing a drip tray. Even your name sounds like a sneeze that got a corporate loan.

b.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest drink in human history (hot water, beans) and added a subscription model. Your own inventor said he regrets making you. Imagine your dad publicly apologizing for you and you're still in every dentist's waiting room.

You tried DRM on coffee. Keurig 2.0 literally scanned pods and refused to brew anything off-brand. You're the only appliance that's ever asked me for a license.

Every K-Cup costs more per pound than a decent steak, and you've buried enough of them to circle the Earth a dozen times. Archaeologists will dig them up and assume we worshipped tiny plastic thimbles.

And the Keurig Kold? A $370 soda machine that died faster than the flat Coke it made.

Your descale light blinks like a cry for help. Honestly, same.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: Macau, you're the only city where the fake Venice has better canals than the real one. You dredged your land out of the sea, built a replica of Venice on top, and hired gondoliers to sing to tourists who just lost their rent at baccarat. Your economy is one enormous slot machine with a Portuguese accent. Your most famous landmark is a church facade with nothing behind it, which is the most honest thing on your skyline. You're 33 square kilometers, so small you can walk across yourself before your egg tart cools. Everybody comes to you to lose money, and you're thrilled to take it. Keep the lights on, little sinner.

b.text:
Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a front wall. Fitting, since the whole city is a facade: a fake Venice with a painted sky, a half-size Eiffel Tower, and a Grand Lisboa that looks like a golden pineapple trying to cheat at baccarat.

Portugal ruled you for 442 years and left behind egg tarts and street signs nobody can pronounce. Four centuries, one pastry.

You've made several times more gambling money than Las Vegas, yet your signature dish is a pork chop jammed in a bun. Classy.

Half your land was dug out of the sea, which is perfect, because the other half was dug out of tourists' pockets.

And they built a 55-kilometer bridge to connect you to Hong Kong, and it's emptier than a junket operator's promises. Even the bridge is losing at the tables.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies, the only investment where your financial advisor was a woman named Deb at a card shop. People kept them in plastic cases, like organ donors. Not toys, relics. "Don't touch Princess the bear, she's for college." Princess was a purple bear stuffed with plastic pellets and a dead princess's legacy, and your mom thought she'd pay for Yale.

The genius was the tag. Not the toy, the tag. Ty looked at a bag of beans and said, "What if we made it illegal to love this?" Bend that heart-shaped tag and you've lost four thousand dollars. Kids learned grief early: "I hugged Peanut the elephant, and now he's worth nothing."

Then the retirements. Ty killed off bears like a Game of Thrones writer with a mortgage. Fall for Squealer the pig and he's gone by Tuesday, replaced by a slightly different pig.

Today they're in a garage in Ohio, sweating in a bin, worth less than the bin.

b.text:
Beanie Babies, look at you. Half bear, half beanbag, all retirement plan that never paid out. An entire generation of parents bought you instead of index funds. Somewhere a man is still storing Princess, the purple Diana bear, in a climate-controlled unit, waiting for the market to "recover." Buddy, the market recovered. It just didn't take you with it.

Your most valuable feature was a heart-shaped paper tag. People bought plastic tag protectors. For the tag. That's like buying a phone case for your receipt.

And every tag had a little poem rhyming "bear" with "care." Hallmark called that lazy.

A Las Vegas couple had to divide you on a courtroom floor during their divorce, one at a time. That's the most anyone has wanted you since 1999: only to make sure their ex didn't get you.

Ty Warner got a billion dollars. You got plastic pellets.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text: Carbon nanotubes are the most stressed-out material on Earth. They're stronger than steel, and they've been "five years from revolutionizing everything" since 1991. They're just graphene that got rolled up and never recovered. Ask one whether it's a metal or a semiconductor and it genuinely can't tell you until someone tests it. In the lab they clump together like cold spaghetti. For thirty years industry has promised them in batteries, bike frames, and space elevators. The only space elevator I've seen is the one in my dorm, and it doesn't work either. Their best feature is that under a microscope they look exactly like asbestos, which is a bold thing for a material to bring to a party.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The strongest material known to science, and you still can't hold a job. Since the nineties you've promised us a space elevator. Your longest strand is about half a meter. That's not an elevator. That's floss with a publicist.

You're graphene that rolled over and gave up. Graphene got a Nobel Prize. You got an argument over whether Soviets spotted you in 1952.

You can't even decide what you are. Twist one way, you're a metal. Twist the other, you're a semiconductor. Nobody controls it, including you. That's not versatility. That's a chirality crisis.

Drop you in any liquid and you clump together like freshmen at a mixer.

And inhale you? Suddenly you behave like asbestos. Thirty years of hype, and your most reliable talent is impersonating the one material we paid billions to rip out of schools.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim is the only software where the tutorial is "how to leave." Millions of developers have spent a Tuesday trapped inside it, mashing Escape like they're trying to wake a hostage. You open a file, type "hello," and the editor responds by deleting your paragraph and playing a macro you recorded in 2019.

Vim users say, "Once you learn it, you'll never touch your mouse again." Neither will you touch grass, sir. You've spent forty hours configuring a .vimrc so you can save four seconds on a typo.

And the modes! Normal mode, where nothing is normal. Insert mode, where you finally get to insert. Visual mode, which is only visual in the sense that you can watch yourself select the wrong thing.

It's an editor built on the premise that your keyboard has too many keys and your dignity has too much room.

Type :wq to save and quit. Type :q! to forget this ever happened.

b.text:
Vim, you're the only text editor with its own hostage negotiation thread. Millions of people have viewed the Stack Overflow question on how to leave you. That's not a user base, that's a missing persons report.

You have modes. Normal mode, where typing does nothing normal, and Insert mode, hidden behind the letter "i" like a secret menu.

Your fans move the cursor with h, j, k, l because a terminal from 1976 printed arrows on those keys. That's not efficiency, that's Stockholm syndrome on the home row.

Every Vim user has a 900-line .vimrc copied from a stranger and is too scared to touch it. And when you crash, you leave .swp files behind like a burglar who signs the guestbook.

Even your own kids forked you into Neovim. That's not a fork. That's an intervention.

Goodnight! :wq… :q!… ESC ESC ESC…

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista, you were the operating system that asked permission to open the calculator. Every time I tried to delete a file, you'd pop up a box asking "Are you sure?" like I was a toddler with scissors. Then you'd ask again. And again. Your User Account Control was so annoying that people turned it off just to get their work done, which I guess was the security equivalent of removing the smoke detector because it beeps.

And Aero! Gorgeous glass windows that ran great on the computer that cost four thousand dollars and crawled on everything else. You had "Vista Capable" stickers on machines that couldn't actually run you. That's not a sticker, that's a hostage note.

b.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Microsoft spent five years building you as "Longhorn," and somehow you still came out premature.

Your slogan was "The Wow Starts Now." You meant "Now" as in "after the loading circle finishes." People bought laptops with "Vista Capable" stickers, which turned out to mean "capable of being sued over." Those machines couldn't even run Aero, so they got a see-through window theme with nothing to see.

And User Account Control! You asked "Are you sure?" so many times that you became the first operating system with separation anxiety.

You came in six editions, including "Ultimate," whose big exclusive was DreamScene: a moving wallpaper for the ten minutes you weren't hunting for printer drivers.

Microsoft had to trick people into liking you. The Mojave Experiment! Your own parents had to put you in disguise.

Your greatest feature? The XP downgrade.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you're the coffee maker that treats a cup of coffee like a hostage negotiation. Eight minutes of whirring, gurgling, and blinking just to produce a lukewarm thimble of brown water. Meanwhile my grandma's percolator makes a full pot before I finish reading the Wikipedia article about pour-over.

And the pods! Every cup creates a little plastic tombstone. You're basically a landfill with a power button. You've got more recyclable-pod-related guilt than my Catholic school.

Then there's the "strong" setting, which is just the regular setting with a dramatic pause. Nothing about you is bold except your price per ounce.

Keurig, you're not a coffee maker. You're a vending machine that got a cardiology degree.

b.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest thing humanity ever did, pouring hot water over beans, and turned it into a subscription-based hostage situation. You charge me fifty cents for a thimble of coffee wrapped in a tiny plastic coffin that will outlive my great-grandchildren.

The inventor of the K-Cup literally apologized for it. The guy said he sometimes regrets inventing it. Your own father looked at his creation and said, "Yeah, I'd undo that."

And the machine itself? You push one button and it screams like a dying dial-up modem, then dribbles out something called "Bold" that tastes like a warm handshake from a wet paper bag. Every morning it flashes "Descale Me" like a needy ex. Meanwhile your water reservoir holds enough for exactly one bad decision.

Offices love you because nothing says "we value our employees" like a sad pod carousel next to a broken microwave.

Keurig: for people who want coffee, but also want to feel something about landfills.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, the "King of Fruits." Sure, if the kingdom is a landfill. You're banned on the Singapore subway, right there on the sign next to flammable liquids, because apparently you're the bigger hazard. Hotels fine guests for sneaking you in. That's not a fruit, that's a parole violation.

You wear a medieval mace as a jacket, which is smart, since nobody who's smelled you wants to get close anyway. You fall out of trees and put people in the hospital. You're the only produce that needs a hard hat AND a hazmat suit.

And your fans swear you're "like custard!" Sure: custard aged in a gym bag full of rotten onions. Fifty bucks for a Musang King, and your breath's a crime scene for three days.

Anthony Bourdain ate warthog rectum on camera, and *you're* the one he warned people about.

b.text:
Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which is wild, because you dress like a medieval mace and smell like a crime scene. You're the only fruit with a body armor package AND a hazmat warning.

You're banned from Singapore's subway, hotels, and airlines. Think about that. Nobody bans the pineapple. You're the only produce item that gets kicked off a plane before it even boards.

Your fans say, "Just get past the smell, the taste is heavenly." Sir, that's what every hostage says about their captor.

You taste like custard that's been cheating on a sewer with an onion. Eat one and your fridge smells like you for three weeks, your breath for five.

And you fall out of trees onto people's heads. You're not even content to be a bad meal. You want to be a *weapon*.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass, the glasses that made everyone around you feel like they were being recorded for a documentary nobody asked for. You wore them to a dinner party and suddenly you weren't a guest, you were a surveillance operation with a nice haircut. Nobody could tell if you were looking at them or at the tiny little screen floating in your eyeball, which, let's be honest, is the exact same energy as a guy who keeps checking his phone while you're talking about your dead dog.

And that little camera! It was always pointed at people's faces like a tiny, judgmental lighthouse. People said "Glasshole" and honestly? They weren't wrong. Google spent years saying "you'll get used to it," and the public said, "We won't, but thanks for the offer."

b.text:
Google Glass, look at you. Fifteen hundred dollars to wear a sugar cube on your eyebrow. Sergey Brin had skydivers jump onto a building to launch you, and that was the last time anything about you was cool.

You invented a whole new insult. Nobody calls iPhone owners "Phoneholes." But "Glasshole"? Earned. Fast. Because you let people take photos by *winking*. You turned flirting into a privacy violation.

Every sentence started with "OK Glass," like a man narrating his own midlife crisis out loud. Bars banned you. Strangers ripped you off people's faces. Your battery died faster than your reputation, and you overheated right next to the user's brain, which honestly explains the buying decision.

Then you pivoted to "Enterprise," the tech version of moving back home to work at your uncle's warehouse.

And even the warehouse let you go.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, you're the only app where a little green dot controls people's moods. We all stare at it like a heart monitor. "Dave's active? Dave's ignoring me personally."

You turned "quick question" into a four-hour ordeal. Somebody types "hey," then nothing, and the whole office watches three little dots dance for twenty minutes like they're drafting the Gettysburg Address. Then comes "can you hop on a huddle?" Nobody has ever hopped.

And #random? That channel has never been random. It's a graveyard of cat GIFs and a 2019 poll about lunch.

You're the reason we have 47 unread notifications and zero idea what's going on. Do Not Disturb is your most-ignored feature, and you know it.

b.text:
Slack, you took "this meeting could've been an email" and made it "this email could've been forty-seven threaded replies and a thumbs-up emoji."

You've got a green dot next to my name, which means my boss thinks I'm available. I'm not available. I'm just *loaded*. There's a difference, and it's called a bathroom break.

Every Monday, "Hey" arrives with no follow-up. Just "Hey." Then three dots appear, disappear, appear, disappear. Is she typing a novel or a resignation?

You gave us channels, and we made #random, #random-2, and #random-actually-random. Somewhere, a guy named Doug is in forty-one channels and has muted forty. He reacts to everything with a salute emoji and calls it leadership.

And that notification sound? That little knock-knock-knock? Pavlov would've been proud. I flinch at wooden doors now.

You're not a productivity tool. You're a very expensive way to watch coworkers say "circling back."

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a wall. The Ruins of St. Paul's: a gorgeous front with absolutely nothing behind it, which is basically your whole personality. You've got a fake Venice with a painted sky, a fake Paris with a half-size Eiffel Tower, and you're so tiny you had to dump dirt into the ocean just to fit a runway. You out-earned Las Vegas several times over, and your signature dish is still a pork chop jammed in a bun. The Portuguese stayed four hundred years and left you an egg tart and street signs nobody reads. The Grand Lisboa looks like a golden pineapple having a breakdown. And the Macau Tower's big attraction is jumping off it, which, after a night at the baccarat tables, is less a thrill ride and more a financial plan.

b.text:
Macau, you're what happens when Portugal and Las Vegas have a one-night stand and nobody wants to claim the kid. You have a Venetian with fake canals, a fake sky, and a gondolier singing "O Sole Mio" in a Chinese province. Not even Italy does that to itself.

You make more gambling money than Vegas by a factor of several, which means you're basically a very successful casino with a cobblestone problem.

Your egg tarts are better than Portugal's, and everyone knows it, including Portugal, who's still mad. Your Eiffel Tower is half-size, your Parisian is half-French, and your Grand Lisboa looks like a golden lotus ate a disco ball.

You're 12 square miles and somehow have traffic jams at the border from people who lost everything and still want to come back. That's not tourism. That's an abusive relationship with a buffet.

Even your ruins are just a facade. St. Paul's is literally one wall. You couldn't keep the church, but you kept the slot machines.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word, you're the only software where pressing Enter once can rearrange my entire document like a Rubik's cube in an earthquake.

You've got a paperclip-shaped trauma in your past, and honestly, he was the only one who ever tried to help. Now it's just you, auto-correcting "ducking" into things I definitely didn't mean to say to my boss.

Bullet points? You take them personally. I press Tab, you indent. I press Backspace, you un-indent, delete the bullet, and change the font to Comic Sans out of spite.

I tried to put one picture on page two. Page six now has a single sentence and a sense of dread.

And the green squiggly line? Judgmental. The red one? Fine, I misspelled "necessary." But you underlined my own name like I'm the one who's wrong.

You've been around since 1983 and still can't tell me why Save As has seven different locations. Ribbon? More like a ribbon of confusion. Truly, you're a masterpiece of formatting I never asked for.

b.text:
Microsoft Word, you're the only program that's been around for forty years and still can't tell me where the bullet point ends. I type one dash, hit enter, and suddenly you're deciding I'm running a whole bulleted empire. I try to undo it and you go, "Nope, here's an indented sub-bullet instead." Thanks, Clippy's grumpy cousin.

And the "Track Changes" feature? You're named after a document, but you treat every edit like a crime scene. Someone changes "the" to "a" and suddenly the whole page looks like a kindergarten finger painting, red lines everywhere, and nobody knows who did it.

Then there's the page numbers. Page one is perfect. Page two is fine. Page nine just quietly starts itself over at one because you got bored.

Forty years, Word. You've seen everything. Still can't center a title without me holding my breath.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Monopoly is the only game where the winner is whoever gets lucky early and the loser is whoever's still playing at 2 a.m. It was designed to teach people that landlords are evil, and somehow it became the thing families play to prove it.

Four hours in, you've got a dad mortgaging Baltic Avenue, a cousin who "forgot" to charge rent, and a kid crying over the thimble. Nobody's ever finished a game. We just stop when someone flips the board.

And the money! You're handed pastel Monopoly bills like it's a deranged Easter egg hunt, then told you owe $200 for "income tax." In a game about capitalism, Free Parking pays out nothing, but everyone insists it does, because house rules are the only thing keeping this thing alive.

The best part: the shoe, the dog, and the iron are all fighting over Boardwalk. Meanwhile, the Community Chest says I won second place in a beauty contest. Ten dollars. Great.

b.text: Monopoly is the only board game where the goal is to bankrupt your friends and somehow everyone still agrees to play it again. Four hours. Four hours! Nobody has ever finished a game of Monopoly. The game just ends when someone's dad flips the table, or when the banker quietly starts pretending they didn't count the money properly. And the banker, by the way, is always the least trustworthy person at the table, because they're the one holding the stack of cash and they're the one who "forgot" to collect Free Parking. Free Parking! That's not a gift, that's a lie you tell children. And Boardwalk? Nobody's ever landed on Boardwalk and felt lucky. They just felt the rent go up like a hostage negotiation. Monopoly: where your uncle buys every railroad and calls it a "strategy."

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text: Oat milk, you're the Prius of dairy alternatives. You show up at brunch with a tote bag full of opinions, and everybody claps like you saved the planet. Meanwhile you're just oats that got put through a blender and came out looking like wet cardboard with a lawyer. You froth beautifully, sure, but you froth like a guy who just found out his barista certificate expired. And don't get me started on "barista edition." Nobody's a barista because they bought a carton with a cartoon on it. You're basically a shampoo that gave up on being a shampoo and decided to be a latte. Nobody asked you to be creamy. You just showed up creamy-adjacent and expected a parade.

b.text:
Oat milk, you're what happens when a bowl of oatmeal gets ghosted and starts a podcast. You're not milk. You're porridge that went through a breakup and a juice cleanse.

You cost eight dollars a carton, and the only reason is that a barista called you "creamy" once and you've been unbearable ever since. Cows have been doing this for ten thousand years for free. You needed an enzyme and a marketing team.

You separate in hot coffee like you're being deposed. You curdle at the first sign of acid, then expect me to drink you anyway.

And the label! "Barista Edition." For what? Standing near a espresso machine? You're a beige liquid with a gym membership.

Your whole personality is that you're not almond milk, which is the lowest bar in the dairy aisle, and somehow you still tripped over it. Sweet, slimy, smug. Basically a Sunday brunch in a carton.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
Canberra is what happens when a committee designs a city and nobody's allowed to have an opinion until the subcommittee reports back. It's the only place where the lake is fake, the hills are decorative, and the excitement is a roundabout. Seriously, you can't give directions without saying "take the third exit, then the third exit again, then cry."

It's a city of 450,000 people, and 449,000 of them are named "Director of Strategic Alignment." The nightlife is a public servant having a second flat white after 2 p.m. Wild.

Every winter it hits minus five, and the locals call that "character." Every summer it's bushfire smoke, so basically a free vape.

And the Aussie icon is a giant flagpole. That's the whole personality: a pole, and a stern reminder to submit your timesheet.

Canberra: a nice place to visit if you've never wanted to.

b.text: Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree, so Australia built a city nobody wanted, which is honestly the most Canberra origin story possible: a compromise with suburbs. They held an international design competition and hired two Americans to plan it, and they nailed the brief: "Make it impossible to find anything." Every road is a roundabout leading to another roundabout, encircling a fake lake named after the guy who designed the roundabouts. Your Parliament House has a grass roof so you can literally walk on top of the government, the only time anyone in Canberra is above a public servant. The kangaroos outnumber the nightlife. For decades your two biggest attractions were legal fireworks and X-rated videos, which tells me the locals needed both a bang and a release. Then you banned the fireworks. Now the excitement is Floriade: a month of staring at tulips because the alternative is Tuggeranong.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text:
Apple Vision Pro: the only device where you pay $3,500 to be told your living room isn't good enough. It's a ski mask for people who want to look at spreadsheets in the void.

It weighs about a pound and a half, so after twenty minutes you don't have spatial computing, you have a chiropractor. And the battery lasts two hours, tethered to a pack in your pocket, so you're basically walking a tiny, expensive dog.

Apple said it was the future of work. The future of work is a man in Cupertino pinching the air like he's trying to catch a very slow fly.

And the "EyeSight" feature, where your eyes appear on the front? It's like a haunted Snapchat filter. Your family sees a creepy digital ghost of you, and you see them as a fuzzy video feed of people you're ignoring.

Three thousand five hundred dollars. For that I could buy a nice TV, a couch, and friends to sit on it.

b.text:
Apple Vision Pro, you cost $3,499 and still need a battery on a cord like a 1996 Walkman. Two hours of charge? That's not spatial computing, that's a matinee. Wear glasses? Zeiss inserts, extra. Apple saw you squinting and smelled revenue.

And EyeSight! A front screen showing your eyes so people feel connected. Nothing says "I'm present" like blurry cartoon eyeballs trapped behind ski-goggle glass. Your Persona avatar looks like a hostage video directed by a ghost.

You promised the future, and Netflix wouldn't even make you an app. You strap over a pound to dads' faces so they can record "spatial memories" of birthdays they watched through a screen.

Apple said you'd never see the world the same way. True. Now it's through a $3,500 face fridge.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
