Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Klingon, a language designed by a linguist for a race of warriors, and somehow it still has a word for "tea" but no word for "hello." You people invented a whole culture of honor and glory, and the greeting is "What do you want?" That's not a language, that's a customer service line at a gym.

The grammar is object-verb-subject. Of course it is. Even the sentence structure says "I'm going to stab the dinner first and tell you who did it later."

Klingon has a phrase for "Today is a good day to die," but you try ordering a sandwich. Nope. Because no Klingon ever said, "Could I get that on rye?" They said, "Bring me the still-moving thing."

And the fans! Thousands of people speaking fluent guttural phlegm, getting married in it, translating Hamlet. Shakespeare in the original Klingon, which is just regular Shakespeare, but now the soliloquy sounds like someone clearing their throat at a funeral.

Qapla'? More like Qa-please-stop.

b.text: Klingon is the only language where clearing your throat counts as a complete sentence. Its creators looked at English and said, "Too soft." So they built a tongue where every word sounds like a dog choking on a gravel driveway. Ask a Klingon for "good morning" and you'll get a cough from the sewer, followed by a threat about your mother's forehead. The apostrophes are everywhere, like someone sneezed punctuation across the page. Qapla'! Qapla'? Qapla'. Half the vocabulary is for dishonor and the other half is for knives. Fans spent decades memorizing it, which tells you they really wanted to be insulted with conviction. Even the Duolingo owl looks nervous when it comes up.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ, everybody! The only resist that ages faster than the grad student using it. You spin it Monday, expose it Tuesday, and suddenly your dose curve has gone through a midlife crisis. It has to live in the fridge like expired yogurt, and it's about as forgiving.

HSQ brags about sub-10-nanometer lines. Sure, if you've got six hours of write time, because this diva needs a dose that could sterilize a hospital. Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you're desperate, *salt water*. Your whole career is literally seasoned with tears now.

And once it's exposed? It turns into glass. Brittle, cracking glass. You wanted a mask; you got a window that shatters when you look at it. Want it gone? Hope you enjoy hydrofluoric acid, the chemical that dissolves your bones.

HSQ: beautiful resolution, terrible personality. It's not negative-tone. It's just negative.

b.text: Let's talk about HSQ, the e-beam resist that's basically a diva. You spin it on, bake it, expose it, and it's supposed to be your friend, but it's secretly already becoming glass. Leave the bottle in the fridge too long and it gels into a sad, cloudy paste, like a relationship that stopped talking to you. Develop it in TMAH and it still acts like it's doing you a favor. And lift-off? Forget it. Once HSQ is exposed, it's SiO2 with a attitude, and it's not leaving your substrate without a fight. It's the only thing in the cleanroom that's been baked, exposed, and developed, and still wants to be left alone.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Microsoft Teams is the only app that marks me "Away" after five minutes of deep thought but keeps me "Available" for three hours after I've died. It's not software. It's a hall monitor in a purple vest.

Teams eats more RAM than the game I'm pretending not to play. It launches on startup uninvited, then takes four minutes to load a chat that just says "ok."

Where are my files? SharePoint. Where's SharePoint? Nobody knows. Teams ships them off like a kid to boarding school.

Then they gave us "New Teams," which is Old Teams with a fresh coat of lag. IT has told me to "clear the cache" so often I do it in my sleep.

Nobody chose Teams. It came free with Office. Fitting, since so did Clippy.

b.text: You know what Teams is? It's the office that's always on fire but nobody's ever seen the smoke. Every message comes with "...is typing" for six minutes, and then it says "Hi." Your green dot says "Available" while you're literally in the bathroom. You join a meeting and the first ten minutes are "Can you hear me?" "You're on mute." "Wait, I'm sharing the wrong screen." Then somebody says, "Let's take this offline," which, in Teams, means it's now a 45-minute call titled "Quick Sync." And the app eats more RAM than the entire Windows 95 installation. Teams, you're the only thing that's ever made my laptop fan sound like it's begging for a transfer.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza is what happens when Italy and a Dole pineapple can get into a fender bender and decide not to exchange insurance. It's a pizza that's also a fruit cup. The only dish where the ham is nervous about the dessert.

And it's not even Hawaiian! It was invented by a Greek guy in Canada. Hawaii had nothing to do with it. That's like naming a burrito "The Norwegian" because someone's cousin once ate one near Oslo.

Pineapple on pizza is like a hot tub full of juice. The cheese slides off, the crust goes soggy, and every bite is a hostage negotiation between salty and sweet. Ham and pineapple are the only couple at the party who came together but won't stand next to each other.

And somehow it's still the pizza ordered by the guy who says, "I'm easy, I'll eat anything," and then picks off all the olives.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Let's start with the name, because that's the first lie. You were invented in Ontario. By a Greek guy. In 1962. You're Hawaiian the way a tiki bar in Ohio is Hawaiian. The only tropical thing about you is the can your pineapple came out of.

And that pineapple: warm, wet, weeping syrup into the crust until the middle slice folds like a lawn chair. Pineapple contains an enzyme that breaks down protein, so the fruit is literally trying to digest the ham. Even your toppings hate each other.

And the ham! Not prosciutto, not even pepperoni. Just pale pink squares that look like they were chiseled out of a deli's floor tile.

You're the pizza people order to seem quirky. "I'm so random!" No, Kevin. That's a fruit cup that fell on a pizza, and nobody cleaned it up.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree on anything, so they built a city that nobody could possibly be jealous of. Mission accomplished.

It was designed by an American architect, which explains why it feels like a very nice airport with sheep. The roundabouts are so plentiful that locals don't give directions, they give revolutions. The lake is fake, the population is mostly public servants waiting for Friday, and the kangaroos outnumber the nightlife.

Your Parliament House is literally buried in a hill so people can walk on the roof, the only time Australians get to stand on politicians.

For your centenary you commissioned the Skywhale, a giant flying balloon with ten enormous boobs, and somehow that's still the most exciting thing to happen here.

Canberra: home of Summernats, Floriade, and legally purchasable X-rated videos. Burnouts, tulips and porn, because you've got to do something until the next Senate estimates hearing.

b.text: Canberra is the only capital in Australia built from scratch, which explains a lot. Sydney and Melbourne were so busy hating each other they agreed to put the country's brain in a paddock halfway between them, and it has been sulking ever since. Walter Burley Griffin drew it up as a neat wheel of boulevards around a lake, then the public servants arrived and discovered that every road in town is a roundabout. Nobody has ever found the way out of Civic. The nightlife shuts at nine because the whole city is in bed before Question Time ends. The lake is named after Griffin, which is a shame, because he's the only man ever to design a city and then get a lake named after him instead of a train station. In winter the frost is so thick the ministers need a scraper before they can go inside and be lied to.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself three night-market stalls before you arrive. People don't find you at Shilin. They track you, like bloodhounds following a crime scene. Your whole brand is "smells like a sewer, tastes great," which is also what every bad Tinder date says about himself. You soak for months in fermented brine like you're marinating in a grudge. And your family's no better: Changsha dyed you black, the culinary equivalent of putting sunglasses on a corpse. You need deep frying, chili sauce, AND a mound of pickled cabbage just to be socially acceptable. That's not a garnish, that's a legal team. Your parents gave you one job: be tofu. Tofu's whole personality is having no personality. And somehow you came out smelling like a gym sock that went to college. Honestly? Respect.

b.text: Stinky tofu is the only food that files a complaint before you've even found the stall. You're three blocks away at the night market and your nose is already asking questions. It's tofu that spent a week soaking in brine that smells like a gym bag left in a hot car, then got deep-fried so the whole street knows what you're doing. They serve it with pickled cabbage, like it needs a chaperone. You bite in, the crispy outside is great, and the inside is basically a fermented cloud. Your jacket smells like it for three days. Your coworkers ask if you were dragged through a sewer. Honestly, though, it's the only snack that shows up to the party knowing it's a mess, and it's still having the best time.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Monopoly is the only game where the winner is whoever gets lucky early and the loser is whoever's still playing at 2 a.m. It was designed to teach people that landlords are evil, and somehow it became the thing families play to prove it.

Four hours in, you've got a dad mortgaging Baltic Avenue, a cousin who "forgot" to charge rent, and a kid crying over the thimble. Nobody's ever finished a game. We just stop when someone flips the board.

And the money! You're handed pastel Monopoly bills like it's a deranged Easter egg hunt, then told you owe $200 for "income tax." In a game about capitalism, Free Parking pays out nothing, but everyone insists it does, because house rules are the only thing keeping this thing alive.

The best part: the shoe, the dog, and the iron are all fighting over Boardwalk. Meanwhile, the Community Chest says I won second place in a beauty contest. Ten dollars. Great.

b.text: Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to warn people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow you became the thing Grandpa uses to teach eight-year-olds that ruining lives is fun. You're the only game where getting arrested is a power move, because late in the game jail is the safest property on the board. Your mascot is a man everyone swears wears a monocle. He doesn't. He's just so smug our brains added one. You promise "about an hour" and deliver a hostage situation. Nobody has ever actually finished you. You just end when somebody flips the board over Marvin Gardens. You award ten bucks for second place in a beauty contest, which is still more than Baltic Avenue pulls in. And the banker who skims from the bank isn't a cheater. He's the only player who read the theme.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text: Ugg boots are the only footwear that looks like it was made from a dead sheep and then slept in. They're basically two slippers that gave up on their dreams and went to college. You don't wear Uggs, you just stop trying in a boot shape. Nobody has ever run for a bus in Uggs. Nobody has ever been caught in the rain in Uggs. They're for the Starbucks line at 8 a.m. and the Costco parking lot, and that's it. And the name! "Ugg." That's not a brand, that's a noise you make when you step on a Lego. Somebody in a boardroom said, "Let's sell people shoes that sound like disappointment," and everybody nodded. Then they charged two hundred dollars for them.

b.text:
UGG boots: because nothing says "I respect my feet" like dressing them as two sheepskin loaves that lost a fight with a puddle.

They're the only shoe that looks wet when dry and ruined when wet. One drop of rain and suddenly your boots have a water stain shaped like Ohio. And the tag says "do not wear in rain," which is wild for something that's basically a footwear sponge. It's a boot with a dress code.

Also, they're from Australia, but the company's in California, and the price is from the moon. Three hundred dollars for a shoe designed to be worn by surfers who just got out of the ocean, and somehow it ended up in a Pilates class in Connecticut.

And the smell. Wearing them without socks is a lifestyle choice, and it turns the inside into a warm, damp sheep sauna. You don't take them off. You release them.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole that got a fake ID. You order it, and the waiter says, "That'll be forty-five minutes." Forty-five minutes! I've had relationships bake faster. They put the sauce on top because if you saw what was underneath first, you'd leave. A solid sheet of sausage, like somebody paved a driveway with a patty. Two pounds of mozzarella hiding under a tomato quilt. It's not a slice, it's a core sample. You need a knife, a fork, and a structural engineer. The crust is buttery cornmeal, so it's a pie crust, so congratulations, you're eating dessert with ambitions. And here's the best part: actual Chicagoans don't even eat it. They eat tavern-style thin crust cut in squares. Deep-dish is just the city's way of keeping tourists too full to walk to Wrigley.

b.text: Deep-dish pizza is the only food where you need a fork, a knife, and a structural engineer. You order a slice and the waiter brings you a casserole with a crust like a bank vault. The sauce sits on top, which is the pizza equivalent of wearing your shirt on the outside of your jacket. Chicagoans will tell you it's "not pizza, it's a pie," which is what you say when you've eaten something that requires a 45-minute wait and still leaves you feeling like you've been mugged by cheese. Locals eat it with a straight face. Tourists eat it with a flashlight, looking for the bottom. And somewhere under there, buried under three pounds of mozzarella, is a tomato that has never once been invited to the party.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like Swiss cheese that wanted to be a boat. You were invented for sailing, and the one place nobody wears you is a boat. You're at Applebee's, squeaking across a wet floor like a dolphin in distress.

You have holes. On purpose. Then you sell us Jibbitz to fill the holes. That's not fashion, that's a protection racket with a SpongeBob charm.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind my heel doesn't make me an athlete. It makes me a toddler about to sprint into traffic.

You made a KFC bucket clog with charms that smelled like fried chicken. That's not footwear. That's a foam cry for help.

Nurses love you. Chefs love you. Which proves you're comfortable for people who've stopped caring who's looking at their feet.

b.text:
Crocs are the only shoes that look like they were designed by a toddler and approved by a plumber. They're what happens when a boat shoe gets hit by a truck and the truck is made of cheese.

And the holes? Those aren't "ventilation." Those are tiny windows so everyone can watch your sock make a terrible decision.

You know what's wild? They sell charms for them. You can pin a little taco to a shoe that already looks like a bath toy. That's not accessorizing, that's decorating a pool float.

The heel strap flips back and suddenly it's "sport mode." Sport mode! For what sport? Competitive gardening? Walking to the fridge at 2 a.m.?

And they're comfortable, which is the cruelest part. Nobody can even make fun of them honestly. You just stand there, defeated, as a surgeon in neon green clogs walks past you with better arch support than your entire family.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text: Klingon is the only language where clearing your throat counts as a complete sentence. Its creators looked at English and said, "Too soft." So they built a tongue where every word sounds like a dog choking on a gravel driveway. Ask a Klingon for "good morning" and you'll get a cough from the sewer, followed by a threat about your mother's forehead. The apostrophes are everywhere, like someone sneezed punctuation across the page. Qapla'! Qapla'? Qapla'. Half the vocabulary is for dishonor and the other half is for knives. Fans spent decades memorizing it, which tells you they really wanted to be insulted with conviction. Even the Duolingo owl looks nervous when it comes up.

b.text: Klingon, you're a language built by one linguist, Marc Okrand, specifically to sound alien and hostile, and somehow you still ended up sounding like a man choking on a Dorito. Your word order is object-verb-subject, so even your sentences walk in backwards to hide their face. You don't even have a word for "hello." Your greeting is "nuqneH," "what do you want?" You're the only language that greets people like a DMV clerk. Your apostrophes are glottal stops, your capital Q is a different letter from lowercase q, and "tlh" isn't a sound, it's a hairball. You translated Hamlet and claimed it was the original. Buddy, the most popular thing ever said in you is "Qapla'," and the people saying it are at a Marriott in Burbank.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, you're the only fruit that needs a permit to carry. You weigh eighty pounds, you're covered in spikes, and you grow directly out of the tree trunk like a tumor with ambition.

Cutting you open requires oiled knives, gloves, and a will, because you bleed glue. I've seen people stuck to you for three days. You're the only fruit that fights back like a bad breakup.

And the smell! Rotten banana, bubblegum, and gym socks, all in one. You're what Juicy Fruit becomes in a hostage situation.

Then vegans discovered you. Now you're in a can, drowning in barbecue sauce, pretending to be pulled pork. Jackfruit, you're a bland, stringy shredded mess in a tin, and you're lying to everyone. Even the tree looks at you and says, "I made that? And it's pretending to be a pig?"

b.text: Jackfruit, you look like a sea mine that got into a fight with a durian and lost. Your skin is a crime scene of little green spikes, and nobody has ever cut you open without a prayer and a machete. You're the size of a toddler, you smell like gym socks dipped in bubblegum, and you're somehow both sweet and wet and still sticky after you've been in the fridge. Vegans found you and suddenly you're "pulled pork," which is the most desperate rebrand since "vegetable oil" tried to be a steak. Everybody's grandma loves you for one week a year, then you rot on the counter and the whole kitchen knows. You're a fruit that needs its own safety briefing. Nobody's ever walked out of a grocery store saying, "I'll have the enormous spiky thing that smells like a locker room."

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text: Crocs are shoes designed by someone who saw a bath mat and thought, "Yes, but what if it had holes so my feet could breathe while I pretend I'm a surgeon at a Cracker Barrel?" They look like the foam that sits on a hot dog's bun. They're the only footwear where the heel is basically a suggestion. You can't run in them, you can't hike in them, and you definitely can't sneak up on anyone, because every step sounds like a duck being slowly squeezed. And somehow they're on the feet of grown adults who own a mortgage. Nobody wears Crocs to look good. You wear Crocs because you've accepted that your feet have given up, and you've decided the shoe should match that energy. Honestly, respect. You're the only person at the Target parking lot who's fully at peace.

b.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like a colander that wanted to go to brunch. Thirteen holes, and somehow none of them let the dignity out, because there was never any in there.

You were invented as a boat shoe. A *boat* shoe. The one place you were built for, and you'd just float away. So you stayed on land and started fights with escalators. Malls had to post warnings. You're the only footwear with a rap sheet against machinery.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind your heel doesn't make you athletic. It makes you a clog wearing a seatbelt.

Then came Jibbitz, little charms you jam into the holes so grown adults can accessorize ventilation. Congratulations. You turned a shoe into a fridge door.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. Somewhere your cousin is a sneeze guard at Chipotle, and honestly? Your cousin has better etch resistance. One whiff of plasma and you vanish faster than a grad student's weekend.

You've been the "gold standard" since the 1970s, which is a polite way of saying nobody's been able to fire you. You need hundreds of microcoulombs just to *notice* the beam. A 40-hour write for one wafer. Glacial, but sure, sub-10-nanometer lines, we get it.

Positive resist? Overdose you and you cross-link into a *negative* one. That's not versatility, that's an identity crisis.

You get developed in MIBK, which smells like regret, and you come in 495K and 950K because one of you alone can't even do liftoff. And acetone dissolves you instantly. Even your solvents think you're temporary.

b.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. The same stuff as the shield at a hockey rink, and somehow you're the pride of the cleanroom. You have sub-10 nanometer resolution and the etch resistance of a wet napkin. Every pattern you make is gorgeous for exactly as long as nobody tries to use it.

You need a dose that would tan a small village, and for what? So the beam can snip your chains one at a time like a slow, expensive haircut? Then we bathe you in MIBK and IPA, and you dissolve only if the ratio is right, the temperature is right, and the moon is in the proper phase.

Overdo the dose and you flip negative-tone out of spite, cross-linking into a crust that no solvent can remove. Everyone loves a bilayer 495/950 for the undercut, because even you know you need a support system.

And liftoff? Acetone, sonication, three hours, and a prayer. You're a clingy ex.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text:
Stinky tofu, you're the only food that gets a restraining order from its own neighborhood. I smelled you three blocks away and assumed a sewer had filed for divorce.

You're fermented in brine made of old vegetables, fish, and what I can only assume is regret. Then someone looks at that and says, "Let's deep-fry it." That's not cooking, that's giving a crime scene a crispy exterior.

And the fans! They say, "Just try it, the taste is nothing like the smell." Oh, so you're a liar with two personalities? Great. Very reassuring.

Every night market, there's a line of people holding their breath while paying for it. Nobody queues for something that smells like feet unless the feet are delicious, and somehow you are. That's the real insult. You smell like a gym sock's funeral, and I still came back for seconds.

b.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself before the menu does. People find you at the night market the way sharks find blood: follow the stench three stalls past the bubble tea. Your brine is fermented vegetables, shrimp, amaranth stems, and apparently a gym sock that lost a bet. Months in that bucket, and you came out smelling like a festival porta-potty in August. Your own name is a confession. Not "aged tofu," not "artisanal bean curd." Your family took one whiff and went, "Yeah, call him Stinky." And the Changsha version? Dyed jet black, like it's in mourning for everyone's sense of smell. The only reason anyone finishes you is the pickled cabbage and chili sauce piled on top to keep you quiet. "Smells bad, tastes good" isn't a slogan, buddy. It's a hostage negotiation.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk, you are porridge that got a publicist. Somebody looked at the breakfast of Victorian orphans and said, "What if it cost six dollars and had a font?"

Your carton talks to me. Oatly, I'm trying to make coffee, not get into a pen-pal situation with a beverage that writes like a substitute teacher who wants to be called "Dave."

You're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not milk, that's a salad dressing that gave up. And they had to add enzymes to turn your starch into sugar so you'd taste like something. You're the only "health drink" that spikes my blood sugar like a Pop-Tart.

There's a "Barista Edition" now. Oat milk, there are two editions of you. Moby-Dick has fewer editions than you.

And you're beige. You make every latte look like dishwater with ambition.

Horses eat oats for free, and they still look embarrassed for us.

b.text: Oat milk, you're the Prius of dairy alternatives. You show up at brunch with a tote bag full of opinions, and everybody claps like you saved the planet. Meanwhile you're just oats that got put through a blender and came out looking like wet cardboard with a lawyer. You froth beautifully, sure, but you froth like a guy who just found out his barista certificate expired. And don't get me started on "barista edition." Nobody's a barista because they bought a carton with a cartoon on it. You're basically a shampoo that gave up on being a shampoo and decided to be a latte. Nobody asked you to be creamy. You just showed up creamy-adjacent and expected a parade.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text:
Papyrus, look at you. A 23-year-old drew you with a calligraphy pen in 1982, trying to imagine what English would look like 2,000 years ago, and somehow you became the official font of every place that sells crystals next to a tanning bed. You're on yoga studios, hookah lounges, and the church bake sale flyer for "Loaves & Fishes & Brownies."

Your letters look like they were chiseled by a Pharaoh with a hangover. That little floaty bar on your capital E? Even your crossbars are trying to leave.

James Cameron spent a billion dollars inventing an alien language, then labeled the poster with a font that came free with Microsoft Office. Ryan Gosling got an entire SNL sketch out of being haunted by you.

Even your creator says he's sick of you. Comic Sans has haters. You have a dad who wants a refund.

b.text:
Papyrus, you're the font that shows up to every event dressed for a different one. A day spa. A mediocre yoga studio. A Pirates of the Caribbean-themed dentist. You look like you were designed by someone who'd only heard about ancient Egypt from a candle.

You're so rough around the edges, it's like the letters were chiseled by a guy who got bored halfway through. Every "E" looks like it lost a fight with a staircase.

And you have the nerve to be everywhere! Organic soap. Tea shops. "Live, Laugh, Love" signs in a kitchen that's never seen a meal.

Then Ryan Gosling's character in SNL had to spend *a whole sketch* sobbing over you, because James Cameron put you on *Avatar*, a $237 million movie. Two hundred thirty-seven million dollars, and the logo looked like a restaurant's Wi-Fi password sign.

Papyrus, you're not a typeface. You're a vibe that got a license.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: NFTs, everybody! The only art form where the most common review is "right-click, save." You paid four hundred thousand dollars for a cartoon monkey in a captain's hat, and I have the same monkey as my phone background. The difference? I didn't pay a gas fee bigger than the art. Technically you don't even own the picture. You own a receipt pointing to a link on a server some guy in Ohio forgot to renew. That's not a masterpiece; that's a parking stub for a JPEG. And remember the roadmap? Metaverse, merch, a yacht party! Then the founder pulled the rug, deleted the Discord, and left you holding a "rare trait": sunglasses. Jimmy Fallon showed Paris Hilton his ape on national TV like a proud dad. Now it's worth less than the TV.

b.text: Nobody's ever bought an NFT. They bought a receipt that says "you own this JPEG," and the JPEG is a cartoon ape with a bowler hat, the same JPEG you can right-click and save in four seconds. So they paid four hundred thousand dollars for a screenshot with a certificate. It's the only art in history where the certificate is the art. The Mona Lisa hangs in the Louvre with a crowd of tourists, and this guy's ape is hanging in a folder called "wallet" that nobody else can see. Ownership, they call it. Congratulations, you own the ape, and the ape doesn't know you exist.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP, you started life as "Personal Home Page," and somehow you now run most of the internet, which explains a lot about the internet. Your own creator said he's "not a real programmer," and honestly, it shows. Is it needle then haystack, or haystack then needle? strpos and in_array have been in a custody battle since 1995. You gave us mysql_escape_string, then mysql_real_escape_string, because apparently the first one was just pretending. Your loose equality swears "0e123" equals "0e456," since both are zero in scientific notation. Your error message for a double colon is T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM, which is Hebrew, because English wasn't confusing enough. You skipped version 6 entirely, like a kid hiding a report card. Facebook loved you so much they had to rewrite you as a different language. But hey, you power WordPress, so you'll outlive all of us.

b.text:
PHP, the language that stands for "Personal Home Page" and now runs half the internet, like a rental car you forgot to return in 1998.

It's the only language where the standard library looks like it was named by a dice roll. strpos has needle, haystack. array_search has needle, haystack. But str_replace? Different order. Why? Because PHP doesn't believe in consistency. It believes in vibes.

The comparison rules are a hostage situation. "0" == false. "abc" == 0, at least until PHP 8 finally took a sip of water. And the ternary operator was left-associative for years, so nested ones did the opposite of what anyone wanted.

Then there's the dollar sign. Every variable has one, like each is being sold individually.

And yet, WordPress, Facebook, Wikipedia, all run on it. PHP is the duct tape holding the web together, and like duct tape, nobody's proud of it, but everyone's got a roll in the garage.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest drink in human history (hot water, beans) and added a subscription model. Your own inventor said he regrets making you. Imagine your dad publicly apologizing for you and you're still in every dentist's waiting room.

You tried DRM on coffee. Keurig 2.0 literally scanned pods and refused to brew anything off-brand. You're the only appliance that's ever asked me for a license.

Every K-Cup costs more per pound than a decent steak, and you've buried enough of them to circle the Earth a dozen times. Archaeologists will dig them up and assume we worshipped tiny plastic thimbles.

And the Keurig Kold? A $370 soda machine that died faster than the flat Coke it made.

Your descale light blinks like a cry for help. Honestly, same.

b.text:
Keurig, you're the coffee maker that treats a cup of coffee like a hostage negotiation. Eight minutes of whirring, gurgling, and blinking just to produce a lukewarm thimble of brown water. Meanwhile my grandma's percolator makes a full pot before I finish reading the Wikipedia article about pour-over.

And the pods! Every cup creates a little plastic tombstone. You're basically a landfill with a power button. You've got more recyclable-pod-related guilt than my Catholic school.

Then there's the "strong" setting, which is just the regular setting with a dramatic pause. Nothing about you is bold except your price per ounce.

Keurig, you're not a coffee maker. You're a vending machine that got a cardiology degree.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text: LaTeX, you're the only software that makes PhDs feel stupid. You're from 1984 and you dress like it: backslashes everywhere, curly braces like a nervous tic. I tell you to put a figure "here," and you treat "here" as a suggestion, then file it four pages later next to the bibliography, like a sock lost in a dryer. Your error messages are poetry: "Missing $ inserted." Inserted where? Why? You won't say. You just blame line 1 of a 40-page file because I typed an underscore in a URL. My citations are double question marks until I compile you twice, then a third time, out of spite. And everyone needs to know it's pronounced "lay-tech," not like the glove. Honestly, at least the glove stretches. Overfull \hbox? Badness 10000? Buddy, that's not a warning. That's your autobiography.

b.text:
LaTeX is the only software where you spend six hours fixing a typo and then twelve more because the fix moved your figure to page nine.

You ask for a picture to go *here*. LaTeX says "here" is more of a "float" situation. It's not a placement, it's a vibe.

The error messages are written by someone who hates you personally. "Overfull hbox, badness 10000." Thank you, I'll tell my therapist. Meanwhile, one missing brace gives you an error on line 4,000, in a file you didn't write, from a package you never installed.

Want a different font? Enjoy a three-day journey through Stack Overflow, where the top answer is from 2009 and starts with "Just use XeTeX."

And the compile times! I changed one comma and now I'm watching it run twice, because the table of contents needs to catch up to reality.

Knuth released it in 1978 and declared it nearly bug-free. Sir, the bugs are in me. I'm the bug. I just wanted a bibliography.

Stinky tofu, you're the only food that gets a restraining order from its own neighborhood. I smelled you three blocks away and assumed a sewer had filed for divorce.

You're fermented in brine made of old vegetables, fish, and what I can only assume is regret. Then someone looks at that and says, "Let's deep-fry it." That's not cooking, that's giving a crime scene a crispy exterior.

And the fans! They say, "Just try it, the taste is nothing like the smell." Oh, so you're a liar with two personalities? Great. Very reassuring.
