b.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself three night-market stalls before you arrive. People don't find you at Shilin. They track you, like bloodhounds following a crime scene. Your whole brand is "smells like a sewer, tastes great," which is also what every bad Tinder date says about himself. You soak for months in fermented brine like you're marinating in a grudge. And your family's no better: Changsha dyed you black, the culinary equivalent of putting sunglasses on a corpse. You need deep frying, chili sauce, AND a mound of pickled cabbage just to be socially acceptable. That's not a garnish, that's a legal team. Your parents gave you one job: be tofu. Tofu's whole personality is having no personality. And somehow you came out smelling like a gym sock that went to college. Honestly? Respect.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Monopoly is the only game where the winner is whoever gets lucky early and the loser is whoever's still playing at 2 a.m. It was designed to teach people that landlords are evil, and somehow it became the thing families play to prove it.

Four hours in, you've got a dad mortgaging Baltic Avenue, a cousin who "forgot" to charge rent, and a kid crying over the thimble. Nobody's ever finished a game. We just stop when someone flips the board.

And the money! You're handed pastel Monopoly bills like it's a deranged Easter egg hunt, then told you owe $200 for "income tax." In a game about capitalism, Free Parking pays out nothing, but everyone insists it does, because house rules are the only thing keeping this thing alive.

The best part: the shoe, the dog, and the iron are all fighting over Boardwalk. Meanwhile, the Community Chest says I won second place in a beauty contest. Ten dollars. Great.

b.text:
Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow the lesson everyone learned was "buy Park Place." Then Parker Brothers bought you from a guy who basically stole you, which is the most on-brand origin story in history.

You're the only game where "second prize in a beauty contest" counts as income and jail is solved with a coupon. Your mascot looks like he foreclosed on the Pringles guy, and half of America swears he wears a monocle. He doesn't. We just assumed a man that rich would be hiding something.

Nobody has ever finished you. Games don't end; your cousin just flips the board over Marvin Gardens, which you misspelled, by the way. It's Marven. Even your real estate is a scam.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text: Vim is the only program that greets you with "How do I quit?" as its opening line. You open it by accident, and now you're trapped in a text editor that thinks typing is a crime. You press "i" to insert text, which is hilarious, because nobody who uses Vim has ever inserted anything into their life. Then you hit Escape, and suddenly you're in command mode, where the letters you type don't write anything. They do things. "d" deletes. "x" deletes. "dd" deletes the whole line, and you did not ask for that. Vim doesn't have a save button; it has ":wq," which sounds like a sneeze in a library. Vim users say it's efficient. Sure, if your idea of efficiency is memorizing a secret language just to change one word.

b.text:
Vim is the only software where the tutorial is "how to leave." Millions of developers have spent a Tuesday trapped inside it, mashing Escape like they're trying to wake a hostage. You open a file, type "hello," and the editor responds by deleting your paragraph and playing a macro you recorded in 2019.

Vim users say, "Once you learn it, you'll never touch your mouse again." Neither will you touch grass, sir. You've spent forty hours configuring a .vimrc so you can save four seconds on a typo.

And the modes! Normal mode, where nothing is normal. Insert mode, where you finally get to insert. Visual mode, which is only visual in the sense that you can watch yourself select the wrong thing.

It's an editor built on the premise that your keyboard has too many keys and your dignity has too much room.

Type :wq to save and quit. Type :q! to forget this ever happened.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text: Canberra: the only city where the traffic jam is a roundabout with a sculpture in the middle. A century ago, someone looked at a sheep paddock between Sydney and Melbourne and said, "Let's put the whole country's government here so nobody has to visit." And it worked. Parliament House sits on its hill like a very expensive filing cabinet. The lake is named after an American architect, and it's the most exciting thing that happens here. Winter mornings hit minus four, and the only people outside are joggers with a grudge. Friday night out means the Civic bar, where everyone's a public servant with a lanyard still on. Nobody lives in Canberra. They're just waiting for a posting.

b.text:
Canberra is what happens when a committee designs a city and nobody's allowed to have an opinion until the subcommittee reports back. It's the only place where the lake is fake, the hills are decorative, and the excitement is a roundabout. Seriously, you can't give directions without saying "take the third exit, then the third exit again, then cry."

It's a city of 450,000 people, and 449,000 of them are named "Director of Strategic Alignment." The nightlife is a public servant having a second flat white after 2 p.m. Wild.

Every winter it hits minus five, and the locals call that "character." Every summer it's bushfire smoke, so basically a free vape.

And the Aussie icon is a giant flagpole. That's the whole personality: a pole, and a stern reminder to submit your timesheet.

Canberra: a nice place to visit if you've never wanted to.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text: Ugg boots are the only footwear that looks like it was made from a dead sheep and then slept in. They're basically two slippers that gave up on their dreams and went to college. You don't wear Uggs, you just stop trying in a boot shape. Nobody has ever run for a bus in Uggs. Nobody has ever been caught in the rain in Uggs. They're for the Starbucks line at 8 a.m. and the Costco parking lot, and that's it. And the name! "Ugg." That's not a brand, that's a noise you make when you step on a Lego. Somebody in a boardroom said, "Let's sell people shoes that sound like disappointment," and everybody nodded. Then they charged two hundred dollars for them.

b.text: UGG boots. The only footwear named after a review. Australian surfers made these to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow America decided the ocean was the mall. They're sheepskin, which means a sheep died so you could wear a slipper to the DMV. One puddle and they're covered in salt lines like a topographic map of everywhere you regret going. Zero arch support, so after two weeks your heel caves sideways and you're walking on the boot's ankle like it owes you money. You wear them barefoot, so by February they smell like a wet lamb's final wish. They're as waterproof as a muffin. Oprah put them on her Favorite Things list. She's since moved on. Twenty years later they're back with platform soles, proving even a mistake wants to be taller.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs are the only shoes that look like they were designed by a toddler and approved by a plumber. They're what happens when a boat shoe gets hit by a truck and the truck is made of cheese.

And the holes? Those aren't "ventilation." Those are tiny windows so everyone can watch your sock make a terrible decision.

You know what's wild? They sell charms for them. You can pin a little taco to a shoe that already looks like a bath toy. That's not accessorizing, that's decorating a pool float.

The heel strap flips back and suddenly it's "sport mode." Sport mode! For what sport? Competitive gardening? Walking to the fridge at 2 a.m.?

And they're comfortable, which is the cruelest part. Nobody can even make fun of them honestly. You just stand there, defeated, as a surgeon in neon green clogs walks past you with better arch support than your entire family.

b.text: Crocs are the only shoe that looks like it was designed by a committee of ducks. Every pair is a foam clog with holes in it, like someone started making shoes, got bored halfway through, and said, "Eh, the air can have the rest." Nobody has ever bought Crocs to look good. You buy them because they're the only shoe that can survive a flood, a hospital shift, and a barbecue at the same time. They come with little charms you snap into the holes, which is how you know the company has given up on fashion and moved into hostage negotiation: "Fine, you want a shoe, we'll give you a shoe with a pizza slice stuck in its side." And somehow they're everywhere. Grandpas, nurses, teenagers, and one guy at every Costco who hasn't left the house since 2009. Crocs don't walk, they waddle. That's not a shoe, that's a rubber duck that lost a bet.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text: Brasília is the only city where you need a car to get lost. Lúcio Costa drew it as an airplane, which explains everything: it was built to be admired from 30,000 feet and never walked in. Every superquadra looks identical, so locals give directions like "third block, the one with the tree." Niemeyer's cathedral looks like a concrete UFO that landed in a bad mood. Congress has one bowl facing up and one facing down, which is the most honest thing about the government. The air is so dry your nosebleeds have nosebleeds, the lake looks like a screensaver, and the nearest bar is eleven kilometers away on a highway with no sidewalk.

b.text:
Brasília, you're the only city designed to look like an airplane, and somehow everyone still just wants to leave on one. Politicians fly in Tuesday, take a bribe Wednesday, and they're gone by Thursday like it's a timeshare.

Your addresses read like a Wi-Fi password: "SQS 308, Bloco C, Apartamento 402." I'm not visiting a friend, I'm resetting a router.

Niemeyer gave you gorgeous curves, then Lúcio Costa forgot pedestrians. Want to walk to the bakery? Hope you enjoy the eight-lane Eixão and a light jog through a tesourinha.

Your humidity drops to 10 percent. Your congress has one bowl facing up, one facing down: one for collecting money, the other for hiding it.

And you were built with no corners, so Brazil's capital has no boteco na esquina. That's not urban planning. That's a human rights violation.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP, you're the only language whose name is a recursive acronym, and it still reads like a bug report. Every variable wears a dollar sign like you're charging rent for each one. Your function names were clearly picked by drawing lots: strpos takes the haystack first, array_search takes the needle first, and you just shrug. "0" == false? Sure. "abc" == 0? Why not. Your comparison operator is a coin toss in a trench coat. Half the internet runs on you, and WordPress is the proof. Nobody brags about WordPress, but everybody's sites are built on you. I'd like to hate you more, but I've seen you in production. Everyone loves you secretly, late at night, with error_reporting turned off.

b.text:
PHP. You started as "Personal Home Page," then rebranded as "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a recursive acronym, because even your name couldn't commit to a stable API.

For twenty years, "abc" == 0 was true, and you called it "type juggling," like a clown proud of dropping things.

strpos takes haystack, needle. array_search takes needle, haystack. That's not argument order; that's mood swings.

Your parse error says T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM. That's Hebrew for "double colon" and English for "good luck."

You skipped version 6 entirely. Even your release numbers just wanted to move on.

You shipped mysql_real_escape_string, implying the first one was a hoax.

Facebook loved you so much they invented Hack just to avoid touching you.

But sure, you power most of the web. Mostly WordPress. That's like bragging your biggest fan is a raccoon.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs isn't a text editor, it's an operating system that's still looking for a decent editor. Thirty years of development, and the most reliable feature is the pinky injury.

You press Control-X, Control-S to save. That's not a keyboard shortcut, that's a hostage negotiation with your left hand.

Emacs users say, "It's infinitely customizable!" Sure. So is a blank sheet of paper, but nobody brags about spending three weekends configuring that. Your init.el is 4,000 lines long, and you wrote 12 of them. The rest is a Stack Overflow answer from 2011 that you're afraid to delete.

And the manual calls it "the extensible, self-documenting editor." Self-documenting! Yes, it will tell you exactly what a function does, right after you press Control-H, then K, then wonder why you're reading Lisp.

You can read email in it, browse the web in it, and play Tetris in it. Everything except quit. Nobody remembers how to quit.

b.text:
Emacs is a beautiful operating system. Shame it never shipped with a decent text editor. That's why half its users install evil-mode: they love Emacs so much they turned it into Vim.

Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," which is also the sound your pinky makes on its way to the orthopedic surgeon. Asking for help is C-h, which in a terminal deletes a character. So even your cry for help gets backspaced.

It has a built-in therapist, M-x doctor, which is thoughtful, because nobody else will listen to you explain your init.el. Four thousand lines of Lisp, half copied from a 2003 mailing list, and you still declare "Emacs bankruptcy" every two years.

It plays Tetris. It reads email. It runs your entire life in Org-mode. It still chokes on one long line of JSON.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text: You know what Teams is? It's the office that's always on fire but nobody's ever seen the smoke. Every message comes with "...is typing" for six minutes, and then it says "Hi." Your green dot says "Available" while you're literally in the bathroom. You join a meeting and the first ten minutes are "Can you hear me?" "You're on mute." "Wait, I'm sharing the wrong screen." Then somebody says, "Let's take this offline," which, in Teams, means it's now a 45-minute call titled "Quick Sync." And the app eats more RAM than the entire Windows 95 installation. Teams, you're the only thing that's ever made my laptop fan sound like it's begging for a transfer.

b.text:
Microsoft Teams is the only app that can notify you about a message you're already reading. You've got a red badge, a yellow badge, and a little purple "@" telling you someone said "per my last email" in a chat called "Q3 Sync (Copy) (Final)."

Teams has seven ways to say hello and none of them load. "Joining meeting..." is its resting state. It's the Waiting for Godot of video calls, except Godot eventually shows up and says, "Can everyone see my screen?" No, Greg. We see a spinning circle and your cat.

Every update, it asks you to restart. Not the app. Your life choices.

Teams and Channels are different things, by the way. A channel lives inside a team. Which is inside a tenant. Which is inside a guest account you can't switch out of without signing out of everything and crying.

And the green dot? It goes yellow the second you stop moving your mouse, so your boss thinks you're napping. Ten minutes of reading a document is considered a vacation.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza, you're named after a place you've never been. You were invented in Ontario, by a Greek guy, using canned pineapple. That's not a heritage, that's a witness protection identity.

And the ham? It's Canadian bacon. Even your meat is from Canada. The only Hawaiian thing about you is that people see you and say "aloha," meaning goodbye.

Pineapple has an enzyme that digests protein. You're the only pizza that eats the customer back. Warm fruit juice pooling on mozzarella like a hot tub nobody cleaned.

Italians don't hate you; they pray for you. The president of Iceland said he'd ban you if he could, and Iceland eats fermented shark.

You're not a pizza. You're a fruit cup that fell on a pizza and refused to get up.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Pineapple on bread with ham. Somebody looked at a perfectly good pizza and said, "You know what this needs? Fruit that's been sitting in a can since the Eisenhower administration." And everybody just nodded. Nobody stopped him.

And the ham! It's not even Hawaiian ham. It's Canadian bacon wearing a cheap Hawaiian shirt. It's the pizza version of a guy at a wedding who says, "I'm not a dancer," and then dances anyway.

The pineapple's the real problem, though. It's sweet, it's wet, and it's trying so hard to be a tropical vacation. You bite in, and it's like a sprinkler went off in your mouth, and the cheese just gives up and slides onto your shirt.

Honestly, I respect it. Hawaiian pizza is the only food that makes ham and fruit feel like they're both lost.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest drink in human history (hot water, beans) and added a subscription model. Your own inventor said he regrets making you. Imagine your dad publicly apologizing for you and you're still in every dentist's waiting room.

You tried DRM on coffee. Keurig 2.0 literally scanned pods and refused to brew anything off-brand. You're the only appliance that's ever asked me for a license.

Every K-Cup costs more per pound than a decent steak, and you've buried enough of them to circle the Earth a dozen times. Archaeologists will dig them up and assume we worshipped tiny plastic thimbles.

And the Keurig Kold? A $370 soda machine that died faster than the flat Coke it made.

Your descale light blinks like a cry for help. Honestly, same.

b.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest thing in the world, hot water meeting coffee, and turned it into a subscription-based hostage situation. My grandfather made coffee with a pot and a prayer. I make it by stabbing a tiny plastic hockey puck in the face.

You've created a machine that takes four minutes to warm up just to produce eight ounces of something that tastes like a mug rinsed in a wet cardboard box. And that little pod? Thousands of tiny plastic cups, each one lasting longer than my last three relationships.

Then there's the "descale" light. Every few months it screams at me to run vinegar through it, like a smoke detector for my own laziness. I ignore it, and the machine just sighs and gives me half a cup.

The best part is the "strong" button. It doesn't make it stronger. It makes it smaller. You invented coffee's version of "I'm not mad, I'm just disappointed."

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you are the only thing in the dairy aisle that's named after a nut and still somehow lies about it. Your almond content is roughly the same as the average Tuesday's ambition. Somebody squeezed one almond over a bathtub of water, waved it at the carton, and said, "Yep, that's almond." That's not milk. That's a rumor.

And the color! You look like a glass of wet drywall. Put you next to real milk and you're the sad cousin who showed up to the wedding in the same beige as the tablecloth. Nobody asked you to be white. You're just gray with a vague sense of purpose.

You also taste like you're trying to apologize for something. Every sip says, "I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm sorry." Pour yourself into a latte and the barista's already plotting how to hide the foam.

b.text:
Almond milk, you're the only drink that needs a lawyer to defend its name. The dairy industry sued because, technically, nobody has ever milked an almond. We looked. No nipples.

You're about two percent almonds. The rest is water, gellan gum, and confidence. You're not milk. You're a nut that got waterboarded and called it wellness.

And speaking of water: it takes over a gallon to grow a single almond. California is in a drought so you can be beige in a latte. Bees get trucked across the country like seasonal laborers just to make you, and a lot of them don't come home.

Leave you in the fridge for two days and you separate like you're ashamed of yourself. Fair. I'd need to be shaken too if I cost seven dollars and tasted like a wet sympathy card.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text: Durian, you're the only fruit that needs a gas mask and a hazmat permit just to get through the airport. Airlines ban you like you're a bomb with a bad attitude. Your smell is a mix of gym socks, rotting onions, and a sewage pipe that's been sulking for a week. People hear the word "delicacy" and think you're kidding. Southeast Asians call you the king of fruits, and honestly, that's the only reason you got a crown instead of a restraining order. You look like a medieval mace someone dropped in a swamp, and you're covered in spikes so nobody can hug you. Even the spikes are a warning. Your fans swear you taste like custard and heaven, but they also say that about getting a root canal on Christmas. Smell like a crime scene, taste like a dessert, and still somehow get a hotel room kicked out for eating you.

b.text:
Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which is wild, because you dress like a medieval mace and smell like a crime scene. You're the only fruit with a body armor package AND a hazmat warning.

You're banned from Singapore's subway, hotels, and airlines. Think about that. Nobody bans the pineapple. You're the only produce item that gets kicked off a plane before it even boards.

Your fans say, "Just get past the smell, the taste is heavenly." Sir, that's what every hostage says about their captor.

You taste like custard that's been cheating on a sewer with an onion. Eat one and your fridge smells like you for three weeks, your breath for five.

And you fall out of trees onto people's heads. You're not even content to be a bad meal. You want to be a *weapon*.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript was built in ten days, and honestly, it shows. It's the only language where 0.1 + 0.2 isn't 0.3, and "11" - 1 is 10 but "11" + 1 is 111. Math, but make it improv.

Its typeof null says "object." That's not a bug, that's a 28-year-old typo everyone agreed to live with, like a tattoo of an ex's name.

You want to check if something's an array? Great, typeof says "object." Use Array.isArray. Want to sort numbers? Default sort alphabetically, so 10 comes before 2. Because why would numbers be numbers?

And the ecosystem! One developer deleted an 11-line package called left-pad and half the internet fell over. Your app has 1,400 dependencies and a node_modules folder heavier than a neutron star.

Every Tuesday there's a new framework that's "totally different this time." It's a React with a Vue on top of a Svelte. Meanwhile, NaN is not equal to itself, which is the most self-aware thing this language has ever done.

b.text:
You're the only language where `typeof null` returns "object" and nobody got fired. It's been wrong for thirty years, and instead of fixing it, you just shrugged and kept serving it, like a restaurant that's been selling raw chicken since 1995 and calls it a rustic choice.

You've got two equals signs for comparison, and one of them lies. `0 == ""` is true. `"" == "0"` is false. Zero equals empty string, empty string doesn't equal zero-string. That's not a bug. That's a hostage situation.

And `.sort()` gives you ``, because you sort numbers alphabetically unless someone begs you for a comparator function. You wrote a language that thinks digits are words.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text: Windows Vista, the operating system that asked permission for everything. You wanted to open a folder? Click "Continue." Delete a file? "Are you sure?" Breathe? "Allow this program to breathe?" Your computer needed a bouncer just to check its own coat. And the copy progress bar: "Four minutes remaining." Three hours later it's at 99 percent, forever. Vista didn't crash. It just kept asking if you were sure. And the sidebar! A little clock and a weather widget floating on your desktop like you needed a hall monitor for your screensaver. Microsoft put a "Vista Capable" sticker on computers that could barely run it, and then acted shocked when people were mad. Honestly, Vista, you were the first operating system to make your user feel like the problem.

b.text:
Windows Vista, you were the only operating system that asked permission to ask permission. "Are you sure you want to open Notepad?" Yes, Vista. I've been sure for twenty years.

You called yourself "Capable" on those stickers. Then you needed 15 gigs of RAM just to display a transparent window border. Aero looked gorgeous, though, like a beautiful man dying slowly of a mystery illness.

Remember copying a file? You'd say "Calculating time remaining" for six hours, like a mechanic staring at my engine going, "Hmm."

Microsoft shipped you, then immediately started apologizing with Windows 7. That's not a successor, that's a public apology with a Start button.

And "Vista Ready" laptops that couldn't run Vista? That's like a "Marathon Ready" sticker on a recliner.

Even your sidebar gadgets gave up. The weather widget just sat there, accurately predicting a cloudy future for everyone who bought you.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text: The Apple Vision Pro costs 3,500 dollars, which is a used Honda, for a headset that makes you look like a welder who wandered into the Apple Store. The front screen shows your eyes to everyone around you, so people don't see a person. They see a dead-eyed aquarium. You click by staring at things and pinching the air, like you're trying to hypnotize your own hand. The battery lives in your pocket on a cable, so you're not free, you're tethered to a fanny pack. Apple calls it spatial computing. I call it the only device that lets you wander your living room in a 3,500-dollar blindfold and still walk straight into the couch.

b.text: Apple Vision Pro, everybody! Thirty-five hundred dollars to look like a scuba diver lost in a Best Buy. Apple insists it's not VR, it's "spatial computing," which is like calling a fanny pack "hip luggage." It's so heavy they had to throw in a second strap, and the battery's a separate brick on a cord, so you're basically a lamp that walks. Two hours of charge! That's not a computer, that's a matinee. Then there's EyeSight, the screen that shows your eyes on the front, so your family can watch a dim, blurry you stare at nothing. Most honest feature Apple's ever made. Netflix wouldn't even make an app. Netflix! They're on smart fridges! And your Persona looks like a hostage video filmed inside the uncanny valley.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text: Brasília, you're what happens when an architect gets an entire country's budget and nobody says, "Maybe add a sidewalk?" You're shaped like an airplane, which is fitting, because everyone's goal is to board one by Friday afternoon. Your addresses read like Wi-Fi passwords: "SQS 308, Bloco C, apartamento 402." That's not a home. That's a parking spot on a spaceship. Kubitschek promised "fifty years in five," and you delivered: it's been sixty-five years and you still feel unfinished. Your Congress has one bowl facing up to receive the money and one facing down to hide it. You've got a row of identical ministry buildings so nobody can tell which one the scandal came from. In August the humidity drops so low that the only thing drier than the air is a deputy's sense of shame. Even your lake is fake. Honestly? On brand.

b.text:
Brasília, you're the only city designed from above, which explains why it's miserable from the ground. You're shaped like an airplane, and honestly, that tracks, because everyone's just passing through and nobody's happy about the food.

Oscar Niemeyer built you in 41 months, and it shows. You have addresses like "SQS 308, Bloco C, Apartamento 204." That's not a location, that's a tax form with a doorbell.

You have no street corners. No one has ever bumped into anyone by accident. Pedestrians don't exist; they're a rumor spread by people with cars.

Your cathedral looks like a crown of thorns made by a very expensive lamp company. Your Congress has two bowls, one facing up and one down, because even your architecture can't decide whether it's receiving bribes or hiding them.

Rio gets Carnival. São Paulo gets money. You get a lawmaker who flies in Tuesday and flees Thursday. You're not a capital, you're a very large airport lounge with a flag.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text:
Risk is the only game where you can conquer the entire planet and still lose to the guy who's been hiding in Australia since 7 p.m. Four territories, one entrance, and he just sits there like a guy at a party who won't leave the snack table.

This game has a map drawn by someone who heard about geography once, at a bar. Kamchatka borders Alaska. Ukraine is the size of Brazil. Yakutsk and Irkutsk are vital military objectives, and nobody at the table can find them on a real map.

The rules say the defender wins ties, which is the most realistic thing about it, because nobody actually finishes Risk. They just quit at 2 a.m. when someone's dad flips the board over Siberia.

And the pieces? Little plastic cannons and horses. Napoleonic warfare, global scale, and the whole thing is decided by rolling a 6 against your cousin Greg.

b.text:
Risk is the only game where you spend four hours conquering the world and then lose it because your brother-in-law rolled three sixes in Kamchatka.

"Strategy game," the box says. Sure. Strategy is a dice cup deciding your destiny while you scream at a plastic cannon.

Nobody finishes Risk. It doesn't end, it just gets abandoned, like Napoleon's Russian campaign, except Napoleon had better snacks. Someone eventually says "I have to be up early," which is Risk for "I've been dead since Australia."

Speaking of Australia: everyone knows the whole game is just "hold Australia and pretend you're smart." One entrance, four territories, a bonus. It's the gated community of continents. Meanwhile Asia has twelve territories and a bonus of seven, which is the board's way of saying "go ahead, try it, I'll see you at hour three."

And the alliances! Friendships don't die in Risk. They get negotiated away for a single card.

Happy 60 years, Risk. You've ended more family dinners than politics.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Let's start with the name, because that's the first lie. You were invented in Ontario. By a Greek guy. In 1962. You're Hawaiian the way a tiki bar in Ohio is Hawaiian. The only tropical thing about you is the can your pineapple came out of.

And that pineapple: warm, wet, weeping syrup into the crust until the middle slice folds like a lawn chair. Pineapple contains an enzyme that breaks down protein, so the fruit is literally trying to digest the ham. Even your toppings hate each other.

And the ham! Not prosciutto, not even pepperoni. Just pale pink squares that look like they were chiseled out of a deli's floor tile.

You're the pizza people order to seem quirky. "I'm so random!" No, Kevin. That's a fruit cup that fell on a pizza, and nobody cleaned it up.

b.text: Hawaiian pizza. Ham and pineapple. Somebody in Canada looked at a perfectly good pizza and said, "You know what this needs? Fruit that's been sitting in a can." Pineapple on pizza is a crime with a fruit salad alibi. It's sweet, it's salty, it's wet, and it's confused about what it wants to be, kind of like a dessert that got lost on the way to a breakfast buffet. And the ham? That's not ham, that's a lunch meat that went to college and dropped out. Every bite is a negotiation between a tropical vacation and a Tuesday at the deli counter. Hawaii didn't even invent this thing. A Greek-Canadian guy in Ontario did, in 1962, and then he just let it loose on the world like a dare.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and honestly? It shows. You're named after Java the way a knockoff purse is named after Gucci.

You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number. NaN doesn't even equal itself, which makes it the only thing in you with any self-awareness.

Ask you to sort and you hand back, because you alphabetize numbers like a drunk librarian. "11" plus 1 is "111", but "11" minus 1 is 10. Pick a lane.

You needed a second equals sign just to stop lying, and nobody, including you, knows what "this" means.

January is month zero. One guy unpublishing left-pad broke half the internet. And your node_modules folder is heavier than a black hole.

Every week there's a new framework to fix you. That's not a language. That's a renovation.

b.text: JavaScript, they built you in ten days. That's not a language, that's a bet somebody lost. Your typeof null says "object." Your [] plus {} gives you a string, and a room full of adults nodded at that. You have two equality operators, and one of them lies to your face. Your sort thinks ten comes before two, because you sort numbers as text like a toddler reading a menu. And "this"? Sometimes it's the object, sometimes it's the window, sometimes it's undefined just to keep everybody humble. You once built a whole ecosystem around eleven lines of padding code. Every developer I know has a node_modules folder heavier than their childhood. Keep going, buddy. You're the only language that needed a sequel named TypeScript to apologize for you.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, the only city where you can see the Eiffel Tower, a pyramid, and Venice in one afternoon and still feel like you never left a strip mall in Ohio. You're a city built in the desert out of pure spite and borrowed water. The Colorado River is literally drying up so a fake volcano can erupt every fifteen minutes for a guy in cargo shorts holding a yard-long margarita.

Your casinos have no clocks and no windows, which is smart, because nobody wants to know it's 9 a.m. on a Tuesday and Grandma's on her third oxygen tank at the Wheel of Fortune slots.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas"? Sure. Mostly your 401(k). And now you've got the Sphere, a giant glowing eyeball, so the whole city can watch you make every mistake in 4K.

b.text:
Las Vegas, you're the only city where a $19 buffet requires a two-hour line and a signed waiver. You built a pyramid, a volcano, and the Eiffel Tower, but God forbid anyone find a clock. You've got no windows, no clocks, and no shame. It's 3 p.m. or 3 a.m., and either way a guy dressed as Elvis is selling me a "gentleman's club" flyer.

You call it a resort fee. I call it a cover charge to enter my own hotel room. Forty-five dollars for "amenities," and the amenity is a sad pool with a DJ who keeps yelling "Make some noise!" at dehydrated accountants from Ohio.

You're a desert pretending to be Venice, with gondoliers singing in a mall. It's 112 degrees and the canal is a puddle with a mortgage.

And the slot machines in the airport? Vegas, you're the only place that starts taking your money before you've even claimed your luggage.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.

Oscar Niemeyer built you in 41 months, and it shows. You have addresses like "SQS 308, Bloco C, Apartamento 204." That's not a location, that's a tax form with a doorbell.

Your cathedral looks like a crown of thorns made by a very expensive lamp company. Your Congress has two bowls, one facing up and one down, because even your architecture can't decide whether it's receiving bribes or hiding them.

Rio gets Carnival. São Paulo gets money. You get a lawmaker who flies in Tuesday and flees Thursday. You're not a capital, you're a very large airport lounge with a flag.

b.text: Brasília is the only city where you need a car to get lost. Lúcio Costa drew it as an airplane, which explains everything: it was built to be admired from 30,000 feet and never walked in. Every superquadra looks identical, so locals give directions like "third block, the one with the tree." Niemeyer's cathedral looks like a concrete UFO that landed in a bad mood. Congress has one bowl facing up and one facing down, which is the most honest thing about the government. The air is so dry your nosebleeds have nosebleeds, the lake looks like a screensaver, and the nearest bar is eleven kilometers away on a highway with no sidewalk.

a.text: Vegas, you're the only city where the pyramid has a light beam shooting into space, and somehow the most depressing thing is the hotel. You've got a fake Venice with a gondolier who's clearly on a break from his real job at the Gap. Eiffel Tower at 1/4 scale, so the French are just fine with you as long as you keep the Eiffel Tower a little embarrassed. Your slogan is "What happens here stays here," which is a lie, because I've seen what happens here, and it's all showing up on my credit card statement in the spring. You run on oxygen that's pumped into casinos so nobody notices the clock. Your buffets are all-you-can-eat, which is a dare. You're a city built on the idea that the house always wins, and honestly, Vegas, you're the house.

b.text:
Las Vegas, you're the only city where a $19 buffet requires a two-hour line and a signed waiver. You built a pyramid, a volcano, and the Eiffel Tower, but God forbid anyone find a clock. You've got no windows, no clocks, and no shame. It's 3 p.m. or 3 a.m., and either way a guy dressed as Elvis is selling me a "gentleman's club" flyer.

You call it a resort fee. I call it a cover charge to enter my own hotel room. Forty-five dollars for "amenities," and the amenity is a sad pool with a DJ who keeps yelling "Make some noise!" at dehydrated accountants from Ohio.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, you're the only app where a little green dot controls people's moods. We all stare at it like a heart monitor. "Dave's active? Dave's ignoring me personally."

You turned "quick question" into a four-hour ordeal. Somebody types "hey," then nothing, and the whole office watches three little dots dance for twenty minutes like they're drafting the Gettysburg Address. Then comes "can you hop on a huddle?" Nobody has ever hopped.

And #random? That channel has never been random. It's a graveyard of cat GIFs and a 2019 poll about lunch.

You're the reason we have 47 unread notifications and zero idea what's going on. Do Not Disturb is your most-ignored feature, and you know it.

b.text:
Slack. Named after the one thing you'll never have again.

You promised to kill email, and you did, by replacing it with forty channels that are each email with a typing indicator. Nothing builds dread like "Greg is typing..." for ninety seconds, followed by "hey." Just "hey." Greg, that's not a message, that's a hostage situation.

You gave us threads, so every conversation happens in two places and nobody knows which one's real. You gave us huddles: a meeting that jumps out of a bush. You gave us the green dot, so my boss can monitor my bathroom breaks like a heart rate.

And that knock sound. I hear it in the grocery store. I hear it at funerals.

Slack, you're the only app that needs three gigs of RAM to tell me someone reacted with a dancing parrot.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text: PMMA, you're the world's most expensive Post-it note. Someone spins you onto a silicon wafer at four thousand RPM, bakes you on a hotplate like a sad pizza, then fires electrons at you for six hours, and your big move is to dissolve in MIBK. That's your whole personality. You're a positive resist, which in your case means you only become positive once you've been destroyed. Hit you with a plasma etch and you're gone in ten seconds, so the entire process has to be built around your fragility. You're the lab's most high-maintenance divorcee. But the resolution is incredible, I'll give you that. Sub-20 nanometers, folks. Shame you can't survive a Tuesday.

b.text: PMMA, you're the same plastic as a hockey rink window, and somehow that's your most dignified job. You've been "high resolution" since the 1970s, which is like bragging about your SAT score at your retirement party. Sure, you'll resolve sub-10-nanometer lines, if someone stands there blasting you with electrons for an eternity. Your sensitivity is so low the beam current has gotten tenure. You don't even develop properly without MIBK and IPA holding your hand in a one-to-three ratio. And your whole personality is chain scission: you literally fall apart when someone pays attention to you. Then hit you with too much dose and you crosslink and flip to negative tone, a full identity crisis. And dry etch? You melt in plasma faster than an ice sculpture at a barbecue. Honestly, the only thing you're consistently good at is lift-off: leaving.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only technology that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not an energy source, you're a timeshare pitch.

The sun does you effortlessly. It just sits there being enormous. You need a giant metal donut called a tokamak, magnets colder than deep space, and plasma hotter than the sun's core, and that plasma still escapes like it's late for a better party.

In 2022 you finally got more energy out than you put in! From the lasers. Ignoring the grid power feeding the lasers. That's like bragging you turned a profit because the cashier handed you change.

ITER started at five billion euros, now sits somewhere north of twenty, and keeps sliding its startup date. And your fuel needs tritium, which barely exists, so you'll have to breed it yourself.

Fusion: clean, safe, limitless, and tragically hypothetical.

b.text:
Fusion power, you've been thirty years away since my grandfather was alive. You're the friend who's "five minutes out" and hasn't left the house.

You're so proud of reaching net energy gain. Sure, the laser put out more than the fuel pellet took in, but it needed three hundred megajoules from the wall to make three. That's like bragging you turned a profit because you ignored rent, payroll, and the building.

You heat plasma to a hundred million degrees, then your biggest worry is that it touches something. Your whole job is holding a tiny sun in a magnetic bottle, and the sun does it for free using only gravity and spite.

ITER's budget has more delays than a budget airline. Your fuel, tritium, is rarer than a straight answer from a physicist, so your plan is to breed it inside the reactor you haven't built yet.

Fusion: the energy of the future, and always will be.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word, ladies and gentlemen. It's the only program where nudging a photo one pixel to the left sends three paragraphs to page nine and summons a blank final page you will never, ever delete.

Word has been around for forty years and still can't decide what font it is. Times New Roman, then Calibri, now Aptos. It's having a midlife crisis in 11-point.

It underlines my own name in red. Wavy red. Like *I'm* the typo.

Try making a numbered list. Word says, "Got it, starting at 1." Second item: "Also 1." Third item: "Here's 4. It's indented. It's a letter now."

And Track Changes isn't a feature. It's a crime scene: strikethroughs everywhere, plus forty comments from someone named "Author."

Word, you gave us Clippy, and somehow he was the most helpful part.

b.text:
Microsoft Word, you're the only program that's been around for forty years and still can't tell me where the bullet point ends. I type one dash, hit enter, and suddenly you're deciding I'm running a whole bulleted empire. I try to undo it and you go, "Nope, here's an indented sub-bullet instead." Thanks, Clippy's grumpy cousin.

And the "Track Changes" feature? You're named after a document, but you treat every edit like a crime scene. Someone changes "the" to "a" and suddenly the whole page looks like a kindergarten finger painting, red lines everywhere, and nobody knows who did it.

Then there's the page numbers. Page one is perfect. Page two is fine. Page nine just quietly starts itself over at one because you got bored.

Forty years, Word. You've seen everything. Still can't center a title without me holding my breath.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, you were a $400 Wi-Fi-connected juicer that delivered four tons of force, enough, your engineers bragged, to lift two Teslas, and Bloomberg proved the job could be done by a guy with hands. You raised $120 million from Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins to compete with *squeezing*. Every single customer already owned the competing product. It came in pairs.

You sold $8 bags of chopped produce that had to scan a QR code and phone home before you'd juice them. A juicer that needed internet. Imagine the outage: "Sorry, AWS is down, enjoy your sealed pouch of regret." You'd refuse to press an expired pack, like a bouncer for kale.

Doug Evans compared himself to Steve Jobs. Steve Jobs put a thousand songs in your pocket. Doug put a sack of mush in a vise and asked for your Wi-Fi password. Silicon Valley's most expensive way to say, "Just use your hands."

b.text:
Juicero raised 120 million dollars to build a Wi-Fi-enabled juicer that cost 700 dollars, then 400 after they panicked. It had a press with four tons of force, enough to lift two Teslas. For what? Squeezing a bag of chopped kale.

Then Bloomberg proved you could just squeeze the bag with your hands. Same juice. No Wi-Fi. No app. No shame. Just a human fist doing the job of a venture-backed appliance.

And the packs! Sold separately, with expiration dates, so the machine would refuse to work if the bag was old. It's a juicer with a DRM problem. You couldn't even use your own fruit. It was a printer that squeezes.

The founder looked like someone who'd raised money by describing a smoothie as "infrastructure."

Google Ventures invested, which makes sense. Nobody does disrupting a squeeze like people who've never had to do one.

Juicero shut down in 2017, a rare startup where the customers' hands outperformed the product, and the product still had a better pitch deck.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista, you were the only operating system that asked permission to ask permission. "Are you sure you want to open Notepad?" Yes, Vista. I've been sure for twenty years.

You called yourself "Capable" on those stickers. Then you needed 15 gigs of RAM just to display a transparent window border. Aero looked gorgeous, though, like a beautiful man dying slowly of a mystery illness.

Remember copying a file? You'd say "Calculating time remaining" for six hours, like a mechanic staring at my engine going, "Hmm."

Microsoft shipped you, then immediately started apologizing with Windows 7. That's not a successor, that's a public apology with a Start button.

And "Vista Ready" laptops that couldn't run Vista? That's like a "Marathon Ready" sticker on a recliner.

Even your sidebar gadgets gave up. The weather widget just sat there, accurately predicting a cloudy future for everyone who bought you.

b.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Five years in development as "Longhorn," and the only thing that shipped on time was the disappointment. They cut WinFS but kept the Aero glass. Finally, an operating system you could see right through.

Vista came in six editions, from Starter to Ultimate, which is five more ways to pay for the same crash. Microsoft slapped "Vista Capable" stickers on computers that could barely run Solitaire, then got sued. The only thing Vista ever finished loading was a class action.

And User Account Control! "Are you sure you want to do that?" Every. Single. Click. Vista was the only software that needed permission to exist, and honestly? We should've hit Cancel.

Copying a file: "Calculating time remaining…" Vista, you were calculating until 2009, when Microsoft fixed you, renamed you Windows 7, and pretended you were adopted.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text:
UGG boots look like someone skinned a Muppet and asked you to wear the evidence. They're the only footwear where the sales pitch is "it's like walking on a cloud" and the cloud is a wet sheepdog.

Nobody's ever said "nice UGGs" without a tiny pause for mercy.

They're technically slippers that got promoted past their competence. You can wear them to the grocery store, but God help you if it drizzles, because suede plus water equals two damp loaves of bread strapped to your calves.

And the shape! Your ankle disappears. You walk in and a stranger thinks you have the legs of a Clydesdale. That's not a boot, that's a hoof cozy.

The inside smells like a gym bag in a sauna by month two, because they're meant to be worn sockless, which is a bold design choice for something with no ventilation and a lifetime of regret.

Also, they cost two hundred dollars. For slippers. That Australians apparently wear to surf, which tells you everything about Australians.

b.text: Ugg boots are the only shoe that looks like a sheep ate a pair of slippers and then apologized by giving them back. You didn't buy Uggs, you bought a pair of carpet remnants that wandered into a shoe store and got lucky. Nobody's ever run in them. Nobody's ever been chased in them. They're designed for one thing: standing in a Target parking lot holding an oat milk latte like you just finished a marathon. And the name! "Ugg." That's not a brand, that's a noise you make when you step on a Lego in the dark. Somewhere, a shearling farmer is looking at these and saying, "I didn't raise sheep for this, I raised them to be respected." Stay warm, I guess. You look like a hot dog that gave up.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies, look at you. Half bear, half beanbag, all retirement plan that never paid out. An entire generation of parents bought you instead of index funds. Somewhere a man is still storing Princess, the purple Diana bear, in a climate-controlled unit, waiting for the market to "recover." Buddy, the market recovered. It just didn't take you with it.

Your most valuable feature was a heart-shaped paper tag. People bought plastic tag protectors. For the tag. That's like buying a phone case for your receipt.

And every tag had a little poem rhyming "bear" with "care." Hallmark called that lazy.

A Las Vegas couple had to divide you on a courtroom floor during their divorce, one at a time. That's the most anyone has wanted you since 1999: only to make sure their ex didn't get you.

Ty Warner got a billion dollars. You got plastic pellets.

b.text:
Beanie Babies: the only investment where the advice was "don't remove the tag" and everyone said, "Sounds legit." Parents in 1998 put them in plexiglass cases like they were the Hope Diamond. It was a bean-filled bear named Garcia. You were hedging against a tie-dye pig.

Every one had a poem on the tag. "Legs the Frog" had a poem. Why? Nobody asked Legs to be a poet. Legs just wanted to sit on a shelf and appreciate the lack of structural support.

And the "retired" thing. Ty would announce a toy was retired, like it had served in a war. Suddenly your aunt's driving to a Hallmark in Ohio at 4 a.m. for Princess the Bear, a bear dedicated to a dead woman, which is a hell of a thing to put a price sticker on.

People paid thousands for these. Today they're worth less than the pellets inside. Which is the only part that was ever real: plastic pellets, fear, and a very small heart-shaped tag.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text: Nuclear fusion is the energy source that's always thirty years away, and it has been since your grandpa was in diapers. Scientists figured out how to bottle a star. Unfortunately, the star is 150 million degrees, and it refuses to stay in the bottle. Every time the plasma touches the wall, it's like a toddler discovering the fridge is cold. The machines are shaped like donuts because nothing else can handle the pressure. We got net energy gain for a few billionths of a second, and the press release was longer than the experiment. Meanwhile, the sun does it for free, with no magnets, and it still manages to be more reliable than the people promising us a fusion plant by 2030.

b.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only technology that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not an energy source, you're a timeshare pitch.

The sun does you effortlessly. It just sits there being enormous. You need a giant metal donut called a tokamak, magnets colder than deep space, and plasma hotter than the sun's core, and that plasma still escapes like it's late for a better party.

In 2022 you finally got more energy out than you put in! From the lasers. Ignoring the grid power feeding the lasers. That's like bragging you turned a profit because the cashier handed you change.

ITER started at five billion euros, now sits somewhere north of twenty, and keeps sliding its startup date. And your fuel needs tritium, which barely exists, so you'll have to breed it yourself.

Fusion: clean, safe, limitless, and tragically hypothetical.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text: Microsoft Word is the only program that has a paperclip for a mascot, and it still managed to be the most annoying thing on the screen. You type one space in the middle of a sentence and the whole document rearranges itself like it's moving apartments. Every image you insert becomes a hostage that refuses to stay on page four. And that blue squiggle under your name? Word thinks *you're* the typo. Then there's Compatibility Mode, the program's way of saying, "I've seen your file, and I'm not going to pretend I understand it." Twenty years of updates, and the only thing it's truly mastered is looking shocked when you press Ctrl+S.

b.text:
Microsoft Word, you're the only software where pressing Enter once can rearrange my entire document like a Rubik's cube in an earthquake.

You've got a paperclip-shaped trauma in your past, and honestly, he was the only one who ever tried to help. Now it's just you, auto-correcting "ducking" into things I definitely didn't mean to say to my boss.

Bullet points? You take them personally. I press Tab, you indent. I press Backspace, you un-indent, delete the bullet, and change the font to Comic Sans out of spite.

I tried to put one picture on page two. Page six now has a single sentence and a sense of dread.

And the green squiggly line? Judgmental. The red one? Fine, I misspelled "necessary." But you underlined my own name like I'm the one who's wrong.

You've been around since 1983 and still can't tell me why Save As has seven different locations. Ribbon? More like a ribbon of confusion. Truly, you're a masterpiece of formatting I never asked for.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text:
LaTeX is the only software where you spend three hours making a document look "professional" and one minute actually writing it.

You want a picture next to some text? LaTeX says, "Sure, I'll put it on page nine. Floating. Like your hopes."

The error messages are written by someone who hates you personally. "Missing $ inserted." Missing WHAT? I'm a grad student, I haven't seen a dollar since 2019.

Compile once, and the table of contents is wrong. Compile twice, it's right. Compile three times, and now the bibliography has vanished. It's not software, it's a séance.

Everyone says, "Just use a template!" Sure, let me paste in forty packages I don't understand, and pray hyperref doesn't fight with the other thirty-nine.

And the people who love it? They'll tell you, "It handles equations beautifully." Yes, Greg, and my Honda handles beautifully too, but I don't build the engine from a text file to drive to Costco.

Knuth wrote it in 1978 and said it was done. That's the only deadline in history met by being declared finished.

b.text: LaTeX, you're the only software where "it compiled" counts as an emotional milestone. One missing brace and you blame line 1 of a 400-line file, then sit there with a question mark like we're playing a text adventure from 1985. I put a figure on page 3; you float it to the appendix because you "know better." You have to run twice just to learn your own page numbers, three times if BibTeX shows up, like a guy who needs two friends to remind him his name. Your answer to every problem is another \usepackage, so my preamble is now longer than my thesis. Every paper you touch looks gorgeous, and identical, because everyone on Earth can spot Computer Modern from across a conference hall. And your favorite warning, "Overfull \hbox, badness 10000"? Honestly, that's just how I feel about you.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript was written in ten days, and honestly, it shows. It's the only language where `[] + {}` is a string, `{} + []` is zero, and nobody can explain why without sweating.

You ask JavaScript to compare `"2" > "12"` and it says true, because it's alphabetical. Sorting numbers? Also alphabetical. `.sort()` gives you ``, like a librarian who learned math from a dictionary.

`NaN` stands for "Not a Number," and its type is "number." `NaN !== NaN`. It's the only thing in programming that refuses to identify itself.

Then there's `this`, which means whatever it feels like today. Every callback is a coin flip with your dignity.

And the ecosystem! You wanted to pad a string, so you installed a package, and now your project has 1,400 dependencies and one of them is a guy's feelings.

JavaScript doesn't throw errors. It throws "undefined is not a function" and lets you figure out which of your 40,000 lines it's talking about.

b.text: JavaScript, they built you in ten days. That's not a language, that's a bet somebody lost. Your typeof null says "object." Your [] plus {} gives you a string, and a room full of adults nodded at that. You have two equality operators, and one of them lies to your face. Your sort thinks ten comes before two, because you sort numbers as text like a toddler reading a menu. And "this"? Sometimes it's the object, sometimes it's the window, sometimes it's undefined just to keep everybody humble. You once built a whole ecosystem around eleven lines of padding code. Every developer I know has a node_modules folder heavier than their childhood. Keep going, buddy. You're the only language that needed a sequel named TypeScript to apologize for you.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text: Apple's Vision Pro costs $3,499, which is more than most people's first car and buys you goggles that make you look like you're about to get hypnotized at a Best Buy. The front has a screen that shows your eyeballs to everyone around you, so now you're not just wearing a computer, you're wearing one that makes eye contact with strangers. You click things by pinching the air, which is great, because you already look like you're conducting an invisible orchestra in the middle of Target. The battery lives in a puck on a cable, so you're a tethered astronaut who paid four grand to watch a movie alone in a room full of people staring at your face.

b.text: Apple Vision Pro, everybody! Thirty-five hundred dollars to look like a scuba diver lost in a Best Buy. Apple insists it's not VR, it's "spatial computing," which is like calling a fanny pack "hip luggage." It's so heavy they had to throw in a second strap, and the battery's a separate brick on a cord, so you're basically a lamp that walks. Two hours of charge! That's not a computer, that's a matinee. Then there's EyeSight, the screen that shows your eyes on the front, so your family can watch a dim, blurry you stare at nothing. Most honest feature Apple's ever made. Netflix wouldn't even make an app. Netflix! They're on smart fridges! And your Persona looks like a hostage video filmed inside the uncanny valley.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
