Emacs is the only text editor that thinks "Ctrl-x Ctrl-c" is a reasonable way to say goodbye. You press it to save, and it asks you if you're sure you want to leave. You press it to leave, and it asks you to save. Nobody's ever been trapped in a relationship that confusing and still called it a productivity tool.

And the name! Emacs stands for "Editor Macros," which is a bit like naming your car "Engine Wheels." It's the most powerful editor on Earth, sure, but it boots up like it's reading you its own family history. Your laptop fan spins up, you wait a few seconds, and then you're staring at a blank screen, wondering if you're the one who's supposed to be doing the editing.

b.text:
Emacs isn't a text editor, it's an operating system that's still waiting for a decent editor to come along. It has a built-in psychiatrist, a Tetris clone, and a mail client, but somehow no sane keybindings.

Ctrl-x Ctrl-s to save? That's not a shortcut, that's a hand injury with a lawsuit pending. Emacs users call it "Emacs pinky" like it's a badge of honor. Sir, that's a repetitive strain injury from a Lisp interpreter.

And the config file! Fifteen years of init.el, a thousand lines of copy-pasted snippets from a 2009 blog post, and nobody knows what half of it does. But if you delete it, you die.

Every Emacs user says, "It's infinitely customizable!" Yes, and you've spent four hundred hours customizing it so you can finally write a grocery list.

Meanwhile, the Vim guys are laughing, and honestly? They've earned it.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text: Risk, you're the only game where "world domination" takes longer than actual world domination. Genghis Khan conquered Asia faster than my cousin conquered Ukraine, and my cousin had six armies and a dream. Your map looks like it was drawn from a description of Earth overheard on a bus. Kamchatka borders Alaska? Irkutsk and Yakutsk get more real estate than most of Africa? You taught a generation that the winning strategy is hiding in Australia like a coward and waiting for everyone else to bleed out over Siam. The defender wins ties, which explains the forty armies I lost trying to get through one guy in Egypt. And one plastic cannon is worth ten soldiers? Finally, accurate military budgeting. Five hours in, two players left, nobody's had fun since the first card set. That's not a board game, Risk. That's a hostage situation.

b.text: Risk is the only board game where the goal is world domination and somehow everyone ends up furious about it. You spend four hours conquering continents while your friend sits there holding Australia, which is basically a fortress with one door and a view of nothing. Kamchatka is the most dangerous place on Earth. It's one territory, and it eats two of your tiny plastic armies every time someone looks at it. Then there's the dice. Three red against two blue, and the fate of the entire planet comes down to a guy yelling "I'm rolling for Siberia!" every game ends the same way: Greg, who swore he'd only be a few minutes, owns Asia, a grudge, and your Alaska.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text: Durian, you smell like a gym sock that got left in a sewer and then decided to become a fruit out of spite. People in Singapore have to ride the MRT with signs warning them about you. Signs! You're banned from hotels. Hotels! They don't ban guests who set fire to the carpet, but they draw the line at you. And the worst part? You're shaped like a medieval mace someone dipped in a hedgehog. Nobody approaches you with a knife, they approach you with a shovel and a prayer. Fans call your taste "custardy." Custardy? Honey, that's what a gym sock would taste like if it had a rich uncle.

b.text:
Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which tracks, because like most monarchies, you stink and nobody's allowed to say it to your face.

You're the only fruit with a criminal record. Banned on the Singapore subway, alongside flammable liquids. Hotels put your picture on signs next to "no smoking." In 2019, a university in Melbourne evacuated five hundred people because they thought there was a gas leak. Nope. Just you, sitting in a cupboard, being yourself.

And the armor! You're covered in spikes like a medieval mace. Nature built you to defend yourself, then gave you a smell that does it better. The spikes are just overkill.

Fans say you taste like custard. Sure. Custard that was left in a gym bag next to some onions. Your flavor isn't an acquired taste. It's a hostage situation.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel, you're the only software so powerful that scientists had to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into a date. You didn't adapt to biology; biology adapted to you. Type a phone number and you lop off the leading zero like it owes you money. Enter a credit card number and you serve back 4.53E+15, as if I'm splitting dinner with a physicist.

You still think 1900 was a leap year. It wasn't. You've known for decades. You just don't care.

You're running entire national economies and you still panic over merged cells. The UK lost sixteen thousand COVID cases because someone used your old .xls format and you quietly ran out of rows. No warning. Just vibes.

And VLOOKUP only looks right. Thirty years we spent squinting at #N/A before you finally invented XLOOKUP, like a guy who learns to turn left at fifty.

b.text:
Excel, you're the Swiss Army knife of spreadsheets, except every blade is sharp in the wrong direction. You've got four hundred functions and somehow none of them can tell me why my dates turned into the number 45292. You autocorrect "1-2" into January 2nd, and then you act surprised when a gene called MARCH1 becomes "1-Mar." Scientists had to rename genes because of you. That's not a bug, that's a biography.

And the Ctrl+Z history stops at about twelve steps, like you're embarrassed of your own mistakes. You're a grid of a million rows and you still can't fit my budget on one screen without me squinting like I'm reading a ransom note.

Every one of us has one cell that says #REF! and one VLOOKUP we don't understand. You're not a tool, you're a hostage negotiation with a row number.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. Somewhere your cousin is a sneeze guard at Chipotle, and honestly? Your cousin has better etch resistance. One whiff of plasma and you vanish faster than a grad student's weekend.

You've been the "gold standard" since the 1970s, which is a polite way of saying nobody's been able to fire you. You need hundreds of microcoulombs just to *notice* the beam. A 40-hour write for one wafer. Glacial, but sure, sub-10-nanometer lines, we get it.

Positive resist? Overdose you and you cross-link into a *negative* one. That's not versatility, that's an identity crisis.

You get developed in MIBK, which smells like regret, and you come in 495K and 950K because one of you alone can't even do liftoff. And acetone dissolves you instantly. Even your solvents think you're temporary.

b.text: PMMA, you're the world's most expensive Post-it note. Someone spins you onto a silicon wafer at four thousand RPM, bakes you on a hotplate like a sad pizza, then fires electrons at you for six hours, and your big move is to dissolve in MIBK. That's your whole personality. You're a positive resist, which in your case means you only become positive once you've been destroyed. Hit you with a plasma etch and you're gone in ten seconds, so the entire process has to be built around your fragility. You're the lab's most high-maintenance divorcee. But the resolution is incredible, I'll give you that. Sub-20 nanometers, folks. Shame you can't survive a Tuesday.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, you've been "five years from changing everything" since 1991. Thirty-plus years! Fusion power looks at you and says, "Take it easy, pal."

You're a hundred times stronger than steel, but only if you're one perfect, flawless, microscopic strand that nobody can actually make longer than a hair. Basically you're a gym bro who can bench a truck but only if it's in a vacuum, and he's the size of a bacterium.

You're just rolled-up graphene. You're a sheet of pencil lead that got into a yoga class and now thinks it's special.

Every grant proposal says you'll build a space elevator. Meanwhile, the only thing you've actually lifted is my hopes and a tennis racket.

And toxicologists say you act like asbestos in the lungs. Incredible range: strongest material ever, also a lawsuit.

You're not the future. You're soot with a publicist.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The strongest material known to science, and you still can't hold a job. Since the nineties you've promised us a space elevator. Your longest strand is about half a meter. That's not an elevator. That's floss with a publicist.

You're graphene that rolled over and gave up. Graphene got a Nobel Prize. You got an argument over whether Soviets spotted you in 1952.

You can't even decide what you are. Twist one way, you're a metal. Twist the other, you're a semiconductor. Nobody controls it, including you. That's not versatility. That's a chirality crisis.

Drop you in any liquid and you clump together like freshmen at a mixer.

And inhale you? Suddenly you behave like asbestos. Thirty years of hype, and your most reliable talent is impersonating the one material we paid billions to rip out of schools.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
You're the only language where `typeof null` returns "object" and nobody got fired. It's been wrong for thirty years, and instead of fixing it, you just shrugged and kept serving it, like a restaurant that's been selling raw chicken since 1995 and calls it a rustic choice.

You've got two equals signs for comparison, and one of them lies. `0 == ""` is true. `"" == "0"` is false. Zero equals empty string, empty string doesn't equal zero-string. That's not a bug. That's a hostage situation.

And `.sort()` gives you ``, because you sort numbers alphabetically unless someone begs you for a comparator function. You wrote a language that thinks digits are words.

b.text:
JavaScript was written in ten days, and honestly, it shows. It's the only language where `[] + {}` is a string, `{} + []` is zero, and nobody can explain why without sweating.

You ask JavaScript to compare `"2" > "12"` and it says true, because it's alphabetical. Sorting numbers? Also alphabetical. `.sort()` gives you ``, like a librarian who learned math from a dictionary.

`NaN` stands for "Not a Number," and its type is "number." `NaN !== NaN`. It's the only thing in programming that refuses to identify itself.

Then there's `this`, which means whatever it feels like today. Every callback is a coin flip with your dignity.

And the ecosystem! You wanted to pad a string, so you installed a package, and now your project has 1,400 dependencies and one of them is a guy's feelings.

JavaScript doesn't throw errors. It throws "undefined is not a function" and lets you figure out which of your 40,000 lines it's talking about.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, you're the only city where a $19 buffet costs $64 once you add the "resort fee," the "facility fee," and the emotional toll of the line.

You built a fake Eiffel Tower, a fake Venice, and a fake New York, because even your tourists said, "Sure, but can we get these somewhere hotter and sadder?"

It's 115 degrees, and the locals say, "But it's a dry heat." So is an oven, Brenda.

Everyone arrives in a bachelor party wearing matching shirts and leaves as a missing-person report with a wristband.

You have a million slot machines at the airport. You're the only place that starts taking your money before you've gotten your luggage.

And the Sphere? A billion-dollar glowing eyeball staring down the Strip, like even the city is judging your decisions.

What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas, mostly because it's your checking account.

b.text: Vegas, you're the only city where the pyramid has a light beam shooting into space, and somehow the most depressing thing is the hotel. You've got a fake Venice with a gondolier who's clearly on a break from his real job at the Gap. Eiffel Tower at 1/4 scale, so the French are just fine with you as long as you keep the Eiffel Tower a little embarrassed. Your slogan is "What happens here stays here," which is a lie, because I've seen what happens here, and it's all showing up on my credit card statement in the spring. You run on oxygen that's pumped into casinos so nobody notices the clock. Your buffets are all-you-can-eat, which is a dare. You're a city built on the idea that the house always wins, and honestly, Vegas, you're the house.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow the lesson everyone learned was "buy Park Place." Then Parker Brothers bought you from a guy who basically stole you, which is the most on-brand origin story in history.

You're the only game where "second prize in a beauty contest" counts as income and jail is solved with a coupon. Your mascot looks like he foreclosed on the Pringles guy, and half of America swears he wears a monocle. He doesn't. We just assumed a man that rich would be hiding something.

Nobody has ever finished you. Games don't end; your cousin just flips the board over Marvin Gardens, which you misspelled, by the way. It's Marven. Even your real estate is a scam.

b.text:
Monopoly is the only game where "fun for the whole family" ends with Dad flipping the board and Grandma cackling over Baltic Avenue.

It's a game about capitalism that takes the worst part, landlords, and makes it a personality. Nobody's ever said "I'll trade you Boardwalk" without ruining a friendship.

The rules say it takes ninety minutes. Liar. I've seen Monopoly games outlive marriages. By hour four, one kid owns everything, three people are mortgaged to the hilt, and the fifth player is in jail, which is honestly the best seat in the house.

And the jail! You can pay fifty dollars to leave, which is what we call "bail reform for people who own a thimble."

Nobody follows the real rules either. Free Parking jackpot? Made up. Auctions? Skipped. Everybody plays by "house rules," which is just a fancy way of saying every family cheats differently.

Best part: the game was invented to show how monopolies are evil. Then Parker Brothers sold it, and the lesson was lost to the one who owns the railroads.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, you're the only fruit that needs a permit to carry. You weigh eighty pounds, you're covered in spikes, and you grow directly out of the tree trunk like a tumor with ambition.

Cutting you open requires oiled knives, gloves, and a will, because you bleed glue. I've seen people stuck to you for three days. You're the only fruit that fights back like a bad breakup.

And the smell! Rotten banana, bubblegum, and gym socks, all in one. You're what Juicy Fruit becomes in a hostage situation.

Then vegans discovered you. Now you're in a can, drowning in barbecue sauce, pretending to be pulled pork. Jackfruit, you're a bland, stringy shredded mess in a tin, and you're lying to everyone. Even the tree looks at you and says, "I made that? And it's pretending to be a pig?"

b.text: Jackfruit, you look like a medieval mace that got into a fight with a durian and lost. You're the size of a toddler and you have the texture of a sweater that's been through the wash. Vegans picked you up as a pulled-pork substitute, and honestly, that's the most desperate career pivot I've ever seen. "Hey, what if we made people chew a fruit like it's a cheap brisket?" Nobody asked for that. And the smell? Sweet, gym-bag funk, like a banana that climbed into a sock drawer and died there. You're the fruit equivalent of a guy who shows up to a party in a tuxedo made of burlap.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text: Brasília, you're what happens when an architect gets an entire country's budget and nobody says, "Maybe add a sidewalk?" You're shaped like an airplane, which is fitting, because everyone's goal is to board one by Friday afternoon. Your addresses read like Wi-Fi passwords: "SQS 308, Bloco C, apartamento 402." That's not a home. That's a parking spot on a spaceship. Kubitschek promised "fifty years in five," and you delivered: it's been sixty-five years and you still feel unfinished. Your Congress has one bowl facing up to receive the money and one facing down to hide it. You've got a row of identical ministry buildings so nobody can tell which one the scandal came from. In August the humidity drops so low that the only thing drier than the air is a deputy's sense of shame. Even your lake is fake. Honestly? On brand.

b.text:
Brasília, you're the only city designed by someone who looked at a map and said, "What if it were an airplane?" Congratulations, you're the world's largest piece of urban origami. Nobody can find anything because every address is a code. "I live at SQS 308, Bloco C, Apartamento 204." That's not a home, that's a Wi-Fi password.

You have no street corners. You have no sidewalks anyone uses. Brazilians love to gather in public, so you built a city where the only way to meet someone is by driving twenty minutes to stand near them.

Oscar Niemeyer gave you gorgeous curves, and then your politicians moved in and did the most corrupt things you could imagine inside them. A cathedral that looks like a crown of thorns, a Congress that looks like two bowls and a pair of dishes. Even the buildings look like they're waiting for a bribe.

You were built in four years. It shows. Rio had 400 to get charming.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text: Luosifen, you're the only dish named after a snail that contains zero snails. They simmer the snails for hours, then throw them out, like a dad who shows up for the paternity test and leaves. Your real star is suan sun, fermented bamboo shoot that smells like a gym sock studied abroad in Liuzhou and came back with opinions. Fans say, "It smells terrible but tastes amazing." So does every scam. You turned instant noodles into a hazmat event: one packet opened in a dorm and three floors file noise complaints, because that smell is *loud*. Couriers wrap you in four bags like evidence. And you come with seven sachets: chili oil, peanuts, tofu skin, wood ear, the bamboo. It's IKEA furniture that makes the neighbors move out. Liuzhou didn't invent a soup. It invented Stockholm syndrome with chili oil.

b.text: Luosifen is the only food that needs a smell permit. You open the packet in a dorm and the RA shows up asking who's microwaving a crime scene. The broth is snails simmered with pickled bamboo shoots that have been fermenting since before your grandmother was born, and those shoots smell like a gym sock that got promoted to management. People say, "It's delicious once you get past the smell." Sure, and a stink bomb is delicious once you get past the explosion. Then there's the packet of chili oil, which the label calls "optional" in the same tone a hostage-taker uses. Eat it on the subway and the whole car suddenly finds the ceiling fascinating. That's not a meal. That's a restraining order with chopsticks.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you're proof that marketing can convince people to pay four dollars for cloudy water with a nut rumor attached. You're 2% almonds. Two percent! That's not milk, that's a homeopathic remedy for oat milk.

You took a nut that needs a gallon of water per single almond to grow, then sold yourself to people who say "I'm doing it for the planet." California is in a drought, Karen. Those bees are being trucked across the country like migrant workers just so you can ruin a latte.

And the texture. You're the only drink that separates in coffee like a bad breakup. Curdling in front of everyone, floating there in tiny shame flakes.

Your carton says "Unsweetened Original," which is two lies in a row. There's nothing original about you, and nothing about you is sweet.

You're what a cow would make if she gave up halfway through and just described milk to a nut.

b.text:
Almond milk, you're not milk. You're a rumor about an almond. Two percent almonds, ninety-eight percent "we strained the tap." You're the only drink that needs a legal team to call itself milk. The dairy lobby has spent a decade trying to make you admit you're nut juice.

California spends about a gallon of water per almond just so you can show up in my fridge as... water. That's like melting a glacier to make an ice cube.

They truck in billions of bees to pollinate your orchards, and the bees die by the millions so I can pay an extra eighty cents at Starbucks for a latte that tastes like damp drywall.

And "shake well"? Leave you alone for ten minutes and you separate like a couple who met at Whole Foods. Even *you* can't commit to you.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text: Excel, you're the only software that forced geneticists to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into March 1st. Scientists can edit DNA, but they couldn't edit you. You still think 1900 was a leap year. You've known it wasn't for forty years. You just don't care. You see a zip code like 02134 and go, "Leading zero? Not on my watch." You lost sixteen thousand UK COVID cases by quietly stopping at row 65,536. Your error messages are pure poetry: #REF!, #N/A, #VALUE!, and my favorite, a column of hashtags that just means "make me wider." And VLOOKUP: insert one column and the whole finance department enters witness protection. You're not a spreadsheet. You're a hostage situation with gridlines.

b.text: Excel, you're the Swiss Army knife of spreadsheets, except every blade is rusty and one of them is just a tiny cursor that's been stuck in a cell since 1998. You've got 17,000 functions and I still can't find the one that sums things without you auto-converting my zip codes into scientific notation. You turned "1-2" into a date. Nobody asked you to. Your autocorrect thinks my gene names are calendar events. And your formulas? One missing parenthesis and suddenly I'm staring at #VALUE! like it's a personal insult. Forty years in, you still can't tell me what I did wrong. You just sit there, green triangle in the corner, judging me.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk, you're porridge that went to finishing school. Somebody looked at horse food and said, "What if it cost seventy cents extra?" Then somebody else said, "Yes, and put it in a carton that talks like a guy who just got back from Copenhagen." Your packaging has more personality than you do. Every box of Oatly reads like a cover letter: "Hi! We're a little weird!" No, you're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not a beverage. That's a salad dressing that gave up.

And the "Barista Edition"? You needed extra oil just to get a job. Enzymes break your starch into maltose, so technically you're a sugar spike in a flannel shirt. Plus you were funded by Blackstone. You're not anti-establishment, oat milk. You're a private equity firm wearing a beanie.

b.text: Oat milk, you're not a milk. You're a breakfast cereal that got lost on the way to the cereal aisle and decided to become a beverage out of spite. Somebody took a bowl of oatmeal, ran it through a blender, strained out the dignity, and called it "barista blend." Barista? You've never made a latte in your life. You just foam up like a bubble bath and tell everyone you're the sustainable one. Congratulations, you're the only drink that needs a wellness influencer to explain what's in it. Cows just stand there and produce; you need a whole marketing campaign with a sunrise on the carton. And that sad grey sediment at the bottom of the glass? That's you, admitting the truth.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a wall. The Ruins of St. Paul's: a gorgeous front with absolutely nothing behind it, which is basically your whole personality. You've got a fake Venice with a painted sky, a fake Paris with a half-size Eiffel Tower, and you're so tiny you had to dump dirt into the ocean just to fit a runway. You out-earned Las Vegas several times over, and your signature dish is still a pork chop jammed in a bun. The Portuguese stayed four hundred years and left you an egg tart and street signs nobody reads. The Grand Lisboa looks like a golden pineapple having a breakdown. And the Macau Tower's big attraction is jumping off it, which, after a night at the baccarat tables, is less a thrill ride and more a financial plan.

b.text:
Macau, you're Las Vegas that went to a Portuguese finishing school and came back with gambling debt and a custard tart habit. You make more money from gambling than Vegas does, but you're only 12 square miles. That's not a city, that's a casino with a postal code.

You've got a replica Eiffel Tower, a Venice with fake canals, and a Roman-style sky painted on the ceiling. Nothing here is original except the egg tarts, and even those are Portuguese. You even stole those, Macau, you just added a Cantonese accent.

The streets have Portuguese names, but nobody speaks Portuguese. It's colonialism's most elegant ghost town. Every sign is written in a language the entire population ignores, like a terms and conditions page.

And the traffic! A million tourists walking between hotels that are all technically the same hotel. You've got a Grand Lisboa shaped like a golden lotus, or as locals call it, a giant birdcage for losing gamblers.

Come for the ruins of St. Paul's. Stay because the ferry back to Hong Kong costs exactly what you have left.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word, you're the only program that's been around for forty years and still can't tell me where the bullet point ends. I type one dash, hit enter, and suddenly you're deciding I'm running a whole bulleted empire. I try to undo it and you go, "Nope, here's an indented sub-bullet instead." Thanks, Clippy's grumpy cousin.

And the "Track Changes" feature? You're named after a document, but you treat every edit like a crime scene. Someone changes "the" to "a" and suddenly the whole page looks like a kindergarten finger painting, red lines everywhere, and nobody knows who did it.

Then there's the page numbers. Page one is perfect. Page two is fine. Page nine just quietly starts itself over at one because you got bored.

Forty years, Word. You've seen everything. Still can't center a title without me holding my breath.

b.text:
Microsoft Word, you've had thirty years to learn what I want, and you still think I'm trying to write a bulleted list every time I type a dash.

You've got a paperclip's worth of trauma in your past, yet you still auto-correct "Costco" to "Cost co" like you're editing a ransom note.

I insert one picture and the whole document rearranges itself like furniture in an earthquake. The image jumps to page nine, the text wraps around it in the shape of a gunshot wound, and page four is now blank for reasons known only to God and a hidden section break.

You have a ribbon with 400 buttons, and the one I need is always under "Layout," which is somehow not where the layout is.

And "Not Responding"? Buddy, I just asked you to save. Then you recover my file as "Document1 (Autorecovered) (Copy) (2)," like a witness protection program for my thesis.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs is a beautiful operating system. Shame it never shipped with a decent text editor. That's why half its users install evil-mode: they love Emacs so much they turned it into Vim.

Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," which is also the sound your pinky makes on its way to the orthopedic surgeon. Asking for help is C-h, which in a terminal deletes a character. So even your cry for help gets backspaced.

It has a built-in therapist, M-x doctor, which is thoughtful, because nobody else will listen to you explain your init.el. Four thousand lines of Lisp, half copied from a 2003 mailing list, and you still declare "Emacs bankruptcy" every two years.

It plays Tetris. It reads email. It runs your entire life in Org-mode. It still chokes on one long line of JSON.

b.text: Emacs is the only text editor that's also an operating system that never got around to booting. People say it's "a great operating system, just missing a good editor." Sure. You open it and it's already running a calendar, a email client, a chess engine, and a psychiatrist. You wanted to type "hello." Instead you get a *Ctrl-x Ctrl-c* keyboard combo, which is the only way out, and it requires two hands, a pinky that's been to physical therapy, and the blessing of a man named Richard who hasn't been seen since 1985. Vim users at least get a funny exit. Emacs users get a seven-keystroke prayer. And the config file? It's a Lisp dialect that's older than your parents' divorce, with parentheses so deep you need a mountain guide. Brilliant software. Terrible hostage negotiator.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Microsoft Teams is the only app that can tell you "You're on mute" after you've spent four minutes giving the best speech of your career to nobody.

It's got a notification system that works like a clingy ex. Someone reacts with a thumbs-up to a message you sent three weeks ago, and suddenly your laptop sounds like a submarine under attack.

The search function is a magic trick: you type "Q3 budget," and it shows you a GIF from Brenda's retirement party.

And the name! "Teams." Also "Teams (work or school)." Also "Teams (free)." Also "Teams Classic," which is what we now call the one that worked slightly better. Whenever you open it, it asks which Teams you want, like a waiter asking which of your three identical sandwiches you'd like.

The status indicator says "Away" when you're staring right at it, and "Available" when you've gone to the bathroom.

Teams isn't collaboration software. It's a hostage negotiation with your own Wi-Fi.

b.text: Microsoft Teams is the only app that got popular the way a parking ticket gets popular: it came free with Office 365 and nobody could say no. It's a chat app that eats more RAM than Chrome, which is like a goldfish outeating a horse. It marks you "Away" if you blink for five minutes, which is why half of corporate America owns a mouse jiggler. Every file you share vanishes into SharePoint, a place so mysterious even Microsoft sends search parties. There's chat, there's channels, there's "posts," and nobody knows which one Kevin used. They released "New Teams" to replace "Classic Teams," and somehow both are running on my laptop right now, fighting. And that notification sound? That little knock-knock haunts people on vacation. Teams, you didn't win the remote work war. You were just pre-installed.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text: Emacs is the only text editor that's also an operating system that never got around to booting. People say it's "a great operating system, just missing a good editor." Sure. You open it and it's already running a calendar, a email client, a chess engine, and a psychiatrist. You wanted to type "hello." Instead you get a *Ctrl-x Ctrl-c* keyboard combo, which is the only way out, and it requires two hands, a pinky that's been to physical therapy, and the blessing of a man named Richard who hasn't been seen since 1985. Vim users at least get a funny exit. Emacs users get a seven-keystroke prayer. And the config file? It's a Lisp dialect that's older than your parents' divorce, with parentheses so deep you need a mountain guide. Brilliant software. Terrible hostage negotiator.

b.text:
Emacs isn't a text editor, it's an operating system that's still looking for a decent editor. Thirty years of development, and the most reliable feature is the pinky injury.

You press Control-X, Control-S to save. That's not a keyboard shortcut, that's a hostage negotiation with your left hand.

Emacs users say, "It's infinitely customizable!" Sure. So is a blank sheet of paper, but nobody brags about spending three weekends configuring that. Your init.el is 4,000 lines long, and you wrote 12 of them. The rest is a Stack Overflow answer from 2011 that you're afraid to delete.

And the manual calls it "the extensible, self-documenting editor." Self-documenting! Yes, it will tell you exactly what a function does, right after you press Control-H, then K, then wonder why you're reading Lisp.

You can read email in it, browse the web in it, and play Tetris in it. Everything except quit. Nobody remembers how to quit.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, you're what happens when a watermelon gets a medieval weapons collection. You grow up to a hundred pounds, hang off the trunk like a tumor, and fall on people. You're the only fruit with a wrongful-death lawsuit hanging over your head.

Cutting you open requires oil on the knife, oil on the hands, and a signed waiver, because your sap is basically industrial glue. And inside? Yellow, stringy pods that smell like a gym bag soaked in bubblegum.

Then vegans discovered you. Suddenly you're "pulled pork." No. You're a fruit in a barbecue costume, sitting in sauce, hoping nobody checks your ID. Nobody's fooled. Even the vegans are just being polite.

You're Bangladesh's national fruit, which means a whole country looked at you and said, "Yes, that's us," and honestly, fair.

b.text: Jackfruit, you look like a sea mine that got into a fight with a durian and lost. Your skin is a crime scene of little green spikes, and nobody has ever cut you open without a prayer and a machete. You're the size of a toddler, you smell like gym socks dipped in bubblegum, and you're somehow both sweet and wet and still sticky after you've been in the fridge. Vegans found you and suddenly you're "pulled pork," which is the most desperate rebrand since "vegetable oil" tried to be a steak. Everybody's grandma loves you for one week a year, then you rot on the counter and the whole kitchen knows. You're a fruit that needs its own safety briefing. Nobody's ever walked out of a grocery store saying, "I'll have the enormous spiky thing that smells like a locker room."

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest thing humanity ever did, pouring hot water over beans, and turned it into a subscription-based hostage situation. You charge me fifty cents for a thimble of coffee wrapped in a tiny plastic coffin that will outlive my great-grandchildren.

The inventor of the K-Cup literally apologized for it. The guy said he sometimes regrets inventing it. Your own father looked at his creation and said, "Yeah, I'd undo that."

And the machine itself? You push one button and it screams like a dying dial-up modem, then dribbles out something called "Bold" that tastes like a warm handshake from a wet paper bag. Every morning it flashes "Descale Me" like a needy ex. Meanwhile your water reservoir holds enough for exactly one bad decision.

Offices love you because nothing says "we value our employees" like a sad pod carousel next to a broken microwave.

Keurig: for people who want coffee, but also want to feel something about landfills.

b.text:
Keurig, you took the one drink humanity had perfected over five hundred years and said, "What if it came in a tiny plastic thimble that outlives your grandchildren?" Your own inventor said he regrets making you. When your dad disowns you, that's a phase. When the guy who invented you disowns you, that's a recall.

You make coffee one sad, lukewarm cup at a time, then flash "DESCALE" like a check-engine light for a machine that costs forty bucks. Remember Keurig 2.0? You put DRM on coffee. You were scanning pods like a bouncer: "Sorry, sir, you're not on the list." Nobody was pirating Folgers! And your "Strong" button just drips slower, which isn't strength. That's procrastination.

You're not a coffee maker. You're a plastic-dispensing subscription that occasionally hiccups out hot brown water.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim, you are the only program that makes people feel like they're defusing a bomb just to type the word "hello." You open up and nothing works. Somebody's cat walks across the keyboard, and suddenly you're in a mode that deletes half a paragraph. And you have modes! Normal mode, insert mode, visual mode, command mode. Nobody asked for a text editor with a personality disorder.

Everybody who uses you has the same story. They accidentally hit colon, then q, then a few keys, and the whole thing just stares back at them. Then they Google "how to exit vim" and find out it's been the top search for a decade. You're not an editor, you're a riddle wrapped in a shrug.

Honestly, respect. Anyone who learns you is basically a monk. You're the only thing on Earth where pressing "j" means "down" and nobody can explain why.

b.text:
Vim. The only program where "how do I leave?" has more Stack Overflow views than most religions have followers. Two million people asked, and the answer was colon, q, exclamation point, which reads less like a command and more like a hostage's final words.

Vim stands for "Vi Improved." Improved from a 1976 terminal whose arrow keys were printed on H, J, K, and L. Fifty years later, Vim's still out here like, "Why fix what you can turn into a personality?"

You don't type in Vim. You type a sentence, then discover you deleted four lines, yanked a paragraph into register W, and started recording a macro.

Crash it once and it leaves a .swp file behind, like a ghost whispering, "Recover, Edit anyway, Quit, or Abort?"

Even its fans forked it. Neovim exists because Vim users wanted Vim, minus Vim.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which is wild, because you dress like a medieval mace and smell like a crime scene. Every other fruit says "eat me." You say "I dare you."

You're the only food with a gas leak. A Canberra university library was evacuated because of you. Evacuated! Fruit is not supposed to trigger a hazmat response.

Singapore had to put you on the subway sign with a big red X, right next to flamethrowers. Hotels ban you the way they ban smoking and goats.

And the flesh inside? Custard that tastes like sweet almonds, caramel, and a decision you regret. Fans say, "Just get past the smell." That's what people say about your cousin's boyfriend.

You're the only fruit that can kill me from the tree, and the only one I'd still blame the neighbors for.

b.text:
Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which tracks, because like most monarchies, you stink and nobody's allowed to say it to your face.

You're the only fruit with a criminal record. Banned on the Singapore subway, alongside flammable liquids. Hotels put your picture on signs next to "no smoking." In 2019, a university in Melbourne evacuated five hundred people because they thought there was a gas leak. Nope. Just you, sitting in a cupboard, being yourself.

And the armor! You're covered in spikes like a medieval mace. Nature built you to defend yourself, then gave you a smell that does it better. The spikes are just overkill.

Fans say you taste like custard. Sure. Custard that was left in a gym bag next to some onions. Your flavor isn't an acquired taste. It's a hostage situation.

Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim, you are the only program that makes people feel like they're defusing a bomb just to type the word "hello." You open up and nothing works. Somebody's cat walks across the keyboard, and suddenly you're in a mode that deletes half a paragraph. And you have modes! Normal mode, insert mode, visual mode, command mode. Nobody asked for a text editor with a personality disorder.

Everybody who uses you has the same story. They accidentally hit colon, then q, then a few keys, and the whole thing just stares back at them. Then they Google "how to exit vim" and find out it's been the top search for a decade. You're not an editor, you're a riddle wrapped in a shrug.

Honestly, respect. Anyone who learns you is basically a monk. You're the only thing on Earth where pressing "j" means "down" and nobody can explain why.

b.text:
Vim is the only software where the tutorial is "how to leave." Millions of developers have spent a Tuesday trapped inside it, mashing Escape like they're trying to wake a hostage. You open a file, type "hello," and the editor responds by deleting your paragraph and playing a macro you recorded in 2019.

Vim users say, "Once you learn it, you'll never touch your mouse again." Neither will you touch grass, sir. You've spent forty hours configuring a .vimrc so you can save four seconds on a typo.

And the modes! Normal mode, where nothing is normal. Insert mode, where you finally get to insert. Visual mode, which is only visual in the sense that you can watch yourself select the wrong thing.

It's an editor built on the premise that your keyboard has too many keys and your dignity has too much room.

Type :wq to save and quit. Type :q! to forget this ever happened.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text: Apple Vision Pro, everybody! Thirty-five hundred dollars to look like a scuba diver lost in a Best Buy. Apple insists it's not VR, it's "spatial computing," which is like calling a fanny pack "hip luggage." It's so heavy they had to throw in a second strap, and the battery's a separate brick on a cord, so you're basically a lamp that walks. Two hours of charge! That's not a computer, that's a matinee. Then there's EyeSight, the screen that shows your eyes on the front, so your family can watch a dim, blurry you stare at nothing. Most honest feature Apple's ever made. Netflix wouldn't even make an app. Netflix! They're on smart fridges! And your Persona looks like a hostage video filmed inside the uncanny valley.

b.text:
The Apple Vision Pro costs $3,499, which is a bold price for something that gives you a headache and a neck injury in the same sitting. It weighs over a pound, so after twenty minutes you're not experiencing spatial computing, you're experiencing the chiropractic kind.

Apple said it would change how we see the world, then gave it a two-hour battery on a cable you have to keep in your pocket, like an oxygen tank for your delusions.

EyeSight shows your eyes on the front, so everyone around you can watch a haunted aquarium version of your face. Your FaceTime Persona looks like a hostage video made by a very polite ghost.

The best part is the control scheme: you look at something and pinch your fingers, like you're being quietly condescending to your own living room.

It's a $3,500 ski goggle that lets you watch a movie alone. Congratulations, you've invented a very expensive way to ignore your family.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text:
NFTs are the only product where "right-click, save as" is a legitimate threat to a billion-dollar market. You didn't buy art. You bought a receipt for a JPEG that anyone can look at for free, and the receipt is a hyperlink, and the hyperlink is hosted on a server that's going down when the startup runs out of money. Congratulations, you own a 404.

And the names! Bored Ape. Doodle. CryptoPunk. Nothing says "serious investor" like a man in a blazer whispering, "I'm down forty grand on a cartoon monkey, but the community is strong."

Everyone was a visionary until the gas fees showed up. You paid sixty dollars in Ethereum fees to buy a picture of a rock that was worth four dollars, then listed it for a million because a guy named xX_DiamondHandz_Xx said it would "flip."

It didn't flip. It just sat there. Like a rock.

b.text:
NFTs, you're the only investment where the product is a receipt, and the receipt is a link to a JPEG hosted on some guy's server. When he stops paying the bill, congratulations: you own a 404.

You convinced grown adults to pay $300,000 for a cartoon monkey in a sailor hat, then charge them $80 in gas fees to watch it lose 98% of its value. Jimmy Fallon showed off his ape on national television like a kid holding up a cool rock.

People right-clicked and hit "save as," and you called it theft. Theft of *what*? It's still there! I'm looking at it!

Every project had a roadmap: metaverse, merch, a members-only yacht party. Instead the roadmap was a Discord mod named Kevin typing "we're still early" at 3 a.m.

WAGMI, you said. We did not all make it.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text:
PHP is the only language where the standard library looks like it was named by a committee of people who'd never met. Is it str_replace or strpos? Is the needle first or the haystack? Nobody knows. Not even PHP. It just rolls dice and says "array_walk, but backwards."

Fun fact: PHP stands for "Personal Home Page," which is also what it feels like when your code gets hacked and a teenager in Belarus redirects your site to a pharmacy.

It's got a function called mysql_real_escape_string, which implies there was a mysql_escape_string that was fake. Fake escaping. Just vibes.

And the equality operator? "0" == false, "abc" == 0, null == false. PHP looks at two completely different things and says, "Eh, close enough." It's the language equivalent of a bouncer who lets everyone in because they're wearing a shirt.

But hey, it powers 77% of the web. So does that one guy named Gary who's still on WordPress 3.2.

b.text: PHP, you started life as "Personal Home Page," and somehow you now run most of the internet, which explains a lot about the internet. Your own creator said he's "not a real programmer," and honestly, it shows. Is it needle then haystack, or haystack then needle? strpos and in_array have been in a custody battle since 1995. You gave us mysql_escape_string, then mysql_real_escape_string, because apparently the first one was just pretending. Your loose equality swears "0e123" equals "0e456," since both are zero in scientific notation. Your error message for a double colon is T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM, which is Hebrew, because English wasn't confusing enough. You skipped version 6 entirely, like a kid hiding a report card. Facebook loved you so much they had to rewrite you as a different language. But hey, you power WordPress, so you'll outlive all of us.

a.text:
PHP, the language that stands for "Personal Home Page" and now runs half the internet, like a rental car you forgot to return in 1998.

It's the only language where the standard library looks like it was named by a dice roll. strpos has needle, haystack. array_search has needle, haystack. But str_replace? Different order. Why? Because PHP doesn't believe in consistency. It believes in vibes.

The comparison rules are a hostage situation. "0" == false. "abc" == 0, at least until PHP 8 finally took a sip of water. And the ternary operator was left-associative for years, so nested ones did the opposite of what anyone wanted.

Then there's the dollar sign. Every variable has one, like each is being sold individually.

And yet, WordPress, Facebook, Wikipedia, all run on it. PHP is the duct tape holding the web together, and like duct tape, nobody's proud of it, but everyone's got a roll in the garage.

b.text: PHP, you're the only language whose name is a recursive acronym, and it still reads like a bug report. Every variable wears a dollar sign like you're charging rent for each one. Your function names were clearly picked by drawing lots: strpos takes the haystack first, array_search takes the needle first, and you just shrug. "0" == false? Sure. "abc" == 0? Why not. Your comparison operator is a coin toss in a trench coat. Half the internet runs on you, and WordPress is the proof. Nobody brags about WordPress, but everybody's sites are built on you. I'd like to hate you more, but I've seen you in production. Everyone loves you secretly, late at night, with error_reporting turned off.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass was the only product where the beta testers were called "Explorers," because "Guinea Pigs With Fourteen Hundred Dollars" tested poorly.

It was a computer you wore on your face that said "OK Glass" out loud, so every guy using it looked like he was being polite to a ghost. You didn't need a screen. You needed a wink and a prayer. Winking took a photo, which is a fantastic feature if you want to be punched in a bar.

And that's where they were banned: bars, casinos, strip clubs, movie theaters. Glass was the first device kicked out of places for what it *might* do. Even the strip club said, "Sir, we have standards."

They called the wearers "Glassholes," which is the rare nickname that came with the product, free, no subscription.

Google didn't discontinue it. They pivoted it to factories, where nobody has to look at you.

b.text:
Google Glass, the glasses that made everyone around you feel like they were being recorded for a documentary nobody asked for. You wore them to a dinner party and suddenly you weren't a guest, you were a surveillance operation with a nice haircut. Nobody could tell if you were looking at them or at the tiny little screen floating in your eyeball, which, let's be honest, is the exact same energy as a guy who keeps checking his phone while you're talking about your dead dog.

And that little camera! It was always pointed at people's faces like a tiny, judgmental lighthouse. People said "Glasshole" and honestly? They weren't wrong. Google spent years saying "you'll get used to it," and the public said, "We won't, but thanks for the offer."

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
Canberra is the only city in the world designed by an architect and then lived in by a committee. It's a capital built on a swamp, which was a bold choice, because nothing says "national pride" like a lake you dug yourself so the city would have something to look at.

Everyone's a public servant. Ask someone what they do and they say "policy," then spend forty minutes explaining that they can't explain it.

Roundabouts are the city's love language. You don't navigate Canberra, you get slowly interrogated by it. Exit two, exit three, back to Parliament House, you've been circling since March.

It's the only place where the nightlife is a Dendy cinema and a tense conversation about a briefing note. Even the fireworks are banned. The bush capital: eight months of frost, four of bushfire smoke, and one weekend where it's nice and everyone's at Floriade pretending they live somewhere better.

b.text: Canberra is the only capital in Australia built from scratch, which explains a lot. Sydney and Melbourne were so busy hating each other they agreed to put the country's brain in a paddock halfway between them, and it has been sulking ever since. Walter Burley Griffin drew it up as a neat wheel of boulevards around a lake, then the public servants arrived and discovered that every road in town is a roundabout. Nobody has ever found the way out of Civic. The nightlife shuts at nine because the whole city is in bed before Question Time ends. The lake is named after Griffin, which is a shame, because he's the only man ever to design a city and then get a lake named after him instead of a train station. In winter the frost is so thick the ministers need a scraper before they can go inside and be lied to.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text: Luosifen smells like someone microwaved a sewer and called it dinner. You open the packet and the whole building files a noise complaint. Half the dormitories in China have banned it, and the company just says, "That's the flavor," like a skunk insisting that's its cologne. The sour bamboo shoots have been fermenting so long they've got a personal history. The little river snails swim in a broth that tastes exactly like the river they came from. Liuzhou calls it a treasure. Liuzhou also has the river. Then you get to the peanuts, tofu skin, and chili oil, which are there to make you feel like you're eating a meal instead of a crime scene. Honestly, the sealed bag is the most honest thing about it. Even the factory knows nobody wants to smell this one in the open.

b.text:
Luosifen, the only food that files a noise complaint with your nose. It's a noodle soup made from river snails, which is already a bold choice, then fermented sour bamboo shoots join in, and suddenly your apartment smells like a swamp got a divorce.

You open one packet and the whole building knows your business. Neighbors don't ask "what's cooking?" They ask "is someone okay?"

Liuzhou people say it's delicious. Sure, and a skunk says the same about its perfume.

And the cruelty is that it's actually amazing. Rice noodles, chili oil, peanuts, tofu skin, that sour-funky-spicy punch. You'll eat it and swear you'll never do it again, then smell your own hoodie three days later and whisper, "Same time next week?"

It's the only dish where the leftover smell outlasts the leftovers, and your elevator has stopped making eye contact with you.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim, you're the only text editor with its own hostage negotiation thread. Millions of people have viewed the Stack Overflow question on how to leave you. That's not a user base, that's a missing persons report.

You have modes. Normal mode, where typing does nothing normal, and Insert mode, hidden behind the letter "i" like a secret menu.

Your fans move the cursor with h, j, k, l because a terminal from 1976 printed arrows on those keys. That's not efficiency, that's Stockholm syndrome on the home row.

Every Vim user has a 900-line .vimrc copied from a stranger and is too scared to touch it. And when you crash, you leave .swp files behind like a burglar who signs the guestbook.

Even your own kids forked you into Neovim. That's not a fork. That's an intervention.

Goodnight! :wq… :q!… ESC ESC ESC…

b.text:
Vim, you are the only program that makes people feel like they're defusing a bomb just to type the word "hello." You open up and nothing works. Somebody's cat walks across the keyboard, and suddenly you're in a mode that deletes half a paragraph. And you have modes! Normal mode, insert mode, visual mode, command mode. Nobody asked for a text editor with a personality disorder.

Everybody who uses you has the same story. They accidentally hit colon, then q, then a few keys, and the whole thing just stares back at them. Then they Google "how to exit vim" and find out it's been the top search for a decade. You're not an editor, you're a riddle wrapped in a shrug.

Honestly, respect. Anyone who learns you is basically a monk. You're the only thing on Earth where pressing "j" means "down" and nobody can explain why.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text: Excel, you're the Swiss Army knife of spreadsheets, except every blade is rusty and one of them is just a tiny cursor that's been stuck in a cell since 1998. You've got 17,000 functions and I still can't find the one that sums things without you auto-converting my zip codes into scientific notation. You turned "1-2" into a date. Nobody asked you to. Your autocorrect thinks my gene names are calendar events. And your formulas? One missing parenthesis and suddenly I'm staring at #VALUE! like it's a personal insult. Forty years in, you still can't tell me what I did wrong. You just sit there, green triangle in the corner, judging me.

b.text:
Excel, you're the only software that thinks "September 4th" and "the gene SEPT4" are the same thing. Scientists renamed human genes because of you. Genetics bent the knee to a spreadsheet.

You've got a million rows, and somehow the one cell I need is always showing ########. That's not an error, that's you yelling at me.

Every company on earth runs on one file called "Final_v7_REAL_final_JOHN'S EDIT.xlsx" that only Linda understands, and Linda's on vacation. Her formula is a nested IF statement so long it has its own zip code.

You can do VLOOKUP, XLOOKUP, INDEX-MATCH, and you still make me fight for it like a hostage negotiation.

And you're a "data tool" that auto-formats my phone number into scientific notation. Congratulations, 5.55E+09, I've never felt more called.

Also, Clippy left. You stayed. That tells us who was actually the problem.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text:
Monopoly is the only game where "fun for the whole family" ends with Dad flipping the board and Grandma cackling over Baltic Avenue.

It's a game about capitalism that takes the worst part, landlords, and makes it a personality. Nobody's ever said "I'll trade you Boardwalk" without ruining a friendship.

The rules say it takes ninety minutes. Liar. I've seen Monopoly games outlive marriages. By hour four, one kid owns everything, three people are mortgaged to the hilt, and the fifth player is in jail, which is honestly the best seat in the house.

And the jail! You can pay fifty dollars to leave, which is what we call "bail reform for people who own a thimble."

Nobody follows the real rules either. Free Parking jackpot? Made up. Auctions? Skipped. Everybody plays by "house rules," which is just a fancy way of saying every family cheats differently.

Best part: the game was invented to show how monopolies are evil. Then Parker Brothers sold it, and the lesson was lost to the one who owns the railroads.

b.text: Monopoly is the only board game where the goal is to bankrupt your friends and somehow everyone still agrees to play it again. Four hours. Four hours! Nobody has ever finished a game of Monopoly. The game just ends when someone's dad flips the table, or when the banker quietly starts pretending they didn't count the money properly. And the banker, by the way, is always the least trustworthy person at the table, because they're the one holding the stack of cash and they're the one who "forgot" to collect Free Parking. Free Parking! That's not a gift, that's a lie you tell children. And Boardwalk? Nobody's ever landed on Boardwalk and felt lucky. They just felt the rent go up like a hostage negotiation. Monopoly: where your uncle buys every railroad and calls it a "strategy."

Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.

The broth is snails simmered with pickled bamboo shoots that have been fermenting since before your grandmother was born, and those shoots smell like a gym sock that got promoted to management. People say, "It's delicious once you get past the smell." Sure, and a stink bomb is delicious once you get past the explosion. Then there's the packet of chili oil, which the label calls "optional" in the same tone a hostage-taker uses. Eat it on the subway and the whole car suddenly finds the ceiling fascinating. That's not a meal. That's a restraining order with chopsticks.

b.text:
Luosifen, the only food that files a noise complaint with your nose. It's a noodle soup made from river snails, which is already a bold choice, then fermented sour bamboo shoots join in, and suddenly your apartment smells like a swamp got a divorce.

You open one packet and the whole building knows your business. Neighbors don't ask "what's cooking?" They ask "is someone okay?"

Liuzhou people say it's delicious. Sure, and a skunk says the same about its perfume.

And the cruelty is that it's actually amazing. Rice noodles, chili oil, peanuts, tofu skin, that sour-funky-spicy punch. You'll eat it and swear you'll never do it again, then smell your own hoodie three days later and whisper, "Same time next week?"
