facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text: Juicero built a $400 Wi-Fi press whose entire job was squeezing a bag. Not a fruit. A bag. Somebody looked at a pouch of pre-chopped kale and decided it needed a computer. Then a reporter showed everyone you could wring the packs out with your bare hands, and the venture capitalists went quiet, like they'd just realized their $120 million bought a very expensive pair of hands. The press checked a QR code before it would crush your spinach. That's the most Silicon Valley sentence ever written: the machine needed permission to juice. The packs cost about five bucks each, so you were paying premium prices to do what a Capri Sun does on its own.

b.text:
Juicero raised 120 million dollars to build a $400 Wi-Fi-connected juicer, which is a lot of engineering for a bag you could just squeeze with your hands. And that's exactly what Bloomberg did. Reporters squeezed the pack by hand and got juice faster than the machine. The machine had four tons of force, and the whole thing was basically a very expensive way to say "no thanks, I'll do it myself."

It wouldn't even work offline. Your juice pack had to phone home to check if it was expired. Imagine being a kale-based hostage to a server in California. "Sorry, your carrots are out of date." Brother, I'm holding them. They're orange. They're fine.

And the packs cost eight dollars each. Eight dollars for a bag of chopped salad you'd then have to pretend was fresh-pressed. Silicon Valley looked at a smoothie and said, "What if it had DRM?"

Juicero didn't disrupt juice. It disrupted investors' bank accounts.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text: Oat milk, you're the Prius of dairy alternatives. You show up at brunch with a tote bag full of opinions, and everybody claps like you saved the planet. Meanwhile you're just oats that got put through a blender and came out looking like wet cardboard with a lawyer. You froth beautifully, sure, but you froth like a guy who just found out his barista certificate expired. And don't get me started on "barista edition." Nobody's a barista because they bought a carton with a cartoon on it. You're basically a shampoo that gave up on being a shampoo and decided to be a latte. Nobody asked you to be creamy. You just showed up creamy-adjacent and expected a parade.

b.text:
Oat milk, you're what happens when a bowl of oatmeal gets ghosted and decides to live in a carton. You're not milk. You're oatmeal that went through a breakup and is now "finding itself" in a Brooklyn coffee shop.

You cost seven dollars, and for that, you taste like a wet cereal bowl that someone rinsed with regret. Baristas call you "creamy." You're not creamy. You're just thick, like the guy at the party explaining his podcast.

You separate in hot coffee like you've got commitment issues, then leave a gritty film at the bottom that feels like drinking a handshake from a sandcastle.

And the label says "Barista Edition." Barista Edition? Oh good, you've got a job title now. Cow's milk never needed a LinkedIn.

Your whole personality is "I'm not dairy." Congratulations. Neither is drywall, and it's got a better shelf life.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest thing in the world, hot water meeting coffee, and turned it into a subscription-based hostage situation. My grandfather made coffee with a pot and a prayer. I make it by stabbing a tiny plastic hockey puck in the face.

You've created a machine that takes four minutes to warm up just to produce eight ounces of something that tastes like a mug rinsed in a wet cardboard box. And that little pod? Thousands of tiny plastic cups, each one lasting longer than my last three relationships.

Then there's the "descale" light. Every few months it screams at me to run vinegar through it, like a smoke detector for my own laziness. I ignore it, and the machine just sighs and gives me half a cup.

The best part is the "strong" button. It doesn't make it stronger. It makes it smaller. You invented coffee's version of "I'm not mad, I'm just disappointed."

b.text:
Keurig, you took the one drink humanity had perfected over five hundred years and said, "What if it came in a tiny plastic thimble that outlives your grandchildren?" Your own inventor said he regrets making you. When your dad disowns you, that's a phase. When the guy who invented you disowns you, that's a recall.

You make coffee one sad, lukewarm cup at a time, then flash "DESCALE" like a check-engine light for a machine that costs forty bucks. Remember Keurig 2.0? You put DRM on coffee. You were scanning pods like a bouncer: "Sorry, sir, you're not on the list." Nobody was pirating Folgers! And your "Strong" button just drips slower, which isn't strength. That's procrastination.

You're not a coffee maker. You're a plastic-dispensing subscription that occasionally hiccups out hot brown water.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text: Beanie Babies. The only retirement plan where the retiree was a five-dollar bear stuffed with plastic pellets. A whole generation bought plastic protectors for a toy's ear tag, then sealed the toy in a Ziploc so no child could ever love it. You weren't a stuffed animal; you were a 401(k) with a poem on it. And those poems! Ty Warner doing greeting-card Shakespeare for people who thought Princess the bear would pay for college. Princess paid for nothing. Neither did the Teenie Beanies everyone hoarded from McDonald's while throwing away the actual Happy Meal. A divorcing couple in Las Vegas literally split their collection on a courtroom floor, one Beanie at a time. That's your legacy: custody battles over a moose named Chocolate. Even your creator got busted hiding money from the IRS, because he was the only one who ever made any.

b.text:
Beanie Babies, the only investment where your financial advisor was a woman named Deb at a card shop. People kept them in plastic cases, like organ donors. Not toys, relics. "Don't touch Princess the bear, she's for college." Princess was a purple bear stuffed with plastic pellets and a dead princess's legacy, and your mom thought she'd pay for Yale.

The genius was the tag. Not the toy, the tag. Ty looked at a bag of beans and said, "What if we made it illegal to love this?" Bend that heart-shaped tag and you've lost four thousand dollars. Kids learned grief early: "I hugged Peanut the elephant, and now he's worth nothing."

Then the retirements. Ty killed off bears like a Game of Thrones writer with a mortgage. Fall for Squealer the pig and he's gone by Tuesday, replaced by a slightly different pig.

Today they're in a garage in Ohio, sweating in a bin, worth less than the bin.

b.text:
Beanie Babies: the only investment where the advice was "don't remove the tag" and everyone said, "Sounds legit." Parents in 1998 put them in plexiglass cases like they were the Hope Diamond. It was a bean-filled bear named Garcia. You were hedging against a tie-dye pig.

Every one had a poem on the tag. "Legs the Frog" had a poem. Why? Nobody asked Legs to be a poet. Legs just wanted to sit on a shelf and appreciate the lack of structural support.

And the "retired" thing. Ty would announce a toy was retired, like it had served in a war. Suddenly your aunt's driving to a Hallmark in Ohio at 4 a.m. for Princess the Bear, a bear dedicated to a dead woman, which is a hell of a thing to put a price sticker on.

People paid thousands for these. Today they're worth less than the pellets inside. Which is the only part that was ever real: plastic pellets, fear, and a very small heart-shaped tag.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8 looked at the most successful desktop interface in history and said, "What if we hid the Start button, like a bathroom in a haunted house?" Microsoft designed an operating system for tablets, then shipped it to people with keyboards, mice, and spreadsheets. Nobody asked for this. Accountants were suddenly swiping at monitors like they were trying to wipe off a stain.

Shutting down the computer required a PhD. You had to summon the Charms bar by hovering in the corner of the screen like a stalker, then click Settings, then Power, then pray. My grandmother spent twenty minutes looking for the off switch and just unplugged it. Honestly, she had the right idea.

And those Live Tiles! Forty colorful rectangles flipping around telling me the weather in a city I've never visited. It wasn't an operating system, it was a toddler's busy board.

Microsoft eventually admitted the mistake and brought back the Start button. Windows 8.1 was basically an apology note taped to the door.

b.text:
Windows 8 was Microsoft's big bet that your desktop computer should look like a phone that got into a fight. They took the Start button, the one thing every human had memorized, and deleted it. Then they replaced it with a screen of giant colored tiles that looked like someone's grandma had designed a bank app. You'd click the corner to get back to the desktop, except the corner did something different depending on your mood. It was like a house where the front door only opens if you whistle.

And the tiles! Your Mail tile was always out of date, your Weather tile showed Miami on a Tuesday, and your Games tile was just an ad for a game you didn't ask for. Microsoft looked at a mouse and keyboard and said, "Let's make these people scroll sideways."

They eventually brought the Start button back. Windows 8 wasn't a bad operating system. It was just the one that tried to swipe its way into your life, and nobody swiped back.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel, you're the only software that thinks "September 4th" and "the gene SEPT4" are the same thing. Scientists renamed human genes because of you. Genetics bent the knee to a spreadsheet.

You've got a million rows, and somehow the one cell I need is always showing ########. That's not an error, that's you yelling at me.

Every company on earth runs on one file called "Final_v7_REAL_final_JOHN'S EDIT.xlsx" that only Linda understands, and Linda's on vacation. Her formula is a nested IF statement so long it has its own zip code.

You can do VLOOKUP, XLOOKUP, INDEX-MATCH, and you still make me fight for it like a hostage negotiation.

And you're a "data tool" that auto-formats my phone number into scientific notation. Congratulations, 5.55E+09, I've never felt more called.

Also, Clippy left. You stayed. That tells us who was actually the problem.

b.text:
Excel, you're the only software so powerful that scientists had to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into a date. You didn't adapt to biology; biology adapted to you. Type a phone number and you lop off the leading zero like it owes you money. Enter a credit card number and you serve back 4.53E+15, as if I'm splitting dinner with a physicist.

You still think 1900 was a leap year. It wasn't. You've known for decades. You just don't care.

You're running entire national economies and you still panic over merged cells. The UK lost sixteen thousand COVID cases because someone used your old .xls format and you quietly ran out of rows. No warning. Just vibes.

And VLOOKUP only looks right. Thirty years we spent squinting at #N/A before you finally invented XLOOKUP, like a guy who learns to turn left at fifty.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text: Ugg boots are the only shoe that looks like a sheep ate a pair of slippers and then apologized by giving them back. You didn't buy Uggs, you bought a pair of carpet remnants that wandered into a shoe store and got lucky. Nobody's ever run in them. Nobody's ever been chased in them. They're designed for one thing: standing in a Target parking lot holding an oat milk latte like you just finished a marathon. And the name! "Ugg." That's not a brand, that's a noise you make when you step on a Lego in the dark. Somewhere, a shearling farmer is looking at these and saying, "I didn't raise sheep for this, I raised them to be respected." Stay warm, I guess. You look like a hot dog that gave up.

b.text: UGG boots. Even the name sounds like the noise you make pulling them on. Australian surfers invented them to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow they became snow boots that dissolve in snow. One puddle and you're wearing a salt-stained topographic map. They're sheepskin, so you skip the socks, so by February they smell like the sheep's revenge. Every pair eventually collapses outward until you're walking on the sides of your ankles like a newborn giraffe in a bread costume. And that's the look: two chestnut loaves. You don't walk in UGGs; you shuffle, like the ghost of Paris Hilton still searching for her Juicy tracksuit. And now they're back with platforms, so you can roll an ankle from higher up. It's not footwear. It's a bathrobe that learned to commute.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The strongest material known to science, and you still can't hold a job. Since the nineties you've promised us a space elevator. Your longest strand is about half a meter. That's not an elevator. That's floss with a publicist.

You're graphene that rolled over and gave up. Graphene got a Nobel Prize. You got an argument over whether Soviets spotted you in 1952.

You can't even decide what you are. Twist one way, you're a metal. Twist the other, you're a semiconductor. Nobody controls it, including you. That's not versatility. That's a chirality crisis.

Drop you in any liquid and you clump together like freshmen at a mixer.

And inhale you? Suddenly you behave like asbestos. Thirty years of hype, and your most reliable talent is impersonating the one material we paid billions to rip out of schools.

b.text: Carbon nanotubes, you've been "five years away from changing everything" since 1991. You're stronger than steel, lighter than aluminum, and conduct electricity like a champ, which is impressive until someone asks you to leave the lab. You're a sheet of graphene that rolled itself up and called it a personality. Your big selling point is being incredibly small, and honestly, that's the only thing you've ever fit into. Every time someone tries to disperse you in a solvent, you clump together like a group project at 2 a.m. Meanwhile, the press releases keep calling you "revolutionary," and the only thing you've revolutionized is the grant budget. Stronger than steel, lighter than aluminum, and still the guest nobody's ready to invite into the real world.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's cousin who got into tech because you could "share a link." Congrats: now forty Anonymous Capybaras can watch me botch a VLOOKUP in real time. Your whole personality is "All changes saved in Drive," which is a weird flex when the change was Kevin sorting one column and detaching every employee from their salary. Version history isn't a feature; it's a crime scene. IMPORTRANGE says "Loading..." the way my dad said he was going out for milk. You've got a QUERY function that's just SQL in a fake mustache, yet you freeze if I paste more than twelve rows. And #REF! isn't an error message; it's you shrugging in all caps. You cap out at ten million cells. Ten million. You're the only spreadsheet with a bedtime.

b.text: Google Sheets, you're the spreadsheet that waits until I've typed three paragraphs of data before you tell me I've been editing a "view-only" copy this whole time. You're the only app where "Saving..." becomes a lifestyle. Your formulas are so fragile that one missing comma turns my budget into a column of #REF! like I'm a hacker's ransom note. And VLOOKUP? You make me hunt for the exact column index like it's a secret handshake. Every time I try to add a chart, you act like I asked you to build a cathedral. Sure, you're free, and you're everywhere, but that's just what happens when your whole personality is "well, at least it's not Excel."

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text:
Esperanto: the universal language invented in 1887 by a Polish eye doctor who decided humanity needed Italian with a Slavic accent. Universal, as long as your universe is Europe.

The name means "one who hopes." Over a century later: still hoping. There are roughly a thousand native speakers. Klingon is closing in, and Klingon has an army.

It's so logical that "bad" is "malbona," literally un-good. Orwell called; he wants royalties.

Every noun ends in -o and every adjective in -a, so every sentence sounds like a waiter reciting the specials. And it gave us ĉ, ĝ, ŝ and ŭ: letters with little hats, designed for global communication, then made untypeable on every keyboard on Earth.

Its biggest movie starred William Shatner. Even he couldn't oversell it.

b.text: Esperanto is the language of hope, which is a polite way of saying nobody has needed it since 1887. Dr. Zamenhof built it so everyone on Earth could talk to each other, and it worked beautifully, provided everyone was a Polish optometrist who already spoke German. Every noun ends in -o and every adjective in -a, like the language is labeling its own furniture. Then it split over a rival called Ido, because Esperantists love a universal language so much they needed a second one to be mad at. The conferences are the best part: a thousand people who learned the same made-up language, hugging in a Bulgarian youth hostel, recognizing each other by little green star pins. Then they fly home, and the nearest person they can talk to is the one who only speaks English.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text: Microsoft Teams is the only app that got popular the way a parking ticket gets popular: it came free with Office 365 and nobody could say no. It's a chat app that eats more RAM than Chrome, which is like a goldfish outeating a horse. It marks you "Away" if you blink for five minutes, which is why half of corporate America owns a mouse jiggler. Every file you share vanishes into SharePoint, a place so mysterious even Microsoft sends search parties. There's chat, there's channels, there's "posts," and nobody knows which one Kevin used. They released "New Teams" to replace "Classic Teams," and somehow both are running on my laptop right now, fighting. And that notification sound? That little knock-knock haunts people on vacation. Teams, you didn't win the remote work war. You were just pre-installed.

b.text: Microsoft Teams, you're the only app with the nerve to open itself the second I log in, like a hall monitor who got promoted. Every meeting starts with the same ritual: "Can you hear me?" "You're on mute." "Sorry, you're on mute." Thirty seconds of people unmuting like it's a hostage situation. And that little "Someone is typing..." bubble? It's been there since Tuesday. Nobody's typing, Teams. Nobody's ever typing. You tell me I'm "Available" while I'm literally in a meeting, then ping me four minutes after everyone else has already replied. "Let's take this offline," says the guy, and then he schedules a Teams call about it. Teams, you're not a chat app. You're a conference room that follows you home.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text: You're one atom thick, the only thing about you that's ever been thin. Two guys won a Nobel for peeling you off a lump of pencil lead with Scotch tape. Pencil lead! Your whole family tree is the stuff kids chew in exam halls. You're stronger than steel pound for pound, you conduct electricity, you're transparent, and you still can't get out of the lab. Every year it's "graphene will revolutionize batteries next year." That's been going on for twenty years. Meanwhile companies slap your name on tennis rackets and face cream with about as much of you as a rumor. You're basically a pencil lead that got a personal trainer and a Nobel, and you still can't get a callback from a battery company.

b.text:
Graphene, the "wonder material." Twenty years of wonder, and the only place I've seen you is in press releases.

You're pencil lead that got an agent. You're literally graphite, but one layer thick, because even carbon wants to be an influencer: all surface, no depth.

They discovered you with Scotch tape. Two guys peeled you off a pencil mark and won a Nobel Prize. That's the most successful thing anyone has ever done with office supplies, and you've been coasting on it ever since.

Stronger than steel! Conducts better than copper! Transparent, flexible, and every article says you'll change everything "within five years." You've been five years away since 2004. You're the Cybertruck of chemistry.

And scaling you up? Impossible. You're perfect in a lab and a wrinkled, expensive mess in a factory. Honestly, you're the most impressive thing a pencil ever did, and also its biggest disappointment.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim is the only software where the tutorial is "how to leave." Millions of developers have spent a Tuesday trapped inside it, mashing Escape like they're trying to wake a hostage. You open a file, type "hello," and the editor responds by deleting your paragraph and playing a macro you recorded in 2019.

Vim users say, "Once you learn it, you'll never touch your mouse again." Neither will you touch grass, sir. You've spent forty hours configuring a .vimrc so you can save four seconds on a typo.

And the modes! Normal mode, where nothing is normal. Insert mode, where you finally get to insert. Visual mode, which is only visual in the sense that you can watch yourself select the wrong thing.

It's an editor built on the premise that your keyboard has too many keys and your dignity has too much room.

Type :wq to save and quit. Type :q! to forget this ever happened.

b.text:
Vim. The only program where "how do I leave?" has more Stack Overflow views than most religions have followers. Two million people asked, and the answer was colon, q, exclamation point, which reads less like a command and more like a hostage's final words.

Vim stands for "Vi Improved." Improved from a 1976 terminal whose arrow keys were printed on H, J, K, and L. Fifty years later, Vim's still out here like, "Why fix what you can turn into a personality?"

You don't type in Vim. You type a sentence, then discover you deleted four lines, yanked a paragraph into register W, and started recording a macro.

Crash it once and it leaves a .swp file behind, like a ghost whispering, "Recover, Edit anyway, Quit, or Abort?"

Even its fans forked it. Neovim exists because Vim users wanted Vim, minus Vim.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Microsoft Teams is the only app that can notify you about a message you're already reading. You've got a red badge, a yellow badge, and a little purple "@" telling you someone said "per my last email" in a chat called "Q3 Sync (Copy) (Final)."

Teams has seven ways to say hello and none of them load. "Joining meeting..." is its resting state. It's the Waiting for Godot of video calls, except Godot eventually shows up and says, "Can everyone see my screen?" No, Greg. We see a spinning circle and your cat.

Every update, it asks you to restart. Not the app. Your life choices.

Teams and Channels are different things, by the way. A channel lives inside a team. Which is inside a tenant. Which is inside a guest account you can't switch out of without signing out of everything and crying.

And the green dot? It goes yellow the second you stop moving your mouse, so your boss thinks you're napping. Ten minutes of reading a document is considered a vacation.

b.text:
Microsoft Teams is the only app that marks me "Away" after five minutes of deep thought but keeps me "Available" for three hours after I've died. It's not software. It's a hall monitor in a purple vest.

Teams eats more RAM than the game I'm pretending not to play. It launches on startup uninvited, then takes four minutes to load a chat that just says "ok."

Where are my files? SharePoint. Where's SharePoint? Nobody knows. Teams ships them off like a kid to boarding school.

Then they gave us "New Teams," which is Old Teams with a fresh coat of lag. IT has told me to "clear the cache" so often I do it in my sleep.

Nobody chose Teams. It came free with Office. Fitting, since so did Clippy.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: NFTs, everybody! The only art form where the most common review is "right-click, save." You paid four hundred thousand dollars for a cartoon monkey in a captain's hat, and I have the same monkey as my phone background. The difference? I didn't pay a gas fee bigger than the art. Technically you don't even own the picture. You own a receipt pointing to a link on a server some guy in Ohio forgot to renew. That's not a masterpiece; that's a parking stub for a JPEG. And remember the roadmap? Metaverse, merch, a yacht party! Then the founder pulled the rug, deleted the Discord, and left you holding a "rare trait": sunglasses. Jimmy Fallon showed Paris Hilton his ape on national TV like a proud dad. Now it's worth less than the TV.

b.text:
NFTs: the only product where you pay $300,000 for a receipt, and the receipt is for a JPEG, and the JPEG is still publicly available for free. You can right-click it. The whole business model is a guy pointing at the Mona Lisa saying, "Technically, I own the bookmark."

And the art! Eight thousand identical apes, each with a slightly different hat. That's not a collection, that's a hostage situation at a Hot Topic.

Remember when they said it was "the future of ownership"? Then OpenSea's servers went down and people learned their million-dollar monkey was just a link to a website that could 404. You didn't buy art. You bought a very expensive "Page Not Found."

And the guys who bought them still say "we're early." Early to what? The funeral?

Somewhere right now, a man named Chad is staring at a cartoon ape worth $14, whispering, "Floor price is just a vibe."

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans, you were literally designed for a talking dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the only part of that project that didn't die with dignity. Vincent Connare made you in 1994 for cartoon speech bubbles, and you heard that and thought, "Tombstones. Legal notices. Resignation letters."

Dan Gilbert wrote his furious LeBron James letter in you, and that's why nobody remembers being scared. CERN announced the Higgs boson, the most important physics discovery in fifty years, in you, and the entire scientific community went, "Did a third grader find God?"

People defend you because you help some readers with dyslexia, which is true and lovely, and also the only time you've ever been used responsibly.

You're not a font. You're a bake sale flyer that got tenure. Even Papyrus looks at you and says, "Wow, okay, tone it down."

b.text:
Comic Sans, you're the only font that shows up to a funeral looking like it's about to do a magic show.

Vincent Connare designed you for a cartoon dog's speech bubble in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you escaped into the wild and started writing resignation letters, hospital signage, and the CERN Higgs boson announcement. Scientists found the God particle and presented it like a bake sale flyer.

You look like handwriting from a guy who says "Let's circle back" while wearing a Hawaiian shirt to a layoff. Every letter looks like it's been sitting in a ball pit.

Your fans say you're great for dyslexic readers. Fine. That's your one defense, and you've been hiding behind it like a substitute teacher using a laminated poster.

You're the only font where "Please stop microwaving fish" sounds like a threat from a clown.

Even Papyrus saw you and said, "Wow."

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you are the only thing in the dairy aisle that's named after a nut and still somehow lies about it. Your almond content is roughly the same as the average Tuesday's ambition. Somebody squeezed one almond over a bathtub of water, waved it at the carton, and said, "Yep, that's almond." That's not milk. That's a rumor.

And the color! You look like a glass of wet drywall. Put you next to real milk and you're the sad cousin who showed up to the wedding in the same beige as the tablecloth. Nobody asked you to be white. You're just gray with a vague sense of purpose.

You also taste like you're trying to apologize for something. Every sip says, "I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm sorry." Pour yourself into a latte and the barista's already plotting how to hide the foam.

b.text:
Almond milk, you're proof that marketing can convince people to pay four dollars for cloudy water with a nut rumor attached. You're 2% almonds. Two percent! That's not milk, that's a homeopathic remedy for oat milk.

You took a nut that needs a gallon of water per single almond to grow, then sold yourself to people who say "I'm doing it for the planet." California is in a drought, Karen. Those bees are being trucked across the country like migrant workers just so you can ruin a latte.

And the texture. You're the only drink that separates in coffee like a bad breakup. Curdling in front of everyone, floating there in tiny shame flakes.

Your carton says "Unsweetened Original," which is two lies in a row. There's nothing original about you, and nothing about you is sweet.

You're what a cow would make if she gave up halfway through and just described milk to a nut.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text:
Google Sheets, you're the spreadsheet equivalent of a guy who says "I'm not really a party person" and then shows up to every meeting with a pivot table. You've got 10 million cells and you still can't tell me why my VLOOKUP returned #N/A. Oh, that's not a bug, that's your personality: "Did you mean the other tab?" No, Sheets, I didn't mean the other tab. Nobody ever meant the other tab.

And don't get me started on autocomplete. I type "=SU" and you suggest SUMIF, SUMSQ, and SUBSTITUTE like you're trying to get me to commit to a divorce. Just pick one! You're a grid of cells that refuses to commit to a formula.

Your collaboration features are great, though. My boss can see my edits in real time, which is how I learned he watches me type "asdfgh" when a deadline hits.

b.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's little brother who moved into a browser tab and called it "the cloud." Your whole personality is twelve people's colored cursors circling the same cell like sharks while an Anonymous Capybara silently watches everyone's mistakes. You say "Saving..." with the confidence of a man who has absolutely not saved. Your IMPORTRANGE makes me click "Allow access" like I'm asking my own spreadsheet for permission to see my own spreadsheet. Half my cells just say "Loading..." forever, like a Victorian ghost waiting for a letter. And you'll let anyone sort one column without the others, then shrug while every customer gets someone else's phone number. Version history is your only real feature: it's just a timeline of who ruined everything at 2 a.m. And yes, Gemini can explain my #REF! error now. Great. It's still there.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which is wild, because you dress like a medieval mace and smell like a crime scene. Every other fruit says "eat me." You say "I dare you."

You're the only food with a gas leak. A Canberra university library was evacuated because of you. Evacuated! Fruit is not supposed to trigger a hazmat response.

Singapore had to put you on the subway sign with a big red X, right next to flamethrowers. Hotels ban you the way they ban smoking and goats.

And the flesh inside? Custard that tastes like sweet almonds, caramel, and a decision you regret. Fans say, "Just get past the smell." That's what people say about your cousin's boyfriend.

You're the only fruit that can kill me from the tree, and the only one I'd still blame the neighbors for.

b.text: Durian, you smell like a gym sock that got left in a sewer and then decided to become a fruit out of spite. People in Singapore have to ride the MRT with signs warning them about you. Signs! You're banned from hotels. Hotels! They don't ban guests who set fire to the carpet, but they draw the line at you. And the worst part? You're shaped like a medieval mace someone dipped in a hedgehog. Nobody approaches you with a knife, they approach you with a shovel and a prayer. Fans call your taste "custardy." Custardy? Honey, that's what a gym sock would taste like if it had a rich uncle.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero raised 120 million dollars to build a Wi-Fi-enabled juicer that cost 700 dollars, then 400 after they panicked. It had a press with four tons of force, enough to lift two Teslas. For what? Squeezing a bag of chopped kale.

Then Bloomberg proved you could just squeeze the bag with your hands. Same juice. No Wi-Fi. No app. No shame. Just a human fist doing the job of a venture-backed appliance.

And the packs! Sold separately, with expiration dates, so the machine would refuse to work if the bag was old. It's a juicer with a DRM problem. You couldn't even use your own fruit. It was a printer that squeezes.

The founder looked like someone who'd raised money by describing a smoothie as "infrastructure."

Google Ventures invested, which makes sense. Nobody does disrupting a squeeze like people who've never had to do one.

Juicero shut down in 2017, a rare startup where the customers' hands outperformed the product, and the product still had a better pitch deck.

b.text: Juicero built a $400 Wi-Fi press whose entire job was squeezing a bag. Not a fruit. A bag. Somebody looked at a pouch of pre-chopped kale and decided it needed a computer. Then a reporter showed everyone you could wring the packs out with your bare hands, and the venture capitalists went quiet, like they'd just realized their $120 million bought a very expensive pair of hands. The press checked a QR code before it would crush your spinach. That's the most Silicon Valley sentence ever written: the machine needed permission to juice. The packs cost about five bucks each, so you were paying premium prices to do what a Capri Sun does on its own.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. The same stuff as the shield at a hockey rink, and somehow you're the pride of the cleanroom. You have sub-10 nanometer resolution and the etch resistance of a wet napkin. Every pattern you make is gorgeous for exactly as long as nobody tries to use it.

You need a dose that would tan a small village, and for what? So the beam can snip your chains one at a time like a slow, expensive haircut? Then we bathe you in MIBK and IPA, and you dissolve only if the ratio is right, the temperature is right, and the moon is in the proper phase.

Overdo the dose and you flip negative-tone out of spite, cross-linking into a crust that no solvent can remove. Everyone loves a bilayer 495/950 for the undercut, because even you know you need a support system.

And liftoff? Acetone, sonication, three hours, and a prayer. You're a clingy ex.

b.text: PMMA, you're the same plastic as a hockey rink window, and somehow that's your most dignified job. You've been "high resolution" since the 1970s, which is like bragging about your SAT score at your retirement party. Sure, you'll resolve sub-10-nanometer lines, if someone stands there blasting you with electrons for an eternity. Your sensitivity is so low the beam current has gotten tenure. You don't even develop properly without MIBK and IPA holding your hand in a one-to-three ratio. And your whole personality is chain scission: you literally fall apart when someone pays attention to you. Then hit you with too much dose and you crosslink and flip to negative tone, a full identity crisis. And dry etch? You melt in plasma faster than an ice sculpture at a barbecue. Honestly, the only thing you're consistently good at is lift-off: leaving.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text: Risk is the only board game where the map is the villain. Australia is one continent with four borders, and somehow it's the thing everyone wants to fight over. Kamchatka is a Russian peninsula nobody could find if you paid them, and it becomes the most important place on Earth for six straight hours. You know the game's dragging when you're hoping someone rolls a three just to end the suffering. The dice are cheap six-siders you shake in a cup, so entire wars get decided by two guys who could lose a continent in the time it takes to say "I'm not mad, I'm just disappointed." And there's always that guy eliminated since nine o'clock, still sitting at the table holding his cards like a hostage negotiation, begging someone to betray their ally and save him. Nobody has ever finished Risk. You just stop when the pizza's cold.

b.text:
Risk promises "world domination" and delivers a nine-hour hostage situation with plastic army men. Nobody has ever finished a game of Risk. We just stop when someone's mom needs the dining room table back.

Let's talk about the dice. You attack with three armies, I defend with two, and somehow I lose all three while you lose nothing. Math is a liar, and it lives in that little red cup.

Australia is the only continent anyone wants, because it has one entrance and the emotional stability of a hermit. Meanwhile Asia has seventeen borders, and holding it is like being the manager of a Wetherspoons on Saturday night.

And the alliances! "Let's team up against Dave." Then you betray me in Kamchatka. Kamchatka! A place no one has ever been or will ever visit, and yet it's responsible for more ruined friendships than any ex's Instagram.

Risk isn't a game. It's a divorce with cards.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, you beautiful $120 million monument to Silicon Valley. You launched at seven hundred dollars to squeeze a bag. A bag! Then Bloomberg reporters squeezed that same bag with their bare hands and got basically the same juice, only faster. You got outperformed by a guy with a grip strength of "typing."

Doug Evans bragged you pressed with four tons of force, enough to lift two Teslas. Buddy, it's kale. The kale didn't need a forklift.

And it needed Wi-Fi. It scanned a QR code before it'd let you drink. Your router goes down and suddenly your breakfast is asking for credentials. Who designs a juicer that can be bricked?

Google Ventures funded this. Kleiner Perkins funded this. Somewhere, a man is still holding a lukewarm pouch, waiting for a firmware update so he's allowed to eat a carrot.

b.text: Juicero built a $400 Wi-Fi press whose entire job was squeezing a bag. Not a fruit. A bag. Somebody looked at a pouch of pre-chopped kale and decided it needed a computer. Then a reporter showed everyone you could wring the packs out with your bare hands, and the venture capitalists went quiet, like they'd just realized their $120 million bought a very expensive pair of hands. The press checked a QR code before it would crush your spinach. That's the most Silicon Valley sentence ever written: the machine needed permission to juice. The packs cost about five bucks each, so you were paying premium prices to do what a Capri Sun does on its own.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text: Durian, you're the only fruit that needs a gas mask and a hazmat permit just to get through the airport. Airlines ban you like you're a bomb with a bad attitude. Your smell is a mix of gym socks, rotting onions, and a sewage pipe that's been sulking for a week. People hear the word "delicacy" and think you're kidding. Southeast Asians call you the king of fruits, and honestly, that's the only reason you got a crown instead of a restraining order. You look like a medieval mace someone dropped in a swamp, and you're covered in spikes so nobody can hug you. Even the spikes are a warning. Your fans swear you taste like custard and heaven, but they also say that about getting a root canal on Christmas. Smell like a crime scene, taste like a dessert, and still somehow get a hotel room kicked out for eating you.

b.text:
Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which tracks, because like most monarchies, you stink and nobody's allowed to say it to your face.

You're the only fruit with a criminal record. Banned on the Singapore subway, alongside flammable liquids. Hotels put your picture on signs next to "no smoking." In 2019, a university in Melbourne evacuated five hundred people because they thought there was a gas leak. Nope. Just you, sitting in a cupboard, being yourself.

And the armor! You're covered in spikes like a medieval mace. Nature built you to defend yourself, then gave you a smell that does it better. The spikes are just overkill.

Fans say you taste like custard. Sure. Custard that was left in a gym bag next to some onions. Your flavor isn't an acquired taste. It's a hostage situation.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text: Esperanto was built in 1887 so everyone on Earth could finally talk to each other, and 140 years later the main conversation is still, "Oh, you speak it too? Where are you from?" "Also Esperanto." Silence. Every speaker is one hug away from running out of things to say. The grammar is famously logical: every noun ends in -o, every adjective in -a, and every direct object gets an -n, which is the only place this language ever shows emotion. It promised to be easy to learn, and it kept that promise the way a diet pill does. You master it in a month, then spend the rest of your life waiting for a stranger to answer you back.

b.text:
Esperanto: the language invented to unite humanity, and after 130 years, its greatest achievement is a tiny group of people who all met at the same convention.

Zamenhof wanted world peace. He got a language where the most common sentence is "Hello, are you also here for the Esperanto thing?"

Everything is regular. Every noun ends in O. Every adjective ends in A. It's the only language designed like a filing cabinet, and it sounds like Italian and Polish got stuck in an elevator and decided to name the kids.

And the accusative! They made a language to be easy, then kept the accusative. Fine. It's a hobby.

"Native speakers" of Esperanto number about a thousand, which is what we call "the children of enthusiasts who never got a vote."

The national anthem is "La Espero." The national sport is correcting your pronunciation of "ĉ." And the only country that really speaks it is the Facebook group.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text: Ugg boots are the only footwear that looks like it was made from a dead sheep and then slept in. They're basically two slippers that gave up on their dreams and went to college. You don't wear Uggs, you just stop trying in a boot shape. Nobody has ever run for a bus in Uggs. Nobody has ever been caught in the rain in Uggs. They're for the Starbucks line at 8 a.m. and the Costco parking lot, and that's it. And the name! "Ugg." That's not a brand, that's a noise you make when you step on a Lego. Somebody in a boardroom said, "Let's sell people shoes that sound like disappointment," and everybody nodded. Then they charged two hundred dollars for them.

b.text:
UGG boots look like someone skinned a Muppet and asked you to wear the evidence. They're the only footwear where the sales pitch is "it's like walking on a cloud" and the cloud is a wet sheepdog.

Nobody's ever said "nice UGGs" without a tiny pause for mercy.

They're technically slippers that got promoted past their competence. You can wear them to the grocery store, but God help you if it drizzles, because suede plus water equals two damp loaves of bread strapped to your calves.

And the shape! Your ankle disappears. You walk in and a stranger thinks you have the legs of a Clydesdale. That's not a boot, that's a hoof cozy.

The inside smells like a gym bag in a sauna by month two, because they're meant to be worn sockless, which is a bold design choice for something with no ventilation and a lifetime of regret.

Also, they cost two hundred dollars. For slippers. That Australians apparently wear to surf, which tells you everything about Australians.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text: Stinky tofu is the only food that files a complaint before you've even found the stall. You're three blocks away at the night market and your nose is already asking questions. It's tofu that spent a week soaking in brine that smells like a gym bag left in a hot car, then got deep-fried so the whole street knows what you're doing. They serve it with pickled cabbage, like it needs a chaperone. You bite in, the crispy outside is great, and the inside is basically a fermented cloud. Your jacket smells like it for three days. Your coworkers ask if you were dragged through a sewer. Honestly, though, it's the only snack that shows up to the party knowing it's a mess, and it's still having the best time.

b.text:
Stinky tofu, you're the only food that needs a restraining order from its own neighborhood. I smelled you three blocks away and assumed a sewer had filed for divorce.

You're fermented in brine made of old vegetables, fish, and, as far as I can tell, regret. Then you're deep-fried, because apparently someone looked at a crime scene and said, "Needs crunch."

Everyone says, "Just try it, it tastes better than it smells!" That's not a compliment. That's what people say about a divorce lawyer.

And the fans! They stand in line at the night market, glowing with pride, like they've survived something. Sir, you're eating a gym sock in a pickle costume, and the pickle is also a gym sock.

Still, I'll admit it: the chili sauce is incredible. Which is exactly what you'd say about a hostage situation with good snacks.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text: Graphene, you're one atom thick, and somehow that's still more depth than your business plan. Two hundred times stronger than steel, conducts better than copper, and twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a sticker on a tennis racket. You were discovered with Scotch tape. *Scotch tape!* You're the only Nobel Prize that could've been found in a kindergarten craft drawer. And let's be honest: you're pencil lead that went to grad school. Your cousin graphite has been writing grocery lists for centuries; you've been writing grant proposals. Every year a headline swears you'll revolutionize batteries, chips, water filters. Every year you're still in the lab, like a thirty-year-old in his parents' basement. You can't even be a decent transistor. No bandgap. You literally cannot turn off. Graphene: the material of the future, permanently.

b.text: Graphene, you're one atom thick and still the biggest presence at every party. Scientists keep calling you the strongest material ever measured, which is wild, because you've never once held your own in a conversation. You're basically pencil lead that went to the gym and never came back. Since 2004 we've been told you'll revolutionize batteries, phones, and bridges. Meanwhile, companies slap your name on golf balls and socks like it's a free upgrade. Two Nobel-winning guys isolated you with Scotch tape, which tells you everything. The most advanced substance in the universe was found by somebody with a roll of tape and too much time. And you're still "five years away" from being useful. Honestly, that's the most relatable thing about you.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs are the only shoes that look like they were designed by someone who'd only had shoes described to them over a bad phone connection. "So it's a boat, but for your foot?" "Sure."

And the holes! Ventilation, they say. Which is great, because nothing says "protect my toes" like a shoe with a dozen open invitations for a dropped knife. They're the only footwear where a gentle rain and a kitchen spill both count as a personal attack.

Then there's the Jibbitz. You've taken a shoe that looks like a foam dinosaur egg and decided to accessorize it with a tiny plastic pizza. That's not fashion. That's a toddler's hostage negotiation.

And the strap! Pushed forward, it's "casual." Flipped back, it's "sport mode." Sport for what, Greg? You're carrying a rotisserie chicken to a barbecue.

Yet somehow, they're unbelievably comfortable. Which is the cruelest part. Every nurse, chef, and gardener secretly knows: they look like a mistake, and they feel like a hug. Crocs are ugly on purpose, and they won.

b.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like Swiss cheese that wanted to be a boat. You were invented for sailing, and the one place nobody wears you is a boat. You're at Applebee's, squeaking across a wet floor like a dolphin in distress.

You have holes. On purpose. Then you sell us Jibbitz to fill the holes. That's not fashion, that's a protection racket with a SpongeBob charm.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind my heel doesn't make me an athlete. It makes me a toddler about to sprint into traffic.

You made a KFC bucket clog with charms that smelled like fried chicken. That's not footwear. That's a foam cry for help.

Nurses love you. Chefs love you. Which proves you're comfortable for people who've stopped caring who's looking at their feet.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text:
Graphene, the "wonder material." Twenty years of wonder, and the only place I've seen you is in press releases.

You're pencil lead that got an agent. You're literally graphite, but one layer thick, because even carbon wants to be an influencer: all surface, no depth.

They discovered you with Scotch tape. Two guys peeled you off a pencil mark and won a Nobel Prize. That's the most successful thing anyone has ever done with office supplies, and you've been coasting on it ever since.

Stronger than steel! Conducts better than copper! Transparent, flexible, and every article says you'll change everything "within five years." You've been five years away since 2004. You're the Cybertruck of chemistry.

And scaling you up? Impossible. You're perfect in a lab and a wrinkled, expensive mess in a factory. Honestly, you're the most impressive thing a pencil ever did, and also its biggest disappointment.

b.text: Graphene, you're one atom thick, and somehow that's still more depth than your business plan. Two hundred times stronger than steel, conducts better than copper, and twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a sticker on a tennis racket. You were discovered with Scotch tape. *Scotch tape!* You're the only Nobel Prize that could've been found in a kindergarten craft drawer. And let's be honest: you're pencil lead that went to grad school. Your cousin graphite has been writing grocery lists for centuries; you've been writing grant proposals. Every year a headline swears you'll revolutionize batteries, chips, water filters. Every year you're still in the lab, like a thirty-year-old in his parents' basement. You can't even be a decent transistor. No bandgap. You literally cannot turn off. Graphene: the material of the future, permanently.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs is the only text editor that ships with a psychotherapist, and you'll need it. M-x doctor exists because the developers knew exactly what they were doing to people.

It's a great operating system. It has a mail client, a web browser, Tetris, and a Lisp interpreter. What it lacks is a decent text editor. Its most beloved package is Evil mode, which is just Vim wearing an Emacs costume. That's like buying a Ferrari and installing a horse.

Want to save? C-x C-s. Want to quit? C-x C-c. Want to feel your left pinky again? Too late. Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," and the RSI stands for "you chose this."

Every user has a 4,000-line init.el they don't understand, copied from strangers on Stack Overflow in 2009.

b.text:
Emacs isn't a text editor, it's an operating system that's still looking for a decent editor. Thirty years of development, and the most reliable feature is the pinky injury.

You press Control-X, Control-S to save. That's not a keyboard shortcut, that's a hostage negotiation with your left hand.

Emacs users say, "It's infinitely customizable!" Sure. So is a blank sheet of paper, but nobody brags about spending three weekends configuring that. Your init.el is 4,000 lines long, and you wrote 12 of them. The rest is a Stack Overflow answer from 2011 that you're afraid to delete.

And the manual calls it "the extensible, self-documenting editor." Self-documenting! Yes, it will tell you exactly what a function does, right after you press Control-H, then K, then wonder why you're reading Lisp.

You can read email in it, browse the web in it, and play Tetris in it. Everything except quit. Nobody remembers how to quit.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text: Emacs is the only text editor that's also an operating system that never got around to booting. People say it's "a great operating system, just missing a good editor." Sure. You open it and it's already running a calendar, a email client, a chess engine, and a psychiatrist. You wanted to type "hello." Instead you get a *Ctrl-x Ctrl-c* keyboard combo, which is the only way out, and it requires two hands, a pinky that's been to physical therapy, and the blessing of a man named Richard who hasn't been seen since 1985. Vim users at least get a funny exit. Emacs users get a seven-keystroke prayer. And the config file? It's a Lisp dialect that's older than your parents' divorce, with parentheses so deep you need a mountain guide. Brilliant software. Terrible hostage negotiator.

b.text:
Emacs isn't a text editor, it's an operating system that's still waiting for a decent editor to come along. It has a built-in psychiatrist, a Tetris clone, and a mail client, but somehow no sane keybindings.

Ctrl-x Ctrl-s to save? That's not a shortcut, that's a hand injury with a lawsuit pending. Emacs users call it "Emacs pinky" like it's a badge of honor. Sir, that's a repetitive strain injury from a Lisp interpreter.

And the config file! Fifteen years of init.el, a thousand lines of copy-pasted snippets from a 2009 blog post, and nobody knows what half of it does. But if you delete it, you die.

Every Emacs user says, "It's infinitely customizable!" Yes, and you've spent four hundred hours customizing it so you can finally write a grocery list.

Meanwhile, the Vim guys are laughing, and honestly? They've earned it.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you are the only thing in the dairy aisle that's named after a nut and still somehow lies about it. Your almond content is roughly the same as the average Tuesday's ambition. Somebody squeezed one almond over a bathtub of water, waved it at the carton, and said, "Yep, that's almond." That's not milk. That's a rumor.

And the color! You look like a glass of wet drywall. Put you next to real milk and you're the sad cousin who showed up to the wedding in the same beige as the tablecloth. Nobody asked you to be white. You're just gray with a vague sense of purpose.

You also taste like you're trying to apologize for something. Every sip says, "I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm sorry." Pour yourself into a latte and the barista's already plotting how to hide the foam.

b.text:
Almond milk, you're not milk. You're a rumor about an almond. Two percent almonds, ninety-eight percent "we strained the tap." You're the only drink that needs a legal team to call itself milk. The dairy lobby has spent a decade trying to make you admit you're nut juice.

California spends about a gallon of water per almond just so you can show up in my fridge as... water. That's like melting a glacier to make an ice cube.

They truck in billions of bees to pollinate your orchards, and the bees die by the millions so I can pay an extra eighty cents at Starbucks for a latte that tastes like damp drywall.

And "shake well"? Leave you alone for ten minutes and you separate like a couple who met at Whole Foods. Even *you* can't commit to you.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text:
Apple Vision Pro, you cost $3,499 and still need a battery on a cord like a 1996 Walkman. Two hours of charge? That's not spatial computing, that's a matinee. Wear glasses? Zeiss inserts, extra. Apple saw you squinting and smelled revenue.

And EyeSight! A front screen showing your eyes so people feel connected. Nothing says "I'm present" like blurry cartoon eyeballs trapped behind ski-goggle glass. Your Persona avatar looks like a hostage video directed by a ghost.

You promised the future, and Netflix wouldn't even make you an app. You strap over a pound to dads' faces so they can record "spatial memories" of birthdays they watched through a screen.

Apple said you'd never see the world the same way. True. Now it's through a $3,500 face fridge.

b.text: Apple's Vision Pro costs $3,499, which is more than most people's first car and buys you goggles that make you look like you're about to get hypnotized at a Best Buy. The front has a screen that shows your eyeballs to everyone around you, so now you're not just wearing a computer, you're wearing one that makes eye contact with strangers. You click things by pinching the air, which is great, because you already look like you're conducting an invisible orchestra in the middle of Target. The battery lives in a puck on a cable, so you're a tethered astronaut who paid four grand to watch a movie alone in a room full of people staring at your face.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans, you're the only font that shows up to a funeral looking like it's about to do a magic show for toddlers.

You were designed for a cartoon dog's speech bubble in Microsoft Bob, and somehow ended up on cancer-ward notices, divorce settlements, and "Please Do Not Microwave Fish" signs in the office kitchen. Every message you carry sounds like it was written by a substitute teacher who's given up.

Designers don't hate you. Designers have a support group for you. CERN announced the Higgs boson in you, and physicists everywhere suddenly wondered if the universe was a bake sale flyer.

Your letters look like they were drawn by someone holding the marker in their left hand while riding a bus. The lowercase "a" is the only part of you that's trying.

And yet you're still installed on every computer on Earth, like a clown that nobody invited but nobody can evict.

b.text: Comic Sans, you look like a font that got a job as a birthday clown and then got fired for scaring the kids. Every letter is wearing pajamas. Your "a" is a little round hat with a hook on it, like it's always about to go to a yard sale. Your "g" is a pretzel that lost an argument with itself. You were designed by Vincent Connare in 1994 to look like a comic book speech bubble, and you have been ruining wedding invitations and hospice signs ever since. Nobody ever chose you on purpose. People open a menu, see you, and quietly give up on being taken seriously. You're the only typeface that makes a lost cat poster sound like a ransom note written by a substitute teacher.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text:
Risk is the only game where you can conquer the entire planet and still lose to the guy who's been hiding in Australia since 7 p.m. Four territories, one entrance, and he just sits there like a guy at a party who won't leave the snack table.

This game has a map drawn by someone who heard about geography once, at a bar. Kamchatka borders Alaska. Ukraine is the size of Brazil. Yakutsk and Irkutsk are vital military objectives, and nobody at the table can find them on a real map.

The rules say the defender wins ties, which is the most realistic thing about it, because nobody actually finishes Risk. They just quit at 2 a.m. when someone's dad flips the board over Siberia.

And the pieces? Little plastic cannons and horses. Napoleonic warfare, global scale, and the whole thing is decided by rolling a 6 against your cousin Greg.

b.text:
Risk promises "world domination" and delivers a nine-hour hostage situation with plastic army men. Nobody has ever finished a game of Risk. We just stop when someone's mom needs the dining room table back.

Let's talk about the dice. You attack with three armies, I defend with two, and somehow I lose all three while you lose nothing. Math is a liar, and it lives in that little red cup.
