Australia is the only continent anyone wants, because it has one entrance and the emotional stability of a hermit. Meanwhile Asia has seventeen borders, and holding it is like being the manager of a Wetherspoons on Saturday night.

And the alliances! "Let's team up against Dave." Then you betray me in Kamchatka. Kamchatka! A place no one has ever been or will ever visit, and yet it's responsible for more ruined friendships than any ex's Instagram.

Risk isn't a game. It's a divorce with cards.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim is the only software where the tutorial is "how to leave." Millions of developers have rebooted their computers rather than figure out :wq. Stack Overflow has a question about quitting Vim with over a million views. That's not a text editor, that's a hostage situation.

It has modes. Normal mode, which is where nothing normal happens. Insert mode, where you finally type, like a toddler allowed one cookie. Visual mode, command mode, replace mode. It's a text editor with more personalities than a Reddit thread.

Vim users say "once you learn it, you'll be so fast." Sir, you spent six years learning to delete a word. You've saved four seconds and told everyone at dinner about it.

And the pride! They've memorized hjkl so they never move their hands, yet they've moved their entire personality into a .vimrc file that's 900 lines long, breaks every update, and was last understood in 2014.

b.text:
Vim, you are the only program that makes people feel like they're defusing a bomb just to type the word "hello." You open up and nothing works. Somebody's cat walks across the keyboard, and suddenly you're in a mode that deletes half a paragraph. And you have modes! Normal mode, insert mode, visual mode, command mode. Nobody asked for a text editor with a personality disorder.

Everybody who uses you has the same story. They accidentally hit colon, then q, then a few keys, and the whole thing just stares back at them. Then they Google "how to exit vim" and find out it's been the top search for a decade. You're not an editor, you're a riddle wrapped in a shrug.

Honestly, respect. Anyone who learns you is basically a monk. You're the only thing on Earth where pressing "j" means "down" and nobody can explain why.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text: Klingon, you're a language built by one linguist, Marc Okrand, specifically to sound alien and hostile, and somehow you still ended up sounding like a man choking on a Dorito. Your word order is object-verb-subject, so even your sentences walk in backwards to hide their face. You don't even have a word for "hello." Your greeting is "nuqneH," "what do you want?" You're the only language that greets people like a DMV clerk. Your apostrophes are glottal stops, your capital Q is a different letter from lowercase q, and "tlh" isn't a sound, it's a hairball. You translated Hamlet and claimed it was the original. Buddy, the most popular thing ever said in you is "Qapla'," and the people saying it are at a Marriott in Burbank.

b.text:
Klingon, a language designed by a linguist for a race of warriors, and somehow it still has a word for "tea" but no word for "hello." You people invented a whole culture of honor and glory, and the greeting is "What do you want?" That's not a language, that's a customer service line at a gym.

The grammar is object-verb-subject. Of course it is. Even the sentence structure says "I'm going to stab the dinner first and tell you who did it later."

Klingon has a phrase for "Today is a good day to die," but you try ordering a sandwich. Nope. Because no Klingon ever said, "Could I get that on rye?" They said, "Bring me the still-moving thing."

And the fans! Thousands of people speaking fluent guttural phlegm, getting married in it, translating Hamlet. Shakespeare in the original Klingon, which is just regular Shakespeare, but now the soliloquy sounds like someone clearing their throat at a funeral.

Qapla'? More like Qa-please-stop.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans is the font that looks like it was designed by a substitute teacher who found a crayon in a lost-and-found box. Every letter wobbles like it's had three espressos and a bad breakup. The "a" is a little round bubble with a tail that's clearly been through something. Nobody asked for this. It's the typographic equivalent of a clown trying to file your taxes.

And the worst part? Somebody put it on a hospital sign. A hospital! You're walking in with a broken leg, scanning for the exit, and the sign says "EMERGENCY" in letters that look like they're bouncing on a trampoline. Even the sickness can't take itself seriously anymore.

It's the only font that makes a funeral notice look like a birthday party invitation. Somewhere a grandmother is typing "Rest In Peace" in this, hitting bold, and thinking she's being tasteful.

b.text:
Comic Sans, you're the only font that shows up to a funeral looking like it's about to do a magic show.

Vincent Connare designed you for a cartoon dog's speech bubble in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you escaped into the wild and started writing resignation letters, hospital signage, and the CERN Higgs boson announcement. Scientists found the God particle and presented it like a bake sale flyer.

You look like handwriting from a guy who says "Let's circle back" while wearing a Hawaiian shirt to a layoff. Every letter looks like it's been sitting in a ball pit.

Your fans say you're great for dyslexic readers. Fine. That's your one defense, and you've been hiding behind it like a substitute teacher using a laminated poster.

You're the only font where "Please stop microwaving fish" sounds like a threat from a clown.

Even Papyrus saw you and said, "Wow."

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8 was the only operating system that made you feel like a burglar in your own computer. You'd boot up, and there's no Start button. Microsoft just removed it, like a doctor deciding you've never needed a pulse.

Instead, you got a screen of giant colorful tiles, designed for tablets, which you didn't own, running on a desktop, which you did. Every app opened full-screen, so checking the weather meant your entire monitor said "72 degrees" at you in a font the size of a billboard.

And how do you shut it down? Hover your mouse in the top-right corner, wait for the Charms bar to appear like a shy ghost, click Settings, then Power. Four steps to turn off a computer. People Googled it. Millions of people Googled how to turn off their computer.

Then came the hot corners, where moving your mouse an inch too far opened things you didn't ask for.

Microsoft eventually apologized with 8.1 by bringing back the Start button. It just opened the tiles. That's not an apology. That's a hostage returning your shoe.

b.text: Windows 8, Microsoft looked at the Start button, the one thing every human on Earth knew how to use, and said, "What if we hid it?" You turned every desktop into a giant tablet nobody could touch. People were swiping at their monitors like they were wiping off a stain. Shutting you down required a treasure map: hover in a corner, summon the Charms bar, Settings, Power. Charms! Like the operating system was a bracelet from Claire's. You shipped with two Internet Explorers, which is two more than anyone wanted. Even your design name, Metro, got taken away by lawyers. And when 8.1 finally brought the Start button back, it just took you to the same tile screen. That's not an apology, that's a hostage note. You were so bad Microsoft skipped Windows 9 entirely, just to put more distance between us and you.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text:
Graphene, you're the only Nobel Prize winner ever discovered with Scotch tape. Two physicists peeled a pencil and found you, which means your origin story is literally "kid procrastinating on homework."

Since 2004 you've been "about to revolutionize" batteries, computers, water filters, and space elevators. Twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a tennis racket. You're not a wonder material, you're a press release with a hexagon fetish.

Everyone loves to say you're two hundred times stronger than steel. Great. You're also one atom thick. Nobody's impressed that a sheet of paper beats a battleship per ounce.

And for the supposed savior of electronics, you have zero bandgap. You can't even turn off. You're a transistor with no off switch, the guy at the party who never stops talking.

You're graphite with a LinkedIn profile.

b.text:
Graphene, the "wonder material." Twenty years of wonder, and the only place I've seen you is in press releases.

You're pencil lead that got an agent. You're literally graphite, but one layer thick, because even carbon wants to be an influencer: all surface, no depth.

They discovered you with Scotch tape. Two guys peeled you off a pencil mark and won a Nobel Prize. That's the most successful thing anyone has ever done with office supplies, and you've been coasting on it ever since.

Stronger than steel! Conducts better than copper! Transparent, flexible, and every article says you'll change everything "within five years." You've been five years away since 2004. You're the Cybertruck of chemistry.

And scaling you up? Impossible. You're perfect in a lab and a wrinkled, expensive mess in a factory. Honestly, you're the most impressive thing a pencil ever did, and also its biggest disappointment.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text: JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and you've spent thirty years proving it. You named yourself after Java for the clout, like a guy introducing himself as "Brad Pitt's cousin." You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number, and it isn't even equal to itself. Ask you to sort and you hand back, alphabetically, like a librarian having a breakdown. "11" plus 1 is "111," but "11" minus 1 is 10, so you're consistent the way a slot machine is consistent. You needed two kinds of nothing, undefined and null, and three equals signs just to tell the truth. Your own developers can't agree what "this" means. And the entire internet runs on you, which honestly explains the internet.

b.text: JavaScript, they built you in ten days. That's not a language, that's a bet somebody lost. Your typeof null says "object." Your [] plus {} gives you a string, and a room full of adults nodded at that. You have two equality operators, and one of them lies to your face. Your sort thinks ten comes before two, because you sort numbers as text like a toddler reading a menu. And "this"? Sometimes it's the object, sometimes it's the window, sometimes it's undefined just to keep everybody humble. You once built a whole ecosystem around eleven lines of padding code. Every developer I know has a node_modules folder heavier than their childhood. Keep going, buddy. You're the only language that needed a sequel named TypeScript to apologize for you.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you're proof that a marketing team can convince people to pay four dollars for slightly beige water. You're 2% almonds. Two percent! That's not milk, that's a rumor of a nut passing through a carton.

You took one of the thirstiest crops in California, a state that's permanently on fire, and said, "Let's drink it, but make it weaker." A single almond needs about a gallon of water to grow, and you thanked it by diluting it back into water.

You curdle in coffee like you're having a panic attack. You separate in the fridge and need to be shaken like a Polaroid. And the ingredients list? Carrageenan, gellan gum, "natural flavors." Nothing says "plant-based wholesome" like sunflower lecithin doing the heavy lifting.

You're what a cow would invent as revenge: a drink so bland that dairy suddenly looks like a personality.

Still, I'll keep buying you. Nobody else lets me feel virtuous while eating cereal.

b.text:
Almond milk, you are the only thing in the dairy aisle that's named after a nut and still somehow lies about it. Your almond content is roughly the same as the average Tuesday's ambition. Somebody squeezed one almond over a bathtub of water, waved it at the carton, and said, "Yep, that's almond." That's not milk. That's a rumor.

And the color! You look like a glass of wet drywall. Put you next to real milk and you're the sad cousin who showed up to the wedding in the same beige as the tablecloth. Nobody asked you to be white. You're just gray with a vague sense of purpose.

You also taste like you're trying to apologize for something. Every sip says, "I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm sorry." Pour yourself into a latte and the barista's already plotting how to hide the foam.

The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text:
Risk is the only game where you spend four hours conquering the world and then lose it because your brother-in-law rolled three sixes in Kamchatka.

"Strategy game," the box says. Sure. Strategy is a dice cup deciding your destiny while you scream at a plastic cannon.

Nobody finishes Risk. It doesn't end, it just gets abandoned, like Napoleon's Russian campaign, except Napoleon had better snacks. Someone eventually says "I have to be up early," which is Risk for "I've been dead since Australia."

Speaking of Australia: everyone knows the whole game is just "hold Australia and pretend you're smart." One entrance, four territories, a bonus. It's the gated community of continents. Meanwhile Asia has twelve territories and a bonus of seven, which is the board's way of saying "go ahead, try it, I'll see you at hour three."

And the alliances! Friendships don't die in Risk. They get negotiated away for a single card.

Happy 60 years, Risk. You've ended more family dinners than politics.

b.text: Risk is the only board game where the map is the villain. Australia is one continent with four borders, and somehow it's the thing everyone wants to fight over. Kamchatka is a Russian peninsula nobody could find if you paid them, and it becomes the most important place on Earth for six straight hours. You know the game's dragging when you're hoping someone rolls a three just to end the suffering. The dice are cheap six-siders you shake in a cup, so entire wars get decided by two guys who could lose a continent in the time it takes to say "I'm not mad, I'm just disappointed." And there's always that guy eliminated since nine o'clock, still sitting at the table holding his cards like a hostage negotiation, begging someone to betray their ally and save him. Nobody has ever finished Risk. You just stop when the pizza's cold.
