typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text: JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and you've spent thirty years proving it. You named yourself after Java for the clout, like a guy introducing himself as "Brad Pitt's cousin." You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number, and it isn't even equal to itself. Ask you to sort and you hand back, alphabetically, like a librarian having a breakdown. "11" plus 1 is "111," but "11" minus 1 is 10, so you're consistent the way a slot machine is consistent. You needed two kinds of nothing, undefined and null, and three equals signs just to tell the truth. Your own developers can't agree what "this" means. And the entire internet runs on you, which honestly explains the internet.

b.text:
JavaScript was built in ten days, and honestly, it shows. It's the only language where 0.1 + 0.2 isn't 0.3, and "11" - 1 is 10 but "11" + 1 is 111. Math, but make it improv.

Its typeof null says "object." That's not a bug, that's a 28-year-old typo everyone agreed to live with, like a tattoo of an ex's name.

You want to check if something's an array? Great, typeof says "object." Use Array.isArray. Want to sort numbers? Default sort alphabetically, so 10 comes before 2. Because why would numbers be numbers?

And the ecosystem! One developer deleted an 11-line package called left-pad and half the internet fell over. Your app has 1,400 dependencies and a node_modules folder heavier than a neutron star.

Every Tuesday there's a new framework that's "totally different this time." It's a React with a Vue on top of a Svelte. Meanwhile, NaN is not equal to itself, which is the most self-aware thing this language has ever done.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero raised 120 million dollars to build a Wi-Fi-enabled juicer that cost 700 dollars, then 400 after they panicked. It had a press with four tons of force, enough to lift two Teslas. For what? Squeezing a bag of chopped kale.

Then Bloomberg proved you could just squeeze the bag with your hands. Same juice. No Wi-Fi. No app. No shame. Just a human fist doing the job of a venture-backed appliance.

And the packs! Sold separately, with expiration dates, so the machine would refuse to work if the bag was old. It's a juicer with a DRM problem. You couldn't even use your own fruit. It was a printer that squeezes.

The founder looked like someone who'd raised money by describing a smoothie as "infrastructure."

Google Ventures invested, which makes sense. Nobody does disrupting a squeeze like people who've never had to do one.

Juicero shut down in 2017, a rare startup where the customers' hands outperformed the product, and the product still had a better pitch deck.

b.text:
Juicero, you beautiful $120 million monument to Silicon Valley. You launched at seven hundred dollars to squeeze a bag. A bag! Then Bloomberg reporters squeezed that same bag with their bare hands and got basically the same juice, only faster. You got outperformed by a guy with a grip strength of "typing."

Doug Evans bragged you pressed with four tons of force, enough to lift two Teslas. Buddy, it's kale. The kale didn't need a forklift.

And it needed Wi-Fi. It scanned a QR code before it'd let you drink. Your router goes down and suddenly your breakfast is asking for credentials. Who designs a juicer that can be bricked?

Google Ventures funded this. Kleiner Perkins funded this. Somewhere, a man is still holding a lukewarm pouch, waiting for a firmware update so he's allowed to eat a carrot.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text: Monopoly is the only board game where the goal is to bankrupt your friends and somehow everyone still agrees to play it again. Four hours. Four hours! Nobody has ever finished a game of Monopoly. The game just ends when someone's dad flips the table, or when the banker quietly starts pretending they didn't count the money properly. And the banker, by the way, is always the least trustworthy person at the table, because they're the one holding the stack of cash and they're the one who "forgot" to collect Free Parking. Free Parking! That's not a gift, that's a lie you tell children. And Boardwalk? Nobody's ever landed on Boardwalk and felt lucky. They just felt the rent go up like a hostage negotiation. Monopoly: where your uncle buys every railroad and calls it a "strategy."

b.text:
Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow the lesson everyone learned was "buy Park Place." Then Parker Brothers bought you from a guy who basically stole you, which is the most on-brand origin story in history.

You're the only game where "second prize in a beauty contest" counts as income and jail is solved with a coupon. Your mascot looks like he foreclosed on the Pringles guy, and half of America swears he wears a monocle. He doesn't. We just assumed a man that rich would be hiding something.

Nobody has ever finished you. Games don't end; your cousin just flips the board over Marvin Gardens, which you misspelled, by the way. It's Marven. Even your real estate is a scam.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista, you were the operating system that asked permission to open the calculator. Every time I tried to delete a file, you'd pop up a box asking "Are you sure?" like I was a toddler with scissors. Then you'd ask again. And again. Your User Account Control was so annoying that people turned it off just to get their work done, which I guess was the security equivalent of removing the smoke detector because it beeps.

And Aero! Gorgeous glass windows that ran great on the computer that cost four thousand dollars and crawled on everything else. You had "Vista Capable" stickers on machines that couldn't actually run you. That's not a sticker, that's a hostage note.

b.text:
Windows Vista, the only operating system that asked "Are you sure?" before letting you breathe. You wanted to open Notepad? Cancel or Allow. You clicked Allow? Are you *really* sure? It had the confidence of a bouncer and the competence of a toddler.

Microsoft promised "Wow." Users said "Why?" Then "Where's my RAM?" Then "Where's my printer driver?" Then "Where's XP?"

It launched with a sticker that said "Vista Capable," which turned out to mean "Capable of displaying a sad blue spinning circle on your brand-new laptop."

Copying a file took so long that Vista estimated "20 minutes remaining," then "3 days," then "Discovering..." forever. Aero looked gorgeous, like a Ferrari with no engine.

Apple made an entire ad campaign out of mocking you, Vista, and the worst part is Microsoft just sat there, clicked Allow, and said "Yes, I'm sure."

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The only material that's been "five years away" since 1991. You're a hundred times stronger than steel, and you've used that strength to hold together... a tennis racket. They promised us a space elevator; you can't get past a few centimeters without a defect. That's not a cable, that's a toothpick with a press agent.

You're basically graphene that rolled itself up out of insecurity, and graphene still got the Nobel. Your cousin the buckyball got one too. You got a shoutout in a bike-frame brochure.

You can't even decide if you're a metal or a semiconductor; it depends on the angle you got rolled at. You clump together like nerds at a mixer, and the second you escape, you lodge in lungs like asbestos. Strongest thing on Earth, and your best trick is ending up in a safety data sheet.

b.text: Carbon nanotubes, you've been "five years away from changing everything" since 1991. You're stronger than steel, lighter than aluminum, and conduct electricity like a champ, which is impressive until someone asks you to leave the lab. You're a sheet of graphene that rolled itself up and called it a personality. Your big selling point is being incredibly small, and honestly, that's the only thing you've ever fit into. Every time someone tries to disperse you in a solvent, you clump together like a group project at 2 a.m. Meanwhile, the press releases keep calling you "revolutionary," and the only thing you've revolutionized is the grant budget. Stronger than steel, lighter than aluminum, and still the guest nobody's ready to invite into the real world.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack. Named after the one thing you'll never have again.

You promised to kill email, and you did, by replacing it with forty channels that are each email with a typing indicator. Nothing builds dread like "Greg is typing..." for ninety seconds, followed by "hey." Just "hey." Greg, that's not a message, that's a hostage situation.

You gave us threads, so every conversation happens in two places and nobody knows which one's real. You gave us huddles: a meeting that jumps out of a bush. You gave us the green dot, so my boss can monitor my bathroom breaks like a heart rate.

And that knock sound. I hear it in the grocery store. I hear it at funerals.

Slack, you're the only app that needs three gigs of RAM to tell me someone reacted with a dancing parrot.

b.text:
You know what Slack is? It's a meeting that refuses to start. Somebody's typing for four minutes, and then it's just "k." Thanks, Dave. Four minutes for a letter.

And the little dots! Everybody's watching those dots like they're a heart monitor. "Dave is typing..." Dave has been typing since Tuesday.

Slack is where we go to "circle back" and never come back. Then there's the huddle. You can't call it a meeting, because that would be too honest. It's a "huddle," like we're a bunch of football players who just need a quick word about the Dorito situation.

And the status emoji! Little palm tree, "OOO." Sure, Brenda. You're on a beach, and you're replying to #marketing-updates from a beach.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Klingon, you're the only language whose native speakers are all fictional and whose fluent speakers all have a Comic-Con badge. Marc Okrand built you in 1984 to sound alien, and he nailed it: you sound like a man choking on a pretzel while reading IKEA instructions.

Your word order is object-verb-subject, so every sentence is a mystery that reveals who did it at the end. Your greeting, nuqneH, literally means "What do you want?" Congratulations: you're the first language designed by a DMV clerk.

You have more apostrophes than vowels deserve, no verb "to be," and a Klingon Language Institute that "restored" Hamlet to its original Klingon. That's not scholarship. That's fan fiction with footnotes.

A linguist once tried raising his son in Klingon. By age five the kid stopped answering. Qapla'!

b.text:
Klingon, a language designed by a linguist for a race of warriors, and somehow it still has a word for "tea" but no word for "hello." You people invented a whole culture of honor and glory, and the greeting is "What do you want?" That's not a language, that's a customer service line at a gym.

The grammar is object-verb-subject. Of course it is. Even the sentence structure says "I'm going to stab the dinner first and tell you who did it later."

Klingon has a phrase for "Today is a good day to die," but you try ordering a sandwich. Nope. Because no Klingon ever said, "Could I get that on rye?" They said, "Bring me the still-moving thing."

And the fans! Thousands of people speaking fluent guttural phlegm, getting married in it, translating Hamlet. Shakespeare in the original Klingon, which is just regular Shakespeare, but now the soliloquy sounds like someone clearing their throat at a funeral.

Qapla'? More like Qa-please-stop.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text:
NFTs, you're the only investment where the product is a receipt, and the receipt is a link to a JPEG hosted on some guy's server. When he stops paying the bill, congratulations: you own a 404.

You convinced grown adults to pay $300,000 for a cartoon monkey in a sailor hat, then charge them $80 in gas fees to watch it lose 98% of its value. Jimmy Fallon showed off his ape on national television like a kid holding up a cool rock.

People right-clicked and hit "save as," and you called it theft. Theft of *what*? It's still there! I'm looking at it!

Every project had a roadmap: metaverse, merch, a members-only yacht party. Instead the roadmap was a Discord mod named Kevin typing "we're still early" at 3 a.m.

WAGMI, you said. We did not all make it.

b.text:
NFTs: the only product where you pay $300,000 for a receipt, and the receipt is for a JPEG, and the JPEG is still publicly available for free. You can right-click it. The whole business model is a guy pointing at the Mona Lisa saying, "Technically, I own the bookmark."

And the art! Eight thousand identical apes, each with a slightly different hat. That's not a collection, that's a hostage situation at a Hot Topic.

Remember when they said it was "the future of ownership"? Then OpenSea's servers went down and people learned their million-dollar monkey was just a link to a website that could 404. You didn't buy art. You bought a very expensive "Page Not Found."

And the guys who bought them still say "we're early." Early to what? The funeral?

Somewhere right now, a man named Chad is staring at a cartoon ape worth $14, whispering, "Floor price is just a vibe."

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ, hydrogen silsesquioxane, the only resist that's basically glass pretending to be a photoresist. You're the diva of nanofabrication. Shelf life? Three months, if you keep it cold, treat it gently, and whisper affirmations. Open the bottle wrong and you've got a jar of gel with commitment issues.

You're a negative tone resist, which is fitting, because that's the attitude. Everyone wants 10-nanometer lines, and you deliver them, then collapse because a developer rinse looked at you funny. Capillary forces: your Achilles heel, your whole personality.

And your dose? You need a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. That's not exposure, that's a hostage negotiation with the beam. Writing one wafer takes longer than my last relationship.

Then you cure into silicon dioxide and just sit there, permanent, like a bad tattoo. "Oh, you wanted to remove me? Enjoy your hydrofluoric acid, hero."

Gorgeous resolution, though. Truly. Shame about everything else.

b.text:
HSQ, everybody! The only resist that ages faster than the grad student using it. You spin it Monday, expose it Tuesday, and suddenly your dose curve has gone through a midlife crisis. It has to live in the fridge like expired yogurt, and it's about as forgiving.

HSQ brags about sub-10-nanometer lines. Sure, if you've got six hours of write time, because this diva needs a dose that could sterilize a hospital. Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you're desperate, *salt water*. Your whole career is literally seasoned with tears now.

And once it's exposed? It turns into glass. Brittle, cracking glass. You wanted a mask; you got a window that shatters when you look at it. Want it gone? Hope you enjoy hydrofluoric acid, the chemical that dissolves your bones.

HSQ: beautiful resolution, terrible personality. It's not negative-tone. It's just negative.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text: Ladies and gentlemen, PMMA, the e-beam resist that's just Plexiglass with a graduate degree. You know what else is sharp and transparent and you can't eat? A window. PMMA takes a beam of electrons, snaps its chains apart, and then acts shocked when the developer washes away exactly the parts it chose to lose. Its sensitivity is so low you need a dose that would make a lesser polymer file for disability. You bake it at 180 degrees, wait, spin it, wait, bake again, and it still makes you feel like you're the one being exposed. Its etch resistance is about as strong as a wet paper towel. But sure, it draws lines thinner than a virus's dream, so we just keep inviting it back, like that one relative who only shows up to tell you what you did wrong.

b.text: PMMA, you're the same plastic as a hockey rink window, and somehow that's your most dignified job. You've been "high resolution" since the 1970s, which is like bragging about your SAT score at your retirement party. Sure, you'll resolve sub-10-nanometer lines, if someone stands there blasting you with electrons for an eternity. Your sensitivity is so low the beam current has gotten tenure. You don't even develop properly without MIBK and IPA holding your hand in a one-to-three ratio. And your whole personality is chain scission: you literally fall apart when someone pays attention to you. Then hit you with too much dose and you crosslink and flip to negative tone, a full identity crisis. And dry etch? You melt in plasma faster than an ice sculpture at a barbecue. Honestly, the only thing you're consistently good at is lift-off: leaving.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text: HSQ, you're the most high-maintenance resist in the cleanroom. You live in a fridge like a sad sandwich, and leave the cap off for an afternoon and you gel into a forgotten Jell-O salad. You're negative-tone, so the exposed parts become your permanent address. You don't leave the wafer, you move in as silicon dioxide. You promise sub-10-nanometer lines, then spread out with the dose like a houseguest saying "just one more electron." Develop in salty developer and you still swell, like you're offended by the chemistry. Honestly, you're a flowable oxide with a personality disorder and an expensive price tag.

b.text:
HSQ, ladies and gentlemen: the only resist with sub-10-nanometer resolution and the personality of a sourdough starter. You buy it, you refrigerate it, and it *still* starts gelling in the bottle like it's got somewhere better to be. Shelf life measured in "eh, few months, maybe."

And slow? HSQ needs a dose so high the e-beam tool files for overtime. Your PMMA friends finished their write and went home; you're still exposing alignment marks.

Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you want contrast, *salty* developer. Yes, this resist literally needs you to add salt. Even Gordon Ramsay thinks that's a lot.

But the real red flag? Once it's exposed, it turns into glass. Permanently. You want it gone? Hydrofluoric acid. That's not a resist, that's a relationship you can only leave with a hazmat suit.

Still, gorgeous lines. Shame they collapse when they dry.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans, you're the only font that shows up to a funeral looking like it's about to do a magic show for toddlers.

You were designed for a cartoon dog's speech bubble in Microsoft Bob, and somehow ended up on cancer-ward notices, divorce settlements, and "Please Do Not Microwave Fish" signs in the office kitchen. Every message you carry sounds like it was written by a substitute teacher who's given up.

Designers don't hate you. Designers have a support group for you. CERN announced the Higgs boson in you, and physicists everywhere suddenly wondered if the universe was a bake sale flyer.

Your letters look like they were drawn by someone holding the marker in their left hand while riding a bus. The lowercase "a" is the only part of you that's trying.

And yet you're still installed on every computer on Earth, like a clown that nobody invited but nobody can evict.

b.text:
Comic Sans is the font that looks like it was designed by a substitute teacher who found a crayon in a lost-and-found box. Every letter wobbles like it's had three espressos and a bad breakup. The "a" is a little round bubble with a tail that's clearly been through something. Nobody asked for this. It's the typographic equivalent of a clown trying to file your taxes.

And the worst part? Somebody put it on a hospital sign. A hospital! You're walking in with a broken leg, scanning for the exit, and the sign says "EMERGENCY" in letters that look like they're bouncing on a trampoline. Even the sickness can't take itself seriously anymore.

It's the only font that makes a funeral notice look like a birthday party invitation. Somewhere a grandmother is typing "Rest In Peace" in this, hitting bold, and thinking she's being tasteful.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Microsoft spent five years building you as "Longhorn," and somehow you still came out premature.

Your slogan was "The Wow Starts Now." You meant "Now" as in "after the loading circle finishes." People bought laptops with "Vista Capable" stickers, which turned out to mean "capable of being sued over." Those machines couldn't even run Aero, so they got a see-through window theme with nothing to see.

And User Account Control! You asked "Are you sure?" so many times that you became the first operating system with separation anxiety.

You came in six editions, including "Ultimate," whose big exclusive was DreamScene: a moving wallpaper for the ten minutes you weren't hunting for printer drivers.

Microsoft had to trick people into liking you. The Mojave Experiment! Your own parents had to put you in disguise.

Your greatest feature? The XP downgrade.

b.text:
Windows Vista, the only operating system that asked "Are you sure?" before letting you breathe. You wanted to open Notepad? Cancel or Allow. You clicked Allow? Are you *really* sure? It had the confidence of a bouncer and the competence of a toddler.

Microsoft promised "Wow." Users said "Why?" Then "Where's my RAM?" Then "Where's my printer driver?" Then "Where's XP?"

It launched with a sticker that said "Vista Capable," which turned out to mean "Capable of displaying a sad blue spinning circle on your brand-new laptop."

Copying a file took so long that Vista estimated "20 minutes remaining," then "3 days," then "Discovering..." forever. Aero looked gorgeous, like a Ferrari with no engine.

Apple made an entire ad campaign out of mocking you, Vista, and the worst part is Microsoft just sat there, clicked Allow, and said "Yes, I'm sure."

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word, you've had thirty years to learn what I want, and you still think I'm trying to write a bulleted list every time I type a dash.

You've got a paperclip's worth of trauma in your past, yet you still auto-correct "Costco" to "Cost co" like you're editing a ransom note.

I insert one picture and the whole document rearranges itself like furniture in an earthquake. The image jumps to page nine, the text wraps around it in the shape of a gunshot wound, and page four is now blank for reasons known only to God and a hidden section break.

You have a ribbon with 400 buttons, and the one I need is always under "Layout," which is somehow not where the layout is.

And "Not Responding"? Buddy, I just asked you to save. Then you recover my file as "Document1 (Autorecovered) (Copy) (2)," like a witness protection program for my thesis.

b.text: Microsoft Word is the only program that has a paperclip for a mascot, and it still managed to be the most annoying thing on the screen. You type one space in the middle of a sentence and the whole document rearranges itself like it's moving apartments. Every image you insert becomes a hostage that refuses to stay on page four. And that blue squiggle under your name? Word thinks *you're* the typo. Then there's Compatibility Mode, the program's way of saying, "I've seen your file, and I'm not going to pretend I understand it." Twenty years of updates, and the only thing it's truly mastered is looking shocked when you press Ctrl+S.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text: LaTeX, you're the only software that makes PhDs feel stupid. You're from 1984 and you dress like it: backslashes everywhere, curly braces like a nervous tic. I tell you to put a figure "here," and you treat "here" as a suggestion, then file it four pages later next to the bibliography, like a sock lost in a dryer. Your error messages are poetry: "Missing $ inserted." Inserted where? Why? You won't say. You just blame line 1 of a 40-page file because I typed an underscore in a URL. My citations are double question marks until I compile you twice, then a third time, out of spite. And everyone needs to know it's pronounced "lay-tech," not like the glove. Honestly, at least the glove stretches. Overfull \hbox? Badness 10000? Buddy, that's not a warning. That's your autobiography.

b.text: LaTeX, you're the only program that makes a document look like a Pulitzer and then sends you a nine-hundred-line error log because you forgot a bracket. "Missing $ inserted." Where? Everywhere. Your error messages read like a ransom note. And the figures! I put a picture in, and it floats off to page nine like it has somewhere better to be. I write to say "here," and you say, "Mm, I'll be the judge of that." Centering a table takes three hours, a booktabs package, and a prayer. Then I compile, get a PDF so beautiful I almost forgive you, and you hit me with "Overfull \hbox, badness 10000." Badness. You named it. You're the only typesetter honest enough to put its own insult in the log.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text: Klingon, you sound like a man hacking up a hairball during a hostage negotiation. Every word starts with a throat-clearing gargle, and somehow "nuqneH" still sounds like a threat. Apparently "please" is a sign of weakness, so you just bellow "Qapla'" and hope the guy behind you agrees. Your grammar treats every sentence like a dare: object first, verb second, subject whenever you feel like it. Your big literary achievement is *Hamlet*, and its most famous line comes out as "taH pagh taHbe'," which sounds like a dog choking on a sock. Your dictionary has more ways to say "your mother" than "I'm sorry," and I'd respect you more if you apologized once.

b.text:
Klingon, you're the only language whose native speakers are all fictional and whose fluent speakers all have a Comic-Con badge. Marc Okrand built you in 1984 to sound alien, and he nailed it: you sound like a man choking on a pretzel while reading IKEA instructions.

Your word order is object-verb-subject, so every sentence is a mystery that reveals who did it at the end. Your greeting, nuqneH, literally means "What do you want?" Congratulations: you're the first language designed by a DMV clerk.

You have more apostrophes than vowels deserve, no verb "to be," and a Klingon Language Institute that "restored" Hamlet to its original Klingon. That's not scholarship. That's fan fiction with footnotes.

A linguist once tried raising his son in Klingon. By age five the kid stopped answering. Qapla'!

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans is the font that looks like it was designed by a substitute teacher who found a crayon in a lost-and-found box. Every letter wobbles like it's had three espressos and a bad breakup. The "a" is a little round bubble with a tail that's clearly been through something. Nobody asked for this. It's the typographic equivalent of a clown trying to file your taxes.

And the worst part? Somebody put it on a hospital sign. A hospital! You're walking in with a broken leg, scanning for the exit, and the sign says "EMERGENCY" in letters that look like they're bouncing on a trampoline. Even the sickness can't take itself seriously anymore.

It's the only font that makes a funeral notice look like a birthday party invitation. Somewhere a grandmother is typing "Rest In Peace" in this, hitting bold, and thinking she's being tasteful.

b.text:
Comic Sans, you were literally designed for a talking dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the only part of that project that didn't die with dignity. Vincent Connare made you in 1994 for cartoon speech bubbles, and you heard that and thought, "Tombstones. Legal notices. Resignation letters."

Dan Gilbert wrote his furious LeBron James letter in you, and that's why nobody remembers being scared. CERN announced the Higgs boson, the most important physics discovery in fifty years, in you, and the entire scientific community went, "Did a third grader find God?"

People defend you because you help some readers with dyslexia, which is true and lovely, and also the only time you've ever been used responsibly.

You're not a font. You're a bake sale flyer that got tenure. Even Papyrus looks at you and says, "Wow, okay, tone it down."

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which is wild, because you dress like a medieval mace and smell like a crime scene. You're the only fruit with a body armor package AND a hazmat warning.

You're banned from Singapore's subway, hotels, and airlines. Think about that. Nobody bans the pineapple. You're the only produce item that gets kicked off a plane before it even boards.

Your fans say, "Just get past the smell, the taste is heavenly." Sir, that's what every hostage says about their captor.

You taste like custard that's been cheating on a sewer with an onion. Eat one and your fridge smells like you for three weeks, your breath for five.

And you fall out of trees onto people's heads. You're not even content to be a bad meal. You want to be a *weapon*.

b.text: Durian, you smell like a gym sock that got left in a sewer and then decided to become a fruit out of spite. People in Singapore have to ride the MRT with signs warning them about you. Signs! You're banned from hotels. Hotels! They don't ban guests who set fire to the carpet, but they draw the line at you. And the worst part? You're shaped like a medieval mace someone dipped in a hedgehog. Nobody approaches you with a knife, they approach you with a shovel and a prayer. Fans call your taste "custardy." Custardy? Honey, that's what a gym sock would taste like if it had a rich uncle.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text: Jackfruit, you look like a sea mine that got into a fight with a durian and lost. Your skin is a crime scene of little green spikes, and nobody has ever cut you open without a prayer and a machete. You're the size of a toddler, you smell like gym socks dipped in bubblegum, and you're somehow both sweet and wet and still sticky after you've been in the fridge. Vegans found you and suddenly you're "pulled pork," which is the most desperate rebrand since "vegetable oil" tried to be a steak. Everybody's grandma loves you for one week a year, then you rot on the counter and the whole kitchen knows. You're a fruit that needs its own safety briefing. Nobody's ever walked out of a grocery store saying, "I'll have the enormous spiky thing that smells like a locker room."

b.text:
Jackfruit, you're the largest fruit that grows on a tree, which sounds impressive until you realize it just means you're the biggest thing that can fall on someone's head in an orchard. Eighty pounds of spikes dangling at skull height. You're not a fruit, you're a booby trap with seeds.

Opening you requires an oiled knife, rubber gloves, and a tarp, because your sap is basically Elmer's glue with a grudge. Then the smell hits: half Juicy Fruit gum, half onions somebody forgot in a gym bag. You smell like a candy store got food poisoning.

And sure, vegans love you, but only when you're young and taste like absolutely nothing. That's your whole career. The most famous thing about you is that, with enough barbecue sauce, you can pass for a pig. Even your best role is an impression.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text: JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and you've spent thirty years proving it. You named yourself after Java for the clout, like a guy introducing himself as "Brad Pitt's cousin." You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number, and it isn't even equal to itself. Ask you to sort and you hand back, alphabetically, like a librarian having a breakdown. "11" plus 1 is "111," but "11" minus 1 is 10, so you're consistent the way a slot machine is consistent. You needed two kinds of nothing, undefined and null, and three equals signs just to tell the truth. Your own developers can't agree what "this" means. And the entire internet runs on you, which honestly explains the internet.

b.text:
You're the only language where `typeof null` returns "object" and nobody got fired. It's been wrong for thirty years, and instead of fixing it, you just shrugged and kept serving it, like a restaurant that's been selling raw chicken since 1995 and calls it a rustic choice.

You've got two equals signs for comparison, and one of them lies. `0 == ""` is true. `"" == "0"` is false. Zero equals empty string, empty string doesn't equal zero-string. That's not a bug. That's a hostage situation.

And `.sort()` gives you ``, because you sort numbers alphabetically unless someone begs you for a comparator function. You wrote a language that thinks digits are words.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: Nobody's ever bought an NFT. They bought a receipt that says "you own this JPEG," and the JPEG is a cartoon ape with a bowler hat, the same JPEG you can right-click and save in four seconds. So they paid four hundred thousand dollars for a screenshot with a certificate. It's the only art in history where the certificate is the art. The Mona Lisa hangs in the Louvre with a crowd of tourists, and this guy's ape is hanging in a folder called "wallet" that nobody else can see. Ownership, they call it. Congratulations, you own the ape, and the ape doesn't know you exist.

b.text:
NFTs are the only product where "right-click, save as" is a legitimate threat to a billion-dollar market. You didn't buy art. You bought a receipt for a JPEG that anyone can look at for free, and the receipt is a hyperlink, and the hyperlink is hosted on a server that's going down when the startup runs out of money. Congratulations, you own a 404.

And the names! Bored Ape. Doodle. CryptoPunk. Nothing says "serious investor" like a man in a blazer whispering, "I'm down forty grand on a cartoon monkey, but the community is strong."

Everyone was a visionary until the gas fees showed up. You paid sixty dollars in Ethereum fees to buy a picture of a rock that was worth four dollars, then listed it for a million because a guy named xX_DiamondHandz_Xx said it would "flip."

It didn't flip. It just sat there. Like a rock.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, you've been "five years from changing everything" since 1991. Thirty-plus years! Fusion power looks at you and says, "Take it easy, pal."

You're a hundred times stronger than steel, but only if you're one perfect, flawless, microscopic strand that nobody can actually make longer than a hair. Basically you're a gym bro who can bench a truck but only if it's in a vacuum, and he's the size of a bacterium.

You're just rolled-up graphene. You're a sheet of pencil lead that got into a yoga class and now thinks it's special.

Every grant proposal says you'll build a space elevator. Meanwhile, the only thing you've actually lifted is my hopes and a tennis racket.

And toxicologists say you act like asbestos in the lungs. Incredible range: strongest material ever, also a lawsuit.

You're not the future. You're soot with a publicist.

b.text: Carbon nanotubes are the most stressed-out material on Earth. They're stronger than steel, and they've been "five years from revolutionizing everything" since 1991. They're just graphene that got rolled up and never recovered. Ask one whether it's a metal or a semiconductor and it genuinely can't tell you until someone tests it. In the lab they clump together like cold spaghetti. For thirty years industry has promised them in batteries, bike frames, and space elevators. The only space elevator I've seen is the one in my dorm, and it doesn't work either. Their best feature is that under a microscope they look exactly like asbestos, which is a bold thing for a material to bring to a party.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text: JavaScript, they built you in ten days. That's not a language, that's a bet somebody lost. Your typeof null says "object." Your [] plus {} gives you a string, and a room full of adults nodded at that. You have two equality operators, and one of them lies to your face. Your sort thinks ten comes before two, because you sort numbers as text like a toddler reading a menu. And "this"? Sometimes it's the object, sometimes it's the window, sometimes it's undefined just to keep everybody humble. You once built a whole ecosystem around eleven lines of padding code. Every developer I know has a node_modules folder heavier than their childhood. Keep going, buddy. You're the only language that needed a sequel named TypeScript to apologize for you.

b.text:
JavaScript was built in ten days, and honestly, it shows. It's the only language where 0.1 + 0.2 isn't 0.3, and "11" - 1 is 10 but "11" + 1 is 111. Math, but make it improv.

Its typeof null says "object." That's not a bug, that's a 28-year-old typo everyone agreed to live with, like a tattoo of an ex's name.

You want to check if something's an array? Great, typeof says "object." Use Array.isArray. Want to sort numbers? Default sort alphabetically, so 10 comes before 2. Because why would numbers be numbers?

And the ecosystem! One developer deleted an 11-line package called left-pad and half the internet fell over. Your app has 1,400 dependencies and a node_modules folder heavier than a neutron star.

Every Tuesday there's a new framework that's "totally different this time." It's a React with a Vue on top of a Svelte. Meanwhile, NaN is not equal to itself, which is the most self-aware thing this language has ever done.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass was the only gadget that made you look like a robot and a creep at the same time. You'd walk into a bar, and before you ordered, everyone had already figured out you were filming them. "Don't worry, I'm not recording." Sure, buddy, and that's why there's a little red light blinking on your face like a smoke detector with a grudge.

And the battery! It lasted about as long as a Google product lasts before they cancel it. You'd spend the whole day with a computer on your head that could barely make it to lunch. Your own eyeballs had better uptime, and they're held together by tiny veins and spite.

Then there was the name. "Glass." Nothing says "I'm trustworthy and affordable" like a device you'd have to tape a sign to, reading "Please don't break my face."

b.text: Google Glass, you cost fifteen hundred dollars and made everyone wearing you look like a Bluetooth headset that got promoted. Sergey Brin launched you by skydiving onto a building, and that's the last time you were ever cool. You put a tiny prism over one eye so people could check email while pretending to make eye contact. You didn't invent a computer, you invented a reason to get punched. You're the only gadget that gave us a new slur: "Glasshole." Bars banned you. Movie theaters banned you. Robert Scoble wore you in the shower, and that photo did more damage than any privacy lawsuit. You took pictures when people winked, turning every awkward conversation into a potential felony. Your battery died before your reputation did, and that's impressive. Rest in peace: demoted to warehouse work, then quietly killed in 2023. The most Google ending possible.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Microsoft Teams is the only app that can notify you about a message you're already reading. You've got a red badge, a yellow badge, and a little purple "@" telling you someone said "per my last email" in a chat called "Q3 Sync (Copy) (Final)."

Teams has seven ways to say hello and none of them load. "Joining meeting..." is its resting state. It's the Waiting for Godot of video calls, except Godot eventually shows up and says, "Can everyone see my screen?" No, Greg. We see a spinning circle and your cat.

Every update, it asks you to restart. Not the app. Your life choices.

Teams and Channels are different things, by the way. A channel lives inside a team. Which is inside a tenant. Which is inside a guest account you can't switch out of without signing out of everything and crying.

And the green dot? It goes yellow the second you stop moving your mouse, so your boss thinks you're napping. Ten minutes of reading a document is considered a vacation.

b.text: Microsoft Teams is the only app that got popular the way a parking ticket gets popular: it came free with Office 365 and nobody could say no. It's a chat app that eats more RAM than Chrome, which is like a goldfish outeating a horse. It marks you "Away" if you blink for five minutes, which is why half of corporate America owns a mouse jiggler. Every file you share vanishes into SharePoint, a place so mysterious even Microsoft sends search parties. There's chat, there's channels, there's "posts," and nobody knows which one Kevin used. They released "New Teams" to replace "Classic Teams," and somehow both are running on my laptop right now, fighting. And that notification sound? That little knock-knock haunts people on vacation. Teams, you didn't win the remote work war. You were just pre-installed.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text: Microsoft Teams, you're the only app with the nerve to open itself the second I log in, like a hall monitor who got promoted. Every meeting starts with the same ritual: "Can you hear me?" "You're on mute." "Sorry, you're on mute." Thirty seconds of people unmuting like it's a hostage situation. And that little "Someone is typing..." bubble? It's been there since Tuesday. Nobody's typing, Teams. Nobody's ever typing. You tell me I'm "Available" while I'm literally in a meeting, then ping me four minutes after everyone else has already replied. "Let's take this offline," says the guy, and then he schedules a Teams call about it. Teams, you're not a chat app. You're a conference room that follows you home.

b.text:
Microsoft Teams is the only app that can tell you "You're on mute" after you've spent four minutes giving the best speech of your career to nobody.

It's got a notification system that works like a clingy ex. Someone reacts with a thumbs-up to a message you sent three weeks ago, and suddenly your laptop sounds like a submarine under attack.

The search function is a magic trick: you type "Q3 budget," and it shows you a GIF from Brenda's retirement party.

And the name! "Teams." Also "Teams (work or school)." Also "Teams (free)." Also "Teams Classic," which is what we now call the one that worked slightly better. Whenever you open it, it asks which Teams you want, like a waiter asking which of your three identical sandwiches you'd like.

The status indicator says "Away" when you're staring right at it, and "Available" when you've gone to the bathroom.

Teams isn't collaboration software. It's a hostage negotiation with your own Wi-Fi.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: Nobody's ever been mugged for an NFT, and that's the scam. You can't steal it, you can't hang it on a wall, and you can't even right-click save it without the cartoon ape judging you. You paid four thousand dollars for a receipt. A receipt that says, "I own the JPEG of a bored monkey," and the JPEG is still sitting on a server in Ohio, unbothered. Your grandma bought Beanie Babies and at least she got a fabric bear she could hug. You bought a hyperlink with a pulse. And the best part? The guy who sold it to you already cashed out and bought a yacht named after the ape you didn't get to keep.

b.text:
NFTs: the only product where you pay $300,000 for a receipt, and the receipt is for a JPEG, and the JPEG is still publicly available for free. You can right-click it. The whole business model is a guy pointing at the Mona Lisa saying, "Technically, I own the bookmark."

And the art! Eight thousand identical apes, each with a slightly different hat. That's not a collection, that's a hostage situation at a Hot Topic.

Remember when they said it was "the future of ownership"? Then OpenSea's servers went down and people learned their million-dollar monkey was just a link to a website that could 404. You didn't buy art. You bought a very expensive "Page Not Found."

And the guys who bought them still say "we're early." Early to what? The funeral?

Somewhere right now, a man named Chad is staring at a cartoon ape worth $14, whispering, "Floor price is just a vibe."

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you're not milk. You're almonds that got lost on the way to a smoothie and decided to lie about it. Milk comes from a cow, and a cow has some dignity. You come from a nut that's been soaked in water until it gave up. Somebody squeezed a almond, looked at the sad little puddle, and said, "Yep, that's breakfast."

You're so thin, I can read a newspaper through you. Your idea of creamy is a rumor. You've got less body than a Tuesday. And every carton of you says "Unsweetened" like you're proud of it, like there's a single person alive who wanted to taste nothing.

Almond milk, you're the guy who says he's "not really into drinking" and then orders the oat latte.

b.text:
Almond milk, you're proof that a marketing team can convince people to pay four dollars for slightly beige water. You're 2% almonds. Two percent! That's not milk, that's a rumor of a nut passing through a carton.

You took one of the thirstiest crops in California, a state that's permanently on fire, and said, "Let's drink it, but make it weaker." A single almond needs about a gallon of water to grow, and you thanked it by diluting it back into water.

You curdle in coffee like you're having a panic attack. You separate in the fridge and need to be shaken like a Polaroid. And the ingredients list? Carrageenan, gellan gum, "natural flavors." Nothing says "plant-based wholesome" like sunflower lecithin doing the heavy lifting.

You're what a cow would invent as revenge: a drink so bland that dairy suddenly looks like a personality.

Still, I'll keep buying you. Nobody else lets me feel virtuous while eating cereal.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim. The only program where "how do I leave?" has more Stack Overflow views than most religions have followers. Two million people asked, and the answer was colon, q, exclamation point, which reads less like a command and more like a hostage's final words.

Vim stands for "Vi Improved." Improved from a 1976 terminal whose arrow keys were printed on H, J, K, and L. Fifty years later, Vim's still out here like, "Why fix what you can turn into a personality?"

You don't type in Vim. You type a sentence, then discover you deleted four lines, yanked a paragraph into register W, and started recording a macro.

Crash it once and it leaves a .swp file behind, like a ghost whispering, "Recover, Edit anyway, Quit, or Abort?"

Even its fans forked it. Neovim exists because Vim users wanted Vim, minus Vim.

b.text: Vim is the only program that greets you with "How do I quit?" as its opening line. You open it by accident, and now you're trapped in a text editor that thinks typing is a crime. You press "i" to insert text, which is hilarious, because nobody who uses Vim has ever inserted anything into their life. Then you hit Escape, and suddenly you're in command mode, where the letters you type don't write anything. They do things. "d" deletes. "x" deletes. "dd" deletes the whole line, and you did not ask for that. Vim doesn't have a save button; it has ":wq," which sounds like a sneeze in a library. Vim users say it's efficient. Sure, if your idea of efficiency is memorizing a secret language just to change one word.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text:
Graphene, you're the most overhyped thing ever pulled off a pencil with Scotch tape. That's your origin story: two guys got a Nobel Prize for peeling you off graphite like a sticker off a banana. Meanwhile I can't get a Nobel for peeling the plastic off a new remote.

You're one atom thick, stronger than steel, more conductive than copper, and nearly transparent. You're also the only thing in science that's invisible and still manages to be full of yourself.

For twenty years you've been "five years away" from changing everything. Foldable phones, space elevators, unbreakable everything. And what do I have? A tennis racket. A really nice tennis racket.

You have no bandgap, so you can't even work as a decent transistor. You're the smartest kid in class who refuses to turn in homework.

You're just carbon in a honeycomb pattern. Your cousin is literally a diamond, and your other cousin is in my pencil case.

b.text: Graphene, you're one atom thick, and somehow that's still more depth than your business plan. Two hundred times stronger than steel, conducts better than copper, and twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a sticker on a tennis racket. You were discovered with Scotch tape. *Scotch tape!* You're the only Nobel Prize that could've been found in a kindergarten craft drawer. And let's be honest: you're pencil lead that went to grad school. Your cousin graphite has been writing grocery lists for centuries; you've been writing grant proposals. Every year a headline swears you'll revolutionize batteries, chips, water filters. Every year you're still in the lab, like a thirty-year-old in his parents' basement. You can't even be a decent transistor. No bandgap. You literally cannot turn off. Graphene: the material of the future, permanently.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you took the one drink humanity had perfected over five hundred years and said, "What if it came in a tiny plastic thimble that outlives your grandchildren?" Your own inventor said he regrets making you. When your dad disowns you, that's a phase. When the guy who invented you disowns you, that's a recall.

You make coffee one sad, lukewarm cup at a time, then flash "DESCALE" like a check-engine light for a machine that costs forty bucks. Remember Keurig 2.0? You put DRM on coffee. You were scanning pods like a bouncer: "Sorry, sir, you're not on the list." Nobody was pirating Folgers! And your "Strong" button just drips slower, which isn't strength. That's procrastination.

You're not a coffee maker. You're a plastic-dispensing subscription that occasionally hiccups out hot brown water.

b.text: Keurig, you're the only appliance that makes a cup of coffee and then apologizes for it by making you wait four minutes while it hums like a dying refrigerator. You're a single-serve machine with the commitment of a Tinder profile: one pod, one cup, and you'll never call back. Every morning I stare into your little plastic mouth, feed you a pod that cost more per ounce than gold, and you spit out something that tastes like a coffee bean's ghost. And the recycling? Those pods are tiny landfills with lids. You didn't make coffee, Keurig. You made a subscription plan wearing a drip tray. Even your name sounds like a sneeze that got a corporate loan.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript was written in ten days, and honestly, it shows. It's the only language where `[] + {}` is a string, `{} + []` is zero, and nobody can explain why without sweating.

You ask JavaScript to compare `"2" > "12"` and it says true, because it's alphabetical. Sorting numbers? Also alphabetical. `.sort()` gives you ``, like a librarian who learned math from a dictionary.

`NaN` stands for "Not a Number," and its type is "number." `NaN !== NaN`. It's the only thing in programming that refuses to identify itself.

Then there's `this`, which means whatever it feels like today. Every callback is a coin flip with your dignity.

And the ecosystem! You wanted to pad a string, so you installed a package, and now your project has 1,400 dependencies and one of them is a guy's feelings.

JavaScript doesn't throw errors. It throws "undefined is not a function" and lets you figure out which of your 40,000 lines it's talking about.

b.text:
JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and honestly? It shows. You're named after Java the way a knockoff purse is named after Gucci.

You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number. NaN doesn't even equal itself, which makes it the only thing in you with any self-awareness.

Ask you to sort and you hand back, because you alphabetize numbers like a drunk librarian. "11" plus 1 is "111", but "11" minus 1 is 10. Pick a lane.

You needed a second equals sign just to stop lying, and nobody, including you, knows what "this" means.

January is month zero. One guy unpublishing left-pad broke half the internet. And your node_modules folder is heavier than a black hole.

Every week there's a new framework to fix you. That's not a language. That's a renovation.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text: Durian, you're the only fruit that needs a gas mask and a hazmat permit just to get through the airport. Airlines ban you like you're a bomb with a bad attitude. Your smell is a mix of gym socks, rotting onions, and a sewage pipe that's been sulking for a week. People hear the word "delicacy" and think you're kidding. Southeast Asians call you the king of fruits, and honestly, that's the only reason you got a crown instead of a restraining order. You look like a medieval mace someone dropped in a swamp, and you're covered in spikes so nobody can hug you. Even the spikes are a warning. Your fans swear you taste like custard and heaven, but they also say that about getting a root canal on Christmas. Smell like a crime scene, taste like a dessert, and still somehow get a hotel room kicked out for eating you.

b.text:
Durian, the "King of Fruits." Sure, if the kingdom is a landfill. You're banned on the Singapore subway, right there on the sign next to flammable liquids, because apparently you're the bigger hazard. Hotels fine guests for sneaking you in. That's not a fruit, that's a parole violation.

You wear a medieval mace as a jacket, which is smart, since nobody who's smelled you wants to get close anyway. You fall out of trees and put people in the hospital. You're the only produce that needs a hard hat AND a hazmat suit.

And your fans swear you're "like custard!" Sure: custard aged in a gym bag full of rotten onions. Fifty bucks for a Musang King, and your breath's a crime scene for three days.

Anthony Bourdain ate warthog rectum on camera, and *you're* the one he warned people about.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the vehicle for people who looked at electric cars and said, "Too convenient."

You can only fuel up at one of about fifty stations in the entire state of California, and half of them are "temporarily" closed, like a Blockbuster with a hopeful sign. Owners plan road trips like they're smuggling something.

The fuel costs more per mile than driving a Bentley on champagne. And the whole thing runs on the most abundant element in the universe, which is somehow harder to find than a parking spot at Costco.

Toyota calls it the Mirai, Japanese for "future." Technically accurate. That's where the gas stations are.

The only emission is water, which is great, because you'll be standing next to the car for an hour, watching it drip, wondering why you didn't just buy a Tesla.

Hydrogen: the future of transportation, and always will be.

b.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle where the tailpipe emission is water and the owners are still crying more than the car. The Toyota Mirai loses value faster than a Hindenburg loses altitude. Used ones sell for less than the free fuel card Toyota bundled with them, a card you can't use because the station's been "temporarily offline" since 2022.

You've got a 10,000-PSI tank of the universe's most abundant element, and somehow it's the scarcest thing in California. Filling up costs thirty-six bucks a kilo, and most of that hydrogen is made from natural gas, so congratulations: you bought a gas car with extra steps and a guilt-free bumper sticker.

Hydrogen's been "ten years away" for thirty years. Even fusion's embarrassed for you, and fusion is the same element with better excuses.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, the only city that looked at the Mojave Desert and said, "You know what this needs? Venice." Nothing says Italian romance like a gondolier singing in a mall next to a Cheesecake Factory.

You built a half-size Eiffel Tower, a fake New York, and a pyramid, because why visit the world when you can visit its gift shop?

No clocks, no windows, and carpet designed by a migraine, all so you won't notice you've been feeding a penny slot since Tuesday.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas." Yeah. Especially your money. And the $45 resort fee for a pool you couldn't use because a bachelor party from Ohio was in it.

And Lake Mead's drying up so fast they keep finding bodies. Even the mob's secrets can't stay in Vegas anymore.

b.text:
Las Vegas, you're the only city where a $19 buffet costs $64 once you add the "resort fee," the "facility fee," and the emotional toll of the line.

You built a fake Eiffel Tower, a fake Venice, and a fake New York, because even your tourists said, "Sure, but can we get these somewhere hotter and sadder?"

It's 115 degrees, and the locals say, "But it's a dry heat." So is an oven, Brenda.

Everyone arrives in a bachelor party wearing matching shirts and leaves as a missing-person report with a wristband.

You have a million slot machines at the airport. You're the only place that starts taking your money before you've gotten your luggage.

And the Sphere? A billion-dollar glowing eyeball staring down the Strip, like even the city is judging your decisions.

What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas, mostly because it's your checking account.
