b.text:
Las Vegas, you're the only city where a $19 buffet requires a two-hour line and a signed waiver. You built a pyramid, a volcano, and the Eiffel Tower, but God forbid anyone find a clock. You've got no windows, no clocks, and no shame. It's 3 p.m. or 3 a.m., and either way a guy dressed as Elvis is selling me a "gentleman's club" flyer.

You call it a resort fee. I call it a cover charge to enter my own hotel room. Forty-five dollars for "amenities," and the amenity is a sad pool with a DJ who keeps yelling "Make some noise!" at dehydrated accountants from Ohio.

You're a desert pretending to be Venice, with gondoliers singing in a mall. It's 112 degrees and the canal is a puddle with a mortgage.

And the slot machines in the airport? Vegas, you're the only place that starts taking your money before you've even claimed your luggage.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree on anything, so they built a city that nobody could possibly be jealous of. Mission accomplished.

It was designed by an American architect, which explains why it feels like a very nice airport with sheep. The roundabouts are so plentiful that locals don't give directions, they give revolutions. The lake is fake, the population is mostly public servants waiting for Friday, and the kangaroos outnumber the nightlife.

Your Parliament House is literally buried in a hill so people can walk on the roof, the only time Australians get to stand on politicians.

For your centenary you commissioned the Skywhale, a giant flying balloon with ten enormous boobs, and somehow that's still the most exciting thing to happen here.

Canberra: home of Summernats, Floriade, and legally purchasable X-rated videos. Burnouts, tulips and porn, because you've got to do something until the next Senate estimates hearing.

b.text:
Canberra is what happens when a committee designs a city and nobody's allowed to have an opinion until the subcommittee reports back. It's the only place where the lake is fake, the hills are decorative, and the excitement is a roundabout. Seriously, you can't give directions without saying "take the third exit, then the third exit again, then cry."

It's a city of 450,000 people, and 449,000 of them are named "Director of Strategic Alignment." The nightlife is a public servant having a second flat white after 2 p.m. Wild.

Every winter it hits minus five, and the locals call that "character." Every summer it's bushfire smoke, so basically a free vape.

And the Aussie icon is a giant flagpole. That's the whole personality: a pole, and a stern reminder to submit your timesheet.

Canberra: a nice place to visit if you've never wanted to.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's cousin who got into tech because you could "share a link." Congrats: now forty Anonymous Capybaras can watch me botch a VLOOKUP in real time. Your whole personality is "All changes saved in Drive," which is a weird flex when the change was Kevin sorting one column and detaching every employee from their salary. Version history isn't a feature; it's a crime scene. IMPORTRANGE says "Loading..." the way my dad said he was going out for milk. You've got a QUERY function that's just SQL in a fake mustache, yet you freeze if I paste more than twelve rows. And #REF! isn't an error message; it's you shrugging in all caps. You cap out at ten million cells. Ten million. You're the only spreadsheet with a bedtime.

b.text:
Google Sheets is Excel's cousin who showed up to the family reunion and insisted everyone edit the same potluck dish at once. You open a file called "Untitled spreadsheet" and somehow it's the most permanent document your company owns. It's been "Budget FINAL v3 (Copy of Copy)" since 2017.

The best part is the real-time collaboration. Nothing says teamwork like watching an Anonymous Capybara delete your entire column while you're mid-formula. And you can't even blame Greg, because Greg is a capybara.

IMPORTRANGE is the only function that makes you beg a spreadsheet for permission to read your own spreadsheet. "Allow access." I'm sorry, I made both of these!

Then you hit a hundred thousand rows and the whole thing goes "Working..." That's not a loading message, that's a hostage video.

And QUERY? It's SQL for people who were told SQL was too scary, then handed something scarier.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text:
Beanie Babies: the only investment where the advice was "don't remove the tag" and everyone said, "Sounds legit." Parents in 1998 put them in plexiglass cases like they were the Hope Diamond. It was a bean-filled bear named Garcia. You were hedging against a tie-dye pig.

Every one had a poem on the tag. "Legs the Frog" had a poem. Why? Nobody asked Legs to be a poet. Legs just wanted to sit on a shelf and appreciate the lack of structural support.

And the "retired" thing. Ty would announce a toy was retired, like it had served in a war. Suddenly your aunt's driving to a Hallmark in Ohio at 4 a.m. for Princess the Bear, a bear dedicated to a dead woman, which is a hell of a thing to put a price sticker on.

People paid thousands for these. Today they're worth less than the pellets inside. Which is the only part that was ever real: plastic pellets, fear, and a very small heart-shaped tag.

b.text: Beanie Babies, you're the only toy whose value depends on a tag announcing you're dead. "Retired." That's not a collectible, that's a hospice with a barcode. Ty Warner figured out that if he stopped making a bear, grown adults would panic-buy it like the last lifeboat on the Titanic. Parents mortgaged houses for Peanut the Elephant. Now your grandma's attic holds forty thousand of you, each worth less than the postage to mail it. And you were the only stuffed animal with a birth certificate stapled to your butt. You're not even stuffed with beans. It's plastic pellets. Honestly, that's the most honest thing about you.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text:
Risk promises "world domination" and delivers a nine-hour hostage situation with plastic army men. Nobody has ever finished a game of Risk. We just stop when someone's mom needs the dining room table back.

Let's talk about the dice. You attack with three armies, I defend with two, and somehow I lose all three while you lose nothing. Math is a liar, and it lives in that little red cup.

Australia is the only continent anyone wants, because it has one entrance and the emotional stability of a hermit. Meanwhile Asia has seventeen borders, and holding it is like being the manager of a Wetherspoons on Saturday night.

And the alliances! "Let's team up against Dave." Then you betray me in Kamchatka. Kamchatka! A place no one has ever been or will ever visit, and yet it's responsible for more ruined friendships than any ex's Instagram.

Risk isn't a game. It's a divorce with cards.

b.text: Risk is the only board game where the goal is world domination and somehow everyone ends up furious about it. You spend four hours conquering continents while your friend sits there holding Australia, which is basically a fortress with one door and a view of nothing. Kamchatka is the most dangerous place on Earth. It's one territory, and it eats two of your tiny plastic armies every time someone looks at it. Then there's the dice. Three red against two blue, and the fate of the entire planet comes down to a guy yelling "I'm rolling for Siberia!" every game ends the same way: Greg, who swore he'd only be a few minutes, owns Asia, a grudge, and your Alaska.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text: Apple's Vision Pro costs $3,499, which is more than most people's first car and buys you goggles that make you look like you're about to get hypnotized at a Best Buy. The front has a screen that shows your eyeballs to everyone around you, so now you're not just wearing a computer, you're wearing one that makes eye contact with strangers. You click things by pinching the air, which is great, because you already look like you're conducting an invisible orchestra in the middle of Target. The battery lives in a puck on a cable, so you're a tethered astronaut who paid four grand to watch a movie alone in a room full of people staring at your face.

b.text:
Apple Vision Pro: the only device where you pay $3,500 to be told your living room isn't good enough. It's a ski mask for people who want to look at spreadsheets in the void.

It weighs about a pound and a half, so after twenty minutes you don't have spatial computing, you have a chiropractor. And the battery lasts two hours, tethered to a pack in your pocket, so you're basically walking a tiny, expensive dog.

Apple said it was the future of work. The future of work is a man in Cupertino pinching the air like he's trying to catch a very slow fly.

And the "EyeSight" feature, where your eyes appear on the front? It's like a haunted Snapchat filter. Your family sees a creepy digital ghost of you, and you see them as a fuzzy video feed of people you're ignoring.

Three thousand five hundred dollars. For that I could buy a nice TV, a couch, and friends to sit on it.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that needs a warning label and a fan club. I smell you two blocks before I see the stall. Your aroma is a crime scene. Somebody left a gym sock in a brine barrel for three months, and you're the evidence. Then you get deep-fried so you look like a golden nugget, innocent and crispy, until people bite in and get a faceful of bad decisions. Everyone swears you "taste better than you smell." So does a gas leak, if you're hungry enough. The vendor hands you over with pickled cabbage and chili sauce like he's apologizing on your behalf. Nobody has ever ordered you on a first date.

b.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself before the menu does. People find you at the night market the way sharks find blood: follow the stench three stalls past the bubble tea. Your brine is fermented vegetables, shrimp, amaranth stems, and apparently a gym sock that lost a bet. Months in that bucket, and you came out smelling like a festival porta-potty in August. Your own name is a confession. Not "aged tofu," not "artisanal bean curd." Your family took one whiff and went, "Yeah, call him Stinky." And the Changsha version? Dyed jet black, like it's in mourning for everyone's sense of smell. The only reason anyone finishes you is the pickled cabbage and chili sauce piled on top to keep you quiet. "Smells bad, tastes good" isn't a slogan, buddy. It's a hostage negotiation.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text:
Esperanto: the universal language invented in 1887 by a Polish eye doctor who decided humanity needed Italian with a Slavic accent. Universal, as long as your universe is Europe.

The name means "one who hopes." Over a century later: still hoping. There are roughly a thousand native speakers. Klingon is closing in, and Klingon has an army.

It's so logical that "bad" is "malbona," literally un-good. Orwell called; he wants royalties.

Every noun ends in -o and every adjective in -a, so every sentence sounds like a waiter reciting the specials. And it gave us ĉ, ĝ, ŝ and ŭ: letters with little hats, designed for global communication, then made untypeable on every keyboard on Earth.

Its biggest movie starred William Shatner. Even he couldn't oversell it.

b.text:
Esperanto is the only product in history where the user manual promised world peace and the user base turned out to be eleven guys named Zbigniew arguing about the accusative case.

Zamenhof invented a language to unite humanity, and humanity said, "Cute. Does it have a Starbucks?"

It has sixteen grammar rules and no exceptions, which is exactly what a language sounds like when it's never been used by anyone angry. Try ordering a sandwich in a tongue where nobody has ever cheated on anyone or been cut off in traffic. Where's the slang? Where's the swearing? You can't build a culture on a word for "hello" and a really strong feeling about the letter ĥ.

Its greatest literary achievement is a translation of Hamlet. Even the original works are mostly translations of someone else's feelings.

And the flag is a green star. Not a country. A star. It's a nation-state with a logo and a dating pool smaller than a Dungeons & Dragons convention in Lithuania.

Mi amas vin, Esperanto. Nobody else does.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.

Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that needs a warning label and a fan club. I smell you two blocks before I see the stall. Your aroma is a crime scene. Somebody left a gym sock in a brine barrel for three months, and you're the evidence. Then you get deep-fried so you look like a golden nugget, innocent and crispy, until people bite in and get a faceful of bad decisions. Everyone swears you "taste better than you smell." So does a gas leak, if you're hungry enough. The vendor hands you over with pickled cabbage and chili sauce like he's apologizing on your behalf. Nobody has ever ordered you on a first date.

b.text:
Stinky tofu, you're the only food that needs a restraining order from its own neighborhood. I smelled you three blocks away and assumed a sewer had filed for divorce.

You're fermented in brine made of old vegetables, fish, and, as far as I can tell, regret. Then you're deep-fried, because apparently someone looked at a crime scene and said, "Needs crunch."

Everyone says, "Just try it, it tastes better than it smells!" That's not a compliment. That's what people say about a divorce lawyer.

And the fans! They stand in line at the night market, glowing with pride, like they've survived something. Sir, you're eating a gym sock in a pickle costume, and the pickle is also a gym sock.

Still, I'll admit it: the chili sauce is incredible. Which is exactly what you'd say about a hostage situation with good snacks.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text: Excel, you're the Swiss Army knife of spreadsheets, except every blade is rusty and one of them is just a tiny cursor that's been stuck in a cell since 1998. You've got 17,000 functions and I still can't find the one that sums things without you auto-converting my zip codes into scientific notation. You turned "1-2" into a date. Nobody asked you to. Your autocorrect thinks my gene names are calendar events. And your formulas? One missing parenthesis and suddenly I'm staring at #VALUE! like it's a personal insult. Forty years in, you still can't tell me what I did wrong. You just sit there, green triangle in the corner, judging me.

b.text:
Excel, you're the only software that thinks "September 4th" and "the gene SEPT4" are the same thing. Scientists had to rename human genes because of you. Human genes! Billions of years of evolution, undone by a spreadsheet that thought it was being helpful.

You've got a million rows, and somehow the one cell I need is always hidden in column XFD. Who's ever been to XFD? Nobody. It's the Bermuda Triangle of accounting.

Every company on earth runs on a file called "Budget_FINAL_v3_REAL_final(2).xlsx," and the whole thing depends on one formula written by Linda, who retired in 2011 and took the logic with her.

You turn my phone numbers into scientific notation. You open a CSV and delete my leading zeros like they owe you money. And VLOOKUP? Twenty-five years, and it still can't look left.

You're not software. You're a hostage situation with gridlines.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass was the only product where the beta testers were called "Explorers," because "Guinea Pigs Who Paid fifteen hundred dollars" didn't fit on the box.

It had one camera, one tiny screen, and zero friends. Wearing it in public was a way of telling a stranger, "I may be filming you, and I definitely want to talk about my startup."

Remember the battery? Thirty minutes of recording and it ran hotter than your uncle at Thanksgiving. You didn't have a wearable computer, you had a forehead space heater with a blinking eye.

And the word "Glasshole" wasn't an insult someone invented. It was a consumer review. Bars banned it. Strangers punched it off people's faces. Strangers also asked, "Is that on right now?" which is the sound of privacy dying.

It was the first device that looked like the future and acted like a restraining order.

b.text:
Google Glass, look at you. Fifteen hundred dollars to wear a sugar cube on your eyebrow. Sergey Brin had skydivers jump onto a building to launch you, and that was the last time anything about you was cool.

You invented a whole new insult. Nobody calls iPhone owners "Phoneholes." But "Glasshole"? Earned. Fast. Because you let people take photos by *winking*. You turned flirting into a privacy violation.

Every sentence started with "OK Glass," like a man narrating his own midlife crisis out loud. Bars banned you. Strangers ripped you off people's faces. Your battery died faster than your reputation, and you overheated right next to the user's brain, which honestly explains the buying decision.

Then you pivoted to "Enterprise," the tech version of moving back home to work at your uncle's warehouse.

And even the warehouse let you go.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text: Risk is the only board game where the goal is world domination and somehow everyone ends up furious about it. You spend four hours conquering continents while your friend sits there holding Australia, which is basically a fortress with one door and a view of nothing. Kamchatka is the most dangerous place on Earth. It's one territory, and it eats two of your tiny plastic armies every time someone looks at it. Then there's the dice. Three red against two blue, and the fate of the entire planet comes down to a guy yelling "I'm rolling for Siberia!" every game ends the same way: Greg, who swore he'd only be a few minutes, owns Asia, a grudge, and your Alaska.

b.text:
Risk is the only game where you spend four hours conquering the world and then lose it because your brother-in-law rolled three sixes in Kamchatka.

"Strategy game," the box says. Sure. Strategy is a dice cup deciding your destiny while you scream at a plastic cannon.

Nobody finishes Risk. It doesn't end, it just gets abandoned, like Napoleon's Russian campaign, except Napoleon had better snacks. Someone eventually says "I have to be up early," which is Risk for "I've been dead since Australia."

Speaking of Australia: everyone knows the whole game is just "hold Australia and pretend you're smart." One entrance, four territories, a bonus. It's the gated community of continents. Meanwhile Asia has twelve territories and a bonus of seven, which is the board's way of saying "go ahead, try it, I'll see you at hour three."

And the alliances! Friendships don't die in Risk. They get negotiated away for a single card.

Happy 60 years, Risk. You've ended more family dinners than politics.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text: Carbon nanotubes are the most stressed-out material on Earth. They're stronger than steel, and they've been "five years from revolutionizing everything" since 1991. They're just graphene that got rolled up and never recovered. Ask one whether it's a metal or a semiconductor and it genuinely can't tell you until someone tests it. In the lab they clump together like cold spaghetti. For thirty years industry has promised them in batteries, bike frames, and space elevators. The only space elevator I've seen is the one in my dorm, and it doesn't work either. Their best feature is that under a microscope they look exactly like asbestos, which is a bold thing for a material to bring to a party.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes, the material that's been "ten years from changing everything" for thirty years. You're 100 times stronger than steel, and yet somehow you've never held a job.

You're a single sheet of graphene rolled up like a sad burrito, and you still can't decide if you're a metal or a semiconductor. Chirality, right? Your entire personality depends on which way you twist. That's not physics, that's a mood ring.

Scientists say you could build a space elevator. Buddy, you can't even get through a lab without clumping together like earbuds in a pocket. Every researcher spends six months trying to disperse you, then writes "uniform" in the paper anyway.

And the manufacturing! Everyone gets a random mix of types, so sorting you is like trying to separate identical twins by vibe.

Also, you're a nanometer wide and somehow still the biggest thing in everyone's grant proposal.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like Swiss cheese that wanted to be a boat. You were invented for sailing, and the one place nobody wears you is a boat. You're at Applebee's, squeaking across a wet floor like a dolphin in distress.

You have holes. On purpose. Then you sell us Jibbitz to fill the holes. That's not fashion, that's a protection racket with a SpongeBob charm.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind my heel doesn't make me an athlete. It makes me a toddler about to sprint into traffic.

You made a KFC bucket clog with charms that smelled like fried chicken. That's not footwear. That's a foam cry for help.

Nurses love you. Chefs love you. Which proves you're comfortable for people who've stopped caring who's looking at their feet.

b.text: Crocs are shoes designed by someone who saw a bath mat and thought, "Yes, but what if it had holes so my feet could breathe while I pretend I'm a surgeon at a Cracker Barrel?" They look like the foam that sits on a hot dog's bun. They're the only footwear where the heel is basically a suggestion. You can't run in them, you can't hike in them, and you definitely can't sneak up on anyone, because every step sounds like a duck being slowly squeezed. And somehow they're on the feet of grown adults who own a mortgage. Nobody wears Crocs to look good. You wear Crocs because you've accepted that your feet have given up, and you've decided the shoe should match that energy. Honestly, respect. You're the only person at the Target parking lot who's fully at peace.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you're not milk. You're almonds that got lost on the way to a smoothie and decided to lie about it. Milk comes from a cow, and a cow has some dignity. You come from a nut that's been soaked in water until it gave up. Somebody squeezed a almond, looked at the sad little puddle, and said, "Yep, that's breakfast."

You're so thin, I can read a newspaper through you. Your idea of creamy is a rumor. You've got less body than a Tuesday. And every carton of you says "Unsweetened" like you're proud of it, like there's a single person alive who wanted to taste nothing.

Almond milk, you're the guy who says he's "not really into drinking" and then orders the oat latte.

b.text:
Almond milk, you're the only drink that needs a lawyer to defend its name. The dairy industry sued because, technically, nobody has ever milked an almond. We looked. No nipples.

You're about two percent almonds. The rest is water, gellan gum, and confidence. You're not milk. You're a nut that got waterboarded and called it wellness.

And speaking of water: it takes over a gallon to grow a single almond. California is in a drought so you can be beige in a latte. Bees get trucked across the country like seasonal laborers just to make you, and a lot of them don't come home.

Leave you in the fridge for two days and you separate like you're ashamed of yourself. Fair. I'd need to be shaken too if I cost seven dollars and tasted like a wet sympathy card.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, you're the only app where a little green dot controls people's moods. We all stare at it like a heart monitor. "Dave's active? Dave's ignoring me personally."

You turned "quick question" into a four-hour ordeal. Somebody types "hey," then nothing, and the whole office watches three little dots dance for twenty minutes like they're drafting the Gettysburg Address. Then comes "can you hop on a huddle?" Nobody has ever hopped.

And #random? That channel has never been random. It's a graveyard of cat GIFs and a 2019 poll about lunch.

You're the reason we have 47 unread notifications and zero idea what's going on. Do Not Disturb is your most-ignored feature, and you know it.

b.text:
Slack, you started as the internal chat tool for a failed video game called Glitch, and honestly? Still the most accurate name you've ever had.

You promised to kill email. Instead you gave us email that *knocks*. That little wooden knock-brush sound has triggered more cortisol than any boss in history. I hear it in the shower. I hear it at funerals.

You invented the green dot, so now my employer knows I went to the bathroom for nineteen minutes. You invented "is typing…" so my manager can type for four straight minutes and send "ok."

Threads? Nobody can find them. Huddles? A Zoom call that ambushes you. And somehow every company has 400 channels, and the only active one is #random, where Kevin posts his sourdough.

Your name literally stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable. Sure. Try finding that one link from Tuesday. 👀 reacted by 3 people.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text:
Brasília, you're the only city designed by someone who looked at a map and said, "What if it were an airplane?" Congratulations, you're the world's largest piece of urban origami. Nobody can find anything because every address is a code. "I live at SQS 308, Bloco C, Apartamento 204." That's not a home, that's a Wi-Fi password.

You have no street corners. You have no sidewalks anyone uses. Brazilians love to gather in public, so you built a city where the only way to meet someone is by driving twenty minutes to stand near them.

Oscar Niemeyer gave you gorgeous curves, and then your politicians moved in and did the most corrupt things you could imagine inside them. A cathedral that looks like a crown of thorns, a Congress that looks like two bowls and a pair of dishes. Even the buildings look like they're waiting for a bribe.

You were built in four years. It shows. Rio had 400 to get charming.

b.text: Brasília is the only city where the architects designed everything except a reason to go outside. Niemeyer built the Cathedral like a flying saucer that gave up halfway, and Lúcio Costa laid the city out like an airplane, which explains why everyone's been circling the same runway of traffic since 1960. The superquadras all look identical, so when you get lost, you're not lost, you're just on a different block of the same block. There are no corners to lean on, no street to wander, just six lanes and a bus stop that's more of a rumor. The people who clean the ministries live out in Ceilândia and commute two hours to get there. And it's so dry your lips file for divorce.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only technology that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not an energy source, you're a timeshare pitch.

The sun does you effortlessly. It just sits there being enormous. You need a giant metal donut called a tokamak, magnets colder than deep space, and plasma hotter than the sun's core, and that plasma still escapes like it's late for a better party.

In 2022 you finally got more energy out than you put in! From the lasers. Ignoring the grid power feeding the lasers. That's like bragging you turned a profit because the cashier handed you change.

ITER started at five billion euros, now sits somewhere north of twenty, and keeps sliding its startup date. And your fuel needs tritium, which barely exists, so you'll have to breed it yourself.

Fusion: clean, safe, limitless, and tragically hypothetical.

b.text: Nuclear fusion, you're the energy source that's been "thirty years away" since Eisenhower. Every decade there's a press conference, and every decade it's the same promise: "Net energy gain!" for a glorious few seconds, measured very carefully, and then the lights go back to coal. You're trying to recreate the sun, which is impressive, except the sun did it for free with gravity doing all the heavy lifting. You need a doughnut-shaped magnetic bottle hotter than the sun's core, held in place by superconducting magnets that cost more than a small country. ITER was conceived in 1985 and is still "a few years out." Your whole brand is "it'll be ready next year," and somehow you've made nuclear physics sound like a guy promising to fix your sink.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text:
LaTeX is the only software where you spend six hours fixing a typo and then twelve more because the fix moved your figure to page nine.

You ask for a picture to go *here*. LaTeX says "here" is more of a "float" situation. It's not a placement, it's a vibe.

The error messages are written by someone who hates you personally. "Overfull hbox, badness 10000." Thank you, I'll tell my therapist. Meanwhile, one missing brace gives you an error on line 4,000, in a file you didn't write, from a package you never installed.

Want a different font? Enjoy a three-day journey through Stack Overflow, where the top answer is from 2009 and starts with "Just use XeTeX."

And the compile times! I changed one comma and now I'm watching it run twice, because the table of contents needs to catch up to reality.

Knuth released it in 1978 and declared it nearly bug-free. Sir, the bugs are in me. I'm the bug. I just wanted a bibliography.

b.text: LaTeX, you're the only program that makes a document look like a Pulitzer and then sends you a nine-hundred-line error log because you forgot a bracket. "Missing $ inserted." Where? Everywhere. Your error messages read like a ransom note. And the figures! I put a picture in, and it floats off to page nine like it has somewhere better to be. I write to say "here," and you say, "Mm, I'll be the judge of that." Centering a table takes three hours, a booktabs package, and a prayer. Then I compile, get a PDF so beautiful I almost forgive you, and you hit me with "Overfull \hbox, badness 10000." Badness. You named it. You're the only typesetter honest enough to put its own insult in the log.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text:
PHP, the language that stands for "Personal Home Page" and now runs half the internet, like a rental car you forgot to return in 1998.

It's the only language where the standard library looks like it was named by a dice roll. strpos has needle, haystack. array_search has needle, haystack. But str_replace? Different order. Why? Because PHP doesn't believe in consistency. It believes in vibes.

The comparison rules are a hostage situation. "0" == false. "abc" == 0, at least until PHP 8 finally took a sip of water. And the ternary operator was left-associative for years, so nested ones did the opposite of what anyone wanted.

Then there's the dollar sign. Every variable has one, like each is being sold individually.

And yet, WordPress, Facebook, Wikipedia, all run on it. PHP is the duct tape holding the web together, and like duct tape, nobody's proud of it, but everyone's got a roll in the garage.

b.text: PHP, you're the only language whose name is a recursive acronym, and your mascot is an elephant that's been sitting on servers since 1995. You slap a dollar sign on every variable like you're charging us by the letter. Your function names look like they were typed during a power outage: strpos wants the haystack first, array_search wants the needle first, and you just shrugged. You told us "0" == false is true and "1e3" == "1000" is true, and we nodded like that makes sense. Magic quotes, register_globals, mysql_ functions you kept around like a grandma's ugly couch. Somehow you run half the internet. Honestly, that's the scariest part.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text: Monopoly is the only board game where the goal is to bankrupt your friends, and the game itself bankrupts the friendship. It's been around ninety years and nobody has ever finished it. Your cousin Dave, who owns Boardwalk and two hotels, isn't a real estate mogul. He's a man who spent three hours shorting the bank. And the banker! The one person trusted with the stack of pink fives, and every single time he "accidentally" gives himself two hundred bucks. Free Parking is a lie. Nobody has ever landed there and collected the jackpot. The little top hat has been in the same spot since 1935 and still gets no respect. Let's be honest: the only property you can afford is Baltic Avenue, and that's because the game put it there to make you feel bad.

b.text:
Monopoly is the only game where the winner is whoever gets lucky early and the loser is whoever's still playing at 2 a.m. It was designed to teach people that landlords are evil, and somehow it became the thing families play to prove it.

Four hours in, you've got a dad mortgaging Baltic Avenue, a cousin who "forgot" to charge rent, and a kid crying over the thimble. Nobody's ever finished a game. We just stop when someone flips the board.

And the money! You're handed pastel Monopoly bills like it's a deranged Easter egg hunt, then told you owe $200 for "income tax." In a game about capitalism, Free Parking pays out nothing, but everyone insists it does, because house rules are the only thing keeping this thing alive.

The best part: the shoe, the dog, and the iron are all fighting over Boardwalk. Meanwhile, the Community Chest says I won second place in a beauty contest. Ten dollars. Great.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel, you're the only software so powerful that scientists had to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into a date. You didn't adapt to biology; biology adapted to you. Type a phone number and you lop off the leading zero like it owes you money. Enter a credit card number and you serve back 4.53E+15, as if I'm splitting dinner with a physicist.

You still think 1900 was a leap year. It wasn't. You've known for decades. You just don't care.

You're running entire national economies and you still panic over merged cells. The UK lost sixteen thousand COVID cases because someone used your old .xls format and you quietly ran out of rows. No warning. Just vibes.

And VLOOKUP only looks right. Thirty years we spent squinting at #N/A before you finally invented XLOOKUP, like a guy who learns to turn left at fifty.

b.text:
Excel, you're the only software that thinks "September 4th" and "the gene SEPT4" are the same thing. Scientists had to rename human genes because of you. Human genes! Billions of years of evolution, undone by a spreadsheet that thought it was being helpful.

You've got a million rows, and somehow the one cell I need is always hidden in column XFD. Who's ever been to XFD? Nobody. It's the Bermuda Triangle of accounting.

Every company on earth runs on a file called "Budget_FINAL_v3_REAL_final(2).xlsx," and the whole thing depends on one formula written by Linda, who retired in 2011 and took the logic with her.

You turn my phone numbers into scientific notation. You open a CSV and delete my leading zeros like they owe you money. And VLOOKUP? Twenty-five years, and it still can't look left.

You're not software. You're a hostage situation with gridlines.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a wall. The Ruins of St. Paul's: a gorgeous front with absolutely nothing behind it, which is basically your whole personality. You've got a fake Venice with a painted sky, a fake Paris with a half-size Eiffel Tower, and you're so tiny you had to dump dirt into the ocean just to fit a runway. You out-earned Las Vegas several times over, and your signature dish is still a pork chop jammed in a bun. The Portuguese stayed four hundred years and left you an egg tart and street signs nobody reads. The Grand Lisboa looks like a golden pineapple having a breakdown. And the Macau Tower's big attraction is jumping off it, which, after a night at the baccarat tables, is less a thrill ride and more a financial plan.

b.text: Macau, you're the only place where a fake Venice has a fake gondola and the gondolas still lose money. You're about ten Central Parks wide, so your casinos can't spread out and have to go up, like a city that got lost looking for space. Your cathedral is just a facade, a church that gave up on the church part. Your egg tarts are the best thing you've ever exported, and you did it by accident, like a bank robbery that ends with pastries. The bridge to Hong Kong took the better part of a decade, which is the most patience you've ever shown anyone. Nobody comes to Macau to see Macau. They come to lose money, and they leave with an egg tart and a receipt.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word, you're the only software where pressing Enter once can rearrange my entire document like a Rubik's cube in an earthquake.

You've got a paperclip-shaped trauma in your past, and honestly, he was the only one who ever tried to help. Now it's just you, auto-correcting "ducking" into things I definitely didn't mean to say to my boss.

Bullet points? You take them personally. I press Tab, you indent. I press Backspace, you un-indent, delete the bullet, and change the font to Comic Sans out of spite.

I tried to put one picture on page two. Page six now has a single sentence and a sense of dread.

And the green squiggly line? Judgmental. The red one? Fine, I misspelled "necessary." But you underlined my own name like I'm the one who's wrong.

You've been around since 1983 and still can't tell me why Save As has seven different locations. Ribbon? More like a ribbon of confusion. Truly, you're a masterpiece of formatting I never asked for.

b.text:
Microsoft Word, ladies and gentlemen. It's the only program where nudging a photo one pixel to the left sends three paragraphs to page nine and summons a blank final page you will never, ever delete.

Word has been around for forty years and still can't decide what font it is. Times New Roman, then Calibri, now Aptos. It's having a midlife crisis in 11-point.

It underlines my own name in red. Wavy red. Like *I'm* the typo.

Try making a numbered list. Word says, "Got it, starting at 1." Second item: "Also 1." Third item: "Here's 4. It's indented. It's a letter now."

And Track Changes isn't a feature. It's a crime scene: strikethroughs everywhere, plus forty comments from someone named "Author."

Word, you gave us Clippy, and somehow he was the most helpful part.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: Macau, you're the only city where the fake Venice has better canals than the real one. You dredged your land out of the sea, built a replica of Venice on top, and hired gondoliers to sing to tourists who just lost their rent at baccarat. Your economy is one enormous slot machine with a Portuguese accent. Your most famous landmark is a church facade with nothing behind it, which is the most honest thing on your skyline. You're 33 square kilometers, so small you can walk across yourself before your egg tart cools. Everybody comes to you to lose money, and you're thrilled to take it. Keep the lights on, little sinner.

b.text:
Macau, you're what happens when Portugal and Las Vegas have a one-night stand and nobody wants to claim the kid. You have a Venetian with fake canals, a fake sky, and a gondolier singing "O Sole Mio" in a Chinese province. Not even Italy does that to itself.

You make more gambling money than Vegas by a factor of several, which means you're basically a very successful casino with a cobblestone problem.

Your egg tarts are better than Portugal's, and everyone knows it, including Portugal, who's still mad. Your Eiffel Tower is half-size, your Parisian is half-French, and your Grand Lisboa looks like a golden lotus ate a disco ball.

You're 12 square miles and somehow have traffic jams at the border from people who lost everything and still want to come back. That's not tourism. That's an abusive relationship with a buffet.

Even your ruins are just a facade. St. Paul's is literally one wall. You couldn't keep the church, but you kept the slot machines.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript was written in ten days, and honestly, it shows. It's the only language where `[] + {}` is a string, `{} + []` is zero, and nobody can explain why without sweating.

You ask JavaScript to compare `"2" > "12"` and it says true, because it's alphabetical. Sorting numbers? Also alphabetical. `.sort()` gives you ``, like a librarian who learned math from a dictionary.

`NaN` stands for "Not a Number," and its type is "number." `NaN !== NaN`. It's the only thing in programming that refuses to identify itself.

Then there's `this`, which means whatever it feels like today. Every callback is a coin flip with your dignity.

And the ecosystem! You wanted to pad a string, so you installed a package, and now your project has 1,400 dependencies and one of them is a guy's feelings.

JavaScript doesn't throw errors. It throws "undefined is not a function" and lets you figure out which of your 40,000 lines it's talking about.

b.text: JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and you've spent thirty years proving it. You named yourself after Java for the clout, like a guy introducing himself as "Brad Pitt's cousin." You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number, and it isn't even equal to itself. Ask you to sort and you hand back, alphabetically, like a librarian having a breakdown. "11" plus 1 is "111," but "11" minus 1 is 10, so you're consistent the way a slot machine is consistent. You needed two kinds of nothing, undefined and null, and three equals signs just to tell the truth. Your own developers can't agree what "this" means. And the entire internet runs on you, which honestly explains the internet.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text: Apple's Vision Pro costs $3,499, which is more than most people's first car and buys you goggles that make you look like you're about to get hypnotized at a Best Buy. The front has a screen that shows your eyeballs to everyone around you, so now you're not just wearing a computer, you're wearing one that makes eye contact with strangers. You click things by pinching the air, which is great, because you already look like you're conducting an invisible orchestra in the middle of Target. The battery lives in a puck on a cable, so you're a tethered astronaut who paid four grand to watch a movie alone in a room full of people staring at your face.

b.text:
The Apple Vision Pro costs $3,499, which is a bold price for something that gives you a headache and a neck injury in the same sitting. It weighs over a pound, so after twenty minutes you're not experiencing spatial computing, you're experiencing the chiropractic kind.

Apple said it would change how we see the world, then gave it a two-hour battery on a cable you have to keep in your pocket, like an oxygen tank for your delusions.

EyeSight shows your eyes on the front, so everyone around you can watch a haunted aquarium version of your face. Your FaceTime Persona looks like a hostage video made by a very polite ghost.

The best part is the control scheme: you look at something and pinch your fingers, like you're being quietly condescending to your own living room.

It's a $3,500 ski goggle that lets you watch a movie alone. Congratulations, you've invented a very expensive way to ignore your family.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text: Hydrogen fuel-cell cars are the most ambitious thing ever built to avoid a charging cable. Think about it: the whole plan is to take electricity, use it to split water into hydrogen, compress that hydrogen to ten thousand PSI, drive it across the country in a tank that's basically a rocket casing, then turn it back into electricity. That's not a green car, that's a magic trick with a chaperone. And the hydrogen stations? Good luck. You'll find one in California, and it's closed for "maintenance," which I'm pretty sure means someone realized they were hydrogen stations and got nervous. Meanwhile, my Tesla just asks if I'd like to plug in at home, like a normal car.

b.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars are the only vehicles where the fuel is the most abundant element in the universe and somehow still costs more per mile than caviar. Sixteen dollars a kilogram, and you can only buy it at one station in California, which is closed. For "maintenance."

Their big selling point is that the only emissions are water. Fantastic. Most of the hydrogen is made from natural gas, so it's a car that cries clean tears after being force-fed fossil fuels in a basement.

Toyota calls its model the Mirai. That's Japanese for "future." Accurate, because that's when you'll find a pump.

Owners are a special breed. They drive 40 minutes to refuel, then call it freedom. Their car is basically a Prius that got a PhD, went into massive debt, and still can't get a job.

And the tank? Pressurized to 10,000 psi. So it's a zero-emissions vehicle with a tiny, polite bomb in the trunk.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text: You know what Teams is? It's the office that's always on fire but nobody's ever seen the smoke. Every message comes with "...is typing" for six minutes, and then it says "Hi." Your green dot says "Available" while you're literally in the bathroom. You join a meeting and the first ten minutes are "Can you hear me?" "You're on mute." "Wait, I'm sharing the wrong screen." Then somebody says, "Let's take this offline," which, in Teams, means it's now a 45-minute call titled "Quick Sync." And the app eats more RAM than the entire Windows 95 installation. Teams, you're the only thing that's ever made my laptop fan sound like it's begging for a transfer.

b.text:
Microsoft Teams is the only app that can tell you "You're on mute" after you've spent four minutes giving the best speech of your career to nobody.

It's got a notification system that works like a clingy ex. Someone reacts with a thumbs-up to a message you sent three weeks ago, and suddenly your laptop sounds like a submarine under attack.

The search function is a magic trick: you type "Q3 budget," and it shows you a GIF from Brenda's retirement party.

And the name! "Teams." Also "Teams (work or school)." Also "Teams (free)." Also "Teams Classic," which is what we now call the one that worked slightly better. Whenever you open it, it asks which Teams you want, like a waiter asking which of your three identical sandwiches you'd like.

The status indicator says "Away" when you're staring right at it, and "Available" when you've gone to the bathroom.

Teams isn't collaboration software. It's a hostage negotiation with your own Wi-Fi.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text: LaTeX, you're the only program that makes a document look like a Pulitzer and then sends you a nine-hundred-line error log because you forgot a bracket. "Missing $ inserted." Where? Everywhere. Your error messages read like a ransom note. And the figures! I put a picture in, and it floats off to page nine like it has somewhere better to be. I write to say "here," and you say, "Mm, I'll be the judge of that." Centering a table takes three hours, a booktabs package, and a prayer. Then I compile, get a PDF so beautiful I almost forgive you, and you hit me with "Overfull \hbox, badness 10000." Badness. You named it. You're the only typesetter honest enough to put its own insult in the log.

b.text: LaTeX, you're the only software where "it compiled" counts as an emotional milestone. One missing brace and you blame line 1 of a 400-line file, then sit there with a question mark like we're playing a text adventure from 1985. I put a figure on page 3; you float it to the appendix because you "know better." You have to run twice just to learn your own page numbers, three times if BibTeX shows up, like a guy who needs two friends to remind him his name. Your answer to every problem is another \usepackage, so my preamble is now longer than my thesis. Every paper you touch looks gorgeous, and identical, because everyone on Earth can spot Computer Modern from across a conference hall. And your favorite warning, "Overfull \hbox, badness 10000"? Honestly, that's just how I feel about you.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only energy source that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not the future, you're a toddler promising to clean his room after the next funding cycle.

You heat plasma to 150 million degrees, ten times hotter than the core of the sun, and still can't do what the sun does for free while being a ball of gas with no PhD.

ITER started at five billion euros. It's now north of twenty, and it hasn't produced a watt. That's not a reactor, that's a French timeshare.

In 2022 you finally got "net energy gain" by ignoring the 300 megajoules the lasers pulled from the wall. That's like saying your restaurant's profitable if you don't count rent.

And your solution to fuel shortages is mining helium-3 on the moon. Buddy, you can't even make it to Tuesday.

b.text:
Nuclear fusion, you've been "thirty years away" for seventy years. That's not a timeline, that's a hostage situation where the hostage is my electric bill.

You're the only technology whose big breakthrough is "we got more energy out than the laser put in." Not more than the wall socket. Just the laser. That's like bragging you're profitable if we ignore rent, payroll, and the building.

You recreate the core of the sun, which sounds impressive until you remember the sun does it for free, with no PhD, and has been doing it for four billion years without a single press release.

Your containment strategy is "a magnetic bottle for something hotter than anything in the solar system." And your funding pitch never changes: "Give us ten billion dollars and a decade." Every decade.

Fusion, you're the ex who says, "I'm almost ready to commit." Sir, you're a tokamak. You've been going in circles since 1950.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a wall. The Ruins of St. Paul's: a gorgeous front with absolutely nothing behind it, which is basically your whole personality. You've got a fake Venice with a painted sky, a fake Paris with a half-size Eiffel Tower, and you're so tiny you had to dump dirt into the ocean just to fit a runway. You out-earned Las Vegas several times over, and your signature dish is still a pork chop jammed in a bun. The Portuguese stayed four hundred years and left you an egg tart and street signs nobody reads. The Grand Lisboa looks like a golden pineapple having a breakdown. And the Macau Tower's big attraction is jumping off it, which, after a night at the baccarat tables, is less a thrill ride and more a financial plan.

b.text: Macau, you're the only city where the fake Venice has better canals than the real one. You dredged your land out of the sea, built a replica of Venice on top, and hired gondoliers to sing to tourists who just lost their rent at baccarat. Your economy is one enormous slot machine with a Portuguese accent. Your most famous landmark is a church facade with nothing behind it, which is the most honest thing on your skyline. You're 33 square kilometers, so small you can walk across yourself before your egg tart cools. Everybody comes to you to lose money, and you're thrilled to take it. Keep the lights on, little sinner.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text: Hawaiian pizza. Ham and pineapple. Somebody in Canada looked at a perfectly good pizza and said, "You know what this needs? Fruit that's been sitting in a can." Pineapple on pizza is a crime with a fruit salad alibi. It's sweet, it's salty, it's wet, and it's confused about what it wants to be, kind of like a dessert that got lost on the way to a breakfast buffet. And the ham? That's not ham, that's a lunch meat that went to college and dropped out. Every bite is a negotiation between a tropical vacation and a Tuesday at the deli counter. Hawaii didn't even invent this thing. A Greek-Canadian guy in Ontario did, in 1962, and then he just let it loose on the world like a dare.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza is what happens when Italy and a Dole pineapple can get into a fender bender and decide not to exchange insurance. It's a pizza that's also a fruit cup. The only dish where the ham is nervous about the dessert.

And it's not even Hawaiian! It was invented by a Greek guy in Canada. Hawaii had nothing to do with it. That's like naming a burrito "The Norwegian" because someone's cousin once ate one near Oslo.

Pineapple on pizza is like a hot tub full of juice. The cheese slides off, the crust goes soggy, and every bite is a hostage negotiation between salty and sweet. Ham and pineapple are the only couple at the party who came together but won't stand next to each other.

And somehow it's still the pizza ordered by the guy who says, "I'm easy, I'll eat anything," and then picks off all the olives.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.
