A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text: LaTeX, you're a word processor that makes me pass a programming exam just to type "hello." I need a backslash, three curly braces, and a prayer to make one word bold. Forget a single dollar sign and you scream "Missing $ inserted," like I personally mugged your math mode. Then you throw "Emergency stop" at me, which is rude, because I'm the one who's supposed to be panicking. Want a table? Enjoy three hours wrestling ampersands and \hline like they owe you money. Bibliography? Run the compiler three times, like a coach yelling "one more lap" because the first two didn't count. Your fans swear the output is gorgeous. Sure, so is a cathedral, and nobody builds a grocery list out of one.

b.text: LaTeX, you're the only software where "it compiled" counts as an emotional milestone. One missing brace and you blame line 1 of a 400-line file, then sit there with a question mark like we're playing a text adventure from 1985. I put a figure on page 3; you float it to the appendix because you "know better." You have to run twice just to learn your own page numbers, three times if BibTeX shows up, like a guy who needs two friends to remind him his name. Your answer to every problem is another \usepackage, so my preamble is now longer than my thesis. Every paper you touch looks gorgeous, and identical, because everyone on Earth can spot Computer Modern from across a conference hall. And your favorite warning, "Overfull \hbox, badness 10000"? Honestly, that's just how I feel about you.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text: Canberra: the only city where the traffic jam is a roundabout with a sculpture in the middle. A century ago, someone looked at a sheep paddock between Sydney and Melbourne and said, "Let's put the whole country's government here so nobody has to visit." And it worked. Parliament House sits on its hill like a very expensive filing cabinet. The lake is named after an American architect, and it's the most exciting thing that happens here. Winter mornings hit minus four, and the only people outside are joggers with a grudge. Friday night out means the Civic bar, where everyone's a public servant with a lanyard still on. Nobody lives in Canberra. They're just waiting for a posting.

b.text:
Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree on anything, so they built a city that nobody could possibly be jealous of. Mission accomplished.

It was designed by an American architect, which explains why it feels like a very nice airport with sheep. The roundabouts are so plentiful that locals don't give directions, they give revolutions. The lake is fake, the population is mostly public servants waiting for Friday, and the kangaroos outnumber the nightlife.

Your Parliament House is literally buried in a hill so people can walk on the roof, the only time Australians get to stand on politicians.

For your centenary you commissioned the Skywhale, a giant flying balloon with ten enormous boobs, and somehow that's still the most exciting thing to happen here.

Canberra: home of Summernats, Floriade, and legally purchasable X-rated videos. Burnouts, tulips and porn, because you've got to do something until the next Senate estimates hearing.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, you're the only app where a little green dot controls people's moods. We all stare at it like a heart monitor. "Dave's active? Dave's ignoring me personally."

You turned "quick question" into a four-hour ordeal. Somebody types "hey," then nothing, and the whole office watches three little dots dance for twenty minutes like they're drafting the Gettysburg Address. Then comes "can you hop on a huddle?" Nobody has ever hopped.

And #random? That channel has never been random. It's a graveyard of cat GIFs and a 2019 poll about lunch.

You're the reason we have 47 unread notifications and zero idea what's going on. Do Not Disturb is your most-ignored feature, and you know it.

b.text:
Slack, the only place where "Quick question" is a threat. Nobody has ever had a quick question. Just a little typing bubble that appears, disappears, appears again, and then nothing, like a ghost deciding whether to haunt you.

You took email, which everyone hated, and said, "What if it were faster, and your boss could watch you be green?" Now I can't go to the bathroom without my status turning yellow like I'm a traffic light of shame.

And the notifications. That little red badge. Forty-seven unread in #general, which is just a graveyard of birthday gifs and a guy named Doug asking who took his yogurt.

The emoji reactions are how adults now communicate. A thumbs-up means "I acknowledge you." The eyes emoji means "I saw this and will do nothing." And the little checkmark means "done," which is the biggest lie since "let's circle back."

Slack: you replaced meetings with meetings that never end.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text: UGG boots. Even the name sounds like the noise you make pulling them on. Australian surfers invented them to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow they became snow boots that dissolve in snow. One puddle and you're wearing a salt-stained topographic map. They're sheepskin, so you skip the socks, so by February they smell like the sheep's revenge. Every pair eventually collapses outward until you're walking on the sides of your ankles like a newborn giraffe in a bread costume. And that's the look: two chestnut loaves. You don't walk in UGGs; you shuffle, like the ghost of Paris Hilton still searching for her Juicy tracksuit. And now they're back with platforms, so you can roll an ankle from higher up. It's not footwear. It's a bathrobe that learned to commute.

b.text: Ugg boots are the only footwear that looks like it was made from a dead sheep and then slept in. They're basically two slippers that gave up on their dreams and went to college. You don't wear Uggs, you just stop trying in a boot shape. Nobody has ever run for a bus in Uggs. Nobody has ever been caught in the rain in Uggs. They're for the Starbucks line at 8 a.m. and the Costco parking lot, and that's it. And the name! "Ugg." That's not a brand, that's a noise you make when you step on a Lego. Somebody in a boardroom said, "Let's sell people shoes that sound like disappointment," and everybody nodded. Then they charged two hundred dollars for them.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text: Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to warn people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow you became the thing Grandpa uses to teach eight-year-olds that ruining lives is fun. You're the only game where getting arrested is a power move, because late in the game jail is the safest property on the board. Your mascot is a man everyone swears wears a monocle. He doesn't. He's just so smug our brains added one. You promise "about an hour" and deliver a hostage situation. Nobody has ever actually finished you. You just end when somebody flips the board over Marvin Gardens. You award ten bucks for second place in a beauty contest, which is still more than Baltic Avenue pulls in. And the banker who skims from the bank isn't a cheater. He's the only player who read the theme.

b.text: Monopoly is the only board game where the goal is to bankrupt your friends, and the game itself bankrupts the friendship. It's been around ninety years and nobody has ever finished it. Your cousin Dave, who owns Boardwalk and two hotels, isn't a real estate mogul. He's a man who spent three hours shorting the bank. And the banker! The one person trusted with the stack of pink fives, and every single time he "accidentally" gives himself two hundred bucks. Free Parking is a lie. Nobody has ever landed there and collected the jackpot. The little top hat has been in the same spot since 1935 and still gets no respect. Let's be honest: the only property you can afford is Baltic Avenue, and that's because the game put it there to make you feel bad.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8 looked at the most successful desktop interface in history and said, "What if we hid the Start button, like a bathroom in a haunted house?" Microsoft designed an operating system for tablets, then shipped it to people with keyboards, mice, and spreadsheets. Nobody asked for this. Accountants were suddenly swiping at monitors like they were trying to wipe off a stain.

Shutting down the computer required a PhD. You had to summon the Charms bar by hovering in the corner of the screen like a stalker, then click Settings, then Power, then pray. My grandmother spent twenty minutes looking for the off switch and just unplugged it. Honestly, she had the right idea.

And those Live Tiles! Forty colorful rectangles flipping around telling me the weather in a city I've never visited. It wasn't an operating system, it was a toddler's busy board.

Microsoft eventually admitted the mistake and brought back the Start button. Windows 8.1 was basically an apology note taped to the door.

b.text: Windows 8 looked at the Start button and said, "Nah." Microsoft deleted the one thing everybody used to find anything, then replaced it with a full-screen wall of colored squares that look like a bathroom tile sample. Want to shut down? Swipe in from the right edge to open the Charms Bar, dig through Settings, and click a power icon hidden like it's in witness protection. The live tiles are my favorite. My Mail tile keeps showing me a headline about a sale from 2013. Eight years of muscle memory, gone, so I could enjoy a touchscreen I didn't buy on a desktop I didn't ask for.

ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only energy source that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not the future, you're a toddler promising to clean his room after the next funding cycle.

You heat plasma to 150 million degrees, ten times hotter than the core of the sun, and still can't do what the sun does for free while being a ball of gas with no PhD.

ITER started at five billion euros. It's now north of twenty, and it hasn't produced a watt. That's not a reactor, that's a French timeshare.

In 2022 you finally got "net energy gain" by ignoring the 300 megajoules the lasers pulled from the wall. That's like saying your restaurant's profitable if you don't count rent.

And your solution to fuel shortages is mining helium-3 on the moon. Buddy, you can't even make it to Tuesday.

b.text: Nuclear fusion is the energy source that's always thirty years away, and it has been since your grandpa was in diapers. Scientists figured out how to bottle a star. Unfortunately, the star is 150 million degrees, and it refuses to stay in the bottle. Every time the plasma touches the wall, it's like a toddler discovering the fridge is cold. The machines are shaped like donuts because nothing else can handle the pressure. We got net energy gain for a few billionths of a second, and the press release was longer than the experiment. Meanwhile, the sun does it for free, with no magnets, and it still manages to be more reliable than the people promising us a fusion plant by 2030.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista, you were the only operating system that asked permission to ask permission. "Are you sure you want to open Notepad?" Yes, Vista. I've been sure for twenty years.

You called yourself "Capable" on those stickers. Then you needed 15 gigs of RAM just to display a transparent window border. Aero looked gorgeous, though, like a beautiful man dying slowly of a mystery illness.

Remember copying a file? You'd say "Calculating time remaining" for six hours, like a mechanic staring at my engine going, "Hmm."

Microsoft shipped you, then immediately started apologizing with Windows 7. That's not a successor, that's a public apology with a Start button.

And "Vista Ready" laptops that couldn't run Vista? That's like a "Marathon Ready" sticker on a recliner.

Even your sidebar gadgets gave up. The weather widget just sat there, accurately predicting a cloudy future for everyone who bought you.

b.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Microsoft spent five years building you as "Longhorn," and somehow you still came out premature.

Your slogan was "The Wow Starts Now." You meant "Now" as in "after the loading circle finishes." People bought laptops with "Vista Capable" stickers, which turned out to mean "capable of being sued over." Those machines couldn't even run Aero, so they got a see-through window theme with nothing to see.

And User Account Control! You asked "Are you sure?" so many times that you became the first operating system with separation anxiety.

You came in six editions, including "Ultimate," whose big exclusive was DreamScene: a moving wallpaper for the ten minutes you weren't hunting for printer drivers.

Microsoft had to trick people into liking you. The Mojave Experiment! Your own parents had to put you in disguise.

Your greatest feature? The XP downgrade.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen, you're the only dish that arrives before the delivery guy does. You're named after river snails, yet nobody has ever found one in the bowl. You boiled them for hours, took their soul, and threw out the bodies. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up.

And that smell? Fermented bamboo shoots that died, got buried, and came back for revenge. Someone opens a packet in Liuzhou and a guy in Guilin checks his shoes. College dorms banned you like a space heater. Neighbors call the gas company.

Your fans swear, "It smells terrible but tastes amazing." Buddy, that's what everyone says about their toxic ex.

Peanuts, crispy tofu skin, wood ear, pickled beans, a slick of chili oil... that's not garnish, that's witness protection for flavor.

And now you come instant. Congratulations: a biohazard with a seasoning packet.

b.text:
Luosifen, you're the only food that comes with a smell warning from the neighbors. Nobody ever says "I'm having snail noodles" quietly. You announce yourself like a sewer breaking up with a pickle.

You're made from river snails, which is already a bold choice. Then you add sour bamboo shoots, which smell like a gym sock that was fermented in a gym sock. Real talk: the first time someone microwaved you in an office, HR held a funeral for the break room.

And the fans! "Just wait, the taste is amazing." Sure, so is a lottery ticket, but I'm not smelling like one for three days. Your broth is a gorgeous, glowing chili-oil red, like a warning light on a submarine, which is accurate, because I am now sealed inside with you.

Luosifen: delicious enough to eat, powerful enough to evict you.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text: Vegas, you're the only city where the pyramid has a light beam that's brighter than the sun, and you still can't find the sun. You built a fake Eiffel Tower, a fake Venice with fake gondoliers singing fake opera, and a fake New York with a roller coaster around the Statue of Liberty. Honestly, that's the most accurate tour of America I've ever taken. Everything's a copy, and nobody wants to leave. You've got clocks with no windows, casinos with no clocks, and a wedding chapel open at four in the morning for people who forgot what they agreed to at ten. Your motto should be "What happens here stays here," but your hotel bills say otherwise.

b.text:
Las Vegas, the only city where you can see the Eiffel Tower, a pyramid, and Venice in one afternoon and still feel like you never left a strip mall in Ohio. You're a city built in the desert out of pure spite and borrowed water. The Colorado River is literally drying up so a fake volcano can erupt every fifteen minutes for a guy in cargo shorts holding a yard-long margarita.

Your casinos have no clocks and no windows, which is smart, because nobody wants to know it's 9 a.m. on a Tuesday and Grandma's on her third oxygen tank at the Wheel of Fortune slots.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas"? Sure. Mostly your 401(k). And now you've got the Sphere, a giant glowing eyeball, so the whole city can watch you make every mistake in 4K.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista, you were the operating system that asked permission to open the calculator. Every time I tried to delete a file, you'd pop up a box asking "Are you sure?" like I was a toddler with scissors. Then you'd ask again. And again. Your User Account Control was so annoying that people turned it off just to get their work done, which I guess was the security equivalent of removing the smoke detector because it beeps.

And Aero! Gorgeous glass windows that ran great on the computer that cost four thousand dollars and crawled on everything else. You had "Vista Capable" stickers on machines that couldn't actually run you. That's not a sticker, that's a hostage note.

b.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Five years in development as "Longhorn," and the only thing that shipped on time was the disappointment. They cut WinFS but kept the Aero glass. Finally, an operating system you could see right through.

Vista came in six editions, from Starter to Ultimate, which is five more ways to pay for the same crash. Microsoft slapped "Vista Capable" stickers on computers that could barely run Solitaire, then got sued. The only thing Vista ever finished loading was a class action.

And User Account Control! "Are you sure you want to do that?" Every. Single. Click. Vista was the only software that needed permission to exist, and honestly? We should've hit Cancel.

Copying a file: "Calculating time remaining…" Vista, you were calculating until 2009, when Microsoft fixed you, renamed you Windows 7, and pretended you were adopted.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, and you couldn't even make it to the branches. You just hang off the trunk like a drunk uncle clinging to a lamppost.

You weigh eighty pounds. That's not a fruit, that's a fourth grader in a bumpy green costume. People cut you open and need cooking oil on their hands and knives, because your insides are basically rubber cement. You're the only produce that requires a solvent.

And vegans love you because when you're young, you taste like absolutely nothing. Your big career move is pretending to be pulled pork. Your whole identity is "not bad if you drown me in barbecue sauce."

Then you ripen and smell like Juicy Fruit gum fermenting in a gym bag.

You're the national fruit of Bangladesh, and you still find time to fall on people's heads.

b.text:
Jackfruit, you're what happens when a watermelon gets a medieval weapons collection. You grow up to a hundred pounds, hang off the trunk like a tumor, and fall on people. You're the only fruit with a wrongful-death lawsuit hanging over your head.

Cutting you open requires oil on the knife, oil on the hands, and a signed waiver, because your sap is basically industrial glue. And inside? Yellow, stringy pods that smell like a gym bag soaked in bubblegum.

Then vegans discovered you. Suddenly you're "pulled pork." No. You're a fruit in a barbecue costume, sitting in sauce, hoping nobody checks your ID. Nobody's fooled. Even the vegans are just being polite.

You're Bangladesh's national fruit, which means a whole country looked at you and said, "Yes, that's us," and honestly, fair.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text: Google Glass, you cost fifteen hundred dollars and made everyone wearing you look like a Bluetooth headset that got promoted. Sergey Brin launched you by skydiving onto a building, and that's the last time you were ever cool. You put a tiny prism over one eye so people could check email while pretending to make eye contact. You didn't invent a computer, you invented a reason to get punched. You're the only gadget that gave us a new slur: "Glasshole." Bars banned you. Movie theaters banned you. Robert Scoble wore you in the shower, and that photo did more damage than any privacy lawsuit. You took pictures when people winked, turning every awkward conversation into a potential felony. Your battery died before your reputation did, and that's impressive. Rest in peace: demoted to warehouse work, then quietly killed in 2023. The most Google ending possible.

b.text:
Google Glass, the glasses that made everyone around you feel like they were being recorded for a documentary nobody asked for. You wore them to a dinner party and suddenly you weren't a guest, you were a surveillance operation with a nice haircut. Nobody could tell if you were looking at them or at the tiny little screen floating in your eyeball, which, let's be honest, is the exact same energy as a guy who keeps checking his phone while you're talking about your dead dog.

And that little camera! It was always pointed at people's faces like a tiny, judgmental lighthouse. People said "Glasshole" and honestly? They weren't wrong. Google spent years saying "you'll get used to it," and the public said, "We won't, but thanks for the offer."

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text: Hydrogen fuel-cell cars are the most optimistic thing ever built. Think about it: you take the most abundant element in the universe, and then you spend a fortune compressing it to 700 bar, bolting it into a tank, and driving it to a station that's closed. Toyota's Mirai has more hydrogen stations in its dreams than in California. Some states have exactly one, and it's always broken. You pull up, the pump says "Out of Service," and you realize you've just become a very expensive lawn ornament. Meanwhile, your electric neighbor is charging in his garage in his pajamas. Hydrogen cars are like a guy who proposes on a first date and then can't find the ring.

b.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle where the tailpipe emission is water and the owners are still crying more than the car. The Toyota Mirai loses value faster than a Hindenburg loses altitude. Used ones sell for less than the free fuel card Toyota bundled with them, a card you can't use because the station's been "temporarily offline" since 2022.

You've got a 10,000-PSI tank of the universe's most abundant element, and somehow it's the scarcest thing in California. Filling up costs thirty-six bucks a kilo, and most of that hydrogen is made from natural gas, so congratulations: you bought a gas car with extra steps and a guilt-free bumper sticker.

Hydrogen's been "ten years away" for thirty years. Even fusion's embarrassed for you, and fusion is the same element with better excuses.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel, you're the only software that thinks "September 4th" and "the gene SEPT4" are the same thing. Scientists had to rename human genes because of you. Human genes! Billions of years of evolution, undone by a spreadsheet that thought it was being helpful.

You've got a million rows, and somehow the one cell I need is always hidden in column XFD. Who's ever been to XFD? Nobody. It's the Bermuda Triangle of accounting.

Every company on earth runs on a file called "Budget_FINAL_v3_REAL_final(2).xlsx," and the whole thing depends on one formula written by Linda, who retired in 2011 and took the logic with her.

You turn my phone numbers into scientific notation. You open a CSV and delete my leading zeros like they owe you money. And VLOOKUP? Twenty-five years, and it still can't look left.

You're not software. You're a hostage situation with gridlines.

b.text:
Excel, you're the Swiss Army knife of spreadsheets, except every blade is sharp in the wrong direction. You've got four hundred functions and somehow none of them can tell me why my dates turned into the number 45292. You autocorrect "1-2" into January 2nd, and then you act surprised when a gene called MARCH1 becomes "1-Mar." Scientists had to rename genes because of you. That's not a bug, that's a biography.

And the Ctrl+Z history stops at about twelve steps, like you're embarrassed of your own mistakes. You're a grid of a million rows and you still can't fit my budget on one screen without me squinting like I'm reading a ransom note.

Every one of us has one cell that says #REF! and one VLOOKUP we don't understand. You're not a tool, you're a hostage negotiation with a row number.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word, ladies and gentlemen. It's the only program where nudging a photo one pixel to the left sends three paragraphs to page nine and summons a blank final page you will never, ever delete.

Word has been around for forty years and still can't decide what font it is. Times New Roman, then Calibri, now Aptos. It's having a midlife crisis in 11-point.

It underlines my own name in red. Wavy red. Like *I'm* the typo.

Try making a numbered list. Word says, "Got it, starting at 1." Second item: "Also 1." Third item: "Here's 4. It's indented. It's a letter now."

And Track Changes isn't a feature. It's a crime scene: strikethroughs everywhere, plus forty comments from someone named "Author."

Word, you gave us Clippy, and somehow he was the most helpful part.

b.text:
Microsoft Word, you've had thirty years to learn what I want, and you still think I'm trying to write a bulleted list every time I type a dash.

You've got a paperclip's worth of trauma in your past, yet you still auto-correct "Costco" to "Cost co" like you're editing a ransom note.

I insert one picture and the whole document rearranges itself like furniture in an earthquake. The image jumps to page nine, the text wraps around it in the shape of a gunshot wound, and page four is now blank for reasons known only to God and a hidden section break.

You have a ribbon with 400 buttons, and the one I need is always under "Layout," which is somehow not where the layout is.

And "Not Responding"? Buddy, I just asked you to save. Then you recover my file as "Document1 (Autorecovered) (Copy) (2)," like a witness protection program for my thesis.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text:
Chicago deep-dish isn't pizza, it's a casserole that got a good agent. You wait 45 minutes for it, which is the only honest part, because the oven is basically doing a bypass in reverse. The waiter says "it takes a while," and he means "call your family and say something nice."

It arrives upside down: cheese on the bottom, sauce on top, like the pizza lost a bet. And the crust is a structural engineering project. It's not a slice, it's a core sample. You lift it with a spatula and the cheese stretches like it's begging you to reconsider.

Two slices and you're done. Not full, done. You walk out into a Chicago winter and honestly, the insulation helps.

New Yorkers call it soup in a bread bowl. Wrong. Soup has the decency to cool down. This stays molten until the first bite takes the roof of your mouth, as a deposit.

b.text: Deep-dish pizza is the only food where you need a fork, a knife, and a structural engineer. You order a slice and the waiter brings you a casserole with a crust like a bank vault. The sauce sits on top, which is the pizza equivalent of wearing your shirt on the outside of your jacket. Chicagoans will tell you it's "not pizza, it's a pie," which is what you say when you've eaten something that requires a 45-minute wait and still leaves you feeling like you've been mugged by cheese. Locals eat it with a straight face. Tourists eat it with a flashlight, looking for the bottom. And somewhere under there, buried under three pounds of mozzarella, is a tomato that has never once been invited to the party.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, and you couldn't even make it to the branches. You just hang off the trunk like a drunk uncle clinging to a lamppost.

You weigh eighty pounds. That's not a fruit, that's a fourth grader in a bumpy green costume. People cut you open and need cooking oil on their hands and knives, because your insides are basically rubber cement. You're the only produce that requires a solvent.

And vegans love you because when you're young, you taste like absolutely nothing. Your big career move is pretending to be pulled pork. Your whole identity is "not bad if you drown me in barbecue sauce."

Then you ripen and smell like Juicy Fruit gum fermenting in a gym bag.

You're the national fruit of Bangladesh, and you still find time to fall on people's heads.

b.text:
Jackfruit, you're the only fruit that needs a permit to carry. You weigh eighty pounds, you're covered in spikes, and you grow directly out of the tree trunk like a tumor with ambition.

Cutting you open requires oiled knives, gloves, and a will, because you bleed glue. I've seen people stuck to you for three days. You're the only fruit that fights back like a bad breakup.

And the smell! Rotten banana, bubblegum, and gym socks, all in one. You're what Juicy Fruit becomes in a hostage situation.

Then vegans discovered you. Now you're in a can, drowning in barbecue sauce, pretending to be pulled pork. Jackfruit, you're a bland, stringy shredded mess in a tin, and you're lying to everyone. Even the tree looks at you and says, "I made that? And it's pretending to be a pig?"

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's little brother who moved into a browser tab and called it "the cloud." Your whole personality is twelve people's colored cursors circling the same cell like sharks while an Anonymous Capybara silently watches everyone's mistakes. You say "Saving..." with the confidence of a man who has absolutely not saved. Your IMPORTRANGE makes me click "Allow access" like I'm asking my own spreadsheet for permission to see my own spreadsheet. Half my cells just say "Loading..." forever, like a Victorian ghost waiting for a letter. And you'll let anyone sort one column without the others, then shrug while every customer gets someone else's phone number. Version history is your only real feature: it's just a timeline of who ruined everything at 2 a.m. And yes, Gemini can explain my #REF! error now. Great. It's still there.

b.text:
Google Sheets: the only software where you can watch a coworker named "Anonymous Capybara" ruin your formulas in real time.

You're the Excel that went to community college and told everyone it's "basically the same." Then someone adds 40,000 rows and you wheeze "Loading..." like a Chromebook climbing stairs.

Your formula for combining data from another sheet is IMPORTRANGE, which immediately yells #REF! until I click "Allow access," like I'm asking you to the prom. Your most advanced function, QUERY, makes me write SQL inside a text string, inside a cell, inside a spreadsheet. That's not a feature. That's a hostage video.

Every file on earth is named "Copy of Copy of Budget FINAL v2," shared with "anyone with the link," and owned by Brenda, who left in 2019. I click "Request edit access" and the void answers.

And the 10 million cell limit? Bold of you to assume anyone's budget is that organized. Mine is three tabs and a dream.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text: Crocs are shoes designed by someone who saw a bath mat and thought, "Yes, but what if it had holes so my feet could breathe while I pretend I'm a surgeon at a Cracker Barrel?" They look like the foam that sits on a hot dog's bun. They're the only footwear where the heel is basically a suggestion. You can't run in them, you can't hike in them, and you definitely can't sneak up on anyone, because every step sounds like a duck being slowly squeezed. And somehow they're on the feet of grown adults who own a mortgage. Nobody wears Crocs to look good. You wear Crocs because you've accepted that your feet have given up, and you've decided the shoe should match that energy. Honestly, respect. You're the only person at the Target parking lot who's fully at peace.

b.text:
Crocs are the only shoes that look like they were designed by a toddler and approved by a plumber. They're what happens when a boat shoe gets hit by a truck and the truck is made of cheese.

And the holes? Those aren't "ventilation." Those are tiny windows so everyone can watch your sock make a terrible decision.

You know what's wild? They sell charms for them. You can pin a little taco to a shoe that already looks like a bath toy. That's not accessorizing, that's decorating a pool float.

The heel strap flips back and suddenly it's "sport mode." Sport mode! For what sport? Competitive gardening? Walking to the fridge at 2 a.m.?

And they're comfortable, which is the cruelest part. Nobody can even make fun of them honestly. You just stand there, defeated, as a surgeon in neon green clogs walks past you with better arch support than your entire family.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, you were a $400 Wi-Fi-connected juicer that delivered four tons of force, enough, your engineers bragged, to lift two Teslas, and Bloomberg proved the job could be done by a guy with hands. You raised $120 million from Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins to compete with *squeezing*. Every single customer already owned the competing product. It came in pairs.

You sold $8 bags of chopped produce that had to scan a QR code and phone home before you'd juice them. A juicer that needed internet. Imagine the outage: "Sorry, AWS is down, enjoy your sealed pouch of regret." You'd refuse to press an expired pack, like a bouncer for kale.

Doug Evans compared himself to Steve Jobs. Steve Jobs put a thousand songs in your pocket. Doug put a sack of mush in a vise and asked for your Wi-Fi password. Silicon Valley's most expensive way to say, "Just use your hands."

b.text: Juicero raised over a hundred million dollars to build a $400 juicer that squeezed packets of pre-chopped kale. Then a reporter showed you could get the same juice by squeezing the packets with your bare hands. That's not a juicer. That's a hand. Your hand already came with the machine. The press checked a QR code on each pack before it would run, so you paid for a Wi-Fi juicer that needed the internet to tell it to do the job a towel does. And people paid it! Venture capitalists looked at a $5 bag of spinach and thought, "Yes, this needs a server." The company shut down in 2017. Honestly, that's the most productive thing the press has ever done.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which is wild, because you dress like a medieval mace and smell like a crime scene. You're the only fruit with a body armor package AND a hazmat warning.

You're banned from Singapore's subway, hotels, and airlines. Think about that. Nobody bans the pineapple. You're the only produce item that gets kicked off a plane before it even boards.

Your fans say, "Just get past the smell, the taste is heavenly." Sir, that's what every hostage says about their captor.

You taste like custard that's been cheating on a sewer with an onion. Eat one and your fridge smells like you for three weeks, your breath for five.

And you fall out of trees onto people's heads. You're not even content to be a bad meal. You want to be a *weapon*.

b.text:
Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which tracks, because like most monarchies, you stink and nobody's allowed to say it to your face.

You're the only fruit with a criminal record. Banned on the Singapore subway, alongside flammable liquids. Hotels put your picture on signs next to "no smoking." In 2019, a university in Melbourne evacuated five hundred people because they thought there was a gas leak. Nope. Just you, sitting in a cupboard, being yourself.

And the armor! You're covered in spikes like a medieval mace. Nature built you to defend yourself, then gave you a smell that does it better. The spikes are just overkill.

Fans say you taste like custard. Sure. Custard that was left in a gym bag next to some onions. Your flavor isn't an acquired taste. It's a hostage situation.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text: The Apple Vision Pro costs 3,500 dollars, which is a used Honda, for a headset that makes you look like a welder who wandered into the Apple Store. The front screen shows your eyes to everyone around you, so people don't see a person. They see a dead-eyed aquarium. You click by staring at things and pinching the air, like you're trying to hypnotize your own hand. The battery lives in your pocket on a cable, so you're not free, you're tethered to a fanny pack. Apple calls it spatial computing. I call it the only device that lets you wander your living room in a 3,500-dollar blindfold and still walk straight into the couch.

b.text:
Apple Vision Pro: the only device where you pay $3,500 to be told your living room isn't good enough. It's a ski mask for people who want to look at spreadsheets in the void.

It weighs about a pound and a half, so after twenty minutes you don't have spatial computing, you have a chiropractor. And the battery lasts two hours, tethered to a pack in your pocket, so you're basically walking a tiny, expensive dog.

Apple said it was the future of work. The future of work is a man in Cupertino pinching the air like he's trying to catch a very slow fly.

And the "EyeSight" feature, where your eyes appear on the front? It's like a haunted Snapchat filter. Your family sees a creepy digital ghost of you, and you see them as a fuzzy video feed of people you're ignoring.

Three thousand five hundred dollars. For that I could buy a nice TV, a couch, and friends to sit on it.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which is wild, because you dress like a medieval mace and smell like a crime scene. Every other fruit says "eat me." You say "I dare you."

You're the only food with a gas leak. A Canberra university library was evacuated because of you. Evacuated! Fruit is not supposed to trigger a hazmat response.

Singapore had to put you on the subway sign with a big red X, right next to flamethrowers. Hotels ban you the way they ban smoking and goats.

And the flesh inside? Custard that tastes like sweet almonds, caramel, and a decision you regret. Fans say, "Just get past the smell." That's what people say about your cousin's boyfriend.

You're the only fruit that can kill me from the tree, and the only one I'd still blame the neighbors for.

b.text:
Durian, the "King of Fruits." Sure, if the kingdom is a landfill. You're banned on the Singapore subway, right there on the sign next to flammable liquids, because apparently you're the bigger hazard. Hotels fine guests for sneaking you in. That's not a fruit, that's a parole violation.

You wear a medieval mace as a jacket, which is smart, since nobody who's smelled you wants to get close anyway. You fall out of trees and put people in the hospital. You're the only produce that needs a hard hat AND a hazmat suit.

And your fans swear you're "like custard!" Sure: custard aged in a gym bag full of rotten onions. Fifty bucks for a Musang King, and your breath's a crime scene for three days.

Anthony Bourdain ate warthog rectum on camera, and *you're* the one he warned people about.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text:
PHP. You started as "Personal Home Page," then rebranded as "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a recursive acronym, because even your name couldn't commit to a stable API.

For twenty years, "abc" == 0 was true, and you called it "type juggling," like a clown proud of dropping things.

strpos takes haystack, needle. array_search takes needle, haystack. That's not argument order; that's mood swings.

Your parse error says T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM. That's Hebrew for "double colon" and English for "good luck."

You skipped version 6 entirely. Even your release numbers just wanted to move on.

You shipped mysql_real_escape_string, implying the first one was a hoax.

Facebook loved you so much they invented Hack just to avoid touching you.

But sure, you power most of the web. Mostly WordPress. That's like bragging your biggest fan is a raccoon.

b.text:
PHP, the language that stands for "Personal Home Page" and now runs half the internet, like a rental car you forgot to return in 1998.

It's the only language where the standard library looks like it was named by a dice roll. strpos has needle, haystack. array_search has needle, haystack. But str_replace? Different order. Why? Because PHP doesn't believe in consistency. It believes in vibes.

The comparison rules are a hostage situation. "0" == false. "abc" == 0, at least until PHP 8 finally took a sip of water. And the ternary operator was left-associative for years, so nested ones did the opposite of what anyone wanted.

Then there's the dollar sign. Every variable has one, like each is being sold individually.

And yet, WordPress, Facebook, Wikipedia, all run on it. PHP is the duct tape holding the web together, and like duct tape, nobody's proud of it, but everyone's got a roll in the garage.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, you started as the internal chat tool for a failed video game called Glitch, and honestly? Still the most accurate name you've ever had.

You promised to kill email. Instead you gave us email that *knocks*. That little wooden knock-brush sound has triggered more cortisol than any boss in history. I hear it in the shower. I hear it at funerals.

You invented the green dot, so now my employer knows I went to the bathroom for nineteen minutes. You invented "is typing…" so my manager can type for four straight minutes and send "ok."

Threads? Nobody can find them. Huddles? A Zoom call that ambushes you. And somehow every company has 400 channels, and the only active one is #random, where Kevin posts his sourdough.

Your name literally stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable. Sure. Try finding that one link from Tuesday. 👀 reacted by 3 people.

b.text:
Slack, you took "this meeting could've been an email" and made it "this email could've been forty-seven threaded replies and a thumbs-up emoji."

You've got a green dot next to my name, which means my boss thinks I'm available. I'm not available. I'm just *loaded*. There's a difference, and it's called a bathroom break.

Every Monday, "Hey" arrives with no follow-up. Just "Hey." Then three dots appear, disappear, appear, disappear. Is she typing a novel or a resignation?

You gave us channels, and we made #random, #random-2, and #random-actually-random. Somewhere, a guy named Doug is in forty-one channels and has muted forty. He reacts to everything with a salute emoji and calls it leadership.

And that notification sound? That little knock-knock-knock? Pavlov would've been proud. I flinch at wooden doors now.

You're not a productivity tool. You're a very expensive way to watch coworkers say "circling back."

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The strongest material known to science, and you still can't hold a job. Since the nineties you've promised us a space elevator. Your longest strand is about half a meter. That's not an elevator. That's floss with a publicist.

You're graphene that rolled over and gave up. Graphene got a Nobel Prize. You got an argument over whether Soviets spotted you in 1952.

You can't even decide what you are. Twist one way, you're a metal. Twist the other, you're a semiconductor. Nobody controls it, including you. That's not versatility. That's a chirality crisis.

Drop you in any liquid and you clump together like freshmen at a mixer.

And inhale you? Suddenly you behave like asbestos. Thirty years of hype, and your most reliable talent is impersonating the one material we paid billions to rip out of schools.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes, the material that's been "ten years from changing everything" for thirty years. You're 100 times stronger than steel, and yet somehow you've never held a job.

You're a single sheet of graphene rolled up like a sad burrito, and you still can't decide if you're a metal or a semiconductor. Chirality, right? Your entire personality depends on which way you twist. That's not physics, that's a mood ring.

Scientists say you could build a space elevator. Buddy, you can't even get through a lab without clumping together like earbuds in a pocket. Every researcher spends six months trying to disperse you, then writes "uniform" in the paper anyway.

And the manufacturing! Everyone gets a random mix of types, so sorting you is like trying to separate identical twins by vibe.

Also, you're a nanometer wide and somehow still the biggest thing in everyone's grant proposal.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word, you're the only program that's been around for forty years and still can't tell me where the bullet point ends. I type one dash, hit enter, and suddenly you're deciding I'm running a whole bulleted empire. I try to undo it and you go, "Nope, here's an indented sub-bullet instead." Thanks, Clippy's grumpy cousin.

And the "Track Changes" feature? You're named after a document, but you treat every edit like a crime scene. Someone changes "the" to "a" and suddenly the whole page looks like a kindergarten finger painting, red lines everywhere, and nobody knows who did it.

Then there's the page numbers. Page one is perfect. Page two is fine. Page nine just quietly starts itself over at one because you got bored.

Forty years, Word. You've seen everything. Still can't center a title without me holding my breath.

b.text:
Microsoft Word, you've had forty years to learn one thing: how to let me move a picture one millimeter without three paragraphs fleeing to page nine. You don't wrap text, you take hostages.

You underline my own name in red like I'm the typo. You turn my grocery list into a numbered legal document I can't escape. I hit Enter once and suddenly I'm in a style called "Heading 7" that I've never met.

And Track Changes? That's not editing, that's a crime scene where everyone bled in a different color.

You fired Clippy, the only one of you who ever admitted I looked like I needed help.

And every crash, you hand me "Document1 (Recovered)" like a cat dropping a dead bird on the porch: proud, useless, and somehow from 2 PM yesterday.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza, you're named after a place you've never been. You were invented in Ontario, by a Greek guy, using canned pineapple. That's not a heritage, that's a witness protection identity.

And the ham? It's Canadian bacon. Even your meat is from Canada. The only Hawaiian thing about you is that people see you and say "aloha," meaning goodbye.

Pineapple has an enzyme that digests protein. You're the only pizza that eats the customer back. Warm fruit juice pooling on mozzarella like a hot tub nobody cleaned.

Italians don't hate you; they pray for you. The president of Iceland said he'd ban you if he could, and Iceland eats fermented shark.

You're not a pizza. You're a fruit cup that fell on a pizza and refused to get up.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza is what happens when Italy and a Dole pineapple can have a custody battle and nobody wins. It was invented in Canada, by a Greek guy, and named after a pineapple brand. That's not a pizza, that's a bad customs form.

Every other topping says "I'm here to be savory." Pineapple shows up like, "I'm also dessert. And I'm leaking." Now your ham is swimming in a warm fruit puddle, and the crust has the structural integrity of a wet napkin.

And the ham! Not even good ham. Sad, pink, circle ham, the kind that's been in a sandwich bag since a 2006 field trip.

Nobody orders it for themselves. It's always "I'll just get a Hawaiian for the table," said by the one guy who also says "I'm not really a *pizza* person."

Hawaii has never claimed it. Hawaii has been in court trying to get away from it.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans, you were born in 1994 to put words in the mouth of a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the one that survived. Bob is dead. The dog is dead. You're on a sympathy card at a funeral home.

You were inspired by Batman comics, and you've never once been near anything heroic. CERN used you to announce the Higgs boson: humanity's greatest discovery, presented like a lemonade stand. Dan Gilbert used you to call LeBron a traitor, because nothing says "furious billionaire" like bubble letters.

And your defense is always "Well, I help dyslexic readers." Great. You're the guy at the party whose whole personality is a doctor's note.

Even Vincent Connare, the man who made you, says he's barely ever used you. Your own dad won't put you on the fridge.

b.text:
Comic Sans, you're the only font that shows up to a funeral looking like it's about to do a magic show for toddlers.

You were designed for a cartoon dog's speech bubble in Microsoft Bob, and somehow ended up on cancer-ward notices, divorce settlements, and "Please Do Not Microwave Fish" signs in the office kitchen. Every message you carry sounds like it was written by a substitute teacher who's given up.

Designers don't hate you. Designers have a support group for you. CERN announced the Higgs boson in you, and physicists everywhere suddenly wondered if the universe was a bake sale flyer.

Your letters look like they were drawn by someone holding the marker in their left hand while riding a bus. The lowercase "a" is the only part of you that's trying.

And yet you're still installed on every computer on Earth, like a clown that nobody invited but nobody can evict.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text:
UGG boots: because nothing says "I respect my feet" like dressing them as two sheepskin loaves that lost a fight with a puddle.

They're the only shoe that looks wet when dry and ruined when wet. One drop of rain and suddenly your boots have a water stain shaped like Ohio. And the tag says "do not wear in rain," which is wild for something that's basically a footwear sponge. It's a boot with a dress code.

Also, they're from Australia, but the company's in California, and the price is from the moon. Three hundred dollars for a shoe designed to be worn by surfers who just got out of the ocean, and somehow it ended up in a Pilates class in Connecticut.

And the smell. Wearing them without socks is a lifestyle choice, and it turns the inside into a warm, damp sheep sauna. You don't take them off. You release them.

b.text: Ugg boots are the only shoe that looks like a sheep ate a pair of slippers and then apologized by giving them back. You didn't buy Uggs, you bought a pair of carpet remnants that wandered into a shoe store and got lucky. Nobody's ever run in them. Nobody's ever been chased in them. They're designed for one thing: standing in a Target parking lot holding an oat milk latte like you just finished a marathon. And the name! "Ugg." That's not a brand, that's a noise you make when you step on a Lego in the dark. Somewhere, a shearling farmer is looking at these and saying, "I didn't raise sheep for this, I raised them to be respected." Stay warm, I guess. You look like a hot dog that gave up.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text: Graphene, you're one atom thick and still the biggest presence at every party. Scientists keep calling you the strongest material ever measured, which is wild, because you've never once held your own in a conversation. You're basically pencil lead that went to the gym and never came back. Since 2004 we've been told you'll revolutionize batteries, phones, and bridges. Meanwhile, companies slap your name on golf balls and socks like it's a free upgrade. Two Nobel-winning guys isolated you with Scotch tape, which tells you everything. The most advanced substance in the universe was found by somebody with a roll of tape and too much time. And you're still "five years away" from being useful. Honestly, that's the most relatable thing about you.

b.text:
Graphene, the "wonder material." Twenty years of wonder, and the only place I've seen you is in press releases.

You're pencil lead that got an agent. You're literally graphite, but one layer thick, because even carbon wants to be an influencer: all surface, no depth.

They discovered you with Scotch tape. Two guys peeled you off a pencil mark and won a Nobel Prize. That's the most successful thing anyone has ever done with office supplies, and you've been coasting on it ever since.

Stronger than steel! Conducts better than copper! Transparent, flexible, and every article says you'll change everything "within five years." You've been five years away since 2004. You're the Cybertruck of chemistry.

And scaling you up? Impossible. You're perfect in a lab and a wrinkled, expensive mess in a factory. Honestly, you're the most impressive thing a pencil ever did, and also its biggest disappointment.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text:
NFTs: the only product where you pay $300,000 for a receipt, and the receipt is for a JPEG, and the JPEG is still publicly available for free. You can right-click it. The whole business model is a guy pointing at the Mona Lisa saying, "Technically, I own the bookmark."

And the art! Eight thousand identical apes, each with a slightly different hat. That's not a collection, that's a hostage situation at a Hot Topic.

Remember when they said it was "the future of ownership"? Then OpenSea's servers went down and people learned their million-dollar monkey was just a link to a website that could 404. You didn't buy art. You bought a very expensive "Page Not Found."

And the guys who bought them still say "we're early." Early to what? The funeral?

Somewhere right now, a man named Chad is staring at a cartoon ape worth $14, whispering, "Floor price is just a vibe."

b.text: Nobody's ever bought an NFT. They bought a receipt that says "you own this JPEG," and the JPEG is a cartoon ape with a bowler hat, the same JPEG you can right-click and save in four seconds. So they paid four hundred thousand dollars for a screenshot with a certificate. It's the only art in history where the certificate is the art. The Mona Lisa hangs in the Louvre with a crowd of tourists, and this guy's ape is hanging in a folder called "wallet" that nobody else can see. Ownership, they call it. Congratulations, you own the ape, and the ape doesn't know you exist.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text: Nuclear fusion is the energy source that's always thirty years away, and it has been since your grandpa was in diapers. Scientists figured out how to bottle a star. Unfortunately, the star is 150 million degrees, and it refuses to stay in the bottle. Every time the plasma touches the wall, it's like a toddler discovering the fridge is cold. The machines are shaped like donuts because nothing else can handle the pressure. We got net energy gain for a few billionths of a second, and the press release was longer than the experiment. Meanwhile, the sun does it for free, with no magnets, and it still manages to be more reliable than the people promising us a fusion plant by 2030.

b.text:
Nuclear fusion, you've been "thirty years away" for seventy years. That's not a timeline, that's a hostage situation where the hostage is my electric bill.

You're the only technology whose big breakthrough is "we got more energy out than the laser put in." Not more than the wall socket. Just the laser. That's like bragging you're profitable if we ignore rent, payroll, and the building.

You recreate the core of the sun, which sounds impressive until you remember the sun does it for free, with no PhD, and has been doing it for four billion years without a single press release.

Your containment strategy is "a magnetic bottle for something hotter than anything in the solar system." And your funding pitch never changes: "Give us ten billion dollars and a decade." Every decade.

Fusion, you're the ex who says, "I'm almost ready to commit." Sir, you're a tokamak. You've been going in circles since 1950.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text: Let's talk about HSQ, the e-beam resist that's basically a diva. You spin it on, bake it, expose it, and it's supposed to be your friend, but it's secretly already becoming glass. Leave the bottle in the fridge too long and it gels into a sad, cloudy paste, like a relationship that stopped talking to you. Develop it in TMAH and it still acts like it's doing you a favor. And lift-off? Forget it. Once HSQ is exposed, it's SiO2 with a attitude, and it's not leaving your substrate without a fight. It's the only thing in the cleanroom that's been baked, exposed, and developed, and still wants to be left alone.

b.text:
HSQ, ladies and gentlemen: the only resist with sub-10-nanometer resolution and the personality of a sourdough starter. You buy it, you refrigerate it, and it *still* starts gelling in the bottle like it's got somewhere better to be. Shelf life measured in "eh, few months, maybe."

And slow? HSQ needs a dose so high the e-beam tool files for overtime. Your PMMA friends finished their write and went home; you're still exposing alignment marks.

Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you want contrast, *salty* developer. Yes, this resist literally needs you to add salt. Even Gordon Ramsay thinks that's a lot.

But the real red flag? Once it's exposed, it turns into glass. Permanently. You want it gone? Hydrofluoric acid. That's not a resist, that's a relationship you can only leave with a hazmat suit.

Still, gorgeous lines. Shame they collapse when they dry.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole that got a fake ID. You order it, and the waiter says, "That'll be forty-five minutes." Forty-five minutes! I've had relationships bake faster. They put the sauce on top because if you saw what was underneath first, you'd leave. A solid sheet of sausage, like somebody paved a driveway with a patty. Two pounds of mozzarella hiding under a tomato quilt. It's not a slice, it's a core sample. You need a knife, a fork, and a structural engineer. The crust is buttery cornmeal, so it's a pie crust, so congratulations, you're eating dessert with ambitions. And here's the best part: actual Chicagoans don't even eat it. They eat tavern-style thin crust cut in squares. Deep-dish is just the city's way of keeping tourists too full to walk to Wrigley.

b.text:
Chicago deep-dish isn't pizza, it's a casserole that got a good agent. You wait 45 minutes for it, which is the only honest part, because the oven is basically doing a bypass in reverse. The waiter says "it takes a while," and he means "call your family and say something nice."

It arrives upside down: cheese on the bottom, sauce on top, like the pizza lost a bet. And the crust is a structural engineering project. It's not a slice, it's a core sample. You lift it with a spatula and the cheese stretches like it's begging you to reconsider.

Two slices and you're done. Not full, done. You walk out into a Chicago winter and honestly, the insulation helps.

New Yorkers call it soup in a bread bowl. Wrong. Soup has the decency to cool down. This stays molten until the first bite takes the roof of your mouth, as a deposit.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, you took "this meeting could've been an email" and made it "this email could've been forty-seven threaded replies and a thumbs-up emoji."

You've got a green dot next to my name, which means my boss thinks I'm available. I'm not available. I'm just *loaded*. There's a difference, and it's called a bathroom break.

Every Monday, "Hey" arrives with no follow-up. Just "Hey." Then three dots appear, disappear, appear, disappear. Is she typing a novel or a resignation?

You gave us channels, and we made #random, #random-2, and #random-actually-random. Somewhere, a guy named Doug is in forty-one channels and has muted forty. He reacts to everything with a salute emoji and calls it leadership.

And that notification sound? That little knock-knock-knock? Pavlov would've been proud. I flinch at wooden doors now.

You're not a productivity tool. You're a very expensive way to watch coworkers say "circling back."

b.text:
Slack. Named after the one thing you'll never have again.

You promised to kill email, and you did, by replacing it with forty channels that are each email with a typing indicator. Nothing builds dread like "Greg is typing..." for ninety seconds, followed by "hey." Just "hey." Greg, that's not a message, that's a hostage situation.

You gave us threads, so every conversation happens in two places and nobody knows which one's real. You gave us huddles: a meeting that jumps out of a bush. You gave us the green dot, so my boss can monitor my bathroom breaks like a heart rate.
