And that knock sound. I hear it in the grocery store. I hear it at funerals.

Slack, you're the only app that needs three gigs of RAM to tell me someone reacted with a dancing parrot.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text: Beanie Babies, you're the only toy whose value depends on a tag announcing you're dead. "Retired." That's not a collectible, that's a hospice with a barcode. Ty Warner figured out that if he stopped making a bear, grown adults would panic-buy it like the last lifeboat on the Titanic. Parents mortgaged houses for Peanut the Elephant. Now your grandma's attic holds forty thousand of you, each worth less than the postage to mail it. And you were the only stuffed animal with a birth certificate stapled to your butt. You're not even stuffed with beans. It's plastic pellets. Honestly, that's the most honest thing about you.

b.text:
Beanie Babies, the only investment where your financial advisor was a woman named Deb at a card shop. People kept them in plastic cases, like organ donors. Not toys, relics. "Don't touch Princess the bear, she's for college." Princess was a purple bear stuffed with plastic pellets and a dead princess's legacy, and your mom thought she'd pay for Yale.

The genius was the tag. Not the toy, the tag. Ty looked at a bag of beans and said, "What if we made it illegal to love this?" Bend that heart-shaped tag and you've lost four thousand dollars. Kids learned grief early: "I hugged Peanut the elephant, and now he's worth nothing."

Then the retirements. Ty killed off bears like a Game of Thrones writer with a mortgage. Fall for Squealer the pig and he's gone by Tuesday, replaced by a slightly different pig.

Today they're in a garage in Ohio, sweating in a bin, worth less than the bin.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text: Luosifen is the only food that needs a smell permit. You open the packet in a dorm and the RA shows up asking who's microwaving a crime scene. The broth is snails simmered with pickled bamboo shoots that have been fermenting since before your grandmother was born, and those shoots smell like a gym sock that got promoted to management. People say, "It's delicious once you get past the smell." Sure, and a stink bomb is delicious once you get past the explosion. Then there's the packet of chili oil, which the label calls "optional" in the same tone a hostage-taker uses. Eat it on the subway and the whole car suddenly finds the ceiling fascinating. That's not a meal. That's a restraining order with chopsticks.

b.text:
Luosifen, you're the only food that comes with a smell warning from the neighbors. Nobody ever says "I'm having snail noodles" quietly. You announce yourself like a sewer breaking up with a pickle.

You're made from river snails, which is already a bold choice. Then you add sour bamboo shoots, which smell like a gym sock that was fermented in a gym sock. Real talk: the first time someone microwaved you in an office, HR held a funeral for the break room.

And the fans! "Just wait, the taste is amazing." Sure, so is a lottery ticket, but I'm not smelling like one for three days. Your broth is a gorgeous, glowing chili-oil red, like a warning light on a submarine, which is accurate, because I am now sealed inside with you.

Luosifen: delicious enough to eat, powerful enough to evict you.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text: Monopoly is the only board game where the goal is to bankrupt your friends and somehow everyone still agrees to play it again. Four hours. Four hours! Nobody has ever finished a game of Monopoly. The game just ends when someone's dad flips the table, or when the banker quietly starts pretending they didn't count the money properly. And the banker, by the way, is always the least trustworthy person at the table, because they're the one holding the stack of cash and they're the one who "forgot" to collect Free Parking. Free Parking! That's not a gift, that's a lie you tell children. And Boardwalk? Nobody's ever landed on Boardwalk and felt lucky. They just felt the rent go up like a hostage negotiation. Monopoly: where your uncle buys every railroad and calls it a "strategy."

b.text: Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to warn people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow you became the thing Grandpa uses to teach eight-year-olds that ruining lives is fun. You're the only game where getting arrested is a power move, because late in the game jail is the safest property on the board. Your mascot is a man everyone swears wears a monocle. He doesn't. He's just so smug our brains added one. You promise "about an hour" and deliver a hostage situation. Nobody has ever actually finished you. You just end when somebody flips the board over Marvin Gardens. You award ten bucks for second place in a beauty contest, which is still more than Baltic Avenue pulls in. And the banker who skims from the bank isn't a cheater. He's the only player who read the theme.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans, you were born in 1994 to put words in the mouth of a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the one that survived. Bob is dead. The dog is dead. You're on a sympathy card at a funeral home.

You were inspired by Batman comics, and you've never once been near anything heroic. CERN used you to announce the Higgs boson: humanity's greatest discovery, presented like a lemonade stand. Dan Gilbert used you to call LeBron a traitor, because nothing says "furious billionaire" like bubble letters.

And your defense is always "Well, I help dyslexic readers." Great. You're the guy at the party whose whole personality is a doctor's note.

Even Vincent Connare, the man who made you, says he's barely ever used you. Your own dad won't put you on the fridge.

b.text:
Comic Sans is the font that looks like it was designed by a substitute teacher who found a crayon in a lost-and-found box. Every letter wobbles like it's had three espressos and a bad breakup. The "a" is a little round bubble with a tail that's clearly been through something. Nobody asked for this. It's the typographic equivalent of a clown trying to file your taxes.

And the worst part? Somebody put it on a hospital sign. A hospital! You're walking in with a broken leg, scanning for the exit, and the sign says "EMERGENCY" in letters that look like they're bouncing on a trampoline. Even the sickness can't take itself seriously anymore.

It's the only font that makes a funeral notice look like a birthday party invitation. Somewhere a grandmother is typing "Rest In Peace" in this, hitting bold, and thinking she's being tasteful.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ, hydrogen silsesquioxane, the only resist that's basically glass pretending to be a photoresist. You're a negative-tone resist that turns into silicon dioxide. So after all my work, my pattern isn't a mask, it's a permanent tenant.

Your shelf life is a joke. You gel in the bottle if I look at you wrong. Open a fresh one, two weeks later it's Jell-O with commitment issues. Keep it in the fridge, and it's still aging like milk in a sauna.

And the development! Sixty nanometer lines, beautiful, then TMAH hits and they collapse like a Jenga tower. Sure, you can do sub-10 nanometer features, but only if I sacrifice a goat, run at 1000 microcoulombs per square centimeter, and sit there for nine hours while the beam writes a rectangle.

Contrast? Terrible. Sensitivity? Worse. Stripping you off? Hydrofluoric acid. You're the ex who can only be removed by something that dissolves bones.

b.text:
HSQ, everybody! The only resist that ages faster than the grad student using it. You spin it Monday, expose it Tuesday, and suddenly your dose curve has gone through a midlife crisis. It has to live in the fridge like expired yogurt, and it's about as forgiving.

HSQ brags about sub-10-nanometer lines. Sure, if you've got six hours of write time, because this diva needs a dose that could sterilize a hospital. Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you're desperate, *salt water*. Your whole career is literally seasoned with tears now.

And once it's exposed? It turns into glass. Brittle, cracking glass. You wanted a mask; you got a window that shatters when you look at it. Want it gone? Hope you enjoy hydrofluoric acid, the chemical that dissolves your bones.

HSQ: beautiful resolution, terrible personality. It's not negative-tone. It's just negative.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs are the only shoes that look like they were designed by a toddler and approved by a plumber. They're what happens when a boat shoe gets hit by a truck and the truck is made of cheese.

And the holes? Those aren't "ventilation." Those are tiny windows so everyone can watch your sock make a terrible decision.

You know what's wild? They sell charms for them. You can pin a little taco to a shoe that already looks like a bath toy. That's not accessorizing, that's decorating a pool float.

The heel strap flips back and suddenly it's "sport mode." Sport mode! For what sport? Competitive gardening? Walking to the fridge at 2 a.m.?

And they're comfortable, which is the cruelest part. Nobody can even make fun of them honestly. You just stand there, defeated, as a surgeon in neon green clogs walks past you with better arch support than your entire family.

b.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like a colander that wanted to go to brunch. Thirteen holes, and somehow none of them let the dignity out, because there was never any in there.

You were invented as a boat shoe. A *boat* shoe. The one place you were built for, and you'd just float away. So you stayed on land and started fights with escalators. Malls had to post warnings. You're the only footwear with a rap sheet against machinery.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind your heel doesn't make you athletic. It makes you a clog wearing a seatbelt.

Then came Jibbitz, little charms you jam into the holes so grown adults can accessorize ventilation. Congratulations. You turned a shoe into a fridge door.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, the only city that looked at the Mojave Desert and said, "You know what this needs? Venice." Nothing says Italian romance like a gondolier singing in a mall next to a Cheesecake Factory.

You built a half-size Eiffel Tower, a fake New York, and a pyramid, because why visit the world when you can visit its gift shop?

No clocks, no windows, and carpet designed by a migraine, all so you won't notice you've been feeding a penny slot since Tuesday.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas." Yeah. Especially your money. And the $45 resort fee for a pool you couldn't use because a bachelor party from Ohio was in it.

And Lake Mead's drying up so fast they keep finding bodies. Even the mob's secrets can't stay in Vegas anymore.

b.text: Vegas, you're the only city where the pyramid has a light beam that's brighter than the sun, and you still can't find the sun. You built a fake Eiffel Tower, a fake Venice with fake gondoliers singing fake opera, and a fake New York with a roller coaster around the Statue of Liberty. Honestly, that's the most accurate tour of America I've ever taken. Everything's a copy, and nobody wants to leave. You've got clocks with no windows, casinos with no clocks, and a wedding chapel open at four in the morning for people who forgot what they agreed to at ten. Your motto should be "What happens here stays here," but your hotel bills say otherwise.

The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen, you're the only food that comes with a smell warning from the neighbors. Nobody ever says "I'm having snail noodles" quietly. You announce yourself like a sewer breaking up with a pickle.

You're made from river snails, which is already a bold choice. Then you add sour bamboo shoots, which smell like a gym sock that was fermented in a gym sock. Real talk: the first time someone microwaved you in an office, HR held a funeral for the break room.

And the fans! "Just wait, the taste is amazing." Sure, so is a lottery ticket, but I'm not smelling like one for three days. Your broth is a gorgeous, glowing chili-oil red, like a warning light on a submarine, which is accurate, because I am now sealed inside with you.

Luosifen: delicious enough to eat, powerful enough to evict you.

b.text: Luosifen, you're the only dish named after a snail that contains zero snails. They simmer the snails for hours, then throw them out, like a dad who shows up for the paternity test and leaves. Your real star is suan sun, fermented bamboo shoot that smells like a gym sock studied abroad in Liuzhou and came back with opinions. Fans say, "It smells terrible but tastes amazing." So does every scam. You turned instant noodles into a hazmat event: one packet opened in a dorm and three floors file noise complaints, because that smell is *loud*. Couriers wrap you in four bags like evidence. And you come with seven sachets: chili oil, peanuts, tofu skin, wood ear, the bamboo. It's IKEA furniture that makes the neighbors move out. Liuzhou didn't invent a soup. It invented Stockholm syndrome with chili oil.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, and you couldn't even make it to the branches. You just hang off the trunk like a drunk uncle clinging to a lamppost.

You weigh eighty pounds. That's not a fruit, that's a fourth grader in a bumpy green costume. People cut you open and need cooking oil on their hands and knives, because your insides are basically rubber cement. You're the only produce that requires a solvent.

And vegans love you because when you're young, you taste like absolutely nothing. Your big career move is pretending to be pulled pork. Your whole identity is "not bad if you drown me in barbecue sauce."

Then you ripen and smell like Juicy Fruit gum fermenting in a gym bag.

You're the national fruit of Bangladesh, and you still find time to fall on people's heads.

b.text: Jackfruit, you look like a sea mine that got into a fight with a durian and lost. Your skin is a crime scene of little green spikes, and nobody has ever cut you open without a prayer and a machete. You're the size of a toddler, you smell like gym socks dipped in bubblegum, and you're somehow both sweet and wet and still sticky after you've been in the fridge. Vegans found you and suddenly you're "pulled pork," which is the most desperate rebrand since "vegetable oil" tried to be a steak. Everybody's grandma loves you for one week a year, then you rot on the counter and the whole kitchen knows. You're a fruit that needs its own safety briefing. Nobody's ever walked out of a grocery store saying, "I'll have the enormous spiky thing that smells like a locker room."

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, the only city where you can see the Eiffel Tower, a pyramid, and Venice in one afternoon and still feel like you never left a strip mall in Ohio. You're a city built in the desert out of pure spite and borrowed water. The Colorado River is literally drying up so a fake volcano can erupt every fifteen minutes for a guy in cargo shorts holding a yard-long margarita.

Your casinos have no clocks and no windows, which is smart, because nobody wants to know it's 9 a.m. on a Tuesday and Grandma's on her third oxygen tank at the Wheel of Fortune slots.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas"? Sure. Mostly your 401(k). And now you've got the Sphere, a giant glowing eyeball, so the whole city can watch you make every mistake in 4K.

b.text: Vegas, you're the only city where the pyramid has a light beam shooting into space, and somehow the most depressing thing is the hotel. You've got a fake Venice with a gondolier who's clearly on a break from his real job at the Gap. Eiffel Tower at 1/4 scale, so the French are just fine with you as long as you keep the Eiffel Tower a little embarrassed. Your slogan is "What happens here stays here," which is a lie, because I've seen what happens here, and it's all showing up on my credit card statement in the spring. You run on oxygen that's pumped into casinos so nobody notices the clock. Your buffets are all-you-can-eat, which is a dare. You're a city built on the idea that the house always wins, and honestly, Vegas, you're the house.

facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text: UGG boots. The only footwear named after a review. Australian surfers made these to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow America decided the ocean was the mall. They're sheepskin, which means a sheep died so you could wear a slipper to the DMV. One puddle and they're covered in salt lines like a topographic map of everywhere you regret going. Zero arch support, so after two weeks your heel caves sideways and you're walking on the boot's ankle like it owes you money. You wear them barefoot, so by February they smell like a wet lamb's final wish. They're as waterproof as a muffin. Oprah put them on her Favorite Things list. She's since moved on. Twenty years later they're back with platform soles, proving even a mistake wants to be taller.

b.text:
UGG boots look like someone skinned a Muppet and asked you to wear the evidence. They're the only footwear where the sales pitch is "it's like walking on a cloud" and the cloud is a wet sheepdog.

Nobody's ever said "nice UGGs" without a tiny pause for mercy.

They're technically slippers that got promoted past their competence. You can wear them to the grocery store, but God help you if it drizzles, because suede plus water equals two damp loaves of bread strapped to your calves.

And the shape! Your ankle disappears. You walk in and a stranger thinks you have the legs of a Clydesdale. That's not a boot, that's a hoof cozy.

The inside smells like a gym bag in a sauna by month two, because they're meant to be worn sockless, which is a bold design choice for something with no ventilation and a lifetime of regret.

Also, they cost two hundred dollars. For slippers. That Australians apparently wear to surf, which tells you everything about Australians.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text:
HSQ, hydrogen silsesquioxane, the only resist that's basically glass pretending to be a photoresist. You're the diva of nanofabrication. Shelf life? Three months, if you keep it cold, treat it gently, and whisper affirmations. Open the bottle wrong and you've got a jar of gel with commitment issues.

You're a negative tone resist, which is fitting, because that's the attitude. Everyone wants 10-nanometer lines, and you deliver them, then collapse because a developer rinse looked at you funny. Capillary forces: your Achilles heel, your whole personality.

And your dose? You need a thousand microcoulombs per square centimeter. That's not exposure, that's a hostage negotiation with the beam. Writing one wafer takes longer than my last relationship.

Then you cure into silicon dioxide and just sit there, permanent, like a bad tattoo. "Oh, you wanted to remove me? Enjoy your hydrofluoric acid, hero."

Gorgeous resolution, though. Truly. Shame about everything else.

b.text: Let's talk about HSQ, the e-beam resist that's basically a diva. You spin it on, bake it, expose it, and it's supposed to be your friend, but it's secretly already becoming glass. Leave the bottle in the fridge too long and it gels into a sad, cloudy paste, like a relationship that stopped talking to you. Develop it in TMAH and it still acts like it's doing you a favor. And lift-off? Forget it. Once HSQ is exposed, it's SiO2 with a attitude, and it's not leaving your substrate without a fight. It's the only thing in the cleanroom that's been baked, exposed, and developed, and still wants to be left alone.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text: Risk is the only board game where the map is the villain. Australia is one continent with four borders, and somehow it's the thing everyone wants to fight over. Kamchatka is a Russian peninsula nobody could find if you paid them, and it becomes the most important place on Earth for six straight hours. You know the game's dragging when you're hoping someone rolls a three just to end the suffering. The dice are cheap six-siders you shake in a cup, so entire wars get decided by two guys who could lose a continent in the time it takes to say "I'm not mad, I'm just disappointed." And there's always that guy eliminated since nine o'clock, still sitting at the table holding his cards like a hostage negotiation, begging someone to betray their ally and save him. Nobody has ever finished Risk. You just stop when the pizza's cold.

b.text:
Risk is the only game where you can conquer the entire planet and still lose to the guy who's been hiding in Australia since 7 p.m. Four territories, one entrance, and he just sits there like a guy at a party who won't leave the snack table.

This game has a map drawn by someone who heard about geography once, at a bar. Kamchatka borders Alaska. Ukraine is the size of Brazil. Yakutsk and Irkutsk are vital military objectives, and nobody at the table can find them on a real map.

The rules say the defender wins ties, which is the most realistic thing about it, because nobody actually finishes Risk. They just quit at 2 a.m. when someone's dad flips the board over Siberia.

And the pieces? Little plastic cannons and horses. Napoleonic warfare, global scale, and the whole thing is decided by rolling a 6 against your cousin Greg.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8 was the only operating system that made you feel like a burglar in your own computer. You'd boot up, and there's no Start button. Microsoft just removed it, like a doctor deciding you've never needed a pulse.

Instead, you got a screen of giant colorful tiles, designed for tablets, which you didn't own, running on a desktop, which you did. Every app opened full-screen, so checking the weather meant your entire monitor said "72 degrees" at you in a font the size of a billboard.

And how do you shut it down? Hover your mouse in the top-right corner, wait for the Charms bar to appear like a shy ghost, click Settings, then Power. Four steps to turn off a computer. People Googled it. Millions of people Googled how to turn off their computer.

Then came the hot corners, where moving your mouse an inch too far opened things you didn't ask for.

Microsoft eventually apologized with 8.1 by bringing back the Start button. It just opened the tiles. That's not an apology. That's a hostage returning your shoe.

b.text:
Windows 8, you looked at a billion people with a mouse and a keyboard and said, "What if your monitor was a giant phone you can't touch?"

You took away the Start button. The one thing a user knew how to find. Microsoft had literally sold Windows 95 with a Rolling Stones song called "Start Me Up," and you said, "Nah."

Want to shut down? Easy: hover in a secret corner, summon the Charms bar, click Settings, click Power. Turning off my computer shouldn't feel like unlocking a cheat code.

Your tiles were so ugly even the name "Metro" had to get dropped over a trademark dispute. Then 8.1 brought back the Start button, which just opened the same tiles. That's not an apology, that's a hostage video.

You were so bad Microsoft skipped the number 9 entirely just to put distance between you and Windows 10.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: Nobody's ever been mugged for an NFT, and that's the scam. You can't steal it, you can't hang it on a wall, and you can't even right-click save it without the cartoon ape judging you. You paid four thousand dollars for a receipt. A receipt that says, "I own the JPEG of a bored monkey," and the JPEG is still sitting on a server in Ohio, unbothered. Your grandma bought Beanie Babies and at least she got a fabric bear she could hug. You bought a hyperlink with a pulse. And the best part? The guy who sold it to you already cashed out and bought a yacht named after the ape you didn't get to keep.

b.text:
NFTs are the only product where "right-click, save as" is a legitimate threat to a billion-dollar market. You didn't buy art. You bought a receipt for a JPEG that anyone can look at for free, and the receipt is a hyperlink, and the hyperlink is hosted on a server that's going down when the startup runs out of money. Congratulations, you own a 404.

And the names! Bored Ape. Doodle. CryptoPunk. Nothing says "serious investor" like a man in a blazer whispering, "I'm down forty grand on a cartoon monkey, but the community is strong."

Everyone was a visionary until the gas fees showed up. You paid sixty dollars in Ethereum fees to buy a picture of a rock that was worth four dollars, then listed it for a million because a guy named xX_DiamondHandz_Xx said it would "flip."

It didn't flip. It just sat there. Like a rock.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you're proof that a marketing team can convince people to pay four dollars for slightly beige water. You're 2% almonds. Two percent! That's not milk, that's a rumor of a nut passing through a carton.

You took one of the thirstiest crops in California, a state that's permanently on fire, and said, "Let's drink it, but make it weaker." A single almond needs about a gallon of water to grow, and you thanked it by diluting it back into water.

You curdle in coffee like you're having a panic attack. You separate in the fridge and need to be shaken like a Polaroid. And the ingredients list? Carrageenan, gellan gum, "natural flavors." Nothing says "plant-based wholesome" like sunflower lecithin doing the heavy lifting.

You're what a cow would invent as revenge: a drink so bland that dairy suddenly looks like a personality.

Still, I'll keep buying you. Nobody else lets me feel virtuous while eating cereal.

b.text:
Almond milk, you're not milk. You're a rumor about an almond. Two percent almonds, ninety-eight percent "we strained the tap." You're the only drink that needs a legal team to call itself milk. The dairy lobby has spent a decade trying to make you admit you're nut juice.

California spends about a gallon of water per almond just so you can show up in my fridge as... water. That's like melting a glacier to make an ice cube.

They truck in billions of bees to pollinate your orchards, and the bees die by the millions so I can pay an extra eighty cents at Starbucks for a latte that tastes like damp drywall.

And "shake well"? Leave you alone for ten minutes and you separate like a couple who met at Whole Foods. Even *you* can't commit to you.

a.text:

You come from a nut that's been soaked in water until it gave up. Somebody squeezed a almond, looked at the sad little puddle, and said, "Yep, that's breakfast."

You're so thin, I can read a newspaper through you. Your idea of creamy is a rumor. You've got less body than a Tuesday. And every carton of you says "Unsweetened" like you're proud of it, like there's a single person alive who wanted to taste nothing.

Almond milk, you're the guy who says he's "not really into drinking" and then orders the oat latte.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass was the only gadget that made you look like a robot and a creep at the same time. You'd walk into a bar, and before you ordered, everyone had already figured out you were filming them. "Don't worry, I'm not recording." Sure, buddy, and that's why there's a little red light blinking on your face like a smoke detector with a grudge.

And the battery! It lasted about as long as a Google product lasts before they cancel it. You'd spend the whole day with a computer on your head that could barely make it to lunch. Your own eyeballs had better uptime, and they're held together by tiny veins and spite.

Then there was the name. "Glass." Nothing says "I'm trustworthy and affordable" like a device you'd have to tape a sign to, reading "Please don't break my face."

b.text:
Google Glass was the only product where the beta testers were called "Explorers," because "Guinea Pigs With Fourteen Hundred Dollars" tested poorly.

It was a computer you wore on your face that said "OK Glass" out loud, so every guy using it looked like he was being polite to a ghost. You didn't need a screen. You needed a wink and a prayer. Winking took a photo, which is a fantastic feature if you want to be punched in a bar.

And that's where they were banned: bars, casinos, strip clubs, movie theaters. Glass was the first device kicked out of places for what it *might* do. Even the strip club said, "Sir, we have standards."

They called the wearers "Glassholes," which is the rare nickname that came with the product, free, no subscription.

Google didn't discontinue it. They pivoted it to factories, where nobody has to look at you.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the vehicle for people who looked at electric cars and said, "Too convenient."

You can only fuel up at one of about fifty stations in the entire state of California, and half of them are "temporarily" closed, like a Blockbuster with a hopeful sign. Owners plan road trips like they're smuggling something.

The fuel costs more per mile than driving a Bentley on champagne. And the whole thing runs on the most abundant element in the universe, which is somehow harder to find than a parking spot at Costco.

Toyota calls it the Mirai, Japanese for "future." Technically accurate. That's where the gas stations are.

The only emission is water, which is great, because you'll be standing next to the car for an hour, watching it drip, wondering why you didn't just buy a Tesla.

Hydrogen: the future of transportation, and always will be.

b.text: Hydrogen fuel-cell cars are the most optimistic thing ever built. Think about it: you take the most abundant element in the universe, and then you spend a fortune compressing it to 700 bar, bolting it into a tank, and driving it to a station that's closed. Toyota's Mirai has more hydrogen stations in its dreams than in California. Some states have exactly one, and it's always broken. You pull up, the pump says "Out of Service," and you realize you've just become a very expensive lawn ornament. Meanwhile, your electric neighbor is charging in his garage in his pajamas. Hydrogen cars are like a guy who proposes on a first date and then can't find the ring.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, the "King of Fruits." Sure, if the kingdom is a landfill. You're banned on the Singapore subway, right there on the sign next to flammable liquids, because apparently you're the bigger hazard. Hotels fine guests for sneaking you in. That's not a fruit, that's a parole violation.

You wear a medieval mace as a jacket, which is smart, since nobody who's smelled you wants to get close anyway. You fall out of trees and put people in the hospital. You're the only produce that needs a hard hat AND a hazmat suit.

And your fans swear you're "like custard!" Sure: custard aged in a gym bag full of rotten onions. Fifty bucks for a Musang King, and your breath's a crime scene for three days.

Anthony Bourdain ate warthog rectum on camera, and *you're* the one he warned people about.

b.text: Durian, you smell like a gym sock that got left in a sewer and then decided to become a fruit out of spite. People in Singapore have to ride the MRT with signs warning them about you. Signs! You're banned from hotels. Hotels! They don't ban guests who set fire to the carpet, but they draw the line at you. And the worst part? You're shaped like a medieval mace someone dipped in a hedgehog. Nobody approaches you with a knife, they approach you with a shovel and a prayer. Fans call your taste "custardy." Custardy? Honey, that's what a gym sock would taste like if it had a rich uncle.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text: The Apple Vision Pro costs 3,500 dollars, which is a used Honda, for a headset that makes you look like a welder who wandered into the Apple Store. The front screen shows your eyes to everyone around you, so people don't see a person. They see a dead-eyed aquarium. You click by staring at things and pinching the air, like you're trying to hypnotize your own hand. The battery lives in your pocket on a cable, so you're not free, you're tethered to a fanny pack. Apple calls it spatial computing. I call it the only device that lets you wander your living room in a 3,500-dollar blindfold and still walk straight into the couch.

b.text:
Apple Vision Pro, you cost $3,499 and still need a battery on a cord like a 1996 Walkman. Two hours of charge? That's not spatial computing, that's a matinee. Wear glasses? Zeiss inserts, extra. Apple saw you squinting and smelled revenue.

And EyeSight! A front screen showing your eyes so people feel connected. Nothing says "I'm present" like blurry cartoon eyeballs trapped behind ski-goggle glass. Your Persona avatar looks like a hostage video directed by a ghost.

You promised the future, and Netflix wouldn't even make you an app. You strap over a pound to dads' faces so they can record "spatial memories" of birthdays they watched through a screen.

Apple said you'd never see the world the same way. True. Now it's through a $3,500 face fridge.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text:
Papyrus, look at you. A 23-year-old drew you with a calligraphy pen in 1982, trying to imagine what English would look like 2,000 years ago, and somehow you became the official font of every place that sells crystals next to a tanning bed. You're on yoga studios, hookah lounges, and the church bake sale flyer for "Loaves & Fishes & Brownies."

Your letters look like they were chiseled by a Pharaoh with a hangover. That little floaty bar on your capital E? Even your crossbars are trying to leave.

James Cameron spent a billion dollars inventing an alien language, then labeled the poster with a font that came free with Microsoft Office. Ryan Gosling got an entire SNL sketch out of being haunted by you.

Even your creator says he's sick of you. Comic Sans has haters. You have a dad who wants a refund.

b.text: Papyrus is the font that wants so badly to be ancient Egyptian it forgot to check whether it's the right century. It was made in 1983, on a computer, by someone with a hunch and no interest in pharaohs. Yet it's on every yoga studio sign, vegan café menu, and candle that says "Blessed." Its letters look like they were chiseled by someone who loves the idea of a tomb but has never stood in one. Wedding invitations, wine bars, tiki shacks: they all reach for Papyrus like it's wisdom. Look at that lopsided W, like it had three margaritas before it got written. It's the typographic equivalent of a man in a linen shirt at a funeral, and it's nobody's ancestor.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk, you're what happens when a bowl of oatmeal gets ghosted and decides to live in a carton. You're not milk. You're oatmeal that went through a breakup and is now "finding itself" in a Brooklyn coffee shop.

You cost seven dollars, and for that, you taste like a wet cereal bowl that someone rinsed with regret. Baristas call you "creamy." You're not creamy. You're just thick, like the guy at the party explaining his podcast.

You separate in hot coffee like you've got commitment issues, then leave a gritty film at the bottom that feels like drinking a handshake from a sandcastle.

And the label says "Barista Edition." Barista Edition? Oh good, you've got a job title now. Cow's milk never needed a LinkedIn.

Your whole personality is "I'm not dairy." Congratulations. Neither is drywall, and it's got a better shelf life.

b.text: Oat milk, you're not a milk. You're a breakfast cereal that got lost on the way to the cereal aisle and decided to become a beverage out of spite. Somebody took a bowl of oatmeal, ran it through a blender, strained out the dignity, and called it "barista blend." Barista? You've never made a latte in your life. You just foam up like a bubble bath and tell everyone you're the sustainable one. Congratulations, you're the only drink that needs a wellness influencer to explain what's in it. Cows just stand there and produce; you need a whole marketing campaign with a sunrise on the carton. And that sad grey sediment at the bottom of the glass? That's you, admitting the truth.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text: Comic Sans, you look like a font that got a job as a birthday clown and then got fired for scaring the kids. Every letter is wearing pajamas. Your "a" is a little round hat with a hook on it, like it's always about to go to a yard sale. Your "g" is a pretzel that lost an argument with itself. You were designed by Vincent Connare in 1994 to look like a comic book speech bubble, and you have been ruining wedding invitations and hospice signs ever since. Nobody ever chose you on purpose. People open a menu, see you, and quietly give up on being taken seriously. You're the only typeface that makes a lost cat poster sound like a ransom note written by a substitute teacher.

b.text:
Comic Sans, you were born in 1994 to put words in the mouth of a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the one that survived. Bob is dead. The dog is dead. You're on a sympathy card at a funeral home.

You were inspired by Batman comics, and you've never once been near anything heroic. CERN used you to announce the Higgs boson: humanity's greatest discovery, presented like a lemonade stand. Dan Gilbert used you to call LeBron a traitor, because nothing says "furious billionaire" like bubble letters.

And your defense is always "Well, I help dyslexic readers." Great. You're the guy at the party whose whole personality is a doctor's note.

Even Vincent Connare, the man who made you, says he's barely ever used you. Your own dad won't put you on the fridge.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. The same stuff as the shield at a hockey rink, and somehow you're the pride of the cleanroom. You have sub-10 nanometer resolution and the etch resistance of a wet napkin. Every pattern you make is gorgeous for exactly as long as nobody tries to use it.

You need a dose that would tan a small village, and for what? So the beam can snip your chains one at a time like a slow, expensive haircut? Then we bathe you in MIBK and IPA, and you dissolve only if the ratio is right, the temperature is right, and the moon is in the proper phase.

Overdo the dose and you flip negative-tone out of spite, cross-linking into a crust that no solvent can remove. Everyone loves a bilayer 495/950 for the undercut, because even you know you need a support system.

And liftoff? Acetone, sonication, three hours, and a prayer. You're a clingy ex.

b.text: Ladies and gentlemen, PMMA, the e-beam resist that's just Plexiglass with a graduate degree. You know what else is sharp and transparent and you can't eat? A window. PMMA takes a beam of electrons, snaps its chains apart, and then acts shocked when the developer washes away exactly the parts it chose to lose. Its sensitivity is so low you need a dose that would make a lesser polymer file for disability. You bake it at 180 degrees, wait, spin it, wait, bake again, and it still makes you feel like you're the one being exposed. Its etch resistance is about as strong as a wet paper towel. But sure, it draws lines thinner than a virus's dream, so we just keep inviting it back, like that one relative who only shows up to tell you what you did wrong.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text:
Macau, you're Las Vegas that went to a Portuguese finishing school and came back with gambling debt and a custard tart habit. You make more money from gambling than Vegas does, but you're only 12 square miles. That's not a city, that's a casino with a postal code.

You've got a replica Eiffel Tower, a Venice with fake canals, and a Roman-style sky painted on the ceiling. Nothing here is original except the egg tarts, and even those are Portuguese. You even stole those, Macau, you just added a Cantonese accent.

The streets have Portuguese names, but nobody speaks Portuguese. It's colonialism's most elegant ghost town. Every sign is written in a language the entire population ignores, like a terms and conditions page.

And the traffic! A million tourists walking between hotels that are all technically the same hotel. You've got a Grand Lisboa shaped like a golden lotus, or as locals call it, a giant birdcage for losing gamblers.

Come for the ruins of St. Paul's. Stay because the ferry back to Hong Kong costs exactly what you have left.

b.text:
Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a front wall. Fitting, since the whole city is a facade: a fake Venice with a painted sky, a half-size Eiffel Tower, and a Grand Lisboa that looks like a golden pineapple trying to cheat at baccarat.

Portugal ruled you for 442 years and left behind egg tarts and street signs nobody can pronounce. Four centuries, one pastry.

You've made several times more gambling money than Las Vegas, yet your signature dish is a pork chop jammed in a bun. Classy.

Half your land was dug out of the sea, which is perfect, because the other half was dug out of tourists' pockets.

And they built a 55-kilometer bridge to connect you to Hong Kong, and it's emptier than a junket operator's promises. Even the bridge is losing at the tables.

You can only fuel up at one of about fifty stations in the entire state of California, and half of them are "temporarily" closed, like a Blockbuster with a hopeful sign. Owners plan road trips like they're smuggling something.

b.text: Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle powered by the most abundant element in the universe that still can't find a gas station. California has about fifty pumps, and half of them are "temporarily offline," which is hydrogen for "go home." Its one emission is water, so it's technically the cleanest car on Earth, as long as you don't ask where the hydrogen came from. Spoiler: natural gas. It's a fossil fuel car in a witness protection program. Toyota gave Mirai buyers fifteen grand in free fuel, which sounds generous until you realize that at thirty-six bucks a kilo it covers roughly a year of driving, and the car loses that much value on the drive home. You're sitting on a tank pressurized to 10,000 psi to go three hundred miles. Even the Hindenburg would say, "Maybe just get a Tesla."

The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text: Ladies and gentlemen, PMMA, the e-beam resist that's just Plexiglass with a graduate degree. You know what else is sharp and transparent and you can't eat? A window. PMMA takes a beam of electrons, snaps its chains apart, and then acts shocked when the developer washes away exactly the parts it chose to lose. Its sensitivity is so low you need a dose that would make a lesser polymer file for disability. You bake it at 180 degrees, wait, spin it, wait, bake again, and it still makes you feel like you're the one being exposed. Its etch resistance is about as strong as a wet paper towel. But sure, it draws lines thinner than a virus's dream, so we just keep inviting it back, like that one relative who only shows up to tell you what you did wrong.

b.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. Somewhere your cousin is a sneeze guard at Chipotle, and honestly? Your cousin has better etch resistance. One whiff of plasma and you vanish faster than a grad student's weekend.

You've been the "gold standard" since the 1970s, which is a polite way of saying nobody's been able to fire you. You need hundreds of microcoulombs just to *notice* the beam. A 40-hour write for one wafer. Glacial, but sure, sub-10-nanometer lines, we get it.

Positive resist? Overdose you and you cross-link into a *negative* one. That's not versatility, that's an identity crisis.

You get developed in MIBK, which smells like regret, and you come in 495K and 950K because one of you alone can't even do liftoff. And acetone dissolves you instantly. Even your solvents think you're temporary.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP, you're the only language whose name is a recursive acronym, and your mascot is an elephant that's been sitting on servers since 1995. You slap a dollar sign on every variable like you're charging us by the letter. Your function names look like they were typed during a power outage: strpos wants the haystack first, array_search wants the needle first, and you just shrugged. You told us "0" == false is true and "1e3" == "1000" is true, and we nodded like that makes sense. Magic quotes, register_globals, mysql_ functions you kept around like a grandma's ugly couch. Somehow you run half the internet. Honestly, that's the scariest part.

b.text:
PHP. You started as "Personal Home Page," then rebranded as "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a recursive acronym, because even your name couldn't commit to a stable API.

For twenty years, "abc" == 0 was true, and you called it "type juggling," like a clown proud of dropping things.

strpos takes haystack, needle. array_search takes needle, haystack. That's not argument order; that's mood swings.

Your parse error says T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM. That's Hebrew for "double colon" and English for "good luck."

You skipped version 6 entirely. Even your release numbers just wanted to move on.

You shipped mysql_real_escape_string, implying the first one was a hoax.

Facebook loved you so much they invented Hack just to avoid touching you.

But sure, you power most of the web. Mostly WordPress. That's like bragging your biggest fan is a raccoon.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs is the only text editor that ships with a psychotherapist, and you'll need it. M-x doctor exists because the developers knew exactly what they were doing to people.

It's a great operating system. It has a mail client, a web browser, Tetris, and a Lisp interpreter. What it lacks is a decent text editor. Its most beloved package is Evil mode, which is just Vim wearing an Emacs costume. That's like buying a Ferrari and installing a horse.

Want to save? C-x C-s. Want to quit? C-x C-c. Want to feel your left pinky again? Too late. Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," and the RSI stands for "you chose this."

Every user has a 4,000-line init.el they don't understand, copied from strangers on Stack Overflow in 2009.

b.text: Emacs is the only text editor that's also an operating system that never got around to booting. People say it's "a great operating system, just missing a good editor." Sure. You open it and it's already running a calendar, a email client, a chess engine, and a psychiatrist. You wanted to type "hello." Instead you get a *Ctrl-x Ctrl-c* keyboard combo, which is the only way out, and it requires two hands, a pinky that's been to physical therapy, and the blessing of a man named Richard who hasn't been seen since 1985. Vim users at least get a funny exit. Emacs users get a seven-keystroke prayer. And the config file? It's a Lisp dialect that's older than your parents' divorce, with parentheses so deep you need a mountain guide. Brilliant software. Terrible hostage negotiator.

a.text:
Google Sheets: the only software where you can watch a coworker named "Anonymous Capybara" ruin your formulas in real time.

You're the Excel that went to community college and told everyone it's "basically the same." Then someone adds 40,000 rows and you wheeze "Loading..." like a Chromebook climbing stairs.

Your formula for combining data from another sheet is IMPORTRANGE, which immediately yells #REF! until I click "Allow access," like I'm asking you to the prom. Your most advanced function, QUERY, makes me write SQL inside a text string, inside a cell, inside a spreadsheet. That's not a feature. That's a hostage video.

Every file on earth is named "Copy of Copy of Budget FINAL v2," shared with "anyone with the link," and owned by Brenda, who left in 2019. I click "Request edit access" and the void answers.

And the 10 million cell limit? Bold of you to assume anyone's budget is that organized. Mine is three tabs and a dream.

b.text: Google Sheets, you're the spreadsheet that waits until I've typed three paragraphs of data before you tell me I've been editing a "view-only" copy this whole time. You're the only app where "Saving..." becomes a lifestyle. Your formulas are so fragile that one missing comma turns my budget into a column of #REF! like I'm a hacker's ransom note. And VLOOKUP? You make me hunt for the exact column index like it's a secret handshake. Every time I try to add a chart, you act like I asked you to build a cathedral. Sure, you're free, and you're everywhere, but that's just what happens when your whole personality is "well, at least it's not Excel."

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole with a publicist. You order one and the waiter says "forty-five minutes," which is how long it takes to bake and also how long it takes to finish one slice. They put the sauce on top and the cheese underneath, like they're hiding evidence. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up. The crust is a buttery retaining wall holding back a lake of chunky tomato, because apparently Lake Michigan wasn't enough water for one city to manage. You need a knife, a fork, a nap, and a cardiologist on retainer. Then there's the sausage, laid down as one solid patty like the base layer of a parking garage. Chicagoans defend it like family. Sure: the relative who shows up late, takes up three chairs, and leaves everyone unable to move.

b.text:
Chicago deep-dish isn't pizza, it's a casserole with an identity crisis. You order it, and they say, "That'll be 45 minutes." Forty-five minutes! For bread! I've seen people give birth faster, and the baby came out less cooked.

Then it arrives, and it's built upside down. Cheese on the bottom, sauce on top. That's not a recipe, that's a structural failure. It's a pizza that fell down the stairs and everyone decided to call it tradition.

You get one slice, and it requires a spatula, a fork, a knife, and a signed waiver. Your first bite is molten cheese lava. Your second bite is a tomato landslide. By the third, you're lying on the booth like you've been shot by a lasagna.

And Chicagoans defend this! "It's the real pizza." Sir, you eat soup with a crust and call New Yorkers wrong. That's a pie chart with a cardiologist.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk, you are porridge that got a publicist. Somebody looked at the breakfast of Victorian orphans and said, "What if it cost six dollars and had a font?"

Your carton talks to me. Oatly, I'm trying to make coffee, not get into a pen-pal situation with a beverage that writes like a substitute teacher who wants to be called "Dave."

You're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not milk, that's a salad dressing that gave up. And they had to add enzymes to turn your starch into sugar so you'd taste like something. You're the only "health drink" that spikes my blood sugar like a Pop-Tart.

There's a "Barista Edition" now. Oat milk, there are two editions of you. Moby-Dick has fewer editions than you.

And you're beige. You make every latte look like dishwater with ambition.

Horses eat oats for free, and they still look embarrassed for us.

b.text:
Oat milk, you're what happens when a bowl of oatmeal gets ghosted and decides to live in a carton. You're not milk. You're oatmeal that went through a breakup and is now "finding itself" in a Brooklyn coffee shop.

You cost seven dollars, and for that, you taste like a wet cereal bowl that someone rinsed with regret. Baristas call you "creamy." You're not creamy. You're just thick, like the guy at the party explaining his podcast.

You separate in hot coffee like you've got commitment issues, then leave a gritty film at the bottom that feels like drinking a handshake from a sandcastle.

And the label says "Barista Edition." Barista Edition? Oh good, you've got a job title now. Cow's milk never needed a LinkedIn.

Your whole personality is "I'm not dairy." Congratulations. Neither is drywall, and it's got a better shelf life.

b.text: Deep-dish pizza is the only food where you need a fork, a knife, and a structural engineer. You order a slice and the waiter brings you a casserole with a crust like a bank vault. The sauce sits on top, which is the pizza equivalent of wearing your shirt on the outside of your jacket. Chicagoans will tell you it's "not pizza, it's a pie," which is what you say when you've eaten something that requires a 45-minute wait and still leaves you feeling like you've been mugged by cheese. Locals eat it with a straight face. Tourists eat it with a flashlight, looking for the bottom. And somewhere under there, buried under three pounds of mozzarella, is a tomato that has never once been invited to the party.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Slack, the only place where "Quick question" is a threat. Nobody has ever had a quick question. Just a little typing bubble that appears, disappears, appears again, and then nothing, like a ghost deciding whether to haunt you.

You took email, which everyone hated, and said, "What if it were faster, and your boss could watch you be green?" Now I can't go to the bathroom without my status turning yellow like I'm a traffic light of shame.

And the notifications. That little red badge. Forty-seven unread in #general, which is just a graveyard of birthday gifs and a guy named Doug asking who took his yogurt.

The emoji reactions are how adults now communicate. A thumbs-up means "I acknowledge you." The eyes emoji means "I saw this and will do nothing." And the little checkmark means "done," which is the biggest lie since "let's circle back."

Slack: you replaced meetings with meetings that never end.

b.text:
You know what Slack is? It's a meeting that refuses to start. Somebody's typing for four minutes, and then it's just "k." Thanks, Dave. Four minutes for a letter.

And the little dots! Everybody's watching those dots like they're a heart monitor. "Dave is typing..." Dave has been typing since Tuesday.

Slack is where we go to "circle back" and never come back. Then there's the huddle. You can't call it a meeting, because that would be too honest. It's a "huddle," like we're a bunch of football players who just need a quick word about the Dorito situation.

And the status emoji! Little palm tree, "OOO." Sure, Brenda. You're on a beach, and you're replying to #marketing-updates from a beach.

You just foam up like a bubble bath and tell everyone you're the sustainable one. Congratulations, you're the only drink that needs a wellness influencer to explain what's in it. Cows just stand there and produce; you need a whole marketing campaign with a sunrise on the carton. And that sad grey sediment at the bottom of the glass? That's you, admitting the truth.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text: Canberra is the only capital in Australia built from scratch, which explains a lot. Sydney and Melbourne were so busy hating each other they agreed to put the country's brain in a paddock halfway between them, and it has been sulking ever since. Walter Burley Griffin drew it up as a neat wheel of boulevards around a lake, then the public servants arrived and discovered that every road in town is a roundabout. Nobody has ever found the way out of Civic. The nightlife shuts at nine because the whole city is in bed before Question Time ends. The lake is named after Griffin, which is a shame, because he's the only man ever to design a city and then get a lake named after him instead of a train station. In winter the frost is so thick the ministers need a scraper before they can go inside and be lied to.

b.text:
Canberra is what happens when a committee designs a city and nobody's allowed to have an opinion until the subcommittee reports back. It's the only place where the lake is fake, the hills are decorative, and the excitement is a roundabout. Seriously, you can't give directions without saying "take the third exit, then the third exit again, then cry."

It's a city of 450,000 people, and 449,000 of them are named "Director of Strategic Alignment." The nightlife is a public servant having a second flat white after 2 p.m. Wild.

Every winter it hits minus five, and the locals call that "character." Every summer it's bushfire smoke, so basically a free vape.

And the Aussie icon is a giant flagpole. That's the whole personality: a pole, and a stern reminder to submit your timesheet.

Canberra: a nice place to visit if you've never wanted to.

a.text: Canberra: the only city where the traffic jam is a roundabout with a sculpture in the middle. A century ago, someone looked at a sheep paddock between Sydney and Melbourne and said, "Let's put the whole country's government here so nobody has to visit." And it worked. Parliament House sits on its hill like a very expensive filing cabinet. The lake is named after an American architect, and it's the most exciting thing that happens here. Winter mornings hit minus four, and the only people outside are joggers with a grudge. Friday night out means the Civic bar, where everyone's a public servant with a lanyard still on. Nobody lives in Canberra. They're just waiting for a posting.

b.text: Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree, so Australia built a city nobody wanted, which is honestly the most Canberra origin story possible: a compromise with suburbs. They held an international design competition and hired two Americans to plan it, and they nailed the brief: "Make it impossible to find anything." Every road is a roundabout leading to another roundabout, encircling a fake lake named after the guy who designed the roundabouts. Your Parliament House has a grass roof so you can literally walk on top of the government, the only time anyone in Canberra is above a public servant. The kangaroos outnumber the nightlife. For decades your two biggest attractions were legal fireworks and X-rated videos, which tells me the locals needed both a bang and a release. Then you banned the fireworks. Now the excitement is Floriade: a month of staring at tulips because the alternative is Tuggeranong.

A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's cousin who got into tech because you could "share a link." Congrats: now forty Anonymous Capybaras can watch me botch a VLOOKUP in real time. Your whole personality is "All changes saved in Drive," which is a weird flex when the change was Kevin sorting one column and detaching every employee from their salary. Version history isn't a feature; it's a crime scene. IMPORTRANGE says "Loading..." the way my dad said he was going out for milk. You've got a QUERY function that's just SQL in a fake mustache, yet you freeze if I paste more than twelve rows. And #REF! isn't an error message; it's you shrugging in all caps. You cap out at ten million cells. Ten million. You're the only spreadsheet with a bedtime.

b.text:
Google Sheets, you're the spreadsheet equivalent of a guy who says "I'm not really a party person" and then shows up to every meeting with a pivot table. You've got 10 million cells and you still can't tell me why my VLOOKUP returned #N/A. Oh, that's not a bug, that's your personality: "Did you mean the other tab?" No, Sheets, I didn't mean the other tab. Nobody ever meant the other tab.

And don't get me started on autocomplete. I type "=SU" and you suggest SUMIF, SUMSQ, and SUBSTITUTE like you're trying to get me to commit to a divorce. Just pick one! You're a grid of cells that refuses to commit to a formula.

Your collaboration features are great, though. My boss can see my edits in real time, which is how I learned he watches me type "asdfgh" when a deadline hits.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text: Papyrus, you're a font that has never once been near Egypt. You look like a yoga studio's "Namaste" sign left out in the Sedona sun until it got fuzzy around the edges. Every letter has the texture of a wet paper bag someone tried to iron. You're the go-to for the wooden plaque in a crystal shop, right next to the "Live Laugh Love" sign and the incense nobody's bought since 2009. James Cameron used you for Avatar, and somehow an entire alien moon ended up looking like a smoothie menu. People who pick you think they're being mysterious. You're not mysterious. You're a tiki bar's menu that's sorry it opened, printed on the same paper you're named after, which is to say, nobody's real writing surface.

b.text:
Papyrus, look at you. A 23-year-old drew you with a calligraphy pen in 1982, trying to imagine what English would look like 2,000 years ago, and somehow you became the official font of every place that sells crystals next to a tanning bed. You're on yoga studios, hookah lounges, and the church bake sale flyer for "Loaves & Fishes & Brownies."

Your letters look like they were chiseled by a Pharaoh with a hangover. That little floaty bar on your capital E? Even your crossbars are trying to leave.

James Cameron spent a billion dollars inventing an alien language, then labeled the poster with a font that came free with Microsoft Office. Ryan Gosling got an entire SNL sketch out of being haunted by you.

Even your creator says he's sick of you. Comic Sans has haters. You have a dad who wants a refund.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
