Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, you beautiful $120 million monument to Silicon Valley. You launched at seven hundred dollars to squeeze a bag. A bag! Then Bloomberg reporters squeezed that same bag with their bare hands and got basically the same juice, only faster. You got outperformed by a guy with a grip strength of "typing."

Doug Evans bragged you pressed with four tons of force, enough to lift two Teslas. Buddy, it's kale. The kale didn't need a forklift.

And it needed Wi-Fi. It scanned a QR code before it'd let you drink. Your router goes down and suddenly your breakfast is asking for credentials. Who designs a juicer that can be bricked?

Google Ventures funded this. Kleiner Perkins funded this. Somewhere, a man is still holding a lukewarm pouch, waiting for a firmware update so he's allowed to eat a carrot.

b.text: Juicero raised over a hundred million dollars to build a $400 juicer that squeezed packets of pre-chopped kale. Then a reporter showed you could get the same juice by squeezing the packets with your bare hands. That's not a juicer. That's a hand. Your hand already came with the machine. The press checked a QR code on each pack before it would run, so you paid for a Wi-Fi juicer that needed the internet to tell it to do the job a towel does. And people paid it! Venture capitalists looked at a $5 bag of spinach and thought, "Yes, this needs a server." The company shut down in 2017. Honestly, that's the most productive thing the press has ever done.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text: Beanie Babies, you're the only toy whose value depends on a tag announcing you're dead. "Retired." That's not a collectible, that's a hospice with a barcode. Ty Warner figured out that if he stopped making a bear, grown adults would panic-buy it like the last lifeboat on the Titanic. Parents mortgaged houses for Peanut the Elephant. Now your grandma's attic holds forty thousand of you, each worth less than the postage to mail it. And you were the only stuffed animal with a birth certificate stapled to your butt. You're not even stuffed with beans. It's plastic pellets. Honestly, that's the most honest thing about you.

b.text:
Beanie Babies, look at you. Half bear, half beanbag, all retirement plan that never paid out. An entire generation of parents bought you instead of index funds. Somewhere a man is still storing Princess, the purple Diana bear, in a climate-controlled unit, waiting for the market to "recover." Buddy, the market recovered. It just didn't take you with it.

Your most valuable feature was a heart-shaped paper tag. People bought plastic tag protectors. For the tag. That's like buying a phone case for your receipt.

And every tag had a little poem rhyming "bear" with "care." Hallmark called that lazy.

A Las Vegas couple had to divide you on a courtroom floor during their divorce, one at a time. That's the most anyone has wanted you since 1999: only to make sure their ex didn't get you.

Ty Warner got a billion dollars. You got plastic pellets.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8 looked at the most successful desktop interface in history and said, "What if we hid the Start button, like a bathroom in a haunted house?" Microsoft designed an operating system for tablets, then shipped it to people with keyboards, mice, and spreadsheets. Nobody asked for this. Accountants were suddenly swiping at monitors like they were trying to wipe off a stain.

Shutting down the computer required a PhD. You had to summon the Charms bar by hovering in the corner of the screen like a stalker, then click Settings, then Power, then pray. My grandmother spent twenty minutes looking for the off switch and just unplugged it. Honestly, she had the right idea.

And those Live Tiles! Forty colorful rectangles flipping around telling me the weather in a city I've never visited. It wasn't an operating system, it was a toddler's busy board.

Microsoft eventually admitted the mistake and brought back the Start button. Windows 8.1 was basically an apology note taped to the door.

b.text: Windows 8, Microsoft looked at the Start button, the one thing every human on Earth knew how to use, and said, "What if we hid it?" You turned every desktop into a giant tablet nobody could touch. People were swiping at their monitors like they were wiping off a stain. Shutting you down required a treasure map: hover in a corner, summon the Charms bar, Settings, Power. Charms! Like the operating system was a bracelet from Claire's. You shipped with two Internet Explorers, which is two more than anyone wanted. Even your design name, Metro, got taken away by lawyers. And when 8.1 finally brought the Start button back, it just took you to the same tile screen. That's not an apology, that's a hostage note. You were so bad Microsoft skipped Windows 9 entirely, just to put more distance between us and you.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Comic Sans, you were literally designed for a talking dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the only part of that project that didn't die with dignity. Vincent Connare made you in 1994 for cartoon speech bubbles, and you heard that and thought, "Tombstones. Legal notices. Resignation letters."

Dan Gilbert wrote his furious LeBron James letter in you, and that's why nobody remembers being scared. CERN announced the Higgs boson, the most important physics discovery in fifty years, in you, and the entire scientific community went, "Did a third grader find God?"

People defend you because you help some readers with dyslexia, which is true and lovely, and also the only time you've ever been used responsibly.

You're not a font. You're a bake sale flyer that got tenure. Even Papyrus looks at you and says, "Wow, okay, tone it down."

b.text: Comic Sans, you look like a font that got a job as a birthday clown and then got fired for scaring the kids. Every letter is wearing pajamas. Your "a" is a little round hat with a hook on it, like it's always about to go to a yard sale. Your "g" is a pretzel that lost an argument with itself. You were designed by Vincent Connare in 1994 to look like a comic book speech bubble, and you have been ruining wedding invitations and hospice signs ever since. Nobody ever chose you on purpose. People open a menu, see you, and quietly give up on being taken seriously. You're the only typeface that makes a lost cat poster sound like a ransom note written by a substitute teacher.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8 was the only operating system that made you feel like a burglar in your own computer. You'd boot up, and there's no Start button. Microsoft just removed it, like a doctor deciding you've never needed a pulse.

Instead, you got a screen of giant colorful tiles, designed for tablets, which you didn't own, running on a desktop, which you did. Every app opened full-screen, so checking the weather meant your entire monitor said "72 degrees" at you in a font the size of a billboard.

And how do you shut it down? Hover your mouse in the top-right corner, wait for the Charms bar to appear like a shy ghost, click Settings, then Power. Four steps to turn off a computer. People Googled it. Millions of people Googled how to turn off their computer.

Then came the hot corners, where moving your mouse an inch too far opened things you didn't ask for.

Microsoft eventually apologized with 8.1 by bringing back the Start button. It just opened the tiles. That's not an apology. That's a hostage returning your shoe.

b.text:
Windows 8 was Microsoft's big bet that your desktop computer should look like a phone that got into a fight. They took the Start button, the one thing every human had memorized, and deleted it. Then they replaced it with a screen of giant colored tiles that looked like someone's grandma had designed a bank app. You'd click the corner to get back to the desktop, except the corner did something different depending on your mood. It was like a house where the front door only opens if you whistle.

And the tiles! Your Mail tile was always out of date, your Weather tile showed Miami on a Tuesday, and your Games tile was just an ad for a game you didn't ask for. Microsoft looked at a mouse and keyboard and said, "Let's make these people scroll sideways."

They eventually brought the Start button back. Windows 8 wasn't a bad operating system. It was just the one that tried to swipe its way into your life, and nobody swiped back.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text: Oat milk, you're not a milk. You're a breakfast cereal that got lost on the way to the cereal aisle and decided to become a beverage out of spite. Somebody took a bowl of oatmeal, ran it through a blender, strained out the dignity, and called it "barista blend." Barista? You've never made a latte in your life. You just foam up like a bubble bath and tell everyone you're the sustainable one. Congratulations, you're the only drink that needs a wellness influencer to explain what's in it. Cows just stand there and produce; you need a whole marketing campaign with a sunrise on the carton. And that sad grey sediment at the bottom of the glass? That's you, admitting the truth.

b.text:
Oat milk, you're what happens when a bowl of oatmeal gets ghosted and starts a podcast. You're not milk. You're porridge that went through a breakup and a juice cleanse.

You cost eight dollars a carton, and the only reason is that a barista called you "creamy" once and you've been unbearable ever since. Cows have been doing this for ten thousand years for free. You needed an enzyme and a marketing team.

You separate in hot coffee like you're being deposed. You curdle at the first sign of acid, then expect me to drink you anyway.

And the label! "Barista Edition." For what? Standing near a espresso machine? You're a beige liquid with a gym membership.

Your whole personality is that you're not almond milk, which is the lowest bar in the dairy aisle, and somehow you still tripped over it. Sweet, slimy, smug. Basically a Sunday brunch in a carton.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text:
Luosifen, you're the only dish that arrives before the delivery guy does. You're named after river snails, yet nobody has ever found one in the bowl. You boiled them for hours, took their soul, and threw out the bodies. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up.

And that smell? Fermented bamboo shoots that died, got buried, and came back for revenge. Someone opens a packet in Liuzhou and a guy in Guilin checks his shoes. College dorms banned you like a space heater. Neighbors call the gas company.

Your fans swear, "It smells terrible but tastes amazing." Buddy, that's what everyone says about their toxic ex.

Peanuts, crispy tofu skin, wood ear, pickled beans, a slick of chili oil... that's not garnish, that's witness protection for flavor.

And now you come instant. Congratulations: a biohazard with a seasoning packet.

b.text:
Luosifen, the only food that files a noise complaint with your nose. It's a noodle soup made from river snails, which is already a bold choice, then fermented sour bamboo shoots join in, and suddenly your apartment smells like a swamp got a divorce.

You open one packet and the whole building knows your business. Neighbors don't ask "what's cooking?" They ask "is someone okay?"

Liuzhou people say it's delicious. Sure, and a skunk says the same about its perfume.

And the cruelty is that it's actually amazing. Rice noodles, chili oil, peanuts, tofu skin, that sour-funky-spicy punch. You'll eat it and swear you'll never do it again, then smell your own hoodie three days later and whisper, "Same time next week?"

It's the only dish where the leftover smell outlasts the leftovers, and your elevator has stopped making eye contact with you.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text: Papyrus is the font that wants so badly to be ancient Egyptian it forgot to check whether it's the right century. It was made in 1983, on a computer, by someone with a hunch and no interest in pharaohs. Yet it's on every yoga studio sign, vegan café menu, and candle that says "Blessed." Its letters look like they were chiseled by someone who loves the idea of a tomb but has never stood in one. Wedding invitations, wine bars, tiki shacks: they all reach for Papyrus like it's wisdom. Look at that lopsided W, like it had three margaritas before it got written. It's the typographic equivalent of a man in a linen shirt at a funeral, and it's nobody's ancestor.

b.text:
Papyrus, you're the font that shows up to every event dressed for a different one. A day spa. A mediocre yoga studio. A Pirates of the Caribbean-themed dentist. You look like you were designed by someone who'd only heard about ancient Egypt from a candle.

You're so rough around the edges, it's like the letters were chiseled by a guy who got bored halfway through. Every "E" looks like it lost a fight with a staircase.

And you have the nerve to be everywhere! Organic soap. Tea shops. "Live, Laugh, Love" signs in a kitchen that's never seen a meal.

Then Ryan Gosling's character in SNL had to spend *a whole sketch* sobbing over you, because James Cameron put you on *Avatar*, a $237 million movie. Two hundred thirty-seven million dollars, and the logo looked like a restaurant's Wi-Fi password sign.

Papyrus, you're not a typeface. You're a vibe that got a license.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. The same stuff as the shield at a hockey rink, and somehow you're the pride of the cleanroom. You have sub-10 nanometer resolution and the etch resistance of a wet napkin. Every pattern you make is gorgeous for exactly as long as nobody tries to use it.

You need a dose that would tan a small village, and for what? So the beam can snip your chains one at a time like a slow, expensive haircut? Then we bathe you in MIBK and IPA, and you dissolve only if the ratio is right, the temperature is right, and the moon is in the proper phase.

Overdo the dose and you flip negative-tone out of spite, cross-linking into a crust that no solvent can remove. Everyone loves a bilayer 495/950 for the undercut, because even you know you need a support system.

And liftoff? Acetone, sonication, three hours, and a prayer. You're a clingy ex.

b.text: PMMA, you're the world's most expensive Post-it note. Someone spins you onto a silicon wafer at four thousand RPM, bakes you on a hotplate like a sad pizza, then fires electrons at you for six hours, and your big move is to dissolve in MIBK. That's your whole personality. You're a positive resist, which in your case means you only become positive once you've been destroyed. Hit you with a plasma etch and you're gone in ten seconds, so the entire process has to be built around your fragility. You're the lab's most high-maintenance divorcee. But the resolution is incredible, I'll give you that. Sub-20 nanometers, folks. Shame you can't survive a Tuesday.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text: HSQ, you're the most high-maintenance resist in the cleanroom. You live in a fridge like a sad sandwich, and leave the cap off for an afternoon and you gel into a forgotten Jell-O salad. You're negative-tone, so the exposed parts become your permanent address. You don't leave the wafer, you move in as silicon dioxide. You promise sub-10-nanometer lines, then spread out with the dose like a houseguest saying "just one more electron." Develop in salty developer and you still swell, like you're offended by the chemistry. Honestly, you're a flowable oxide with a personality disorder and an expensive price tag.

b.text:
HSQ, hydrogen silsesquioxane, the only resist that's basically glass pretending to be a photoresist. You're a negative-tone resist that turns into silicon dioxide. So after all my work, my pattern isn't a mask, it's a permanent tenant.

Your shelf life is a joke. You gel in the bottle if I look at you wrong. Open a fresh one, two weeks later it's Jell-O with commitment issues. Keep it in the fridge, and it's still aging like milk in a sauna.

And the development! Sixty nanometer lines, beautiful, then TMAH hits and they collapse like a Jenga tower. Sure, you can do sub-10 nanometer features, but only if I sacrifice a goat, run at 1000 microcoulombs per square centimeter, and sit there for nine hours while the beam writes a rectangle.

Contrast? Terrible. Sensitivity? Worse. Stripping you off? Hydrofluoric acid. You're the ex who can only be removed by something that dissolves bones.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, the material that's been "ten years from changing everything" for thirty years. You're 100 times stronger than steel, and yet somehow you've never held a job.

You're a single sheet of graphene rolled up like a sad burrito, and you still can't decide if you're a metal or a semiconductor. Chirality, right? Your entire personality depends on which way you twist. That's not physics, that's a mood ring.

Scientists say you could build a space elevator. Buddy, you can't even get through a lab without clumping together like earbuds in a pocket. Every researcher spends six months trying to disperse you, then writes "uniform" in the paper anyway.

And the manufacturing! Everyone gets a random mix of types, so sorting you is like trying to separate identical twins by vibe.

Also, you're a nanometer wide and somehow still the biggest thing in everyone's grant proposal.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The only material that's been "five years away" since 1991. You're a hundred times stronger than steel, and you've used that strength to hold together... a tennis racket. They promised us a space elevator; you can't get past a few centimeters without a defect. That's not a cable, that's a toothpick with a press agent.

You're basically graphene that rolled itself up out of insecurity, and graphene still got the Nobel. Your cousin the buckyball got one too. You got a shoutout in a bike-frame brochure.

You can't even decide if you're a metal or a semiconductor; it depends on the angle you got rolled at. You clump together like nerds at a mixer, and the second you escape, you lodge in lungs like asbestos. Strongest thing on Earth, and your best trick is ending up in a safety data sheet.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text: My mom bought forty Beanie Babies in 1998 because a man on the news said they'd pay for my college. They didn't. They're in a bin in her garage, each one still wrapped in its plastic tag protector like a tiny hostage. Ty Warner pulled off the greatest con in toy history. He retired a bear, announced it like a celebrity death, and watched grown adults panic-buy the thing they were supposed to play with. You weren't allowed to touch it, though. Touching meant fingerprints, and fingerprints meant it was worth nothing. So you didn't get a teddy bear. You got a bag of plastic pellets with a face, sitting on a shelf, guarded like the Crown Jewels.

b.text: Beanie Babies. The only retirement plan where the retiree was a five-dollar bear stuffed with plastic pellets. A whole generation bought plastic protectors for a toy's ear tag, then sealed the toy in a Ziploc so no child could ever love it. You weren't a stuffed animal; you were a 401(k) with a poem on it. And those poems! Ty Warner doing greeting-card Shakespeare for people who thought Princess the bear would pay for college. Princess paid for nothing. Neither did the Teenie Beanies everyone hoarded from McDonald's while throwing away the actual Happy Meal. A divorcing couple in Las Vegas literally split their collection on a courtroom floor, one Beanie at a time. That's your legacy: custody battles over a moose named Chocolate. Even your creator got busted hiding money from the IRS, because he was the only one who ever made any.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text: LaTeX, you're a word processor that makes me pass a programming exam just to type "hello." I need a backslash, three curly braces, and a prayer to make one word bold. Forget a single dollar sign and you scream "Missing $ inserted," like I personally mugged your math mode. Then you throw "Emergency stop" at me, which is rude, because I'm the one who's supposed to be panicking. Want a table? Enjoy three hours wrestling ampersands and \hline like they owe you money. Bibliography? Run the compiler three times, like a coach yelling "one more lap" because the first two didn't count. Your fans swear the output is gorgeous. Sure, so is a cathedral, and nobody builds a grocery list out of one.

b.text:
LaTeX is the only software where you spend six hours fixing a typo and then twelve more because the fix moved your figure to page nine.

You ask for a picture to go *here*. LaTeX says "here" is more of a "float" situation. It's not a placement, it's a vibe.

The error messages are written by someone who hates you personally. "Overfull hbox, badness 10000." Thank you, I'll tell my therapist. Meanwhile, one missing brace gives you an error on line 4,000, in a file you didn't write, from a package you never installed.

Want a different font? Enjoy a three-day journey through Stack Overflow, where the top answer is from 2009 and starts with "Just use XeTeX."

And the compile times! I changed one comma and now I'm watching it run twice, because the table of contents needs to catch up to reality.

Knuth released it in 1978 and declared it nearly bug-free. Sir, the bugs are in me. I'm the bug. I just wanted a bibliography.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you took the one drink humanity had perfected over five hundred years and said, "What if it came in a tiny plastic thimble that outlives your grandchildren?" Your own inventor said he regrets making you. When your dad disowns you, that's a phase. When the guy who invented you disowns you, that's a recall.

You make coffee one sad, lukewarm cup at a time, then flash "DESCALE" like a check-engine light for a machine that costs forty bucks. Remember Keurig 2.0? You put DRM on coffee. You were scanning pods like a bouncer: "Sorry, sir, you're not on the list." Nobody was pirating Folgers! And your "Strong" button just drips slower, which isn't strength. That's procrastination.

You're not a coffee maker. You're a plastic-dispensing subscription that occasionally hiccups out hot brown water.

b.text:
Keurig, you're the coffee maker that treats a cup of coffee like a hostage negotiation. Eight minutes of whirring, gurgling, and blinking just to produce a lukewarm thimble of brown water. Meanwhile my grandma's percolator makes a full pot before I finish reading the Wikipedia article about pour-over.

And the pods! Every cup creates a little plastic tombstone. You're basically a landfill with a power button. You've got more recyclable-pod-related guilt than my Catholic school.

Then there's the "strong" setting, which is just the regular setting with a dramatic pause. Nothing about you is bold except your price per ounce.

Keurig, you're not a coffee maker. You're a vending machine that got a cardiology degree.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text: Crocs are the only shoe that looks like it was designed by a committee of ducks. Every pair is a foam clog with holes in it, like someone started making shoes, got bored halfway through, and said, "Eh, the air can have the rest." Nobody has ever bought Crocs to look good. You buy them because they're the only shoe that can survive a flood, a hospital shift, and a barbecue at the same time. They come with little charms you snap into the holes, which is how you know the company has given up on fashion and moved into hostage negotiation: "Fine, you want a shoe, we'll give you a shoe with a pizza slice stuck in its side." And somehow they're everywhere. Grandpas, nurses, teenagers, and one guy at every Costco who hasn't left the house since 2009. Crocs don't walk, they waddle. That's not a shoe, that's a rubber duck that lost a bet.

b.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like Swiss cheese that wanted to be a boat. You were invented for sailing, and the one place nobody wears you is a boat. You're at Applebee's, squeaking across a wet floor like a dolphin in distress.

You have holes. On purpose. Then you sell us Jibbitz to fill the holes. That's not fashion, that's a protection racket with a SpongeBob charm.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind my heel doesn't make me an athlete. It makes me a toddler about to sprint into traffic.

You made a KFC bucket clog with charms that smelled like fried chicken. That's not footwear. That's a foam cry for help.

Nurses love you. Chefs love you. Which proves you're comfortable for people who've stopped caring who's looking at their feet.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text:
Google Glass was the only gadget that made you look like a robot and a creep at the same time. You'd walk into a bar, and before you ordered, everyone had already figured out you were filming them. "Don't worry, I'm not recording." Sure, buddy, and that's why there's a little red light blinking on your face like a smoke detector with a grudge.

And the battery! It lasted about as long as a Google product lasts before they cancel it. You'd spend the whole day with a computer on your head that could barely make it to lunch. Your own eyeballs had better uptime, and they're held together by tiny veins and spite.

Then there was the name. "Glass." Nothing says "I'm trustworthy and affordable" like a device you'd have to tape a sign to, reading "Please don't break my face."

b.text:
Google Glass, look at you. Fifteen hundred dollars to wear a sugar cube on your eyebrow. Sergey Brin had skydivers jump onto a building to launch you, and that was the last time anything about you was cool.

You invented a whole new insult. Nobody calls iPhone owners "Phoneholes." But "Glasshole"? Earned. Fast. Because you let people take photos by *winking*. You turned flirting into a privacy violation.

Every sentence started with "OK Glass," like a man narrating his own midlife crisis out loud. Bars banned you. Strangers ripped you off people's faces. Your battery died faster than your reputation, and you overheated right next to the user's brain, which honestly explains the buying decision.

Then you pivoted to "Enterprise," the tech version of moving back home to work at your uncle's warehouse.

And even the warehouse let you go.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Microsoft Teams is the only app that can tell you "You're on mute" after you've spent four minutes giving the best speech of your career to nobody.

It's got a notification system that works like a clingy ex. Someone reacts with a thumbs-up to a message you sent three weeks ago, and suddenly your laptop sounds like a submarine under attack.

The search function is a magic trick: you type "Q3 budget," and it shows you a GIF from Brenda's retirement party.

And the name! "Teams." Also "Teams (work or school)." Also "Teams (free)." Also "Teams Classic," which is what we now call the one that worked slightly better. Whenever you open it, it asks which Teams you want, like a waiter asking which of your three identical sandwiches you'd like.

The status indicator says "Away" when you're staring right at it, and "Available" when you've gone to the bathroom.

Teams isn't collaboration software. It's a hostage negotiation with your own Wi-Fi.

b.text:
Microsoft Teams is the only app that marks me "Away" after five minutes of deep thought but keeps me "Available" for three hours after I've died. It's not software. It's a hall monitor in a purple vest.

Teams eats more RAM than the game I'm pretending not to play. It launches on startup uninvited, then takes four minutes to load a chat that just says "ok."

Where are my files? SharePoint. Where's SharePoint? Nobody knows. Teams ships them off like a kid to boarding school.

Then they gave us "New Teams," which is Old Teams with a fresh coat of lag. IT has told me to "clear the cache" so often I do it in my sleep.

Nobody chose Teams. It came free with Office. Fitting, since so did Clippy.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text: Luosifen smells like someone microwaved a sewer and called it dinner. You open the packet and the whole building files a noise complaint. Half the dormitories in China have banned it, and the company just says, "That's the flavor," like a skunk insisting that's its cologne. The sour bamboo shoots have been fermenting so long they've got a personal history. The little river snails swim in a broth that tastes exactly like the river they came from. Liuzhou calls it a treasure. Liuzhou also has the river. Then you get to the peanuts, tofu skin, and chili oil, which are there to make you feel like you're eating a meal instead of a crime scene. Honestly, the sealed bag is the most honest thing about it. Even the factory knows nobody wants to smell this one in the open.

b.text:
Luosifen, you're the only food that comes with a smell warning from the neighbors. Nobody ever says "I'm having snail noodles" quietly. You announce yourself like a sewer breaking up with a pickle.

You're made from river snails, which is already a bold choice. Then you add sour bamboo shoots, which smell like a gym sock that was fermented in a gym sock. Real talk: the first time someone microwaved you in an office, HR held a funeral for the break room.

And the fans! "Just wait, the taste is amazing." Sure, so is a lottery ticket, but I'm not smelling like one for three days. Your broth is a gorgeous, glowing chili-oil red, like a warning light on a submarine, which is accurate, because I am now sealed inside with you.

Luosifen: delicious enough to eat, powerful enough to evict you.

facts: Launched in 1983 as 'Multi-Tool Word' for Xenix and MS-DOS.
Clippy, the animated paperclip assistant, arrived in Office 97 and was removed in Office 2007; Microsoft itself ran ads mocking it in 2001.
Its .docx format, Office Open XML, was fast-tracked to ISO standard 29500 in 2008 as a roughly 6,000-page specification, amid accusations that national committees had been packed.
Older spell checkers, Word's included, offered 'Cupertino' as a correction for a mistyped 'cooperation', and the resulting 'Cupertino effect' made it into published NATO, EU and UN-agency documents.

a.text:
Microsoft Word, you've had forty years to learn one thing: how to let me move a picture one millimeter without three paragraphs fleeing to page nine. You don't wrap text, you take hostages.

You underline my own name in red like I'm the typo. You turn my grocery list into a numbered legal document I can't escape. I hit Enter once and suddenly I'm in a style called "Heading 7" that I've never met.

And Track Changes? That's not editing, that's a crime scene where everyone bled in a different color.

You fired Clippy, the only one of you who ever admitted I looked like I needed help.

And every crash, you hand me "Document1 (Recovered)" like a cat dropping a dead bird on the porch: proud, useless, and somehow from 2 PM yesterday.

b.text: Microsoft Word is the only program that has a paperclip for a mascot, and it still managed to be the most annoying thing on the screen. You type one space in the middle of a sentence and the whole document rearranges itself like it's moving apartments. Every image you insert becomes a hostage that refuses to stay on page four. And that blue squiggle under your name? Word thinks *you're* the typo. Then there's Compatibility Mode, the program's way of saying, "I've seen your file, and I'm not going to pretend I understand it." Twenty years of updates, and the only thing it's truly mastered is looking shocked when you press Ctrl+S.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim, you're the only text editor with its own hostage negotiation thread. Millions of people have viewed the Stack Overflow question on how to leave you. That's not a user base, that's a missing persons report.

You have modes. Normal mode, where typing does nothing normal, and Insert mode, hidden behind the letter "i" like a secret menu.

Your fans move the cursor with h, j, k, l because a terminal from 1976 printed arrows on those keys. That's not efficiency, that's Stockholm syndrome on the home row.

Every Vim user has a 900-line .vimrc copied from a stranger and is too scared to touch it. And when you crash, you leave .swp files behind like a burglar who signs the guestbook.

Even your own kids forked you into Neovim. That's not a fork. That's an intervention.

Goodnight! :wq… :q!… ESC ESC ESC…

b.text:
Vim is the only software where the tutorial is "how to leave." Millions of developers have rebooted their computers rather than figure out :wq. Stack Overflow has a question about quitting Vim with over a million views. That's not a text editor, that's a hostage situation.

It has modes. Normal mode, which is where nothing normal happens. Insert mode, where you finally type, like a toddler allowed one cookie. Visual mode, command mode, replace mode. It's a text editor with more personalities than a Reddit thread.

Vim users say "once you learn it, you'll be so fast." Sir, you spent six years learning to delete a word. You've saved four seconds and told everyone at dinner about it.

And the pride! They've memorized hjkl so they never move their hands, yet they've moved their entire personality into a .vimrc file that's 900 lines long, breaks every update, and was last understood in 2014.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text: Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle powered by the most abundant element in the universe that still can't find a gas station. California has about fifty pumps, and half of them are "temporarily offline," which is hydrogen for "go home." Its one emission is water, so it's technically the cleanest car on Earth, as long as you don't ask where the hydrogen came from. Spoiler: natural gas. It's a fossil fuel car in a witness protection program. Toyota gave Mirai buyers fifteen grand in free fuel, which sounds generous until you realize that at thirty-six bucks a kilo it covers roughly a year of driving, and the car loses that much value on the drive home. You're sitting on a tank pressurized to 10,000 psi to go three hundred miles. Even the Hindenburg would say, "Maybe just get a Tesla."

b.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars are the only vehicles where the fuel is the most abundant element in the universe and somehow still costs more per mile than caviar. Sixteen dollars a kilogram, and you can only buy it at one station in California, which is closed. For "maintenance."

Their big selling point is that the only emissions are water. Fantastic. Most of the hydrogen is made from natural gas, so it's a car that cries clean tears after being force-fed fossil fuels in a basement.

Toyota calls its model the Mirai. That's Japanese for "future." Accurate, because that's when you'll find a pump.

Owners are a special breed. They drive 40 minutes to refuel, then call it freedom. Their car is basically a Prius that got a PhD, went into massive debt, and still can't get a job.

And the tank? Pressurized to 10,000 psi. So it's a zero-emissions vehicle with a tiny, polite bomb in the trunk.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like a colander that wanted to go to brunch. Thirteen holes, and somehow none of them let the dignity out, because there was never any in there.

You were invented as a boat shoe. A *boat* shoe. The one place you were built for, and you'd just float away. So you stayed on land and started fights with escalators. Malls had to post warnings. You're the only footwear with a rap sheet against machinery.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind your heel doesn't make you athletic. It makes you a clog wearing a seatbelt.

Then came Jibbitz, little charms you jam into the holes so grown adults can accessorize ventilation. Congratulations. You turned a shoe into a fridge door.

b.text: Crocs are the only shoe that looks like it was designed by a committee of ducks. Every pair is a foam clog with holes in it, like someone started making shoes, got bored halfway through, and said, "Eh, the air can have the rest." Nobody has ever bought Crocs to look good. You buy them because they're the only shoe that can survive a flood, a hospital shift, and a barbecue at the same time. They come with little charms you snap into the holes, which is how you know the company has given up on fashion and moved into hostage negotiation: "Fine, you want a shoe, we'll give you a shoe with a pizza slice stuck in its side." And somehow they're everywhere. Grandpas, nurses, teenagers, and one guy at every Costco who hasn't left the house since 2009. Crocs don't walk, they waddle. That's not a shoe, that's a rubber duck that lost a bet.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text: Windows Vista, the operating system that asked permission for everything. You wanted to open a folder? Click "Continue." Delete a file? "Are you sure?" Breathe? "Allow this program to breathe?" Your computer needed a bouncer just to check its own coat. And the copy progress bar: "Four minutes remaining." Three hours later it's at 99 percent, forever. Vista didn't crash. It just kept asking if you were sure. And the sidebar! A little clock and a weather widget floating on your desktop like you needed a hall monitor for your screensaver. Microsoft put a "Vista Capable" sticker on computers that could barely run it, and then acted shocked when people were mad. Honestly, Vista, you were the first operating system to make your user feel like the problem.

b.text:
Windows Vista, the only operating system that asked "Are you sure?" before letting you breathe. You wanted to open Notepad? Cancel or Allow. You clicked Allow? Are you *really* sure? It had the confidence of a bouncer and the competence of a toddler.

Microsoft promised "Wow." Users said "Why?" Then "Where's my RAM?" Then "Where's my printer driver?" Then "Where's XP?"

It launched with a sticker that said "Vista Capable," which turned out to mean "Capable of displaying a sad blue spinning circle on your brand-new laptop."

Copying a file took so long that Vista estimated "20 minutes remaining," then "3 days," then "Discovering..." forever. Aero looked gorgeous, like a Ferrari with no engine.

Apple made an entire ad campaign out of mocking you, Vista, and the worst part is Microsoft just sat there, clicked Allow, and said "Yes, I'm sure."

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: Macau, you're the only place where a fake Venice has a fake gondola and the gondolas still lose money. You're about ten Central Parks wide, so your casinos can't spread out and have to go up, like a city that got lost looking for space. Your cathedral is just a facade, a church that gave up on the church part. Your egg tarts are the best thing you've ever exported, and you did it by accident, like a bank robbery that ends with pastries. The bridge to Hong Kong took the better part of a decade, which is the most patience you've ever shown anyone. Nobody comes to Macau to see Macau. They come to lose money, and they leave with an egg tart and a receipt.

b.text:
Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a front wall. Fitting, since the whole city is a facade: a fake Venice with a painted sky, a half-size Eiffel Tower, and a Grand Lisboa that looks like a golden pineapple trying to cheat at baccarat.

Portugal ruled you for 442 years and left behind egg tarts and street signs nobody can pronounce. Four centuries, one pastry.

You've made several times more gambling money than Las Vegas, yet your signature dish is a pork chop jammed in a bun. Classy.

Half your land was dug out of the sea, which is perfect, because the other half was dug out of tourists' pockets.

And they built a 55-kilometer bridge to connect you to Hong Kong, and it's emptier than a junket operator's promises. Even the bridge is losing at the tables.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text: The Apple Vision Pro costs 3,500 dollars, which is a used Honda, for a headset that makes you look like a welder who wandered into the Apple Store. The front screen shows your eyes to everyone around you, so people don't see a person. They see a dead-eyed aquarium. You click by staring at things and pinching the air, like you're trying to hypnotize your own hand. The battery lives in your pocket on a cable, so you're not free, you're tethered to a fanny pack. Apple calls it spatial computing. I call it the only device that lets you wander your living room in a 3,500-dollar blindfold and still walk straight into the couch.

b.text:
The Apple Vision Pro costs $3,499, which is a bold price for something that gives you a headache and a neck injury in the same sitting. It weighs over a pound, so after twenty minutes you're not experiencing spatial computing, you're experiencing the chiropractic kind.

Apple said it would change how we see the world, then gave it a two-hour battery on a cable you have to keep in your pocket, like an oxygen tank for your delusions.

EyeSight shows your eyes on the front, so everyone around you can watch a haunted aquarium version of your face. Your FaceTime Persona looks like a hostage video made by a very polite ghost.

The best part is the control scheme: you look at something and pinch your fingers, like you're being quietly condescending to your own living room.

It's a $3,500 ski goggle that lets you watch a movie alone. Congratulations, you've invented a very expensive way to ignore your family.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text: Klingon, you're a language built by one linguist, Marc Okrand, specifically to sound alien and hostile, and somehow you still ended up sounding like a man choking on a Dorito. Your word order is object-verb-subject, so even your sentences walk in backwards to hide their face. You don't even have a word for "hello." Your greeting is "nuqneH," "what do you want?" You're the only language that greets people like a DMV clerk. Your apostrophes are glottal stops, your capital Q is a different letter from lowercase q, and "tlh" isn't a sound, it's a hairball. You translated Hamlet and claimed it was the original. Buddy, the most popular thing ever said in you is "Qapla'," and the people saying it are at a Marriott in Burbank.

b.text: Klingon, you sound like a man hacking up a hairball during a hostage negotiation. Every word starts with a throat-clearing gargle, and somehow "nuqneH" still sounds like a threat. Apparently "please" is a sign of weakness, so you just bellow "Qapla'" and hope the guy behind you agrees. Your grammar treats every sentence like a dare: object first, verb second, subject whenever you feel like it. Your big literary achievement is *Hamlet*, and its most famous line comes out as "taH pagh taHbe'," which sounds like a dog choking on a sock. Your dictionary has more ways to say "your mother" than "I'm sorry," and I'd respect you more if you apologized once.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text:
Excel, you're the only software that thinks "September 4th" and "the gene SEPT4" are the same thing. Scientists renamed human genes because of you. Genetics bent the knee to a spreadsheet.

You've got a million rows, and somehow the one cell I need is always showing ########. That's not an error, that's you yelling at me.

Every company on earth runs on one file called "Final_v7_REAL_final_JOHN'S EDIT.xlsx" that only Linda understands, and Linda's on vacation. Her formula is a nested IF statement so long it has its own zip code.

You can do VLOOKUP, XLOOKUP, INDEX-MATCH, and you still make me fight for it like a hostage negotiation.

And you're a "data tool" that auto-formats my phone number into scientific notation. Congratulations, 5.55E+09, I've never felt more called.

Also, Clippy left. You stayed. That tells us who was actually the problem.

b.text:
Excel, you're the Swiss Army knife of spreadsheets, except every blade is sharp in the wrong direction. You've got four hundred functions and somehow none of them can tell me why my dates turned into the number 45292. You autocorrect "1-2" into January 2nd, and then you act surprised when a gene called MARCH1 becomes "1-Mar." Scientists had to rename genes because of you. That's not a bug, that's a biography.

And the Ctrl+Z history stops at about twelve steps, like you're embarrassed of your own mistakes. You're a grid of a million rows and you still can't fit my budget on one screen without me squinting like I'm reading a ransom note.

Every one of us has one cell that says #REF! and one VLOOKUP we don't understand. You're not a tool, you're a hostage negotiation with a row number.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text: Beanie Babies, you're the only toy whose value depends on a tag announcing you're dead. "Retired." That's not a collectible, that's a hospice with a barcode. Ty Warner figured out that if he stopped making a bear, grown adults would panic-buy it like the last lifeboat on the Titanic. Parents mortgaged houses for Peanut the Elephant. Now your grandma's attic holds forty thousand of you, each worth less than the postage to mail it. And you were the only stuffed animal with a birth certificate stapled to your butt. You're not even stuffed with beans. It's plastic pellets. Honestly, that's the most honest thing about you.

b.text: Beanie Babies. The only retirement plan where the retiree was a five-dollar bear stuffed with plastic pellets. A whole generation bought plastic protectors for a toy's ear tag, then sealed the toy in a Ziploc so no child could ever love it. You weren't a stuffed animal; you were a 401(k) with a poem on it. And those poems! Ty Warner doing greeting-card Shakespeare for people who thought Princess the bear would pay for college. Princess paid for nothing. Neither did the Teenie Beanies everyone hoarded from McDonald's while throwing away the actual Happy Meal. A divorcing couple in Las Vegas literally split their collection on a courtroom floor, one Beanie at a time. That's your legacy: custody battles over a moose named Chocolate. Even your creator got busted hiding money from the IRS, because he was the only one who ever made any.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself three night-market stalls before you arrive. People don't find you at Shilin. They track you, like bloodhounds following a crime scene. Your whole brand is "smells like a sewer, tastes great," which is also what every bad Tinder date says about himself. You soak for months in fermented brine like you're marinating in a grudge. And your family's no better: Changsha dyed you black, the culinary equivalent of putting sunglasses on a corpse. You need deep frying, chili sauce, AND a mound of pickled cabbage just to be socially acceptable. That's not a garnish, that's a legal team. Your parents gave you one job: be tofu. Tofu's whole personality is having no personality. And somehow you came out smelling like a gym sock that went to college. Honestly? Respect.

b.text:
Stinky tofu, you're the only food that needs a restraining order from its own neighborhood. I smelled you three blocks away and assumed a sewer had filed for divorce.

You're fermented in brine made of old vegetables, fish, and, as far as I can tell, regret. Then you're deep-fried, because apparently someone looked at a crime scene and said, "Needs crunch."

Everyone says, "Just try it, it tastes better than it smells!" That's not a compliment. That's what people say about a divorce lawyer.

And the fans! They stand in line at the night market, glowing with pride, like they've survived something. Sir, you're eating a gym sock in a pickle costume, and the pickle is also a gym sock.

Still, I'll admit it: the chili sauce is incredible. Which is exactly what you'd say about a hostage situation with good snacks.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: Macau, you're the only city where the fake Venice has better canals than the real one. You dredged your land out of the sea, built a replica of Venice on top, and hired gondoliers to sing to tourists who just lost their rent at baccarat. Your economy is one enormous slot machine with a Portuguese accent. Your most famous landmark is a church facade with nothing behind it, which is the most honest thing on your skyline. You're 33 square kilometers, so small you can walk across yourself before your egg tart cools. Everybody comes to you to lose money, and you're thrilled to take it. Keep the lights on, little sinner.

b.text:
Macau, you're Las Vegas that went to a Portuguese finishing school and came back with gambling debt and a custard tart habit. You make more money from gambling than Vegas does, but you're only 12 square miles. That's not a city, that's a casino with a postal code.

You've got a replica Eiffel Tower, a Venice with fake canals, and a Roman-style sky painted on the ceiling. Nothing here is original except the egg tarts, and even those are Portuguese. You even stole those, Macau, you just added a Cantonese accent.

The streets have Portuguese names, but nobody speaks Portuguese. It's colonialism's most elegant ghost town. Every sign is written in a language the entire population ignores, like a terms and conditions page.

And the traffic! A million tourists walking between hotels that are all technically the same hotel. You've got a Grand Lisboa shaped like a golden lotus, or as locals call it, a giant birdcage for losing gamblers.

Come for the ruins of St. Paul's. Stay because the ferry back to Hong Kong costs exactly what you have left.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text: LaTeX, you're the only software where "it compiled" counts as an emotional milestone. One missing brace and you blame line 1 of a 400-line file, then sit there with a question mark like we're playing a text adventure from 1985. I put a figure on page 3; you float it to the appendix because you "know better." You have to run twice just to learn your own page numbers, three times if BibTeX shows up, like a guy who needs two friends to remind him his name. Your answer to every problem is another \usepackage, so my preamble is now longer than my thesis. Every paper you touch looks gorgeous, and identical, because everyone on Earth can spot Computer Modern from across a conference hall. And your favorite warning, "Overfull \hbox, badness 10000"? Honestly, that's just how I feel about you.

b.text:
LaTeX is the only software where you spend six hours fixing a typo and then twelve more because the fix moved your figure to page nine.

You ask for a picture to go *here*. LaTeX says "here" is more of a "float" situation. It's not a placement, it's a vibe.

The error messages are written by someone who hates you personally. "Overfull hbox, badness 10000." Thank you, I'll tell my therapist. Meanwhile, one missing brace gives you an error on line 4,000, in a file you didn't write, from a package you never installed.

Want a different font? Enjoy a three-day journey through Stack Overflow, where the top answer is from 2009 and starts with "Just use XeTeX."

And the compile times! I changed one comma and now I'm watching it run twice, because the table of contents needs to catch up to reality.

Knuth released it in 1978 and declared it nearly bug-free. Sir, the bugs are in me. I'm the bug. I just wanted a bibliography.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text:
Windows 8, you looked at a billion people with a mouse and a keyboard and said, "What if your monitor was a giant phone you can't touch?"

You took away the Start button. The one thing a user knew how to find. Microsoft had literally sold Windows 95 with a Rolling Stones song called "Start Me Up," and you said, "Nah."

Want to shut down? Easy: hover in a secret corner, summon the Charms bar, click Settings, click Power. Turning off my computer shouldn't feel like unlocking a cheat code.

Your tiles were so ugly even the name "Metro" had to get dropped over a trademark dispute. Then 8.1 brought back the Start button, which just opened the same tiles. That's not an apology, that's a hostage video.

You were so bad Microsoft skipped the number 9 entirely just to put distance between you and Windows 10.

b.text:
Windows 8 looked at the most successful desktop interface in history and said, "What if we hid the Start button, like a bathroom in a haunted house?" Microsoft designed an operating system for tablets, then shipped it to people with keyboards, mice, and spreadsheets. Nobody asked for this. Accountants were suddenly swiping at monitors like they were trying to wipe off a stain.

Shutting down the computer required a PhD. You had to summon the Charms bar by hovering in the corner of the screen like a stalker, then click Settings, then Power, then pray. My grandmother spent twenty minutes looking for the off switch and just unplugged it. Honestly, she had the right idea.

And those Live Tiles! Forty colorful rectangles flipping around telling me the weather in a city I've never visited. It wasn't an operating system, it was a toddler's busy board.

Microsoft eventually admitted the mistake and brought back the Start button. Windows 8.1 was basically an apology note taped to the door.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text:
Klingon, you're the only language whose native speakers are all fictional and whose fluent speakers all have a Comic-Con badge. Marc Okrand built you in 1984 to sound alien, and he nailed it: you sound like a man choking on a pretzel while reading IKEA instructions.

Your word order is object-verb-subject, so every sentence is a mystery that reveals who did it at the end. Your greeting, nuqneH, literally means "What do you want?" Congratulations: you're the first language designed by a DMV clerk.

You have more apostrophes than vowels deserve, no verb "to be," and a Klingon Language Institute that "restored" Hamlet to its original Klingon. That's not scholarship. That's fan fiction with footnotes.

A linguist once tried raising his son in Klingon. By age five the kid stopped answering. Qapla'!

b.text:
Klingon, a language designed by a linguist so warriors could sound like they're clearing their throats at you in anger. Every sentence sounds like a cat being strangled by a Scrabble bag of Q's and apostrophes.

You have a word for "disruptor" but not "please." Because apparently when a Klingon wants something, he doesn't ask. He just reorders his grammar until the object is afraid.

Your verbs go at the end, so by the time someone finishes threatening me, I've already left for lunch. "I will crush your skull and... " Hold on, I'm still waiting for the verb. Honestly, that's the most polite thing about you.

And Okrand wrote an entire dictionary, yet there's no word for "sorry" because "it's a weakness." Meanwhile, there's a proverb about revenge being a dish best served cold. You're a language with an open-mic problem and a fridge full of leftovers.

Fluent speakers: about twelve. All of them are named Gary, and all of them are using you to ask for the check.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text:
Chicago deep-dish isn't pizza, it's a casserole that got a good agent. You wait 45 minutes for it, which is the only honest part, because the oven is basically doing a bypass in reverse. The waiter says "it takes a while," and he means "call your family and say something nice."

It arrives upside down: cheese on the bottom, sauce on top, like the pizza lost a bet. And the crust is a structural engineering project. It's not a slice, it's a core sample. You lift it with a spatula and the cheese stretches like it's begging you to reconsider.

Two slices and you're done. Not full, done. You walk out into a Chicago winter and honestly, the insulation helps.

New Yorkers call it soup in a bread bowl. Wrong. Soup has the decency to cool down. This stays molten until the first bite takes the roof of your mouth, as a deposit.

b.text: Deep-dish pizza is the only food that makes you wait forty-five minutes for a meal and then spends the next three hours in your stomach like a sofa somebody moved in without asking. It's not a pizza. It's a casserole that got a library card. You bite in and the cheese pulls up like it's auditioning for a Lysol commercial, and the sauce sits on top like it lost a bet with the crust. Chicagoans will tell you it's "a whole different thing," which is what people say when they're hoping you won't check the ingredients. Nobody in Chicago has ever finished a whole deep dish alone. They just stare at the last slice in the box like it owes them money, then eat it cold at 1 a.m. over the sink, which is the only honest way to eat it.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text: Comic Sans 这字体我真服了。它本来是给微软一个卡通小狗助手配对话框用的，设计师想的是"亲切"，结果亲切过头了。医院墙上贴一张"此处禁止吸烟"，字歪歪扭扭、圆滚滚的，像小朋友在跟你过家家。葬礼讣告也用它，逝者一辈子的故事底下压着一排蹦蹦跳跳的字，好像在说"哎呀别难过啦"。你看那个大写C，弯得跟喝多了似的，连感叹号都在晃。说它正经吧，它一点不正经；说它可爱吧，它偏偏在最不该可爱的地方可爱。

b.text:
Comic Sans 你们知道怎么来的吗？1994年，微软有个软件叫 Bob，里面有只卡通狗。设计师一看，狗的对话气泡用的是 Times New Roman，狗说话像在发律师函。于是他就设计了 Comic Sans。

这字体出生的使命，就是让一只狗说话别那么严肃。

结果现在呢？它跑出来了，什么都写。小区通知"电梯停用，恢复时间待定"，用 Comic Sans。体检中心"您的筛查结果异常"，也是 Comic Sans。2012年，欧洲核子研究中心宣布发现希格斯玻色子，人类物理学最高光时刻，PPT 上还是 Comic Sans。

全世界最聪明的一群人，用一只电脑狗的语气告诉你："我们找到上帝粒子啦～"

这字体最气人的是，它每个 a 都只有一个圈，每个字母都孤零零的，不连笔，还要假装是手写。就像一个人不会签名，只会画笑脸。
